landin-citations 1
C	10	Line comments	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0010	`--` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.\n\n    -- [0010] Line comment, to end of line.
C	20	Block comments, which nest	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0020	`--(` opens a block comment and `)--` closes it. A block comment may sit between two tokens on one line.\n\n    --( [0020] Block comment. Nests properly.\n        --( so this inner one is fine )--\n    )--\n\nBecause block comments nest, you can comment out a region that already contains one.\n\nA block comment that is never closed runs to the end of the file, and the compiler reports it there.
C	30	Doc comments	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0030	`---` starts a doc comment, which documents the declaration on the next line.\n\n    --- [0030] Doc comment. Attaches to the declaration that follows.\n\nA doc comment changes nothing about what the program means. Spec [2000] says which lines count as a declaration's doc comment.
C	40	Declaring a name	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0040	A declaration gives a name, a type and a value, in that order. The name is immutable unless you say otherwise ([0060]).\n\n    greeting: utf8 = "hello"
C	50	Letting the type come from the value	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0050	Leave out the type and write `:=`, and the name takes the type of its value.\n\n    count := 7
C	60	Mutable variables	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0060	`mut` makes a binding you can assign again.\n\n    mut total: u32 = 0
C	70	Two separate questions about a reference	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0070	A reference raises two independent questions. May the name be pointed somewhere else? `mut` on the binding answers that. May the thing it points at be written? `mut` inside the type answers that. Nothing else answers either.\n\n    two_questions: () -> (seen: u32) =\n        mut first_reading: u32 = 1\n        mut dial_setting: u32 = 2\n        mut cursor: ptr u32 = addr first_reading -- re-pointable, reads only\n        knob: ptr mut u32 = addr dial_setting -- fixed, writes\n        cursor = addr dial_setting -- allowed: the binding is mut\n        knob.val = 3 -- allowed: the type is ptr mut\n        seen = cursor.val -- 3\n    end two_questions\n\n`addr` takes an address and `.val` is the thing pointed at. [0430] explains pointers properly, and [0460] points one at a fixed hardware address.
C	80	Declaring now, assigning later	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0080	A declaration may leave out the value. The name must then be assigned before anything reads it.\n\n    mut result: u32
C	90	Making a name public	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0090	`public` exports a name to other modules. Without it, the name is private to its module.\n\n    public version: u32 = 3\n\n`public` is about modules, not the linker. A public function or datum is still a local symbol inside the program's image, so no C library or linked object can collide with it. To give C or the linker a name, see [1600] and [1610].\n\nExact rules: spec [1975].
C	100	Several names in one declaration	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0100	Several names may share one declaration, as fields in a struct already do.\n\n    public red, green, blue: u8\n    north, south, east, west: atom\n\nThe shared form means the same as one declaration per name, written in the same order. Each name gets its own storage, and each gets everything written around the list: `mut`, `public`, a parameter convention, `at` or `from`. So in a parameter list, `inout low, high: i32` makes both parameters `inout`.\n\n    mut low_mark, high_mark: u32 = 10 -- two variables, both start at 10\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- A shared value is computed once, for the first name, and the other names start as copies of it: `mut low, high: u32 = next_seed()` calls `next_seed` once.\n- The shared form needs a written type, because `low, high := bounds()` reads as taking apart a multiple result ([0990]).\n- These take one name each: type declarations, functions, type and fixed formals, variant parts and condition bindings.
C	110	The name is always on the left	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0110	Left of `:` is always the name being introduced. Right of `:` is what fills it: a type, or, with `=`, a value.\n\nIn a local declaration, the written type and the value both see only the names visible before the declaration. If an outer `t` names a type, `mut t: t = value` uses that type and then introduces the local `t`, and the statements after it see the local. A binding in a condition follows the same rule ([1070]).\n\nModule declarations and function signatures see all their names at once ([0130], [1290]).\n\nControl words are reserved everywhere a name could go (spec [1760]). `begin`, `match`, `loop`, `break` and `unchecked` cannot be variables, parameters, fields or labels, so `begin = 10` is an error. Call it `begin_value` instead. There is no escape for using a keyword as a name: writing `(begin)` does not make one.
C	120	Declaring a type	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0120	A type is declared like any other name, with `type` as its type.\n\n    point: type = struct\n        x: f32\n        y: f32\n    end point
C	130	Order does not matter in a module	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0130	Inside a module, you may use a name above the line that declares it. The compiler collects every name before resolving any.\n\n    twice_answer: () -> (n: i32) =\n        n = 2 * answer_value -- answer_value is declared below\n    end twice_answer\n\n    answer_value: i32 = 21\n\nThe one exception is `linker.library` directives, which keep their source order for linking ([1590]).
C	140	Shadowing	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0140	A name in an inner scope may hide the same name from an outer one.\n\n    step_limit: u32 = 100\n\n    shadow_demo: (extra: u32) -> (result: u32) =\n        result = step_limit\n        begin\n            step_limit := extra -- a new local; the module's step_limit is untouched\n            result += step_limit\n        end\n    end shadow_demo\n\nTwo declarations of one name in the same scope are an error (spec [1850]).
C	150	Integer types	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0150	The integer types are `u8`, `u16`, `u32` and `u64`, and the signed `i8`, `i16`, `i32` and `i64`.\n\n128-bit integers are not in Landin yet. They are planned, for when a program needs them (Language evolution, in the roadmap).\n\nOdd widths such as `u4` or `u12` exist only as fields of packed register images ([0730]):\n\n- Reading one gives you the next ordinary width up, so a `u1` field reads as a `u8` holding 0 or 1.\n- A one-bit flag is spelt `bool`, and a `u1` does not convert to or from `bool` on its own.
C	160	Pointer-sized integers	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0160	`usize` and `isize` are as wide as a pointer on the target.
C	170	Floating point	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0170	The float types are `f32` and `f64`. There is no `f80`.\n\nThere is no `f16` yet either: neither baseline x86-64 nor Cortex-M0 has a half-precision instruction. It is planned (Language evolution, in the roadmap).
C	180	Booleans	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0180	`bool` holds `true` or `false`.
C	190	Integer literals take their type from where they are used	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0190	An integer literal has no type of its own. It takes the type its context expects, and the compiler checks that it fits.\n\n    tiny: u8 = 5\n    large: u64 = 5\n    -- bad: u8 = 300      is a compile error\n\nSpec [1880] says exactly what counts as a context.
C	200	With no context, an integer is an `i32`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0200	When nothing says what type an integer literal should be, it is an `i32`.\n\n    plain := 5
C	210	Float literals always have a point	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0210	A float literal always looks like one, so an integer never quietly becomes a float, nor a float an integer.\n\n    ratio: f32 = 5.0\n    -- bad: f32 = 5     is a compile error\n    half := 1.0 / 2.0 -- 0.5\n    zero := 1 / 2 -- 0, integer division\n\nWhen nothing says what type a float literal should be, it is an `f32`.
C	220	Bases, separators and exponents	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0220	Integers may be written in hex, binary or octal, and long numbers may use `_` to group digits. A float may carry an exponent.\n\n    hex_value: u32 = 0xDEAD_BEEF -- too big for the default i32\n    bin_value := 0b1010_0101\n    oct_value := 0o755\n    big_value := 1_000_000\n    sci_value := 1.5e10\n    neg_exp := 1.0e-6\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- A digit run starts and ends with a digit of its base. Underscores go only between digits, and may repeat, as in `1__000`.\n- A base prefix alone, such as `0x`, and a trailing underscore are errors.\n- In a float, both sides of the point and a written exponent need digits, with the same underscore rule.\n- A number has no suffix. A letter directly after one is part of it, so `1u64` is an error: put the type on the binding, as in `mask: u64 = 1`.
C	230	Hex floats, for exact values	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0230	A hex float literal states a float's bits exactly, subnormals included.\n\n    pi_exact: f64 = 0x1.921fb54442d18p+1\n    smallest_subnormal: f32 = 0x1.0p-149\n    smallest_normal: f32 = 0x1.0p-126
C	240	Infinity, NaN and negative zero	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0240	The IEEE special values are named values of the float types, and unary minus gives their negative forms.\n\n    neg_zero: f64 = -0.0\n    pos_inf: f64 = f64.infinity\n    neg_inf: f64 = -f64.infinity\n    quiet_nan: f64 = f64.nan\n    neg_nan: f64 = -f64.nan\n\nConstant folding keeps a literal's sign. The sign of a NaN that arithmetic produces is not specified.
C	250	Character literals	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0250	A character literal is one Unicode scalar, and its type is `u32`.\n\n    letter_a := 'a'\n\nA byte is a `u8`, so comparing one with a character takes a conversion:\n\n    is_newline: (byte: u8) -> (yes: bool) =\n        yes = byte == u8('\\n')\n    end is_newline
C	260	Text literals take their type from where they are used	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0260	Like integers, a text literal takes its type from its context: `utf8`, `[]u8`, `utf16` or `cstring`. With no context, it is `utf8`.\n\n    name: utf8 = "hello"\n    cname: cstring = "hello"\n\nEvery text literal ends with a NUL byte that its length does not count, so passing one to C costs nothing.\n\nA literal lives in read-only storage, so you can never write through a reference to one, however the binding is declared ([0070]). For writable text, copy it into storage you asked for.\n\n    -- greeting: []u8 = "abc"\n    -- greeting[0] = 0x78          -- error, the literal is static
C	270	Escapes	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0270	A backslash starts an escape. The set is small and closed:\n\n| escape | means |\n|---|---|\n| `\\n` `\\r` `\\t` `\\e` | newline, carriage return, tab, escape |\n| `\\\\` `\\"` `\\'` | the character itself |\n| `\\xNN` | one byte, exactly two hex digits |\n| `\\u{...}` | one Unicode scalar, any number of hex digits |\n\n    line := "col\\tsep\\n"\n    smile := "\\u{1F600}"\n    byte: []u8 = "\\xFF" -- byte escapes require []u8 context\n\nThere is no octal escape and no `\\0`; write `\\x00`. An unknown escape is a compile error, never silently the character. `\\xNN` is allowed only where bytes are meant, in a `[]u8`, and `\\u{...}` only where text is meant, so a text literal can never hold invalid UTF-8.
C	280	Raw text literals	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0280	A raw literal sits between runs of at least three quotes, and nothing in it is escaped. If the text itself contains three quotes in a row, use four.\n\n    help := """\n            usage: tool [options]\n              -v    verbose\n            """\n\nThe closing quotes' indentation is stripped from every line, so the block can sit indented in your code and still start at the left margin.\n\nEvery line end between the quotes is part of the text. That includes the one just after the opening quotes and the one before a closer on its own line, so `help` begins and ends with a line end: `"\\nusage: tool [options]\\n  -v    verbose\\n"`.\n\nFor text that should start with its first line, as expected output usually should, start it on the opener's line. Nothing is stripped from that line, and the closer's indentation is still stripped from the lines after it.\n\n    expected := """usage: tool [options]\n                -v verbose\n                """\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- The whole opening run of quotes sets the count. Six quotes in a row are one opener of six, not an empty literal, and a matching closer must follow later.\n- For empty text, write `""`.
C	290	Arithmetic	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0290	The arithmetic operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%`. Integer division truncates toward zero, and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend, as in C.\n\n    q := -7 / 2 -- -3\n    r := -7 % 2 -- -1
C	300	Overflow traps; wrapping is a separate operator	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0300	Integer overflow traps. When you want wrap-around, say so with `+%`, `-%` or `*%`. Each has an assignment form, such as `+%=` ([0390]).\n\n    wrap_demo: () -> (ticks: u8) =\n        ticks = 255\n        ticks +%= 1 -- wraps to 0\n    end wrap_demo
C	310	Conversions are written out	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0310	Nothing converts implicitly, except that a writable reference passes where a read-only one is expected ([0440]). To convert, apply the type to the value, like a call.\n\n- If the value is known at compile time, an impossible conversion is a compile error; otherwise it traps at run time.\n- A float converts to an integer by truncating toward zero.\n- An integer converts to a float by rounding, and that never traps.\n\n    -- bad: u8 = u8(300)        compile error\n    narrow_reading: (reading: u32) -> (small: u8) =\n        small = u8(reading) -- traps if reading is above 255\n    end narrow_reading\n\n    greeting_bytes: []u8 = []u8(greeting) -- the same bytes, not a copy\n    whole_part := i64(45.7) -- 45: truncates toward zero\n\nYou can write the type directly, as `[]u8(greeting)` does here, rather than declaring an alias for it first. Either spelling means the same conversion.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- Type prefixes nest as they do in declarations: `[][2]u8(value)` converts to a slice of two-byte arrays, and `tag(u32, 7)(value)` to a parameterized type with every parameter given. The last parentheses hold the one value.\n- As with a call result, bind the result before you index it, select a field or call it.\n- A converted reference still refers to the same storage, and keeps its origin: where that storage lives, and so how long ([0770]).\n- `ptr u8(value)` applies the type `ptr u8`: it can take the pointer out of a distinct type ([0650]), but it never turns an integer into a pointer. `ptr(address)` does that, taking its pointer type from the declaration ([0460]).\n- A conversion does not say what type a float literal is, so the literal is an `f32` ([0210]). `u64(1.0e18)` would truncate the `f32` nearest 10^18, which is 999,999,984,306,749,440, so the compiler refuses it; write `u64(f64(1.0e18))` for the number written. `i64(45.7)` gives 45 at either width and is converted as it stands.
C	320	Shifts	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0320	`<<` and `>>` shift. Bits shifted out are gone and zeros come in, and a signed `>>` keeps the sign. There is one form of each.\n\n    z: u32 = 1 << 40 -- 0 in a u32 context\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- The amount has the same type as the value being shifted.\n- An amount at or past the width gives zero on every shift, signed `>>` included; the amount never wraps around.\n- A negative amount is refused when the compiler knows it and traps when it does not.\n\nExact rules: spec [1950].
C	330	Bitwise operators	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0330	The bitwise operators are `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>`. Unlike in C, they bind tighter than comparisons, so the usual mask test needs no parentheses.\n\n    count_is_even := count & 1 == 0 -- means (count & 1) == 0
C	340	Logical operators	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0340	The logical operators are words: `and`, `or` and `not`. That leaves `!` free for errors.\n\n    finished: bool = false\n    keep_going := count < 10 and not finished
C	350	Comparison	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0350	The comparisons are `==`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Inequality is `<>`, not `!=`. Comparisons do not chain (spec [1820]).
C	360	Ranges	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0360	A range is written in a `for` header or a slice: `0..9` includes 9, and `0..<10` stops before 10.\n\n    digit_sum: () -> (total: i32) =\n        total = 0\n        for i in 0..9 do\n            total += i\n        end for\n    end digit_sum\n\nThe same bounds select part of a slice, as in `items[0..<10]`. A range is not a value: you cannot store, pass or return `0..<10` on its own. There is no form that excludes the left end. For custom stepping, a library supplies an iterable value ([1330]).
C	370	`sizeof`, `alignof`, `lenof` and `offsetof`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0370	These four measure things: the size of a type, its alignment, a length, and where a struct field begins.\n\n    w1 := sizeof u32 -- 4\n    a1 := alignof u64 -- 8\n    o1 := offsetof reading_head.value -- 2: one byte of padding after sensor\n\n    reading_head: type = struct\n        sensor: u8\n        value: u16\n    end reading_head\n\n    roll_die: () -> (face: u8) =\n        face = 4\n    end roll_die\n\n    measure_demo: (words: []u32) -> (total: usize) =\n        samples: [8]u16 = zeroed\n        total = lenof samples -- 8, known at compile time\n        total += lenof words -- the slice's length, at run time\n        total += lenof ([roll_die(), roll_die()]) -- 2; roll_die is not called\n    end measure_demo\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- `lenof` measures a name, a field or element reached through it, or what a call returns.\n- A call whose result is measured runs. The elements of a measured literal, like the `roll_die()` calls above, are checked to have one scalar type but not evaluated.\n- An array that a name or path reaches is not read, because its type holds its length.\n- `offsetof` gives a field's offset in bytes from the start of its struct type, through nested structs.\n- `lenof` and `offsetof` are not reserved: everywhere else, they are ordinary names.
C	380	`addr` and `.val`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0380	`addr` takes an address, and `.val` is the thing a pointer points at. On the right of an assignment `.val` reads it, and on the left `.val` writes it. [0430] shows both.
C	390	Assignment is a statement	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0390	Assignment is a statement, never an expression, so it cannot hide inside a condition.\n\nThe assignment operators are `=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=` and `>>=`, plus the wrapping `+%=`, `-%=` and `*%=` ([0300]).
C	400	No `++` and no `--`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0400	There is no `++` or `--`. The statements `inc` and `dec` do the job, though `x += 1` says the same thing.\n\n    inc total\n    dec total
C	410	Evaluation order is fixed	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0410	Landin fixes the order in which things are evaluated, so you can see where costs happen:\n\n- operands and call arguments, left to right;\n- a struct's fields, in the order you write them, whatever order the layout puts them in;\n- `and` and `or`, left to right, stopping as soon as the answer is known;\n- an assignment, its destination first, then the value.\n\nA deferred call is the one thing not evaluated where it is written; [1100] says when it runs.
C	420	What the dot means	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0420	The dot always selects a member of something:\n\n| example | selects |\n|---|---|\n| `p.val` | what a pointer points at |\n| `t.less` | an entry of a concept |\n| `http.get` | a member of a module |\n| `f64.nan` | a named value of a type |\n\nThe tokens `..` (a range), `...` (an inferred error set) and the decimal point are separate things.
C	430	`ptr`, `addr` and `.val`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0430	`ptr u32` is a pointer to a `u32`. `addr` takes an address, and `.val` is the thing pointed at, on either side of an assignment.\n\n    mut value: u32 = 42\n    p: ptr mut u32 = addr value\n    v := p.val -- read through p\n    p.val = 43 -- write through p\n    ro: ptr u32 = addr value -- same address, read-only\n    -- ro.val = 1 -- error: ro cannot write\n\n`mut` inside the type is what lets you write through the pointer. `addr` of a mutable variable gives a `ptr mut`, and `addr` of an immutable one a plain `ptr`.\n\nWhat `addr` is applied to decides which address you get:\n\n- `addr p.val` is the address of the thing `p` points at.\n- `addr items[i]` is the address of a slice's element.\n- `addr p` is something else: the address of the variable `p` itself, which may live on the stack.
C	440	A writable pointer passes where a read-only one is expected	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0440	A writable reference is accepted where a read-only one is expected, and the call needs no conversion spelled out.\n\n    add_up: (xs: []i32) -> (total: i32) =\n        total = 0\n        for x in xs do\n            total += x\n        end for\n    end add_up\n\n    add_written: (writable_slice: []mut i32) -> (total: i32) =\n        total = add_up(writable_slice) -- fine: []mut i32 relaxes to []i32\n    end add_written\n\nNo bit changes; the callee simply forgets that it could write. This is the only implicit relaxation in the language, and it only goes this way: a read-only reference never becomes a writable one.
C	450	Permission is shallow	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0450	Read-only applies to one level only. An immutable binding, or an `in` parameter, protects the value it holds, not what that value points at. A list handed over as `in` still has writable elements if its storage is writable.\n\nProtecting deeper would mean knowing which references a value owns and which it borrows, and Landin does not track ownership ([0910]). When you want to hand out a read-only view, hand out a read-only reference; an accessor is how.
C	460	A pointer to a fixed address	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0460	`ptr(...)` turns an address into a pointer. The pointer type comes from the declaration.\n\n    gpio: ptr mut u32 = ptr(0x4001_0000)\n\nThis binding is immutable, but the register behind it is written: the two questions of [0070] really are separate.\n\nNothing in the pointer's type makes access to it a device transaction. The operation that reads or writes does that ([0850]).
C	470	Converting between pointers and integers	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0470	A pointer and an integer convert both ways like any other conversion ([0700]): apply the type. Here `gpio` is the pointer from [0460].\n\n    gpio_round_trip: () -> (back: ptr mut u32) =\n        address := usize(gpio) -- pointer to integer\n        back = ptr(address) -- integer to pointer: no origin\n    end gpio_round_trip\n\nThe cost is on the way back. An integer has no origin, so a pointer made from one borrows nothing as far as the compiler knows, and the compiler will say nothing more about that pointer's lifetime. This is the one place inside the language where lifetime checking is left behind, much as at the C boundary.
C	480	There is no null	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0480	"Maybe a pointer" is a union of an atom and a pointer type. With a single atom, the compiler stores it as a plain pointer, with 0 meaning the atom.\n\n    none_found: atom\n    maybe_ptr: type = none_found | ptr mut u32\n\n    lookup: (key: u32, cell: ptr mut u32) -> (found: maybe_ptr from cell) =\n        if key == 0 then\n            found = none_found\n        else\n            found = cell\n        end if\n    end lookup\n\n    read: (m: maybe_ptr, fallback: u32) -> (value: u32) =\n        match m\n            none_found: value = fallback\n            ptr (p): value = p.val\n        end match\n    end read\n\nA pointer goes into the union with nothing extra to write. Getting it out takes a `match`, and the `match` has to name both cases: `ptr (p)` is the present case, with the pointer bound to `p`.\n\nTo ask only which case the union holds, compare with the atom: `m == none_found` or `m <> none_found`. That reads no address, so it needs no `match`. Two such unions do not compare with each other.\n\nA union may also hold several atoms beside the pointer; it then takes two cells instead of one.\n\nExact rules: spec [1870].
C	490	What to use instead of a pointer	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0490	Before you reach for a pointer, see whether one of these does the job:\n\n| you want | use |\n|---|---|\n| a run of elements, to read or to write | a slice ([0570]) |\n| one element of an array you already have | its index |\n| a service such as an allocator | a handle: a small value that refers to state kept elsewhere ([1360]) |\n\nEach says more than a pointer would: a slice carries its length, an index is checked against that length, and a handle's type says what it is for.
C	500	No pointer arithmetic outside the library	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0500	There is no `p + n` on pointers, and no built-in operation that turns a pointer into a slice.\n\nCode that really needs to compute an address converts to an integer and back ([0470]), and gives up lifetime checking when it does. Inside the standard library, `core/mem` does this for you, behind its private storage operations.\n\nIf you need an element's address, take it from a slice that you know is not empty: `addr items[0]`.
C	510	Storage that is not filled yet: `mem.storage(t)`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0510	A growing array has room for more items than it holds. The empty slots contain no `t` yet, so no slice may cover them: a `[]mut t` over them would claim values that do not exist. Neither may they be zero-filled, because many types, pointers among them, have no zero value ([0540]).\n\n`core/mem`'s `storage(t)` is the answer. It holds a block of storage, counts how many slots at its start are initialized, and only ever shows you that initialized prefix. Its representation is the private type `raw(t)`: you can hold one but not look inside.\n\n| operation | what it does |\n|---|---|\n| `capacity`, `length` | how many slots there are, and how many are initialized |\n| `admit` | initialize the next slot |\n| `get`, `replace` | read or overwrite an initialized slot |\n| `used` | the initialized prefix as a `[]mut t` |\n| `withdraw`, `clear` | drop the last item, or every item |\n| `transfer` | copy one item onto the end of another `storage`, for growing |\n| `dispose` | hand the block back once it is empty |\n\nThe four ways of asking for something impossible are ordinary failures: `full`, `out_of_bounds`, `empty` and `not_empty`.\n\nGrowing. To grow, reserve a bigger block and `transfer` every item into it. A `transfer` copies and leaves its source as it was, so the old block is unchanged until you are done: if a step fails, release the new block and carry on with the old one. Only after every item is copied do you empty and dispose of the old block and publish the new one.\n\nThis keeps the empty slots out of reach. It does not make raw storage safe: the allocation you supply must be live, aligned and as large as you say ([1720]).
C	520	Arrays are values	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0520	`[n]t` is `n` elements of type `t`, stored inline. Assignment copies the whole array. The length is part of the type, so `[4]f32` and `[8]f32` are different types.\n\n    grid: [4]f32 = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]\n    mut next: [4]f32\n    next = [grid[0], grid[1], grid[2], grid[3]]\n\nAssigning a literal. Assigning a literal to an existing array, as `next = [...]` does, fills the array in place, in written order. Each element is evaluated and stored before the next one starts, and no hidden temporary copy is made. Two things follow: a later element sees an earlier write, and a failure part-way leaves the written prefix changed. The repeated forms of [0560] fill in the same order.\n\nThe length. The length must be a constant the compiler works out without running anything. You may write:\n\n- integer literals;\n- fixed parameters ([1520]);\n- compiler facts such as `compiler.word_size` [1500];\n- `sizeof` of a built-in scalar type, such as `sizeof usize`;\n- immutable module integers;\n- parentheses, unary `-` and plain `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` to combine them.\n\nCalls, wrapping operators, bitwise operators, shifts and measurements of your own types are not allowed.\n\nA fact and a scalar's size are the selected target's, so `[sizeof usize]u8` is `[8]u8` on a 64-bit target and `[4]u8` on Cortex-M0. A module integer counts only when its own value is such a constant. A `mut` one never counts, because the program may write it. With `path_max: usize = 4096`, `[path_max]u8` is the same type as `[4096]u8`.\n\nFine print:\n\n- The compiler refuses a negative length. A length of zero is fine and gives a zero-length array, but there is no empty array literal, and the repeated forms of [0560] cannot fill a zero-length array.\n- An index is a `usize`, and the array's size in bytes must fit the target's `usize`.\n- A computed index is evaluated and bounds-checked once, before the element is used. Indexing exposes no pointer and does not change how arrays are copied.\n- An array keeps its complete element type, permissions included, through a pointer, a slice, a generic call or a stored field. An `any C` element keeps its own data and its evidence for `C`.
C	530	Letting the literal set the length	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0530	With `:=`, the literal supplies both the length and the element type.\n\n    triple := [1.0, 2.0, 3.0] -- [3]f32\n\nThe first element decides the element type, whether it is a number, a slice, a pointer or a struct. Every later element must have that type.
C	540	`zeroed`: the all-zero value	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0540	`zeroed` is the value of a type whose bits are all zero.\n\nIn this example `point` is [0120]'s struct and `compass` [0640]'s enumeration:\n\n    mut buffer: [256]u8 = zeroed\n    buffer = zeroed -- clear the existing array as a whole\n    corner: point = zeroed -- fine: both fields are floats\n    -- facing_now: compass = zeroed -- error, write 'north'\n    -- p: ptr u32 = zeroed -- error, no zero image\n\nTwo separate questions decide where you may write `zeroed`.\n\nDoes the type have a zero image? It does when all-zero bits are a valid value of it. That is what lets a surrounding struct or array be zeroed. Pointers and `any` have none, because there is no null ([0480]), and neither does a function address. A struct or an active variant payload that contains a function address must spell that field out instead of using whole or trailing `zeroed`.\n\nDoes the type accept the word? Only when its zero has one obvious reading:\n\n- Numbers, `bool`, ranges that contain zero, and aggregates of those accept it.\n- Named value sets do not: write the name.\n- A distinct type [0650] has its base's zero image, so a record holding one zeroes fine. But an identity such as a user id has no obvious zero, so write `user_id(0)` rather than `zeroed` for it.\n\nWhere the destination gives the context, `zeroed` writes the complete zero image as one value, as the assignment to `buffer` does.\n\nA packed struct ([0730]) is a raw image, so `zeroed` is allowed even when an encoded field's zero pattern has no name. Reading that field then traps; copying the image keeps its bits.\n\nLibrary code has a narrow cousin, `uninit`, which leaves a private array field unwritten. It is not another spelling of `zeroed` and cannot initialize a stand-alone array.
C	550	Asking for a zero image: `zeroable`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0550	`zeroable` is the concept that says a type has a zero image, the first of [0540]'s two questions. Generic code can therefore require it. Concepts come in [1240]; for now read one as a named property a type can have.\n\n    -- compiler-owned; a program does not repeat this declaration\n    zeroable: type = concept (t: type)\n    end zeroable\n\nOnly the compiler knows a type's bit patterns, so only the compiler supplies conformances to `zeroable`, and a program cannot declare one. It is the one concept like that. These types conform:\n\n- the enabled scalars;\n- a fixed array exactly when its element is zeroable, even at length zero;\n- a struct exactly when its all-zero shape, recursively, has a zero image;\n- a distinct type exactly when its base is zeroable.\n\nAtoms, functions, pointers and slices do not. It is a closed list, not reflection over arbitrary types.\n\nRequiring `zeroable` is how a container that needs a filler value for storage it has not used yet says so, instead of pretending: see `cleared` at [1350] and the reason at [0510].
C	560	Filling an array with one value	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0560	`[n of v]` is an array of `n` copies of `v`. It suits fixed patterns, which an immutable module binding can keep in flash.\n\n    pattern: [256]u8 = [256 of 0xFF]\n    filled: [256]u8 = [of 0xFF] -- length from the type\n\n    read_header: () -> none =\n        header: [8]u8 = [0x7F, 0x45, of 0]\n    end read_header\n\nThere are three forms. They differ in where the length comes from:\n\n| form | where the length comes from |\n|---|---|\n| `[n of v]` | the count `n`; it can also infer a local or module binding's type |\n| `[of v]` | the destination's written type |\n| `[e1, ..., ek, of v]` | the destination's written type, with `1 <= k < N` |\n\n`v` is evaluated once, not once per element. The last form is the mixed form: it writes the prefix left to right, then evaluates `v` once and fills the rest.\n\nAn assignment to an existing array may use any of the three forms:\n\n    header_image: [8]u8 = [0x7F, 0x45, of 0]\n\n    refill: (seed: u32) -> (row: [4]u32) =\n        row = [of seed] -- the length comes from row\n        row = [seed, seed + 1, of 0] -- the prefix first, then the fill\n        copies := [4 of seed] -- [4]u32\n        row = copies\n    end refill\n\nFine print:\n\n- The mixed form needs one of three destinations: an explicitly typed local or module binding, an assignment to a mutable fixed array, or a fixed-array argument of the same length, which it fills. It cannot be inferred, nested or returned. At module level every element must be a compile-time known scalar [1460].\n- An inferred `[n of v]` takes `v`'s scalar type, and an untyped integer becomes `i32`. Its size must fit the target's `usize`.\n- Refused: `row := [of 0]`, which has no length to give, and a zero count or a zero-length destination.\n- `of` is a contextual word: if `of` names a binding, `[of, other, of]` and `[of + 1]` are ordinary literals.
C	570	Slices are views	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0570	A slice `[]t` is a pointer and a length. It copies nothing. `mut` inside the type says its elements may be written.\n\n    mut cells: [4]f32 = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]\n    view: []f32 = cells[0..<2] -- read-only elements\n    edit: []mut f32 = cells[0..<2] -- writable, since cells is mut\n\nYou can pass an array straight to a slice parameter. The array lends a slice of all its elements:\n\n- A named array lends its own storage.\n- An array literal is built in the caller's frame for the duration of the call, so a list of values needs no binding of its own. A literal lends read-only elements only, so it cannot go to a `[]mut t` parameter.\n\n    added: (values: []f32) -> (sum: f32) =\n        sum = 0.0\n        for value in values do\n            sum += value\n        end for\n    end added\n\n    both_sums: () -> (both: f32) =\n        both = added(grid) + added([1.0, 2.0])\n    end both_sums
C	580	The empty slice	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0580	`[]` is the empty slice. Its length is zero, and a `for` over it runs no iteration.\n\nIt is never null. Its base is the lowest positive address aligned for the element type: 1 for bytes and 4 for a `u32`. Indexing checks the length first, so that base is never dereferenced.
C	590	Arithmetic on whole arrays	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0590	Fixed arrays are also Landin's vector type: arithmetic on numeric arrays works element by element. There is no second type with the same shape and different rules.\n\n    sum_four: (values: [4]f32) -> (sum: f32) =\n        sum = 0.0\n        for value in values do\n            sum += value\n        end for\n    end sum_four\n\n    array_example: () -> (sc: [4]f32, s: f32) =\n        va: [4]f32 = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]\n        vb := va * va\n        sc = va * 2.0 -- a scalar on either side is fine\n        s = sum_four(vb) -- ordinary function, not a reduction builtin\n    end array_example\n\nThe rules:\n\n- `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and unary `-` work on numeric arrays; `%`, `+%`, `-%` and `*%` on integer arrays.\n- Two arrays must have the same element type and length. A scalar of the element type is applied to every element; an array of another length is not.\n- Each operand is evaluated once, left to right, as a complete value before any element is computed. So `a += a` and other overlapping assignments see the old values, not their own earlier writes.\n- Elements go in ascending index order under the ordinary scalar rules for traps, wrapping and floating point. Nothing is reassociated, so `sum_four` adds in order starting from positive zero.\n\nArrays do not compare, not even with `==` or `<>`. Whole-array equality and per-element masks are both plausible meanings, so write the function you mean.\n\nThe cost is visible in the type: `[4096]f32 + [4096]f32` needs a 16 KB result and may keep copies of its operands as well. Vector instructions are an optimisation, never needed for a correct result.
C	600	Text: `utf8`, `utf16` and `cstring`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0600	Landin has no single string type. It has three distinct views over plain storage:\n\n| type | view over | holds |\n|---|---|---|\n| `utf8` | `[]u8` | validated shortest-form UTF-8 |\n| `utf16` | `[]u16` | UTF-16 code units |\n| `cstring` | `ptr u8` | bytes up to a NUL; no length |\n\nThe three types stay distinct from each other and from their backing types through calls, structs and generics. `lenof` on `utf8` and `utf16` counts code units, not characters.\n\nLiterals. A quoted or raw literal can be any of the three, and is `utf8` when nothing says otherwise. Every literal has one trailing zero code unit, which slice lengths leave out. Equal literals of the same width may share one read-only copy. A `cstring` literal is valid UTF-8; a `cstring` that comes from C promises only readable bytes up to its first NUL, with its encoding unchecked.\n\nConverting. Conversion between text and bytes is the ordinary explicit conversion, and these are all there are:\n\n| from | to | what it does |\n|---|---|---|\n| `[]u8` (read-only) | `utf8` | validates, and traps on invalid UTF-8 |\n| `utf8` | `[]u8` (read-only) | nothing: same base, same length |\n| `cstring` | `[]u8` (read-only) | scans to the first NUL |\n| `cstring` | `utf8` | scans to the first NUL and validates |\n\nThere is no conversion from a pointer to `cstring`, none with a writable result, and none for `utf16`. An empty result keeps its source's base and origin.\n\n`compiler.utf8_unvalidated(bytes)` [1560] is for bytes a program knows are UTF-8, because it has just checked them or wrote only whole characters. They become `utf8` without being read again, with the same base, length and origin. The call is allowed only inside `unchecked` [1120], and bytes that are not UTF-8 then go unnoticed.\n\nSlicing. `utf8` and `utf16` slice by range, as `word[3..3]` in [0610] does. The result is the same text type, read-only, over the same storage.\n\n- The `usize` bounds count bytes or UTF-16 code units, not characters.\n- Both bounds must fall where a Unicode scalar starts; a bound out of range or inside an encoding traps.\n- A half-open range may end at the length; an inclusive range takes the whole scalar that starts at its upper bound.\n- A `cstring` has no length and cannot be sliced.\n\nTraversal. `for c in text` yields each Unicode scalar as a `u32` [1320]; on a `cstring` it stops before the first NUL. Traversal declares no error, so text from C is validated as it is decoded and malformed encoding traps, even inside `unchecked`.\n\n**`core/text`.** When invalid text is input to handle rather than a bug, `text.from_bytes` and `text.from_c` validate the same way but fail with `invalid_text` instead of trapping; call them before traversing. The module also has exact byte equality, substring search, decimal parsing and bounded writing into a buffer you supply. It never normalizes or silently truncates. It allocates only in a builder made by `text.growing`, which takes an allocator.\n\n`core/text` counts positions as byte offsets of the opaque type `text.position`:\n\n- On plain `[]u8`, the functions are `first`, `at_end`, `next`, `advance`, `offset`, `byte` and `slice`. Reading a byte at the end fails with `past_end`, and a slice keeps its source's origin.\n- On `utf8`, the same positions step a whole scalar with `start`, `step`, `done` and `width`. `find` returns where a match begins, so the text around it slices out by range with nothing copied.
C	610	Indexing text by scalar or by position	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0610	Indexing a `utf8` gives the Unicode scalar there as a `u32`, the type a character literal [0250] and a traversal [1320] already give it. The index type picks the operation:\n\n- a `usize` counts scalars from the start, so `word[2]` is the third one; the compiler finds it by scanning;\n- a `core/text.position` is a byte offset, decoded directly in O(1).\n\n    word: utf8 = "\\u{e9}t\\u{e9}"\n    last := word[2] -- 233, the u32 of é, found by scanning\n    same := last == '\\u{e9}' -- true\n    bytes: utf8 = word[3..3] -- é again, at byte 3: two bytes, no copy\n\nA count past the end traps, and so does a position at the end or on a continuation byte. Neither index type converts implicitly to the other.\n\nThe scalar is decoded, so it is a value, not a place: `addr word[2]` and `word[2] = 'e'` are errors. To get its bytes, take a one-scalar range as [0600] describes: its bounds count bytes, and the result is still `utf8`.\n\nA `utf8` converted to `[]u8` loses scalar indexing and has the ordinary slice operations instead.
C	620	Storing a collection field by field (deferred)	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0620	DEFERRED: not in Landin yet; it is planned (Language evolution, in the roadmap).\n\nA collection could be stored transposed: one array per field instead of one array of structs, so that one field of every element is a contiguous slice. It would be written `soa [4096]entity`.\n\nThe feature touches aliasing, generics, slicing, `addr`, layout, debug information and the optimiser all at once, and no program has needed it yet. Until one does, generate the arrays with a program that writes the source ([1540]).
C	630	Atoms	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0630	An atom is a name that is its own value and its own type. Declaring one gives you both at once, because for an atom the value and the type are the same thing.\n\n    not_found: atom\n    no_access: atom\n\nAtoms compare with `==` and `<>`, and nothing else. Two atoms are equal when they are the same declaration, even when the values come from two different atom sets:\n\n    is_missing: (outcome: not_found | no_access) -> (missing: bool) =\n        missing = outcome == not_found\n    end is_missing\n\nAs far as your program can tell, an atom has no number behind it: it is not ordered, and it does not convert to or from an integer.
C	640	Enumerations are unions of atoms	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0640	An enumeration is a union of atoms. The atoms `north`, `south`, `east` and `west` were declared at [0100].\n\n    compass: type = north | south | east | west\n\nYou may also write the union in place, as the type of a binding, a parameter, a return or a field. It is then the same type as the declared name: `facing: (way: north | south) -> (ahead: bool)` takes a `compass` value that is north or south. As the element of an array, a slice or a pointer, the union needs its name.\n\nAn atom set can be an array element, a struct field or a variant payload, and it stays that set there. A write needs one of its members, and reading it back gives you an atom, not an integer.
C	650	Distinct types	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0650	`distinct` makes a new type that has its base's representation and never mixes with its base or any other type. Comparison comes along, and so do the bit operations of an unsigned base. Arithmetic does not.\n\n    meter: type = distinct f32\n    second: type = distinct f32\n\nYou cannot add a `meter` to a `second`. You cannot even add two `meter` values, because `f32`'s arithmetic stays with `f32`. To get a value in or out, apply the type, as for any conversion ([0700]):\n\n    length: meter = meter(2.5)\n    raw: f32 = f32(length)\n\nThat separation is the whole point: the compiler keeps the type apart from its base and from every other distinct type, at no runtime cost. Generic deduction and conformances tell it apart too, and an alias of it keeps its identity.\n\nA few things do carry over, because they ask nothing of what the value means:\n\n- Equality. `==` and `<>` work when the base has them: a scalar, an atom set, a pointer or a function value. A descriptor compares without taking its number out.\n- Ordering, when the base is a scalar. `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` order as the base does.\n- Flags, when the base is an unsigned integer. `&`, `^`, `|` and `~` give the same distinct type, and `&=`, `^=` and `|=` update in place, so a set of flags stays one.\n- The zero image. A record that holds a distinct value may be `zeroed` ([0540]), though `zeroed` written for the distinct type itself does not construct it.\n\n    farther: (a: meter, b: meter) -> (yes: bool) =\n        yes = a > b\n    end farther\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- Shifts stay with the base, as arithmetic does.\n- A distinct value meets its base or any other type only through a conversion, and that includes comparing with it.\n- A wrapped reference keeps its origin.\n\nExact rules: spec [1890].
C	660	Range subtypes	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0660	A range subtype is an integer type limited to a run of its values. The range is checked when a value goes in.\n\n    percent: type = u8 range 0..100\n\nThe check happens at a binding, a parameter, a named return and a conversion. When a value is outside the range, the compiler refuses it if it knows, and the program traps if it does not. Arithmetic on a `percent` gives a plain `u8`: the range is not part of the result.\n\nA range subtype is not allowed as a struct field, an array element, a pointer or slice target, a generic argument, or something `addr` can point at. In each of those, a write through the base type could reach the storage unchecked. To keep a checked value in storage, wrap it: a `distinct` type that only a checking function constructs carries the proof ([1730]).\n\nA guard on an ordinary integer does not make it a `percent`. If you reject bad input with a `fail` guard and then store the integer as `percent`, that store still has its trapping check. Once the value is in a `percent` place, passing it to another `percent` place needs no second check.
C	670	Structs	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0670	A struct is written either as a block or inline in parentheses. The two forms mean the same thing. The inline form is also how parameter lists, return lists and payloads are written.\n\n    size2: type = (w: u32, h: u32)\n\nA struct is nominal in either form: two separately declared structs with the same fields are different types. An alias keeps the original identity.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- Either form may take type and fixed parameters, and `layout` ([0750]) applies to either. The parameters are compile-time names: they add no field and no hidden runtime argument.\n- Each fully applied instance of a parameterized struct is its own type. The declaration and all its arguments identify it, even an argument the fields do not use. Aliases of the arguments make no new type. A different argument does, even when the fields and layout come out equal.\n- A struct may mention itself, or another struct that mentions it back, in a function parameter or result. A function field is one code address, so the layout stays finite.
C	680	Structs with a variant part	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0680	A struct may end in a variant part: one of several cases, each with its own fields. The fields that every case shares are ordinary fields of the struct.\n\n    figure: type = struct\n        label: utf8\n        area: f32\n        kind: variant\n            circle: (radius: f32) |\n            rectangle: (width: f32, height: f32)\n        end kind\n    end figure
C	690	Cases with no payload	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0690	A case with no fields is written bare. A bare case is an atom, like any other ([1700]), so a variant part reads as a union of its cases.\n\n    node_kind: type = struct\n        kind: variant\n            leaf |\n            branch: (first: u32, count: u32)\n        end kind\n    end node_kind\n\nYou write a case where its variant part is the context: when you construct into that part, and when you name an arm of a match on it. A case is not a value apart from its part, and the part is not a value apart from its struct: copy the struct, or match it.\n\nSelecting a case costs the size of that case, not the size of the largest one, because of what it writes:\n\n- Selecting a bare case writes only its tag.\n- Selecting a case with fields zeros that case's fields first, then writes the ones you gave.\n- The bytes of the inactive cases and the padding are unspecified afterwards, though `zeroed` still writes the whole struct as zeros.
C	700	Constructing values and converting them	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0700	Construction and conversion look the same: a type applied to arguments.\n\n    origin := point(x: 0.0, y: 0.0)\n    metres := meter(1.5)\n\nA variant case is built the same way, with the case name applied to its fields. To read a case back, use `match` ([1210]).\n\n    mut f: figure = (label: "disc", area: 0.0, kind: circle(radius: 2.0))\n    f.kind = rectangle(width: 3.0, height: 4.0)
C	710	Struct literals take their type from context	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0710	A struct literal has no type of its own, like a number literal. It takes the named struct type that its context wants. A struct type written inline is not yet such a context: declare the type and use its name (spec [1830]).\n\n    here: point = (x: 1.0, y: 2.0)\n\nWhat does not convert is a value that already has an anonymous struct type, such as a call's results. `divide(10, 3)` gives `(quot: i32, rem: i32)`, and that value never becomes a named struct with the same fields. Two anonymous types match when their field names, types and order all match.\n\nAt module scope, a struct literal is a static image that the compiler builds, not code run before the entry point ([1460]).\n\nExact rules: spec [1940].
C	720	Filling the remaining fields with `of`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0720	`of` at the end of a struct literal fills every field that the literal did not name. It is the same word in the same place as in array literals ([0560]).\n\n    window: type = struct\n        width: u32\n        height: u32\n        visible: bool\n        resizable: bool\n    end window\n\n    main_window: window = (width: 640, height: 480, of false)\n    tiny_window: window = (width: 1, of zeroed)\n\nThe fill has to typecheck for each field it fills: `of false` works where the rest are `bool`, and `of zeroed` ([0540]) wherever the rest have a zero image.\n\nThis is not a default value. Declarations have none ([0980]), because a new parameter would then fit every existing call silently. Here whoever writes the literal makes the choice. The trade is theirs too: a literal with `of` picks up a field added later without a word, and one without it breaks loudly.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- A fill other than `zeroed` needs at least one omitted field, and all of the omitted fields must then have exactly the same type, array length and reference permission included.\n- The fill is evaluated once, after the named values, and copied into each remaining field in declaration order.
C	730	Register images: flags, selections and sets	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0730	A hardware register mixes kinds of field, and confusing them is the classic driver bug. Landin describes a register as a packed struct whose fields sit at bit positions you write down.\n\n| kind | what it is | how you write it |\n|---|---|---|\n| flag | one bit | `bool` |\n| selection | one of several named values, encoded as the datasheet says | a union of atoms with encodings |\n| set | several independent flags at once | a packed struct of `bool` |\n| number | a plain number | an unsigned field such as `u12` |\n\nThe examples below use these atoms:\n\n    irq_rx: atom\n    irq_tx: atom\n    irq_err: atom\n\n    internal: atom\n    external: atom\n    pll: atom\n\n    active_low, active_high: atom\n    by_1, by_2: atom\n\nA selection is a union that gives each atom its encoding. The encoding belongs to the union, not to the atom, so the same atom may be encoded differently in another register. The width is the smallest that holds the largest encoding; write a base type only when the datasheet gives the field more room than it needs.\n\n    polarity: type = (active_low = 0 | active_high = 1) -- one bit\n    clock_mode: type = (internal = 0 | external = 1 | pll = 4)\n    divider_sel: type = u4 (by_1 = 0 | by_2 = 1) -- four bits, as given\n\nA set is a packed struct of `bool`, one field per member, each at the bit its member's encoding names.\n\n- Membership is a field read.\n- Adding or removing a member is a field write.\n- Building one is an ordinary struct literal with `of` ([0720]).\n\nThere is no set literal or set operator, because a struct needs none. Inside a larger image the same fields sit at the image's bits, offset by where the set begins.\n\n    irq: type = (irq_rx = 0 | irq_tx = 1 | irq_err = 2)\n\n    irq_set: type = layout(packed, u32) struct\n        irq_rx: bool at 0\n        irq_tx: bool at 1\n        irq_err: bool at 2\n    end irq_set\n\n    control: type = layout(packed) struct\n        enable: bool at 0\n        mode: clock_mode at 4..6\n        irq_rx: bool at 8 -- irq's encodings, from bit 8\n        irq_tx: bool at 9\n        irq_err: bool at 10\n        divider: u12 at 16..27\n    end control\n\nA set earns its place when its members mean something. A numbered bank of lines does not: sixteen output pins are `[16]bool` at `0..15`, not sixteen invented atoms.\n\nPositions are written. Bit positions are never implied by field order, so reordering the fields of a published register is not a hidden breaking change. In a packed struct every field carries a position, or none does. Any bit no field claims is reserved: you cannot name it, no completion list offers it, and a read-modify-write leaves it untouched.\n\nYou rarely write these by hand. A generator reading a vendor's System View Description (SVD) file writes the fields, and the helpers [0740] uses, for every register: `refine svd` generates them (devices), and running a generator as a step of a build belongs to the companion tool. The language has no `set(X)` type former to do it instead.\n\nA field may be an array, which is how a real peripheral packs sixteen two-bit pin settings into one word. The element width times the count must equal the range, and element zero takes the low bits.\n\n    pin_input, pin_output, pin_alternate, pin_analog: atom\n\n    pin_mode: type = (pin_input = 0 | pin_output = 1 | pin_alternate = 2 | pin_analog = 3)\n\n    moder: type = layout(packed) struct\n        pins: [16]pin_mode at 0..31\n    end moder\n\n    set_pin: (inout m: moder, n: usize, mode: pin_mode) -> none =\n        m.pins[n] = mode\n    end set_pin\n\nIndexing such a field with a run-time value is a shift by a computed amount, with a bounds check that stays even in `unchecked`. Do it on an image in memory, never straight on the device ([0740]).\n\nFine print:\n\n- A packed struct is a raw image, and every bit pattern is a valid image. Copying, passing and returning it keep all its bits.\n- Reading an encoded field checks that the bits name a member and traps if they do not, so a `match` on the result can be exhaustive.\n- Writing a field leaves every other bit alone, and a fresh literal starts from zero. A packed field has no address of its own: to update one, pass the whole image.\n- `layout(packed, u32)` keeps a 32-bit carrier even when the highest position would fit a smaller one.\n- Field widths run from `u1` to `u64` inside packed structs only; they add no arbitrary-width arithmetic or calling convention.\n\nExact rules: spec [1870].
C	740	Reading and writing a device register	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0740	A device register is read and written by two operations, and how the register behaves is data you pass them, not a keyword:\n\n- `compiler.register_read(pointer, read_mode)`\n- `compiler.register_write(pointer, image, write_mode, reserved_policy, named_mask)`\n\nThe pointer is an ordinary one to `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64`, and its width is the one transaction the device sees. Modes and policies are atoms, so a generator can describe write-one-to-clear, clear-on-read and whatever the next vendor invents without the language growing a word for each.\n\n    status_raw: (base: usize) -> (raw: u32) =\n        port: ptr u32 = ptr(base + 0x04)\n        raw = compiler.register_read(port, compiler.normal_read)\n    end status_raw\n\n    clear_events: (base: usize, events: u32) -> none =\n        port: ptr mut u32 = ptr(base + 0x08)\n        compiler.register_write(port, events, compiler.one_clears,\n                                compiler.write_zero, 0x0000_0007)\n    end clear_events\n\n| argument | values |\n|---|---|\n| read mode | `compiler.normal_read`, `compiler.clear_on_read` |\n| write mode | `compiler.normal_write`, `compiler.one_clears` |\n| reserved policy | `compiler.preserve`, `compiler.write_zero`, `compiler.write_one` |\n| named mask | a fixed number of the register's width, with a one at every bit a field names |\n\nA register that cannot be read has no read to perform, so `compiler.no_read` is an error rather than a mode, and so is `compiler.no_write`.\n\nThe operation, not the pointer's type, makes an access a device transaction: there is no `volatile ptr` and no `register(t, ...)` wrapper type.\n\nChanging one field. You cannot write a single field of a device register. For an ordinary read/write register, read the whole image, change it locally and write it back whole. The generator of [0730] writes, beside `control`, `control_decode` from the raw `u32` to the image, `control_encode` back, and the constant `control_named_mask`:\n\n    reset_flags: (base: usize) -> none =\n        port: ptr mut u32 = ptr(base)\n        image: control = (enable: true, mode: external, irq_rx: true, of zeroed)\n        compiler.register_write(port, control_encode(image),\n                                compiler.normal_write, compiler.write_zero,\n                                control_named_mask)\n    end reset_flags\n\n    read_modify_write: (base: usize, n: u16) -> none =\n        port: ptr mut u32 = ptr(base)\n        mut image := control_decode(compiler.register_read(port,\n                                                           compiler.normal_read))\n        image.divider = n\n        compiler.register_write(port, control_encode(image),\n                                compiler.normal_write, compiler.preserve,\n                                control_named_mask)\n    end read_modify_write\n\n- A fresh local literal knows nothing of what the hardware holds. To keep reserved bits as the device has them, read the image first, as `read_modify_write` does; `compiler.preserve` never reads behind your back.\n- That read, change and write is not atomic.\n- The read, change and write does not carry over to clear-on-read or one-clears registers: a destructive read consumes state, and a one-clears readback is not a command.\n\nReset values. A register's reset value initializes nothing. It is what the datasheet says the register holds after a reset, generated as a constant so that tools and readers know where they start. The hardware puts it there, not the program.\n\nExact rules: spec [1870].
C	750	Field order and layout	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0750	Fields stay in the order you wrote them, with natural alignment and padding in between. A hexdump matches the source, and the layout does not shift under a new compiler or an optimization flag.\n\n    packet: type = layout(c) struct\n        kind: u8\n        length: u16 -- big-endian as the wire sent it\n        id: u32\n    end packet\n\n    from_big_u16: (wire: u16) -> (value: u16) =\n        value = (wire << 8) | (wire >> 8) -- on a little-endian target\n    end from_big_u16\n\nYou ask for another layout by name:\n\n| layout | what it does |\n|---|---|\n| no `layout` | source order, natural alignment |\n| `layout(optimal)` | sorts fields by descending alignment, but only if that makes the struct strictly smaller |\n| `layout(c)` | the selected target's C rules (spec [1975]) |\n| `layout(c, packed)` | C's byte-packed record: every field at alignment one, no padding |\n| `layout(packed)` | a register image of bits ([0730]) |\n\nByte order is not a property of a field. A field holds the target's own order, which `compiler.byte_order` names ([1560]). When your program reads or writes another order, it converts where the bytes cross, with shifts ([0320]) or an ordinary function, as `from_big_u16` does above. That way the cost is visible where it is paid.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- `layout(optimal)` keeps source order when sorting saves nothing, moves nested structs, arrays and variant parts whole, and never makes a struct fit for C.\n- `layout(c)` does not choose a function's calling convention. A C record holds native-endian scalars, fixed arrays, nested nonempty C structs and callback fields declared with C's convention.\n- A `layout(c, packed)` record's fields are read and written by copy and have no address of their own. C takes such a record through a pointer.\n- A C record's last field may be `[0]T`, C's flexible array member, whose elements follow the record in memory.\n- Every byte count comes from the selected target, 32-bit targets included. Initializers still run in the order you wrote them ([0410]).
C	760	Attributes	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0760	Attributes are prefix words from a closed set. Their arguments are always in parentheses. Where an argument is one of a fixed set of values it is an atom; a linker name is a string. These are the words, with the arguments each takes:\n\n| word | arguments | where it is described |\n|---|---|---|\n| `mut` | none | [0060] |\n| `public` | none | [0090] |\n| `layout` | `c`, `optimal`, `packed`, or `c, packed` | [0730], [0750] |\n| `escaping` | none | [0780] |\n| `caller` | none | [1040] |\n| `fixed` | none | [1490] |\n| `option` | none; it implies `fixed` | [1530] |\n| `link` | `symbol: "..."`, `thread`, `section: "..."`, `region: "..."`, `align: 16`, `vector: 16`, `keep`, `boot_stage` | [1610], [1615], [1640] |\n| `extern` | `c`, `interrupt`, `naked`, and others | [1570] |\n\n`at` gives a field its bit position ([0730]). `at`, `of` and `align` are contextual: a field or an entry may still be called one of them, because nothing reads the word as an attribute there. Placement alignment is `link`'s `align` label ([1640]), not a word of its own. `from` and `with` are reserved and cannot name anything.\n\nLandin has none of these attributes:\n\n- `volatile`: a device access is an operation ([0740]).\n- `big` or `little`: byte order is converted where bytes cross ([0750]).\n- `inline` or `noinline`: inlining is the optimizer's decision ([1310]).\n- `weak`: a whole program links one definition per name, and the compiler-owned vector image does what weak default handlers do in C ([1640]).
C	770	A frame reference cannot leave its function	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0770	A pointer to a local dies with the function. Returning one is an error, and so is storing it anywhere that outlives the function.\n\n    bad: () -> (p: ptr u32) =\n        x: u32 = 42\n        p = addr x -- error: a frame origin escapes\n    end bad\n\nA pointer to module storage is static, so the same shape is fine:\n\n    mut tally: u32 = 0\n\n    tally_cell: () -> (p: ptr mut u32) =\n        p = addr tally -- fine: module storage is static\n    end tally_cell\n\nThe origin travels with the value. A slice of a local array is frame too, and so is an `any` built over a local ([1370]).
C	780	Keeping a pointer you were given: `escaping`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0780	A parameter is non-escaping by default. The callee may read and write through a pointer it was handed, but it may not keep the pointer once it returns.\n\n    increment_cell: (cell: ptr mut u32) -> none =\n        cell.val += 1 -- using the pointer is fine; keeping it would not be\n    end increment_cell\n\n    caller_of_increment: () -> (n: u32) =\n        mut local: u32 = 1\n        increment_cell(addr local) -- fine: the callee does not keep it\n        n = local\n    end caller_of_increment\n\nSo a pointer to a local can go into any call whose parameter does not say `escaping`.\n\nA function that does keep a reference marks the parameter `escaping`. The caller may then pass only something that lives long enough: allocated or static, never frame.\n\nThe next example assumes a struct `node` with a field `next: ptr mut node`. `mem.new` allocates one value through the allocator it is given and returns a pointer to it ([1360]; `core/mem` in the library guide).\n\n    push_front: (escaping inout head: ptr mut node, escaping item: ptr mut node)\n                -> none =\n        item.val.next = head\n        head = item\n    end push_front\n\n    build: (provider: type is mem.allocator, memory: provider,\n            escaping seed: ptr mut node)\n           -> (head: ptr mut node) ! mem.out_of_memory =\n        head = seed\n        n := try mem.new(memory: memory, value: seed.val)\n        push_front(head, n) -- allocated, fine\n\n        mut local: node = seed.val\n        push_front(head, addr local) -- error: a frame origin escapes\n    end build\n\n`push_front` stores each argument where the other can reach it, so both are `escaping`.\n\nWhat counts as keeping:\n\n- "Keeping" means any store that outlives the call: into a module binding, or through a pointer, slice or `inout` field the caller owns.\n- Storing a reference back into storage of the same origin is an update, not keeping, and needs no marker.\n- Storing one parameter's reference into another parameter's storage needs `escaping`, or else `escaping into`.\n\n`escaping into` names the one parameter whose storage keeps the reference. With it, a node on the caller's frame can go onto a list on the caller's frame, provided the node lives as long as the list. The node does so when it is the caller's parameter, static, allocated, or a local declared before the list.\n\nIn the next example each parameter is kept in the other's storage, so each names the other.\n\n    push_kept: (escaping into item inout head: ptr mut node,\n                escaping into head item: ptr mut node) -> none =\n        item.val.next = head\n        head = item\n    end push_kept\n\n    on_the_frame: (escaping seed: ptr mut node) -> none =\n        mut first: node = seed.val\n        mut head: ptr mut node = seed\n        push_kept(head, addr first) -- fine: first is declared before head\n\n        mut late: node = seed.val\n        push_kept(head, addr late) -- error: late is declared after head\n    end on_the_frame\n\nThe function may keep `item` in `head` and nowhere else. A frame reference never goes into a parameter's storage, and a reference from the caller's parameter goes into anything its frame holds.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	790	A returned reference says where it came from: `from`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0790	When a function returns a reference derived from a parameter, its signature says so with `from`. The caller then knows that the thing it passed in has to hold still while it uses the result.\n\nHere a `batch` holds a writable slice of readings and how many of them are filled in:\n\n    batch: type = struct\n        items: []mut u32\n        count: usize\n    end batch\n\n    filled_part: (b: batch) -> (s: []mut u32 from b) = b.items[0..<b.count] end\n\n- `from` names where the reference came from; it says nothing about writing. Write permission is the return type's business ([0430]).\n- `from a, b` borrows from both.\n- No `from` at all means the result is independent: it borrows nothing. That is what an allocator returns, which is why two live allocations from one allocator are unremarkable.\n\nOne accessor is enough. `filled_part` hands out the widest permission the storage has, and a caller who wants less relaxes it ([0440]): `xs: []u32 = filled_part(b)`. There is no const and non-const pair.\n\nThe compiler checks the clause against the body in both directions. Returning something derived from a parameter without naming it is an error, and so is naming a parameter the result did not come from.\n\n`from` is the mirror of `escaping`. `escaping` says the callee keeps what the caller handed in; `from` says the caller keeps something of what the callee handed back. You write both, and the compiler infers neither. So a distant body can never change a signature, and function pointers, concept entries and the C boundary need no special rule.\n\nTwo refinements:\n\n- A read-only result that points into static storage may name a parameter it does not come from, since static storage outlives every parameter.\n- A writable result must name every place it could point to. So a helper that might return module storage takes that storage as a parameter and names it too.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	800	A borrow through `from` lasts across the call	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0800	A result with `from` borrows its source just as a view does in [0830]. The difference is how the compiler learns of the derivation: the signature supplies it, where in [0830] one expression showed it. The fix is the same: take the view again afterwards.\n\n`core/vec`'s `vec.used` is declared with `from`, like [0790]'s `filled_part`:\n\n    import core/mem\n    import core/vec\n    import hosted/heap\n\n    grow_under_view: (inout numbers: vec.list(i32)) -> (n: i32) ! mem.out_of_memory =\n        memory := heap.new()\n        xs := vec.used(numbers)\n        try vec.push(numbers, memory, 5) -- error: numbers is borrowed by xs\n        n = xs[0]\n    end grow_under_view\n\nNothing is written at the call. The convention lives in the declaration, and a caller that misuses the result is told at its next use, just as with `escaping`.
C	810	A pointer made from an integer is not tracked	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0810	Converting an integer to a pointer ([0470]) ends tracking. The integer has no origin, so the pointer borrows nothing, and the compiler says nothing more about its lifetime. Nor does the compiler check that the storage is live or large enough: that stays the library's unsafe obligation ([1720]).\n\n    block_at: (base: ptr mut u8, offset: usize) -> (block: ptr mut u8) =\n        address: usize = usize(base) + offset\n        block = ptr(address) -- no tracked derivation survives\n    end block_at\n\nThis is how `core/arena` returns a block without borrowing the arena, after checking its arithmetic; `core` gets no special privilege for it. [0500] says why there is no `offset` or `slice_from` to do this for you, and [0510] keeps uninitialized storage out of reach.\n\nA signature brings tracking back. A function that indexes a table C gave it writes `from table` on its result, and the compiler checks its callers against that as against any signature. The compiler does not check the function's body against it, since a pointer made from an integer satisfies any `from`. The contract is its author's claim, so keep such functions small.
C	820	Arenas are ordinary allocators you give storage to	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0820	An arena is a library value from `core/arena`: you hand it a block of bytes, it hands out pieces of it, and individual frees do nothing. It is not a builtin type or block. Code that takes any allocator accepts it as a `mem.allocator` provider.\n\n    import core/arena\n    import core/mem\n\n    mut backing: [1024]u8 = zeroed\n    report: () -> (code: i32) =\n        mut space: arena.space = zeroed\n        scratch := arena.over(space, addr backing[0], 1024)\n        code = 1\n        first := mem.new(scratch, u8(7)) else (problem)\n            _ = problem\n            return\n        end\n        second := mem.new(scratch, u8(9)) else (problem)\n            _ = problem\n            return\n        end\n        code = i32(first.val) + i32(second.val)\n    end report\n\n- `arena.over(state, base, size)` takes the backing address, its size in bytes, and an `arena.space` you declare `zeroed` beside it. It returns the arena's handle `from` the space and the backing; copies of the handle share one arena.\n- Allocation aligns the address and advances an offset. A request that does not fit fails with `mem.out_of_memory` before changing anything.\n- `arena.reset` gives everything back at once, and `arena.used` reports the bytes consumed.\n\n`over` takes its backing as `escaping base`, so it accepts module storage or storage from another allocator and refuses a frame array. The reason is that allocations borrow nothing ([0790]): a helper could store one in module storage, and an arena over frame storage would let that pointer outlive the frame.\n\nFor a local buffer whose every use stays inside the frame, `arena.over_unchecked` takes frame backing. You must stop using its results before the buffer ends.\n\nOther providers build on the same idea:\n\n| provider | what it does | what you must do |\n|---|---|---|\n| `core/region.over(ledger, provider)` | records every extent it takes from `provider` in a `region.space` ledger you declare `zeroed` | release all at once with `defer region.release(ledger, provider)`, and stop using its allocations before then |\n| `core/pool.over` | hands out pieces of backing whose origin its handle keeps | keep the backing live until every result is done with |\n\nA region's handle holds a copy of its provider's handle. Its allocations borrow nothing, and its bookkeeping also uses the provider's capacity. A finite provider stays finite: there is no hidden heap fallback.\n\nThe compiler does not do these for you:\n\n- arrange the backing's lifetime and release (`defer`, [1100], runs on every exit);\n- keep overlapping backing apart;\n- stop you using a result after its backing ends or is reused.\n\nResults obey the ordinary origin rules and nothing more. `arena` itself is not a keyword: it is an ordinary name you may declare.
C	830	A view into a local holds the local still	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0830	A view taken from a local borrows it. While the view is still in use, the compiler refuses to pass the local as `inout` or `sink`, because that call could grow, move or replace the storage under the view.\n\n    reset_cells: (inout buffer: [4]i32) -> none =\n        buffer = [9, 9, 9, 9]\n    end reset_cells\n\n    view_then_reset: () -> (n: i32) =\n        mut buffer: [4]i32 = [1, 2, 3, 4]\n        xs := buffer[0..<2]\n        reset_cells(buffer) -- error: buffer is borrowed by xs\n        n = xs[0]\n    end view_then_reset\n\nThe fix is always nearby: finish with the view before the call, or take it again after. The check looks at one function body, so there is nothing to annotate.\n\nOnly `inout` and `sink` trigger the check, since they are the two ways a call can change the storage itself. While the view lives, you may still read the local, pass it `in` or pass it by pointer.\n\nA view needs no name to be in use. The slice a `for` walks is in use until the loop is done, so the loop's body does not pass what it walks `inout` unless it leaves the loop straight after; and a view given to a call is in use until the call returns, so its source is not passed `inout` beside it.\n\nAn unchecked region ([1120]) does not turn the check off: origins and escape are among the checks that stay.
C	840	Mixed origins count as the shortest-lived	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0840	When a value combines origins, it takes the most restrictive one. A struct holding one frame pointer is frame as a whole, and a value chosen between two branches takes the shorter-lived of the two.\n\nA value that holds no references has no origin and goes anywhere, which is one more reason the idiom is handles and indices. A number computed from a view keeps no borrow: saving `lenof xs` saves a number, and you may use it after `xs` or its container changes.\n\nTaking an address or a range is different: that reference keeps the selected storage's origin ([0430], [0790]). Writing through a known address of a local updates the local's origins too. Mixing in a pointer made from an integer ([0810]) does not hide a tracked origin.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	850	Volatile access sits outside the borrow rules	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0850	A volatile access is exempt from the borrow rule and from every aliasing assumption. It is an operation, not a pointer type:\n\n| operation | for |\n|---|---|\n| `compiler.volatile_load`, `compiler.volatile_store` | one scalar |\n| `compiler.register_read`, `compiler.register_write` | a register image ([0740]) |\n\nEach performs exactly one access of its width through an ordinary pointer. That pointer is usually one built from an address ([0460]), and so already outside the lifetime checks ([0470]).\n\nHardware often needs several typed windows on one address, such as a byte view and a word view of the same register, and that is legal on purpose. There is no `volatile ptr`: a second permission on every reference would buy nothing the operations do not.\n\nDirect memory access (DMA) uses ordinary slices. Landin makes no lifetime promise about storage a device is still writing: neither an interrupt nor masking one makes it reusable, and waiting for the device is the driver's own protocol.\n\nExact rules: spec [1990].
C	860	What the lifetime checks do not catch	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0860	The checks know which kind of storage a reference points into. They do not know which allocation it points into, or whether that allocation still exists. So these go through:\n\n- Use after free or reset. The compiler does not know which arena or allocator a pointer came from, or that it has been given back.\n- A pointer that went through longer-lived storage. Inside one function a struct carries its fields' origins ([0840]).
