Store a pointer into a heap node, though, and read it back later through the node: it now has the node's origin, and whatever it pointed to may be gone.\n- Anything across the C boundary.\n\nCatching these would need region-based checking or generation counters, and Landin deliberately has neither.
C	870	Declaring a function	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0870	A function is a name bound to a value of a function type. There is no `fn` keyword. In every function, `=` opens the body and `end` closes it.\n\n    double: (x: i32) -> (r: i32) =\n        r = x * 2\n    end double\n\nResults have names, as parameters do. The body sets `r` by assigning it, and the caller gets whatever `r` holds when the body ends.
C	880	One-line functions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0880	When the body is a single expression, write that expression after `=`. Its value fills the named result. The function still takes an `end`.\n\n    triple_it: (x: i32) -> (r: i32) = x * 3 end
C	890	Returning nothing, and never returning	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0890	`none` means the function returns normally with no value. `noreturn` means it never returns at all.\n\n    log_it: (m: utf8) -> none = end log_it\n    halt_it: () -> noreturn = loop do end loop end halt_it\n\nThe body of a `noreturn` function has to diverge on every reachable path: an unconditional `loop` with no exit, or a call to another `noreturn` function. A conditional loop does not count, even if you expect it to run forever.\n\nA call to a `noreturn` function ends the path it is on, so a branch that calls `halt_it()` needs no value of its own.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- `noreturn` is part of the function's type. A `() -> none` function cannot stand in for a `() -> noreturn` one, and a `() -> noreturn` function cannot stand in for a `() -> none` one.\n- A `noreturn` function declares no errors ([0940]), because failing would return to the caller.\n- Calling a `noreturn` function does not unwind `defer` ([1100]). A deferred `noreturn` call stops the cleanup that would follow it, and the original exit.\n- C declarations may use `noreturn`. Interrupt and naked handlers stay `() -> none`.
C	900	Three parameter conventions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0900	A convention says what the function may do with the value you hand it. It is about the argument itself, never about what the argument points at: the pointer type says that ([0450]).\n\n| convention | what it promises |\n| --- | --- |\n| `in` | I will not change the value. The default, unmarked. |\n| `inout` | I may replace it, and the change comes back to the caller. The argument must be mutable. |\n| `sink` | I consume it. The place the caller named is dead afterwards ([0910]). |\n\nThere is no `out` convention: outputs are named results.\n\nIn this example, `[]u8` is a slice of bytes, a view of someone else's bytes ([0570]):\n\n    process: (source: []u8, inout target: []u8, sink owned: []u8)\n             -> (written: u32) =\n        written = 0\n    end process\n\nBecause a convention is about the argument itself, a function that writes device registers through a pointer, but never re-points it, takes the pointer as `in`. The `mut` lives in the pointer type ([0430]).\n\n`escaping` is a separate word that can go with any of the three conventions. It says that the function may keep what a pointer, slice or `any` refers to after the call returns, so the caller has to show that it lives long enough ([0780]).\n\n`sink` and `escaping` do different jobs: `sink` makes the caller's place unusable afterwards, and `escaping` lets the callee keep a reference. The two can go together. On a type parameter, `escaping` asks nothing when the type holds no references ([0840]).\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- An `inout` argument need not be a binding: a pointer target such as `c.inner.val` is fine.\n- One call may not pass the same variable, or a field of it, to two `inout` parameters.\n- Two different pointer or computed-index paths may still alias. The compiler cannot see that, and does not promise to ([1720]).
C	910	`sink` consumes a place	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0910	A `sink` argument is a place. After the call, that place is dead until you assign it again. A field of a binding is a place, so consuming a struct's field needs no temporary.\n\n    message: type = struct\n        body: []u8\n        size: u32\n    end message\n\n    release: (sink bytes: []u8) -> none = end release\n\n    clear_message: (inout m: message) -> none =\n        release(m.body) -- m.body is dead from here\n        m.body = [] -- and live again from here\n        m.size = 0\n    end clear_message\n\nReading `m.body` between those two lines is an error. The check closes the window between releasing storage and repointing the field, which a temporary binding would have left open.\n\nThis is a use-after-consume check on one place, not ownership. The value is still copyable: a copy made before the sink stays live, and the compiler does not catch consuming through both.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- The place is a path from a binding through fields and literal fixed-array indexes. The compiler refuses a path through a pointer (`p.val.items`), a computed index (`xs[i].items`) or a slice index. A whole slice may be sunk.\n- A field sunk out of an `inout` parameter must be assigned again before every return, failure included. A `defer` or `undo` may do it.\n- Arguments are evaluated left to right first, and the places are consumed as the call begins. So `use(value, value.count)` is fine when `use` sinks its first parameter.\n- The compiler refuses a call that sinks one place twice, or that sinks a place it also passes `inout`.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	920	Several results	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0920	A function can return several named results.\n\n    divide: (a: i32, b: i32) -> (quot: i32, rem: i32) =\n        quot = a / b\n        rem = a % b\n    end divide\n\nTwo or more results travel together as one anonymous struct, laid out in the order you wrote them. A single result is its own type, with no struct around it.
C	930	Every result is assigned before returning	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0930	A function must assign each named result on every path that returns. The compiler checks this, so there is no "uninitialised return value".\n\nA path that fails ([0940]) need not assign the results, and the caller cannot read them on that path.
C	940	Errors: what can fail is in the signature	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0940	A function that can fail lists, after `!`, the atoms it can fail with, and `fail` leaves with one of them. An atom is a declared name that is its own value, such as `port_zero: atom` ([0630]). A caller cannot ignore a failure: at every call to a failing function, it either passes the failure on or handles it.\n\nHere is all of it at once. `port_from` reads a port number with the library's `text.to_u32`, which fails on bad digits, and adds a failure of its own. Its two callers then deal with the result in different ways:\n\n    import core/text\n\n    port_zero: atom\n\n    port_from: (digits: utf8)\n               -> (port: u32)\n               ! text.invalid_number | text.number_overflow | port_zero =\n        port = try text.to_u32(digits)\n        fail port_zero when port == 0\n    end port_from\n\n    listen_port: (setting: utf8) -> (port: u32) =\n        port = port_from(setting) else 8080\n    end listen_port\n\n    port_or_complaint: (setting: utf8) -> (port: u32, complaint: utf8) =\n        complaint = ""\n        port = port_from(setting) else (problem)\n            match problem\n                port_zero: complaint = "port 0 is reserved"\n                _: complaint = "not a port number"\n            end match\n            8080\n        end\n    end port_or_complaint\n\n- `try` passes a failure on: if `text.to_u32` fails, `port_from` fails with the same atom, which is why its `!` lists them ([0960]).\n- `listen_port` cannot fail. Whatever went wrong, 8080 stands in for the result.\n- `port_or_complaint` binds the atom to `problem`, looks at it, and ends the block with the value that stands in ([1030]).\n\nA call to something that can fail takes one of four forms:\n\n| you write | when the call fails |\n|---|---|\n| `try f()` | your function fails with the same atom |\n| `f() else value` | `value` stands in for the result |\n| `f() else (e) ... end` | the block runs with the atom bound to `e` |\n| `f() else none` | nothing; the next statement runs |\n\nThe next entries use a shorter declaration. Its atoms, `not_found` and `no_access`, are the ones declared at [0630]:\n\n    open_file: (path: utf8) -> (handle: u32) ! not_found | no_access =\n        fail no_access when lenof path == 0\n        handle = 1\n    end open_file\n\nThree facts about error sets and their atoms:\n\n- An error set is a set. Aliases flatten, order does not matter, and a function that fails with `a` passes where `a | b` is expected.\n- The atoms carry no payload.\n- The atoms travel in a register of their own, so failing costs about what returning does.\n\nExact rules: spec [1980].
C	950	What deserves an error, and what does not	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0950	A failure ends the operation without a result, and the caller handles it. A diagnostic is reported while the work goes on. Choose by what the caller needs: no result at all, or a result with notes about what was wrong. Where you can see a problem in what you already hold, prefer checking for it and working around it to failing.\n\n`sum_digits` notes a problem instead of failing on it. It adds the digits in a line and counts what it had to skip, so every line still gets a sum:\n\n    --- Adds up the digits in a line and counts what is not a digit.\n    sum_digits: (line: []u8) -> (sum: u32, skipped: u32) =\n        sum = 0\n        skipped = 0\n        for b in line do\n            if b >= u8('0') and b <= u8('9') then\n                sum += u32(b - u8('0'))\n            else\n                inc skipped -- noted, and the work goes on\n            end if\n        end for\n    end sum_digits\n\n- A parser is the usual case: a syntax mistake is entirely in the bytes it is reading, so it records a diagnostic and carries on. One that stops at the first mistake hides the other twelve.\n- Input with no usable answer may well be a failure: [0940]'s `port_from` fails on text that is not a port, because its caller has no port to use.\n- Out of memory, a missing file, an unplugged device: these depend on the world, not on your data, and checking first would only be a race. They are failures.\n\nCollecting diagnostics needs somewhere to put them, and that is an ordinary parameter. The library's destination for diagnostics is the concept `core/diag.log`. A function takes it as `inout log: any diag.log`, meaning any kind of log at all ([1370]). Its `note` entry takes a position in the text, a severity and the message bytes.\n\nRecording a note is a diagnostic; failing to record it is an operation failure. So `note` declares `io.io_failed`, and a function that records notes lists it too.\n\n- A bounded logger never fails. When it is full it stops keeping entries, counts them in `dropped`, and still records whether an error was reported.\n- A streaming logger writes as it goes, and fails with `io_failed` when a write does.\n- Both pass as `any diag.log`, so the producer does not know which policy its caller chose. The sink is a capability ([1680]): passing one makes the destination explicit, though the parameter list alone does not prove that the function cannot make another sink or reach the host.
C	960	Passing a failure on: `try`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0960	`try f()` calls `f`. If `f` fails, your function runs its cleanups ([1100]) and then fails with the same atom. Every atom you might pass on must be in your own `!` set.\n\n    read_config: (path: utf8) -> (data: []u8) ! ... =\n        h := try open_file(path)\n        data = []\n    end read_config\n\nThe `try` sits at the call, so you can see in the source every place a function may leave early.\n\n`! ...` means "whatever my callees can fail with": the compiler works the set out from every `fail` and `try` in the body. An inferred set that comes out empty means the function cannot fail.\n\nUse `! ...` inside a module, where the compiler sees every caller anyway. These must write their set out:\n\n- Anything public, because a public signature is a promise, and a change three modules down must not rewrite it silently.\n- Function types, anonymous functions, concept entries ([1260]) and anything exported to C, because their complete signature is their type.\n\n`try for item in source do ... end for` passes on a failure from any traversal step ([1150]). The enclosing function must declare or infer the atoms, and its caller handles them with the ordinary `else` on that call.\n\nExact rules: spec [1980].
C	970	Leaving early: `return` and `fail`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0970	`return` leaves the function with its named results as they stand, and `fail` leaves with an error. Each takes an optional `when condition`.\n\n    clamp_low: (x: i32, floor: i32) -> (r: i32) =\n        r = floor\n        return when x < floor\n        r = x\n    end clamp_low\n\nOnly exits take `when`: `return`, `fail`, `break` and `continue`.
C	980	Calling: positional, then named	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0980	A call gives its positional arguments first and its named arguments after them. Every parameter gets exactly one argument: there are no default values.\n\n    volume_of: (width: u32, height: u32, depth: u32) -> (v: u32) =\n        v = width * height * depth\n    end volume_of\n\n    volumes: () -> (total: u32) =\n        a := volume_of(2, 3, 4)\n        b := volume_of(2, depth: 4, height: 3)\n        c := volume_of(width: 2, height: 3, depth: 4)\n        total = a + b + c\n    end volumes\n\nThe positional arguments fill parameters in order. The named ones may come in any order after them. An unknown or repeated name is an error.\n\nArguments are evaluated in the order you wrote them. Named arguments work in a call statement as well as in a call expression.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- A call through a stored function uses the parameter names of that value's type. Those names are not part of function-type identity ([1000]).\n- A generic call may name its compile-time arguments in the same list: `copy(t: u8, n: 4, source: bytes)`. Name one and you name them all ([1290]).\n- A C variadic call adds an unnamed tail ([1580]). It does not add optional parameters.
C	990	Using a multiple result	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#0990	The results of a call form an anonymous struct ([0920]). Bind it whole and read its fields, or take it apart by name. You never take it apart by position.\n\n    whole := divide(10, 3)\n    sum := whole.quot + whole.rem\n    (quot, rem) := divide(10, 3)\n    (quot: q2) := divide(20, 3)\n    (quot, _) := divide(30, 3)\n\nThe call runs once. When you take the result apart, you can pick names in any order, leave some out, or rename one after `:`. `_` says that you ignore the rest on purpose.\n\nA whole result can also be the value of an `if`, `match` or block when every branch gives the same names and types.\n\nThe names belong to the call, not to the function's type. Two function types with the same result types in the same order agree, whatever the results are called ([1000]).
C	1000	Functions are values	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1000	A function type is an ordinary type, written the way a signature is. A function is a value of that type: a code address. There is no separate function-pointer type, and you never write `addr` on a function.\n\n    default_handler: () -> none = end default_handler\n    handler: type = () -> none\n    mut current: handler = default_handler\n\nTwo function types agree by their parameter and result types, in order:\n\n- The names inside them only describe the positions.\n- The comparison is recursive when a parameter or result is itself a function.\n- Calling convention and variadicness count too. A C callback type is written `extern(c) (parameters) -> returns`, and a Landin function never matches it.\n\nA module binding set to a named or anonymous function is a fixed code address. A mutable binding may later take any function with the same complete signature. A `ptr` to a function type points at a cell that holds the address, not at the code.\n\nA function captures nothing ([1010]), so a callback is a function and an explicit state pointer:\n\n    on_byte: type = struct\n        call: (state: ptr u8, b: u8) -> none\n        state: ptr u8\n    end on_byte\n\nCall it through the field: `callback.call(callback.state, byte)`. The field keeps its full signature through every copy, assignment, variant payload and array. Whether the field may be replaced depends on the binding that holds the struct. The callee is evaluated before the arguments.
C	1010	Anonymous functions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1010	An anonymous function is a signature and body without a name. It captures nothing: inside, it sees module declarations and its own parameters, results and locals, but none of the enclosing function's.\n\n    less_i32 := (a: i32, b: i32) -> (yes: bool) = a < b end\n\nWriting an anonymous function makes a fixed code address; it does not run the body. State travels as an explicit parameter, as in the callback at [1000].\n\nA bound anonymous function is a value. `less_i32(1, 2)` calls it, and you can pass it wherever its function type is expected. It cannot supply a concept's entry ([1240]).
C	1020	Throwing a result away	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1020	You cannot ignore a result silently. To throw one away, say so with `_ =`.\n\n    _ = double(5)\n\nA function that returns `none` gives the caller nothing to discard. Write its call on its own: `_ =` in front of it is an error (spec [1930]).
C	1030	Handling a failure: `else`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1030	An `else` after a call handles its failure on the spot. The handler either supplies a value in place of the result, or leaves. Leaving is `return`, `fail`, `break` or `continue`, written in a block, as `else begin return end`.\n\n    h1 := open_file(path) else 0\n    h2 := open_file(path) else (e) fail e end\n    h3 := open_file(path) else (e)\n        match e\n            not_found: 0\n            _: fail e\n        end match\n    end\n\n`try f()` is short for the second line's form. A handler that leaves needs no value, the same rule an arm of an `if` follows ([1080]), so nobody invents a placeholder to satisfy the type. The handler supplies the value; it does not assign the binding being initialized.\n\n- `else (e)` binds the atom. `e` has the call's whole error set and exists only inside the block. A `match` on it must cover every atom, or end with one `_` arm for the rest ([1210]).\n- A name the block never reads draws a warning. To run statements without naming the atom at all, give `else` a bare block as its value: `else begin ... end`. The compiler refuses `else (_)`; leave the parentheses out instead.\n- A call that returns nothing has no value to supply. Its block only handles the error, and the statement after the call runs next.\n- The result may have any shape, from a scalar to a struct or several named results.\n\nA failing call needs `try` or `else` even when you throw its result away. `else` handles only declared failure: a result that is a union, such as [0480]'s maybe-pointer, is taken apart with `match`.\n\nInside an `if` arm, `else value` after a call is the `if`'s own `else`, which is how `if c then a() else b() end if` reads. To handle the call's failure there, parenthesize it, `(open_file(path) else 0)`, or bind the error: `else (e)` always belongs to the call, wherever it is written.\n\nA handled call is an expression, so it also works inside a larger one, as an operand or an argument:\n\n    next_handle := (open_file(path) else 0) + 1\n\nWhen a call returns nothing and its failure does not matter where the call is made, one word says so. Here `flush` writes out a buffer and returns nothing:\n\n    flush(out) else none\n\n`else none` is the bound block with nothing in it, minus the name nobody would read: what the call did before it failed stays done, and the next statement runs.\n\nOn a call that returns a value, `else none` is allowed only when the whole call is discarded with `_ =`. Anywhere else, a failure would leave a result unset that something reads. Here `parse_header` returns a value:\n\n    _ = parse_header(input) else none\n\nUsed any other way, that call needs `else value`, a block, or `try`.
C	1040	Passing the call site: `caller`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1040	The compiler fills in a `caller` parameter with where the call was written, so assertions and logging need no macros. The parameter's type is a struct you declare, with exactly these three `u32` fields, in this order:\n\n    site: type = struct\n        file_id: u32\n        line: u32\n        column: u32\n    end site\n\n    report_failure: (where: site) -> none = end report_failure\n\n    assert: (cond: bool, caller where: site) -> none =\n        if not cond then\n            report_failure(where)\n        end if\n    end assert\n\nA call looks like this: `assert(count > 0)`. The caller leaves the parameter out.\n\nInside the function, the parameter is an ordinary immutable struct that you can read, copy and store. It is 12 bytes on every target. Line and column count from one.\n\nThe file number is only a number. The table that maps it to a filename is written beside the program and need not ship with it, which keeps names out of firmware ([1670]).\n\nA wrapper that wants to report its own caller's position passes its `caller` parameter on by name:\n\n    checked: (cond: bool, caller where: site) -> none =\n        assert(cond, where: where)\n    end checked\n\nLeave out `where:` there and the report points at the wrapper's own call instead. Only a `caller` parameter can fill a `caller` position: a copied or constructed `site` cannot.\n\nA check that stops the program gives its `caller` parameter to `compiler.unreachable` ([1560]). The stop is then reported at the call, through any wrappers that passed the parameter on, and not at the check:\n\n    require: (cond: bool, caller where: site) -> none =\n        if not cond then compiler.unreachable(where) end if\n    end require\n\nThis `site` is not the `site` that a panic handler receives at [1670]. That one is a single `u32` number, which the compiler gives a failing check.\n\nExact rules: spec [1920].
C	1050	Branching with `if`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1050	`if` takes a condition, and `then` begins the body. `elsif` and `else` are optional, and `end if` closes the whole thing.\n\n        if x > 0 then\n            out = 1\n        elsif x < 0 then\n            out = -1\n        else\n            out = 0\n        end if\n\nThe condition has type `bool`. No integer or pointer stands in for a `bool`.
C	1060	Every construct fits on one line	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1060	No construct needs a newline. `end` is what closes a construct, so you can write any of them on one line.\n\n        if x > 0 then out = 1 end if\n\n`refine fmt` leaves a one-line form on one line. It never joins lines and never breaks them.
C	1070	Declaring a name in a condition	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1070	An `if`, `elsif` or `while` condition may declare a binding, inferred or with a written type. The binding's value is the condition, so it must be a `bool`; anything else is an ordinary type error.\n\n        if ok := is_ready() then\n            out = 1\n        end if\n\n        while mut more: bool = has_more() do\n            consume_next()\n            more = false\n        end while\n\n- The name exists only in the body that its condition guards. It does not exist in a later `elsif`, in the `else`, in a loop's `complete`, or after the construct.\n- The initializer runs before the name exists, so it cannot refer to the name it initializes.\n- A `while` runs the initializer again before every iteration.\n\nExact rules: spec [1840].
C	1080	Blocks have values	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1080	`if`, `match`, bare blocks and loops are expressions as well as statements. The value is the last expression of the block that ran.\n\n        sign := if x > 0 then 1 else -1 end if\n\n        doubled := begin\n            a := expensive()\n            a * 2\n        end\n\nRust needs a semicolon to tell a block's value from a statement. Landin does not: you always write `_ =` to throw a value away ([1020]), so a bare expression at the end of a block can only be its value.\n\nThe details, arm by arm:\n\n- Every arm that falls through must end with a value of one complete type and shape. An `if` used as a value therefore needs its `else`.\n- An arm that leaves by `return`, `fail`, `break` or `continue` supplies no value and needs no placeholder.\n- When the compiler decides whether a name is assigned after the construct, only the arms that fall through count. An arm that has left proves nothing for the others.\n- Statements and the final expression run in source order. They run after the `if` condition or the `match` subject, and only in the selected arm.\n- In a construct used as a statement, an arm may not end with a value: nothing would take it.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	1090	Bare blocks: `begin ... end`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1090	`begin ... end` opens a scope: names declared inside are gone after its `end`.\n\n        begin\n            tmp := x * 2\n            out = out + tmp\n        end\n\nGive the block a label, `name: begin ... end name`, and a `break name` can leave it early. Its cleanups then run as a loop's do ([1180]).
C	1100	Cleanup on the way out: `defer`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1100	`defer call` runs the call when its block is left: by falling off the end, `return`, `break`, `continue` or a failure. Entries run in reverse order, inner blocks before outer ones.\n\n        defer cleanup()\n\nThere are no destructors, so this is how anything gets closed, flushed or freed.\n\nThe call's arguments are read when it runs, not when the `defer` is written. Here `walk_steps` leaves `trail` at 2, not 1:\n\n    record_step: (inout trail: i32, step: i32) -> none =\n        trail = step\n    end record_step\n\n    walk_steps: (inout trail: i32) -> none =\n        mut step: i32 = 1\n        defer record_step(trail, step)\n        step = 2\n    end walk_steps\n\n- At exit, the callee is evaluated first, including a function field, then the arguments, reading the places they name at that moment. So a `defer` that sinks something sinks it at the end, and the thing stays usable in between. If a place was re-pointed meanwhile, the `defer` sees what is there now.\n- Registering an entry evaluates nothing, costs nothing and reserves nothing.\n- An entry counts only once control has reached it. A `return` above the `defer` does not run it.\n- The block's value, or its failure atom, is settled before the deferred calls run.\n- A trap stops the program and runs no cleanup.
C	1110	Cleanup only on failure: `undo`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1110	`undo call` is a `defer` that runs only when a declared failure leaves its block: a `fail`, a `try` that passes a failure on, or a failure arriving from a deeper call.\n\n        undo release(handle)\n\nIt is its own word, not a flavour of `defer`: to defer is to do it later, and this may never be done at all. It is a compensating action.\n\n- Falling off the end, a successful `return` and `break` skip it. So does a trap: it stops the program and unwinds nothing.\n- A caller's `else` that handles the failure does not leave the caller's block, so the caller's `undo` entries do not run. The failing callee's own entries have already run on the way out.\n- In one block, `defer` and `undo` entries share one order: on failure they run interleaved, in reverse order of writing, inner blocks first.\n- Like `defer`, an `undo` evaluates its callee and arguments only when it runs, and sees their values then.
C	1120	Switching checks off for a region: `unchecked`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1120	An `unchecked` region drops the run-time checks the compiler would emit inside it, and says so where you read it.\n\n        unchecked begin\n            out = out + items[0]\n        end unchecked\n\nThe region is an ordinary block: it has its own scope, `defer` still runs on the way out, and nesting one inside another changes nothing.\n\nThese checks go:\n\n- integer overflow;\n- an element index or a slice range;\n- the destination range of an integer conversion.\n\nTwo things stay:\n\n- Everything the compiler decides at compile time: types, definite assignment, permissions, origins.\n- The checks whose absence would not mean the same thing on every machine: a zero divisor, a negative shift count, a conversion to `bool` or from a float, a text boundary, and converting an integer that is zero at the target's width into a pointer.\n\nA region reaches only the code written inside it. A function called from it is checked as that function is written. A deferred call is checked where you wrote it, not where the exit that runs it stands.
C	1130	Repeating: `loop`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1130	`loop do ... end loop` repeats until something leaves it: `break`, `return` or `fail`. A labelled loop closes with its label.\n\n        counter: loop do\n            break when x == 0\n        end counter
C	1140	Repeating while a condition holds: `while`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1140	`while` tests its condition before every iteration. `continue` goes straight to the next test.\n\n        mut i: u32 = 0\n        while i < 10 do\n            inc i\n            continue when i == 3\n        end while
C	1150	Walking a range or a collection: `for`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1150	`for` binds each item of its source in turn. An optional second name is a `usize` index counting from zero.\n\n        for item in items do\n            out += item\n        end for\n\n        for item, idx in items do\n            item = item + i32(idx) -- items is writable, so this writes\n        end for\n\n        for k in 0..<10 do\n            out += k\n        end for\n\n| source | each item is |\n|---|---|\n| `a..<b`, `a..b` | an integer, ascending; `..<` leaves out `b`, `..` includes it |\n| a slice or fixed array | the element, in place ([1160]) |\n| `utf8`, `utf16`, `cstring` | a Unicode scalar, as a `u32` |\n| a struct or `any C` | what its conformance to `iterable` hands out ([1320]) |\n\n- A range's bounds are evaluated once, left to right. A lower bound above the upper one runs no iteration.\n- A typed bound gives its type to an untyped one, and two untyped bounds are `i32`. So `0..<lenof items` counts in `usize` with no conversion.\n- An element may itself be a fixed array, a slice or an `any C`; the binding keeps its complete type.\n- A struct or `any C` source is evaluated once, and walked through its `first`, `at_end`, `item` and `next` ([1320]). The index advances with `next`.\n- Text yields decoded scalars, not encoded slices. A `cstring` ends at its first NUL, which is not an item. Text from C is validated as [0600] says.\n\n`try for` walks a source whose steps can fail ([1320]'s `fallible_iterable`, or a plain `iterable`). A failure leaves the loop through the function's error set ([0960]). It runs `defer` and `undo` on the way and skips `complete`. `break` and `continue` work as usual.
C	1160	Writing through a loop binding	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1160	A loop binding carries no marker, because the source's type already decides. Over a `[]mut t` the element is a writable place, and over a `[]t` it is not.\n\n    double_all: (xs: []mut i32) -> none =\n        for x in xs do\n            x = x * 2\n        end for\n    end double_all\n\nOver anything else that satisfies `iterable`, the binding is a copy, since `item` ([1320]) hands out a value. Assigning to it is an error rather than a silent write to nothing. Text likewise yields a copied `u32` that cannot be written.\n\n- The cursor and item keep their exact declared types. An `any C` item is still an `any C`: it carries its evidence ([1690]), which is its type's table of C's entries. An `any C` source is handed as it is to its `iterable` entries. Neither is treated as a slice.\n- When the element is a fixed array, slice or `any C`, replacing the whole element follows the same rule. Writing through an inner slice follows that slice's own `mut`.
C	1170	When a loop runs out: `complete`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1170	A `complete` block runs when the loop ends because its source or condition ran out. It does not run when a `break` left the loop.\n\n        for item in items do\n            break when item == 42\n        complete\n            out = -1\n        end for\n\n`loop do` has no natural end, so it takes no `complete`.
C	1180	Labels	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1180	A loop or a bare block may carry a label, written like any other name. `break` and `continue` may name one. An unlabelled `break` or `continue` means the innermost loop.\n\n        outer: for a in items do\n            for b in items do\n                break outer when a == b\n            end for\n        end outer\n\nA `break` naming a bare block leaves it, and whatever loops it crosses, running their cleanups on the way out.\n\n        search: begin\n            for item in items do\n                break search when item == 0\n            end for\n            out = 1 -- no item was zero\n        end search\n\nA bare block has no next iteration and yields no value. So `continue` can target only a loop, and only a loop can produce a value through `break with`.
C	1190	A loop with a value: `break with`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1190	`break with value` leaves the loop and makes the value the loop's result. A search becomes an expression instead of a mutable variable and a flag.\n\n        found := for item in items do\n            break with item when item > 40\n        complete\n            break with 0\n        end for\n        out += found\n\n`with` is required because a bare name after `break` could be either a label or a value.\n\n- Every `break` of a loop used as a value carries `with`, and all of them yield the same type.\n- A loop that can run out needs a `complete` that supplies the value. `loop do` needs none, having no other way out.\n- A loop whose value is unwanted is discarded explicitly ([1020]): `_ = loop do break with 1 end loop`. A statement loop uses plain `break` and cannot silently drop a `with` value.
C	1200	Cleaning up several acquisitions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1200	An entry exists only once control reaches it. A run of fallible acquisitions therefore cleans up exactly what it got: if the first fails, nothing is released; if the second fails, one is; if the third fails, two are.\n\n    close_file: (handle: u32) -> none =\n        -- hand the handle back to the system\n    end close_file\n\n    open_three: (a: utf8, b: utf8, c: utf8)\n                -> (first: u32, second: u32, third: u32) ! not_found | no_access =\n        first = try open_file(a)\n        undo close_file(first)\n        second = try open_file(b)\n        undo close_file(second)\n        third = try open_file(c)\n    end open_three\n\nThe same shape holds for memory. This version is generic over the allocator, which [1290] and [1360] explain:\n\n    new_buffers: (provider: type is mem.allocator,\n                  memory: provider, count: usize)\n                 -> (first: mem.byte_buffer, second: mem.byte_buffer,\n                     third: mem.byte_buffer) ! mem.out_of_memory =\n        first = try mem.new_bytes(memory: memory, count: count)\n        undo mem.delete_bytes(memory, first)\n\n        second = try mem.new_bytes(memory: memory, count: count)\n        undo mem.delete_bytes(memory, second)\n\n        third = try mem.new_bytes(memory: memory, count: count)\n        -- All three owners are published by the successful return.\n    end new_buffers\n\n`undo` cleans up what is still yours. Once you hand a resource on, its cleanup is somebody else's, but your entry is still registered, and there is deliberately no way to call one off. So acquire everything fallible first, commit afterwards, and let nothing fallible stand between the commit and the end of the block.\n\nThe usual alternative is a flag and a conditional `defer`. Forget to set the flag and you free storage that is still in use. Under an arena, where freeing does nothing, that mistake stays silent until the same code runs on a real allocator.
C	1210	Pattern matching: `match`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1210	`match` picks the arm whose case or atom the subject holds. There is no fallthrough, and a missing case is a compile error. This uses `figure` from [0680]:\n\n    area: (f: figure) -> (a: f32) =\n        a = 0.0\n        match f.kind\n            circle(radius):\n                a = 3.14159 * radius * radius\n            rectangle(width, height):\n                a = width * height\n        end match\n    end area\n\nAn arm runs one statement or one expression. For several, make the arm a bare block:\n\n    area_and_corners: (f: figure) -> (a: f32, corners: u32) =\n        corners = 0\n        match f.kind\n            circle(radius): a = 3.14159 * radius * radius\n            rectangle(width, height): begin\n                a = width * height\n                corners = 4\n            end\n        end match\n    end area_and_corners\n\n- The subject is an atom set ([0640]), a variant part ([0680]) or a pointer union ([0480]). An arm names an identity, and a case arm may bind the payload, as `circle(radius)` does.\n- Several labels share one arm, `north, south:`, and each counts toward covering every case. An arm that binds a payload names one case.\n- `_` is an arm of its own and covers whatever is left of an atom set or a pointer union. On an atom set, `_ (rest):` binds the remaining atoms as a set of their own, so they can be passed on where only those are wanted.\n- A variant part takes no `_`: its match names every case, and the cases that share what an arm runs are listed on that arm.\n- A number has no identity to name, so you compare it with `if` and `elsif` instead of matching it.
C	1220	Writing into a matched payload	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1220	A pattern binding takes a parameter convention ([0900]). It is `in` by default; `inout` writes into the payload that was matched.\n\n    store: type = struct\n        kind: variant\n            inline: (buf: [4]i32) |\n            spilled: (heap: []mut i32)\n        end kind\n    end store\n\n    spill: (inout s: store, v: i32) -> none =\n        match s.kind\n            inline(inout buf): buf[0] = v\n            spilled(heap): heap[0] = v\n        end match\n    end spill\n\n`spilled(heap)` needs no `inout`: it writes through the slice, whose own `mut` allows it, and never replaces the slice.\n\nA plain binding reads the payload in place, without copying it; `inout` adds permission to write it, where the matched value may itself be written: `s` above is an `inout` parameter. On a pointer union's `ptr` arm, `ptr (sink p):` passes the pointer on to a `sink` parameter ([0910]), which consumes the matched place.\n\n`describe` matches the `compass` of [0640], two directions in one arm:\n\n    describe: (c: compass) -> (name: utf8) =\n        match c\n            north, south: name = "along"\n            _: name = "across"\n        end match\n    end describe\n\nThe rules for the bindings:\n\n- Both plain and `inout` bindings alias the matched storage, scalars included. So an arm may replace the variant, or an object containing it, only after the aliases' last use ([0830]). Writing through an `inout` alias is a use, as is reading an address derived from it or evaluating a pending cleanup argument.\n- A scalar copied out of a binding keeps no borrow of the payload.\n- Matching a computed value matches a temporary copy, so replacing the original does not change what the arm sees.\n- Assigning a new case selects its tag before evaluating the new payload, so the payload's initializer cannot use an alias of the old one. When constructing a whole containing value, save the scalars you need first.\n\nExact rules: spec [1910].
C	1230	Declaring a concept	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1230	A concept names a bundle of operations, each a complete function signature written in terms of the concept's type parameter.\n\n    ordered: type = concept (t: type)\n        less: (a: t, b: t) -> (yes: bool)\n    end ordered\n\nA concept is an ordinary type declaration, so it lives in a module like any other name. It has no default bodies: each conformance supplies every entry.
C	1240	Making a type conform	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1240	A conformance registers one type against one concept, naming the function that supplies each entry.\n\n    less_than_i32: (a: i32, b: i32) -> (yes: bool) = a < b end less_than_i32\n\n    i32 is ordered (less: less_than_i32)\n\nEach label is an entry of the concept. Each supplying function must have exactly the entry's signature with `t` replaced by `i32`, and it must be a declared function: [1010]'s `less_i32`, a binding that holds an anonymous function, cannot supply an entry.\n\nThere is no implicit conformance. A type with a matching `less` is still not `ordered` until a line like this one says so.
C	1250	A conformance for a generic type	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1250	A conformance for a generic type declares its type variables in front, because it holds for every one of them.\n\nThe examples use two concepts met later: `iterable`, which `for` loops use ([1320]), and `mem.allocator` ([1360]). `counted(provider)` is an allocator that wraps another, and the `pair_...` and `counted_...` names are the functions that supply each entry.\n\n    (t: type) pair(t) is iterable (cur: u8, item_type: t,\n                                   first: pair_first, at_end: pair_at_end,\n                                   item: pair_item, next: pair_next)\n\n    (provider: type is mem.allocator) counted(provider) is mem.allocator\n        (alloc: counted_alloc, grow: counted_grow, resize: counted_resize,\n         free: counted_free)\n\nThe binder is an ordinary parameter list, the same form functions and generic types take. So a variable may carry a constraint, and a `fixed` parameter may appear among them.\n\nThe supplying functions are generic themselves. Instantiating the conformance gives them their type argument and leaves functions of exactly the concept's shape.\n\nThe target must be the whole generic type applied to the binder in order, each variable used once: one conformance covers the whole family `pair(t)`. Another family for the same template and concept is a collision ([1280]), and so is a concrete exception such as `pair(u8) is iterable`.\n\nWithout this form no generic container could be traversed, sorted or handed to other generic code.
C	1260	A concept fixes its error sets	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1260	A concept entry's error set is written out or absent, never inferred with `! ...`. An entry is reached through a table, and [0960] forbids an inferred set there. So the concept fixes the error set once, for every type that will ever satisfy it.\n\nThat is right for allocation, where out of memory is out of memory, but it shapes how you design a concept.\n\nThe same goes for what an implementation is handed: by convention, a concept with no allocator among its parameters says its implementations do not allocate. The compiler does not check that, since any hosted function can make a heap of its own ([1680]).\n\nResist widening a concept until it fits its hungriest implementation; that hands every implementation the sum of everyone's needs. Either the hungry one picks a shape that does not need it, or there are two concepts.
C	1270	One type, several conformances	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1270	A conformance is keyed by the type, the concept and the concept's other input types, so one type may satisfy the same concept more than once.\n\nThe example assumes `position` is a byte-offset type, and `utf8_nth` and `utf8_at_pos` look up a character by count and by position.\n\n    indexable: type = concept (t: type, idx: type, item_type: type)\n        get: (s: t, i: idx) -> (item: item_type)\n    end indexable\n\n    utf8 is indexable (idx: usize, item_type: u32, get: utf8_nth)\n    utf8 is indexable (idx: position, item_type: u32, get: utf8_at_pos)\n\nThe labels for the extra inputs, `idx` and `item_type`, are part of the key; the function labels are not.\n\nWhich concepts exist, and how finely they distinguish what an operation costs, is the standard library's business. The language checks nothing about cost: a guarantee should not depend on how clever the compiler happens to be.
C	1280	Where conformances live, and what collides	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1280	A conformance may be declared in any module, and two for the same key are an error. There is no precedence, no orphan rule and no override: the compiler reports the collision and somebody sorts it out.\n\nWhen two libraries collide, you do not have to change either. Wrap the type in a `distinct` type of your own and conform that, or pass the functions explicitly instead of through a concept.\n\nThe compiler collects every conformance in every module the program reaches before it checks any generic call, whether or not anything uses the conformance. Modules the program does not reach contribute nothing.\n\nA conformance is a registration, not a name, so it needs no `public` and refuses one.
C	1290	Writing a generic function	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1290	A generic function takes the type as an ordinary parameter, constrained with `is`, and calls the concept's entries through that parameter.\n\n    sort: (t: type is ordered, data: []mut t) -> none =\n        for k in 1..<lenof data do\n            mut j := k\n            while j > 0 and t.less(data[j], data[j - 1]) do\n                tmp := data[j]\n                data[j] = data[j - 1]\n                data[j - 1] = tmp\n                dec j\n            end while\n        end for\n    end sort\n\n`t.less` is the `less` of whatever type `t` turns out to be. Because entries are reached through the type parameter, two constrained parameters never collide: `left_type.less` and `right_type.less` are different functions.\n\nType and `fixed` parameters exist only at compile time; they add no runtime argument. A `fixed` parameter is an integer known at compile time, and inside the body it may also be used as an ordinary value. The order of parameters does not matter, so `fill: (inout data: [capacity]u8, fixed capacity: u32)` is as good as putting `capacity` first.\n\nA type parameter may also be unconstrained, for code that only moves values around.\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- Every type parameter is written in the list. A name that is not in scope is a misspelling and an error, never a new type variable, just as a misspelt build option is an error ([1530]).\n- A generic function is not a function value. Only a call picks a concrete instance, so you cannot take `sort` itself and store it.\n- A private `! ...` error set is inferred separately for each concrete instance.\n- The compiler checks the body for each instance a call makes. A generic function nothing calls is checked only for its names and for operands no type could make valid. An error that depends on what `t` turns out to be, such as a view held across a call that may move its source, is reported once a call picks `t`.\n- In the body, `t(value)` converts one value to whatever type `t` turns out to be, by that type's own conversion ([0310]): `t(0)` starts a sum in any numeric type. An instance whose type has no conversion from the value is an error once a call picks it. A type parameter converts and does not construct: `t(a: 1)` is an error.
C	1300	Calling a generic function	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1300	The compiler normally deduces the type from the arguments. You may also name it, in the same named-argument list as the runtime arguments.\n\n    sort_demo: (values: []mut i32) -> none =\n        sort(values)\n        sort(t: i32, data: values)\n    end sort_demo\n\nIt is all or nothing: either every type and `fixed` parameter is deduced, or the call names every one of them. Runtime arguments keep [0980]'s rule, positional first and then named.\n\nDeduction matches each written parameter type against the argument's type, exactly. It never uses the return type, a conversion or a search of the conformances, and it runs no code. Two consequences:\n\n- A writable `[]mut i32` argument still passes where `[]t` is written ([0440]), but deeper inside a type, permission must match exactly.\n- A fixed bound written `capacity * 2` is never solved for `capacity`; it is only checked once another argument has fixed `capacity`.\n\nExact rules: spec [1920].
C	1310	How generic code runs: tables, and specialization as an option	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1310	A call to a generic function passes, invisibly, a table for each conformance the body uses. The table holds the type's size and alignment, then the concept's functions in the order the concept declares them. `t.less(...)` loads `less` from that table and calls it. The same tables carry `any C` values ([1370]), so static generics and runtime dispatch are one mechanism ([1690]).\n\nThe tables are the meaning of generic code. Specialization replaces an indirect call with a direct one where the compiler can prove which table arrives. It is an optimization that never changes what a program does.\n\nTwo independent switches control code generation:\n\n| option | values | default |\n|---|---|---|\n| `--optimize` | `none`, `size`, `speed` | `size` |\n| `--specialize` | `off`, `auto`, `all` | `auto` |\n\nNeither depends on `--build-mode`.\n\nA call is never specialized merely because its source type is known: the compiler needs proof of the table that actually arrives. A call stays indirect when it goes through `any`, through a table the compiler cannot trace, or in an instance whose address is taken. `--build-report=PATH` writes a report of what was specialized and what stayed indirect, and why.
C	1320	Traversal is a concept	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1320	`for x in s` over your own type uses the `iterable` concept. Conform to it and your type works in a `for` loop.\n\n    iterable: type = concept (t: type, cur: type, item_type: type)\n        first: (s: ptr t) -> (c: cur)\n        at_end: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (yes: bool)\n        item: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (v: item_type)\n        next: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (c2: cur)\n    end iterable\n\nThe conformance supplies the cursor type `cur` and the `item_type`, as [1250]'s `pair` does. The labels may come in any order.\n\nThe loop evaluates `s` once and keeps a private copy. Each provider gets a read-only pointer to that copy, so a large struct is copied once, not on every call.\n\nThe four signatures are exact: no permission, error set or `from` clause is inferred or converted. So a provider whose result is declared `from s` does not match.\n\n`item` returns a fresh value for the loop binding, never an alias into the source. A container that wants to hand out references into its storage returns a slice view instead and uses the built-in slice traversal, as `for value in vec.used(numbers)` does.\n\nA source that can fail while streaming conforms to `fallible_iterable`, which adds an error set as a fourth input:\n\n    fallible_iterable: type = concept\n        (t: type, cur: type, item_type: type, errors: type)\n        first: (s: ptr t) -> (c: cur) ! errors\n        at_end: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (yes: bool) ! errors\n        item: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (v: item_type) ! errors\n        next: (s: ptr t, c: cur) -> (c2: cur) ! errors\n    end fallible_iterable\n\n`errors` is an atom set, and all four entries declare exactly that set; a provider may declare an error it never raises. Such a source is walked with `try for` ([0960]). `try for` needs one unambiguous conformance and prefers `fallible_iterable` when both exist; plain `for` only ever uses `iterable`.
C	1330	Integer ranges are not values	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1330	In `for i in 0..<10 do`, the loop evaluates the two bounds once and counts between them directly ([1150]). `0..<10` and `0..9` are loop and slice syntax ([0360]), not expressions, and the header does not go through `iterable`.\n\nFor other stepping, write a struct with its own `iterable` conformance. A library could then offer `for i in step(0, 10, 2) do ... end for`; `core` has no such `step` or `step_range` today.
C	1340	Combining concepts	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1340	A concept may build on others by naming them after `is`. A type that satisfies the combined concept still conforms to each part separately.\n\nThe example assumes a struct `button` with a `text` field, a type `canvas`, and functions `button_draw`, `button_click` and `button_focus` with the entries' signatures.\n\n    drawable: type = concept (t: type)\n        draw: (self: ptr t, target: ptr mut canvas) -> none\n    end drawable\n\n    clickable: type = concept (t: type)\n        click: (self: ptr mut t, x: u32, y: u32) -> none\n    end clickable\n\n    widget: type = concept (t: type) is drawable, clickable\n        focus: (self: ptr mut t) -> none\n    end widget\n\n    button is drawable (draw: button_draw)\n    button is clickable (click: button_click)\n    button is widget (focus: button_focus)\n\nAll three conformances are needed, because `widget`'s supplies only what `widget` adds. Having the parts does not make a type a `widget`, and being a `widget` does not make it `drawable`. Conformance is always declared, even when its list is empty.\n\nThe combined concept has a name of its own, so an `any widget` value still carries one table and stays two words.\n\nIn generic code, `t.entry` must name exactly one declaration across the concept and all its parents:\n\n- A parent reached twice, through two paths, is still one concept.\n- Two different concepts that both declare `entry` make `t.entry` ambiguous.\n- Parent order never decides, and a child's own entry does not override an inherited one.\n- A clash nobody uses is not an error.\n\nExact rules: spec [1920].
C	1350	Generic types	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1350	A type takes parameters through its own declaration form. It is not a function that returns a type: that would be compile-time execution, which Landin does not have. Substitution, not execution.\n\n    pair: type (t: type) = struct\n        first: t\n        second: t\n    end pair\n\n`pair(i32)` and `pair(u8)` are different types, and every use of `pair(i32)` is the same type. A growable container is generic the same way: `core/vec`'s `list(t)` is one, and [0510] explains how it keeps its empty slots out of sight.\n\nA type parameter may carry one concept constraint, and a `fixed` parameter is an integer known at compile time. Here `cmp.hashable` is a concept `core/cmp` provides, and `zeroable` is [0550]'s:\n\n    import core/cmp\n\n    key_value: type (key_type: type is cmp.hashable, value_type: type) = struct\n        key: key_type\n        value: value_type\n    end key_value\n\n    cleared: type (t: type is zeroable, fixed capacity: u32) = struct\n        items: [capacity]t\n        len: u32\n    end cleared\n\nApplications are positional and complete: `key_value(u32, utf8)`, never `key_value(u32)`. A `fixed` argument is an integer literal, or a `fixed` parameter passed on by another generic declaration, and it must fit its declared type. Whether an argument type may go where the body puts it, as a field or an array element, is checked after substitution.\n\nAn alias may be generic too, including a union of atom sets. An alias never makes a new type: `missing | ptr t` keeps the one-word optional pointer of [0480].\n\nThe fine print:\n\n- The compiler checks a generic type's template even if nothing applies it, and reports an error that depends on the argument at each application. A generic function's body is checked per instance instead ([1290]).\n- An unused or phantom parameter still distinguishes instances.\n- A struct may not contain itself by value, even through another template.
C	1360	Allocation is a concept	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1360	An allocator is anything that conforms to `allocator`. The same container runs on the heap, in an arena or on a fixed buffer, and a deliberately failing allocator makes the out-of-memory paths testable, which almost nobody bothers with in C.\n\nThis is `core/mem`'s concept:\n\n    allocator: type = concept (provider: type)\n        alloc: (self: provider, size: usize, alignment: usize)\n               -> (p: ptr mut u8) ! out_of_memory\n        grow: (self: provider, p: ptr mut u8, old_size: usize,\n               new_size: usize, alignment: usize) -> (grown: bool)\n        resize: (self: provider, p: ptr mut u8, old_size: usize,\n                 new_size: usize, alignment: usize)\n                -> (moved: ptr mut u8) ! out_of_memory\n        free: (self: provider, p: ptr mut u8, size: usize) -> none\n    end allocator\n\nA function that adds to a list takes the list `inout` and the allocator as an ordinary argument:\n\n    record_reading: (provider: type is mem.allocator, inout readings: vec.list(u32),\n                     memory: provider, value: u32) -> none ! mem.out_of_memory =\n        try vec.push(readings, memory, value)\n    end record_reading\n\nThe same `record_reading` runs with `heap.new()` as `memory`, or with an arena over a buffer on the stack ([0820]).\n\nThe list is changed, so it is passed `inout`. The allocator is passed as a handle: a small copyable value, passed `in`, that refers to its provider's state. The handle's lifetime is checked once, where the handle is made from that state, and using it does not borrow that state. So several containers can allocate through one handle, and a region can allocate from its parent while both are live.\n\nThe allocator is passed to each call rather than stored in the container. A stored one would be part of the type, `vec.list(t, provider)`, so a list in an arena and a list on the heap would be different types and no function could take both. Passing it keeps the type `vec.list(t)`, at the cost of one argument to every call that can allocate.\n\nThe four entries:\n\n| entry | what it does |\n|---|---|\n| `alloc` | a new block, or `out_of_memory` |\n| `grow` | extend the block where it is; `false`, with nothing changed, if it cannot |\n| `resize` | a new extent, larger or smaller, moving the block if it must |\n| `free` | give the block back, with the size it was allocated with |\n\n`resize` keeps the bytes the old and new extents share, and a refusal reports `out_of_memory` with the block as it was. A concept entry has no default, so a provider that can only move a block calls `mem.relocate`, which allocates, copies and frees through it.\n\nThe standard library's providers and containers:\n\n| module | what it gives |\n|---|---|\n| `core/arena` | a bump allocator over storage you supply |\n| `core/pool` | uniform slots over storage you supply, freed slots reused |\n| `core/fault` | wraps any allocator and fails once a budget of attempts is spent |\n| `hosted/heap` | the operating system's memory, really freed, on every hosted system |\n| `core/vec` | a growable list |\n| `core/spill` | a list that keeps its first items inline and spills to an allocator |\n| `core/map` | an open-addressed hash map |\n\nNone of them has a hidden heap or a fallback. Every failure is `out_of_memory`, reported before anything changes: a container that cannot grow keeps its old storage and contents. The library guide lists each module's calls.\n\nWhen you use the containers directly:\n\n- A map's key needs both an `equatable` and a `hashable` conformance; the combined one does not supply its parent ([1340]). Equality must be an equivalence, equal keys must hash alike, and neither may change while the key is stored, including through a pointer inside the key. The compiler does not check any of this.\n- A map's entry cursor is just a position. Start a new walk after any change to the map, and never resume one on a different map.\n- A map's fields are public. Code that works below its operations must keep the map's invariants itself.\n- A spill list's `spill.used` lends its items `from` the list, so the list cannot spill or be released while that view is still used ([0830]). Its first spill doubles the inline capacity, checking that the result fits `usize`, or takes eight if the inline capacity is zero. If a spill or later growth fails, the list is unchanged.\n\nThese are the providers' contracts. They do not make raw storage safe: storage you hand an arena or a pool must be live, aligned and as large as you say ([1720]).
C	1370	`any C`: a value of some type that satisfies C	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1370	`any C` holds a value of some type that satisfies concept C, decided at run time. It is two words: a pointer to the data and a pointer to C's table of entries for that type.\n\nWhat the pair is, as a value:\n\n- It is an ordinary copyable value, and can sit in a variable, a field or a slice.\n- What it points at is never copied, because its size is unknown. So the pointee must stay alive as long as any copy of the pair can use it. An arena ([0820]) is the usual place for it.\n- It needs no permission of its own: the concept's entries carry it. An entry declared with `self: ptr mut t` can only be satisfied by a pointer that may write, so a stateful implementation behind `any` just works.\n- It does carry its pointee's origin ([0770]), so an `any` over a local cannot go into a list that outlives the frame.\n\nAn `any C` is itself a provider of C and of every concept C builds on ([1340]). So a generic function ([1290]) takes one, and each entry the function calls goes through the value's own table. Here an `any widget` is handed to a function that wants a `drawable`:\n\n    draw_on: (provider: type is drawable, item: ptr provider,\n              target: ptr mut canvas) -> none =\n        provider.draw(item, target)\n    end draw_on\n\n    paint_one: (item: any widget, target: ptr mut canvas) -> none =\n        draw_on(addr item, target)\n    end paint_one\n\nAn `any C` provides no other concept, and the compiler, not the program, declares these conformances. An `any` is not erased again: where an `any C` is wanted, pass the one you have rather than its address.\n\nPrinting is where most programs first meet `any`. `io.write_format` takes its values as a `[]any text.formattable`, each built from a value's address:\n\n    print_born: (host: blocking.host, name: utf8, year: u32) -> none =\n        io.write_format(host, io.out(host), "{} was born in {}.\\n",\n                        [any(addr name), any(addr year)]) else none\n    end print_born\n\n        print_born(host, "Ada", 1815) -- Ada was born in 1815.\n\nIntegers, `bool`, `utf8` and byte strings are formattable, floats not yet, and a type of your own becomes formattable by conforming ([1240]).\n\nThe text is made in a small buffer on the stack and written as it fills, so printing allocates nothing. A template whose `{}` and values differ in number fails with `text.invalid_format` and writes nothing.
C	1380	Building an `any` with `any(...)`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1380	You build an `any` explicitly from a pointer. The concept comes from context where it can; otherwise name it.\n\n    make_widget: (provider: type is mem.allocator, memory: provider)\n                 -> (item: any widget) ! mem.out_of_memory =\n        initial: button = (text: "OK")\n        b := try mem.new(memory: memory, value: initial)\n        item = any(b)\n    end make_widget\n\nHere the result type supplies `widget`. Without a context, `any(pointer)` needs exactly one concept the pointee's type conforms to.\n\nA read-only pointer cannot build an `any` whose concept has an entry taking `self: ptr mut t`. Once the `any` is built, binding mutability controls only replacing the pair, not the write authority its pointer already carries.
C	1390	Calls go through the table	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1390	A call on an `any` looks up the entry in the table and passes the data pointer as the first argument. This is the only place in Landin that reads like a method call.\n\n    paint: (items: []any widget, target: ptr mut canvas) -> none =\n        for w in items do\n            w.draw(target)\n        end for\n    end paint\n\nAn entry is callable this way when it meets two conditions:\n\n- Its first parameter is `self` as `ptr t` or `ptr mut t`, or `self: t` taken by value when `t` is a record.\n- The hidden type `t` appears nowhere else in it.\n\nA by-value `self` is copied out of the data pointer when the call is made. So to put a small handle, such as an allocator handle `memory`, behind `any`, take the address of the variable that holds it: `any(addr memory)`.\n\n`any C` is exactly C: a concept's parent gives no conversion, and two `any` types never convert to each other. The implicit `self` takes part in the same `from`, `escaping` and origin checks as a written pointer argument.\n\nThe compiler checks a call through `any C` even if the program has no conformance of C. Then no `any C` can be made and no value reaches the call, so it compiles to a trap that never runs. A library that takes an erased capability therefore builds in a program that supplies none.
C	1400	What `any` can do that generics cannot	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1400	One slice can hold values of different types. A `[]t` is always one `t`; a `[]any widget` holds buttons, labels and anything else that is a widget.
C	1410	A module is a directory	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1410	Every `.ldn` file directly inside one directory belongs to one module. Those files see each other's declarations without importing anything. Everything is private to its module unless it is marked `public`. There is no separate interface file.\n\n    geometry/area.ldn\n    geometry/shapes.ldn\n    geometry/solid/volume.ldn\n\nHere `geometry` is one module of two files, and `geometry/solid` is a second module.\n\nFine print:\n\n- The compiler reads a module's files in bytewise filename order. It ignores other files, and an empty directory is a legal empty module.\n- Declaration order never affects what is visible. File order does fix identities, the order of diagnostics and the order of active `linker.library` directives [1590].\n- An importer can name public functions, bindings, atoms, types and concepts. A variant case is public when its type is.\n- A public declaration may mention a private one. The private identity flows through the public surface, but an importer cannot name it.
C	1420	Importing a module by its path	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1420	`import net/http` finds a directory `net` holding a directory `http`, under the import roots the compiler was given. It binds the last segment, `http`, as a namespace in this file.\n\n    import net/http\n\nFinding the module. The compiler searches the roots in order, and the first that has the directory wins; a later root is not merged in. From that directory the compiler takes every source file, not recursively, and follows their imports. A subdirectory is a module of its own, reached by its own path. Each module is loaded once, so import cycles are legal.\n\nUsing the namespace. After the import, `http.get`, `http.response` and `http.drawable` name that module's public declarations. Qualification works wherever a value, type, type application, concept, conformance, error atom or match case is named. The first dot after the namespace selects a public declaration; later dots are ordinary value selections. The namespace itself is not a value, type or place.\n\nSpelling the path. A path segment is a plain identifier: lowercase letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit.\n\n- It is lowercase because a case-sensitive and a case-insensitive filesystem must agree on what a name is. The directory entry must have exactly that spelling even on a case-insensitive host.\n- It is an identifier because the last segment becomes a name in your file, so a hyphen would need an alias every time.\n\nThe separator is always `/` in source, on every host.
C	1430	Renaming an import	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1430	`as` gives the namespace another name, for when two imports collide.\n\n    import net/http as h\n\nThis binds `h` only, not `http`. `as` is a contextual word, so outside an import it is an ordinary identifier.
C	1440	Importing selected names	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1440	A parenthesized list brings named declarations into scope directly. There is no wildcard.\n\n    import net/http (get, post)\n\nThis binds `get` and `post` and not the `http` namespace. The rules for the list:\n\n- Every selected name must exist and be public, even if the file never uses it.\n- Each name keeps its original declaration's identity, type and mutability.\n- The list is not empty and has no trailing comma or renaming.\n- A selection cannot be combined with an alias.
C	1450	Imports belong to one file	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1450	Each file has its own imports, so every file reads on its own.\n\n- Imports come first, before every declaration.\n- One file's imports are not visible in its siblings and are never re-exported.\n- Binding one name twice in a file's imports is an error, whether it is the same import twice or a selection colliding with an alias.\n\nShadowing goes like this:\n\n- A parameter or local may shadow an import.\n- A namespace import shadows a same-named module declaration only for qualified lookup; the module's unqualified value stays visible.\n- A selected name shadows the module declaration in both.\n\nThe compiler reports selecting a private member differently from selecting one that does not exist, and the report points at the private declaration.
C	1460	Module-level values are known at compile time	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1460	A value at module level must be known when the compiler reads it, because nothing runs before the entry point. So it cannot call a function. Immutable values can stay in flash; mutable ones cost RAM, and the `mut` makes them conspicuous.\n\n    table: [4]u32 = [1, 2, 4, 8]\n    mut call_count: u32 = 0\n\nArithmetic. Integer arithmetic here is worked out in a wide range first, and only the final value is checked against its type. So a module `value: u8 = 200 + 100 - 100` holds 200, while the same `u8` addition inside a function overflows and traps before the subtraction.\n\nValues from other modules. A value another module exports is known in the same way, named through that module: `limit: u32 = sizes.page * 4`, `ready: flags.state = flags.idle`. Qualifying a name changes where it is found, not whether it is known.\n\nFunctions in a struct. A module struct may hold a function. The field names a declared function, or an anonymous one that captures nothing. What is stored is the function's address; nothing is called. There is no all-zero function address [0540], so such a struct must be written out in full.\n\nExact rules: spec [1940].
C	1470	Packages and versions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1470	A package is a named collection of modules with a version and an origin. Its name has two levels, owner and package, and a directory under a search root is the package it names.\n\nA program holds one version of each package name. Two copies of a package would do three things:\n\n- cost space a 32 KB part does not have;\n- be different types, since types are nominal;\n- put conflicting entries in the single list the whole program keeps of which types conform to which concepts ([1240]).\n\nThe companion tool ([1480]), once it exists, will solve versions and report a conflict as a hard error that asks for an upgrade.\n\nThe current compiler reads no versions or origins. It takes the first matching module directory from the ordered roots [1420], even when a later root holds another version.
C	1480	Where modules come from: the roots	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1480	You tell the compiler where modules are. `refine` takes repeated `--root=DIR` options and then the entry module: its directory, or its source files, which together form one module. With no `--root` you name the source files, and they form one module in the same way.\n\nThe roots are searched in the order you give ([1420]), and that order alone decides: the compiler consults no home directory and adds no system root of its own choosing.\n\nThe library root. The compiler does add one root: the library it ships with, found beside its executable. `core`, `hosted` and `platform` always come from there and from nowhere else, so a root you name cannot replace them. Every other module is searched for in your roots, project first, so a project can override an ordinary module by putting its own copy in its first root. Vendoring a package is just that.\n\nThe companion tool. Fetching packages, solving versions, lock files and naming authority belong to a companion tool. It will ship alongside the compiler but stay separate from it: a compiler you can read is worth more than one that can download things.\n\n- Arranging the roots so that only one version of each package is reachable is that tool's job. So until it exists, the compiler does not enforce [1470]'s one-version rule.\n- The intended root order is the project, then the user's Landin home, then a system-wide one.\n- Whether a path's leading segments name an owner and a package is a convention for people and that tool. The compiler only sees directories.\n\nThe compiler's namespaces. Four source namespaces come with the compiler:\n\n| namespace | holds | available |\n|---|---|---|\n| `core` | the shared freestanding library: `core/mem`, `core/text`, `core/vec` | every module and interface on every target |\n| `hosted` | hosted providers such as `hosted/heap`, `hosted/system` and `hosted/blocking` | on hosted systems |\n| `platform` | interfaces scoped to a target or a system: `platform/c`, the CPU modules and the POSIX layer | each as the next table says |\n| `landin` | the toolchain modules of [1560]: `landin/compiler`, `landin/assembler`, `landin/linker` | everywhere, without an import |\n\nWithin `platform`, availability goes by module:\n\n| `platform` module | available |\n|---|---|\n| `platform/c` | wherever a C ABI (application binary interface) is enabled: the hosted LP64 targets and Cortex-M's AAPCS32 |\n| a CPU module: `platform/cortex_m`, `platform/riscv` or `platform/xtensa` | everywhere, with its operations, submodules and reference descriptions only on its own targets: Cortex-M at any level, `rv32`, `xtensa` |\n| the POSIX layer: `platform/posix` over `platform/linux`, `platform/libc` and `platform/kqueue` | on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD |\n| a `platform` module the compiler gives no scope | nowhere |\n\nFine print:\n\n- An import outside its target's scope is refused by name when the target is checked, for example `hosted/heap` in firmware.\n- The POSIX layer is hosted-only and still under `platform`, not `hosted`: it is the system's own interface, which the `hosted` providers are written over, rather than a provider of its own.\n- A module that declares nothing on some targets can be imported on all of them: a program for every target imports `platform/cortex_m` and calls it from a `fixed if compiler.arch == cortex_m0` arm ([1500]).\n- The toolchain modules are always there, so the bare names `compiler`, `assembler` and `linker` cannot be declared or bound by an import, and an explicit `import landin/compiler` (or `assembler`, or `linker`) is refused by name before any root is searched.\n- Otherwise the namespace names are ordinary identifiers.
C	1490	The word `fixed`	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1490	`fixed` marks something the compiler knows before the program runs. You meet it in three places:\n\n- `fixed if` chooses declarations ([1500]).\n- A fixed parameter is a compile-time value ([1520]).\n- A fixed expression is what a condition, an assertion or an option default is written in ([1500], [1510], [1530]).
C	1500	Choosing declarations by target	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1500	`fixed if` picks which module-level declarations exist in this build. It works on declarations only, not on statements.\n\n    fixed if compiler.arch == arm64 then\n        word_bits: u32 = 64\n    elsif compiler.arch == cortex_m0 then\n        word_bits: u32 = 32\n    end if\n\nThe compiler parses every arm, so a syntax error in an arm you are not building is still an error. Only the selected arm's declarations join the module; the declarations of the other arms have no names, no types and no effect. Arms may nest, an arm may be empty, and an arm opens no scope.\n\nThe facts. The compiler supplies these facts:\n\n| fact | what it says |\n|---|---|\n| `compiler.arch` | `x86_64`, `arm64`, `rv64`, `cortex_m0`, `rv32`, `xtensa` or `synthetic_32` |\n| `compiler.os` | `linux`, `darwin`, `freebsd` or `freestanding` |\n| `compiler.word_size` | the width of `usize`, in bits |\n| `compiler.byte_order` | `little` or `big` |\n| `compiler.build_mode` | `debug`, the default, or `release` |\n| `compiler.c_sysv_lp64`, `compiler.c_darwin_lp64`, `compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64`, `compiler.c_riscv_lp64d`, `compiler.c_aapcs32`, `compiler.c_riscv_ilp32`, `compiler.c_xtensa_windowed_ilp32` | which C ABI the target uses, each true for its own ABI alone |\n| `compiler.c_runtime` | whether C's runtime starts the program and its library is linked |\n| `compiler.feature.NAME` | whether the selected CPU level has feature NAME |\n| `compiler.cache_line` | the line of the device description's cache, in bytes, or 0 without one |\n\nBuild mode is a value you ask for. It does not change runtime checks or optimization.\n\nThe C ABI and the C runtime. Ask the C ABI question directly rather than guessing the answer from the architecture: Linux and Apple arm64 share `compiler.arch == arm64` and answer the C ABI question differently. `compiler.os` is separate from the C ABI because Linux and FreeBSD share a calling convention on each architecture but not every libc record layout.\n\n`compiler.c_runtime` is always true on Darwin and FreeBSD, true on Linux only when the build asks with `--link=libc`, and never true on firmware. A library calls the C library only where this fact says it is there.\n\nCPU features. A build assumes a CPU feature level. You choose it with `--level=`, and it defaults to the oldest processor of the architecture. `compiler.feature.NAME` asks about one feature, such as `bmi2` on x86-64, `lse` on arm64, `idiv` on the M profile or `xtheadba` on RV64. A feature of another architecture is simply false, so you need no `compiler.arch` test first:\n\n    fixed if compiler.feature.idiv then\n        divide_cycles: u32 = 12\n    else\n        divide_cycles: u32 = 40\n    end if\n\nA level changes which instructions the build may use, never a layout or a calling convention, so code built at two levels links together. `spec.md` lists the levels and their features.\n\nValues that differ by target.
