When only a value differs, you need no `fixed if` at all. A module value may read a fact, and a function branches on that value with an ordinary `if`:\n\n    fast_count: bool = compiler.feature.popcnt\n    on_linux: bool = compiler.os == linux\n    word_bytes: usize = compiler.word_size / 8\n\nAn integer fact takes its type from context. You read an atom fact, which is one of `compiler.arch`, `compiler.os`, `compiler.byte_order` and `compiler.build_mode`, by comparing it with one of its atoms.\n\nInside a function. A function body reads no fact directly, except in an array length, which is part of a type [0520], and `fixed if` cannot begin a statement. Instead:\n\n- What differs by value branches on a module value like those above.\n- What needs a call that one system lacks is a function declared in each arm of a module-level `fixed if`.\n\nConditions. A condition is a closed fold: literals, parentheses, unary `-`, integer `+ - * / %` without overflow, integer comparisons, equality, `not`, `and`, `or`, and `sizeof` and `alignof` of the built-in scalar types.\n\n- Sizes count target bytes, so `compiler.word_size == 8 * sizeof usize` holds on 32-bit and 64-bit targets alike.\n- A condition may also read your own options ([1530]).\n- The compiler refuses calls, runtime names, measurements of your own types and aggregate operations, even in an operand that short-circuiting would skip.\n\nForms that do not exist. There is no `public fixed if`, no trailing name after `end if`, and no `fixed if` inside a block, struct, signature or template.\n\nExact rules: spec [1940].
C	1510	Checking a layout at compile time	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1510	`compiler.assert` stops the build when a fixed condition is false.\n\n    compiler.assert(sizeof usize == 8)\n\n`compiler.assert` is a module-level directive, and a selected `fixed if` arm may hold one too. An assertion in an inactive arm does nothing.\n\nThe condition is the same closed fold as in [1500] and must be a bool. A false condition is reported at its own source.\n\nAn assertion may also measure your own types, as in `compiler.assert(sizeof header == 8)`. The compiler then checks it once the type is laid out.\n\n`compiler.assert` is a builtin call rather than a keyword, like the rest of [1560]. That leaves the word `assert` free for an ordinary function of your own, such as the `assert` of [1040].
C	1520	A compile-time value parameter	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1520	A `fixed` parameter is a value the caller supplies at compile time, so it can size an array in the signature.\n\n    make_buffer: (fixed capacity: u32, t: type is zeroable)\n                 -> (b: [capacity]t) = zeroed end\n\nA fixed parameter sits beside the type parameters and works the way they do ([1290]): the call supplies it or deduces it, and it has no storage at run time.
C	1530	Your own build switches	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1530	An `option` declares a typed build switch with a default, which the build can override. A misspelt switch is a compile error, never a silent false.\n\n    option log_level: u32 = 0\n\nRead it in a fixed condition, and set it on the command line with `--option=log_level=2`:\n\n    fixed if log_level > 1 then\n        trace_enabled: bool = true\n    else\n        trace_enabled: bool = false\n    end if\n\nType. An option's type is `bool` or a built-in integer type; `usize` and `isize` take the selected target's bounds. An option has no storage at run time, and its name is visible only in fixed conditions, option defaults and compiler assertions.\n\nDeclaration. Option names are global across the whole program, so each is declared exactly once, unconditionally at module level and never inside a `fixed if` arm: the compiler collects every option before it chooses arms.\n\nNames. An option may not share a name with either of these:\n\n- an active declaration or import in its declaring module, including another file of that module;\n- a compiler-owned atom such as `arm64` or `release`.\n\nOrdinary bindings in unrelated modules may use the same spelling. Fixed configuration still reads the global option, while runtime uses ordinary module/import lookup.\n\nDefaults. A default may refer to another option, even one declared later, and sees that option's overridden value. The compiler refuses cycles, and every default must be valid even when overridden.\n\nOn the command line. `--option=NAME=VALUE` takes `true` or `false`, or signed decimal integer text. Unknown or repeated names, malformed values and values out of range are errors. `--build-mode=debug` or `--build-mode=release` sets the separate built-in build mode.
C	1540	No compile-time execution	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1540	There are no compile-time loops and no compile-time function calls. Nothing of yours runs while the program is being built.\n\nThe builtin modules of [1560] look like an exception and are not one. Their members are operations the compiler recognizes, not your functions run during the build, and nobody can add another. Their inputs differ:\n\n- Some must be fixed, such as assertion conditions, library names and assembly text.\n- Others can be runtime values, such as atomic data and assembly input operands.\n\nWhen you need a generated table or a structure-of-arrays layout, write a program that writes the source, and have the build run it.
C	1550	What the compiler produces	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1550	`refine` compiles the whole program at once into assembly text, and the platform's own assembler and linker turn that into an executable. There is no LLVM and no C in between. Going through C would lose the calling convention, the traps and the debug information Landin is precise about, so every target's backend is Landin's own. The README lists the targets.\n\n- The emitted assembly is deterministic: the same program and options give the same bytes, whatever the build directory, environment or order. The linked executable is not covered by that promise.\n- Every ordinary function and every interrupt handler sets up the frame pointer, so a debugger or a backtrace can always walk the stack. On Cortex-M0 a function with no calls, no assembly and no stack changes may leave it alone (spec [1990]). A naked function ([1570]) owns its frame instead.\n- The whole program is compiled together ([1480]). The compiler may keep private caches, but there is no stable separate-compilation interface.\n\nOn Cortex-M the `cortex_m0` backend emits ARMv6-M Thumb, the default `armv6-m` level.\n\n- Levels. `--level=armv7-m`, `--level=armv7e-m` or `--level=armv8-m.main` lets the backend use that level's instructions too, which the processor must then support. All four levels are little-endian.\n- Floats. Floats are computed in software unless the device description names a float unit. A Cortex-M7's `compiler.float_unit("fpv5-d16")` makes the build hard-float at `armv7e-m`: its f32 and f64 arithmetic becomes VFP instructions, its floats are passed in s and d registers, and `compiler.feature.fp` and `compiler.feature.fp_dp` say so.\n- Firmware. A firmware request emits its own reset code, vector table and linker script. Reset copies initialized data and RAM code out of flash and clears BSS before your code runs.\n- Caches. A Cortex-M7's description may also declare its caches, `compiler.cache("armv7-m-l1", 32)`. Reset then turns them on after those copies and off again if the entry returns, and `compiler.feature.cache` and `compiler.cache_line` say so. A direct memory access (DMA) buffer is kept in step with the caches through `core/cache`.\n\nExact rules: spec [1990].
C	1560	The `compiler`, `assembler` and `linker` modules	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1560	Three builtin modules reach the toolchain. They belong to the reserved `landin` package (`landin/compiler` and its siblings) and are in scope without an import, which is why nobody else can use their bare names.\n\n| module | what it reaches |\n| --- | --- |\n| `compiler` | target, word size, byte order, build mode, CPU features; the atomic, volatile and register intrinsics; the two stack builtins under fibres ([1675]); `compiler.unreachable()`; `compiler.utf8_unvalidated(bytes)` |\n| `assembler` | inline assembly |\n| `linker` | libraries, sections, entry |\n\nTwo of those calls:\n\n- `compiler.unreachable()` is a call that never returns. It stops the program as a failed check does ([1670]). Given a `caller` parameter of the function it is written in, `compiler.unreachable(where)`, it reports the stop at the call that filled the parameter ([1040]).\n- `compiler.utf8_unvalidated(bytes)` is text of bytes known to be UTF-8, made without reading them and only inside `unchecked` ([0600]).\n\nThe members of all three modules are built into the compiler; you cannot write one yourself.\n\nSome arguments must be fixed when the program is compiled:\n\n- `compiler.assert` takes a fixed condition.\n- `linker.library` takes a fixed name.\n- `assembler.block` takes fixed instruction text.\n- An atomic's ordering is always a fixed `compiler` atom.\n\nAtomic and volatile pointer and value operands, and assembly inputs, can be runtime values.\n\nWhat works today:\n\n- Every hosted target has the compiler facts, `compiler.assert`, `linker.library` ([1590]) and the scalar atomics and barriers ([1620]).\n- Firmware targets also have placement annotations ([1640]) and the firmware entry request ([1650]), which hosted targets refuse, and Cortex-M firmware links C archives through `linker.library` ([1590]). The capability inventory names the supported firmware targets and their limits.\n- `assembler.block` is checked on every target ([1630]).\n- Any other tool operation is refused by name.\n\nWhy some things are builtin and others are not: something is builtin when the compiler has to understand it.\n\n- Atomics are builtin, because opaque assembly in a hot loop wrecks the register allocation around it.\n- Masking interrupts is not. A critical section wants nothing moved across it, which is exactly what opaque assembly gives. So `cortex_m.disable_interrupts` and its kin are an ordinary module per target, written with `assembler.block` ([1630]).\n- An operation that comes to mean the same thing on every target, as the atomics do, can move into `compiler`.\n- There are no vector intrinsics: fixed arrays are the vector type and take element-wise operators ([0590]).
C	1570	Calling conventions	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1570	A function's calling convention is written `extern(...)` before its name. Without one, a function uses Landin's own convention.\n\n| convention | for |\n| --- | --- |\n| `extern(c)` | the target's C ABI ([1580], [1600]) |\n| `extern(interrupt)` | an interrupt handler, whose entry, exit and vector placement differ from a call ([1640]) |\n| `extern(naked)` | no prologue at all: the body is one assembly block ([1630]) |\n\nThe convention is an atom, not a keyword, so the set can grow, for example to `extern(aapcs)`, `extern(sysv)` or `extern(win64)`. No other convention is in Landin yet.\n\nThe two machine conventions, `interrupt` and `naked`, are their own function types:\n\n- A definition is nongeneric, exactly `() -> none`, and declares no failures. Its function value can be stored or named by a vector, but not called or converted to an ordinary or C function.\n- An interrupt handler runs an ordinary Landin frame on top of the hardware's exception frame and returns through EXC_RETURN.\n- A naked body is one assembly block with no compiler prologue. The stack, registers, calls and return instruction are yours, and falling off the end traps.\n- Neither convention keeps a function from section garbage collection ([1640]).\n- Naked functions also work on hosted x86-64, arm64 and RV64; `platform/linux`'s process entry is one.
C	1580	Importing from C	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1580	A bodyless `extern(c)` declaration imports a C function. A compilation reads Landin, never C headers: `refine bindings`, a deterministic binding generator, asks Clang what a header declares and writes these declarations for you.\n\n    none_returned: atom\n    allocation: type = none_returned | ptr mut u8\n    extern(c) malloc: (n: usize) -> (p: allocation)\n    extern(c) free: (p: ptr mut u8) -> none\n\nNull. A C pointer may be null and a Landin pointer may not. So a C result or parameter that may be null is [0480]'s one-atom pointer union, which costs no extra bits, and you `match` the result before using the pointer.\n\n- `ptr(0)` is refused, and so is any fixed expression that folds to zero at the target's `usize` width.\n- A pointer built from an integer at run time is checked, and zero traps, even in `unchecked`: losing the origin is not permission to make null.\n- Absent allocator backing is a named union too, never a fake `ptr(1)`.\n\nWhat a header leaves out. A header does not say everything Landin wants to know: whether a pointer may be null, who owns it, what it is `from`, whether C retains it, how to read incoming varargs. The generator takes that from a written policy, not from a handwritten replacement signature.\n\nA function found while the program runs. Such a function, a symbol of a loaded library for example, is just an address. Apply a C function type to it and you have a function value:\n\n    c_adder: type = extern(c) (a: i32, b: i32) -> (r: i32)\n\n    add_at: (address: usize) -> (sum: i32) =\n        add := c_adder(address)\n        sum = add(2, 3)\n    end add_at\n\nNothing can check that code of that type is there, as nothing checks a C cast, and the value is yours to call only while the library stays loaded.\n\nThe supported ABIs. Landin supports five C application binary interfaces (ABIs):\n\n| C ABI | where |\n| --- | --- |\n| SysV AMD64 LP64 | Linux and FreeBSD x86-64 |\n| Apple's arm64 variant of AAPCS64 | macOS |\n| the standard AAPCS64 | Linux and FreeBSD arm64 |\n| RV64 LP64D | Linux RV64 |\n| AAPCS32 | Cortex-M |\n\nUnder Cortex-M's AAPCS32, floats travel in the float unit's registers when the device description has one and in core registers when it has none.\n\nC's types. `platform/c` names them: the signed and unsigned integer widths, `c_size`, `c_ptrdiff`, `c_float`, `c_double` and `c_bool`. It asserts `compiler.c_sysv_lp64 or compiler.c_darwin_lp64 or compiler.c_aapcs64_lp64 or compiler.c_riscv_lp64d or compiler.c_aapcs32`, so it admits exactly those five ABIs; another target with the same pointer width, RV32's or Xtensa's, is not admitted.\n\n- The first four are LP64, with a 64-bit `long`. AAPCS32 is ILP32, so there `c_long` is an `i32` and `c_size` a 32-bit `usize`.\n- Plain `c_char` is the ABI's plain `char`, a number and not a Unicode scalar: `i8` under SysV and Apple's ABI, `u8` under the standard AAPCS64, RV64 and AAPCS32.\n\nWhat crosses the boundary:\n\n| kind | how it crosses |\n| --- | --- |\n| integers, `bool`, pointers, `f32`, `f64`, C function values | by value |\n| nonempty `layout(c)` structs, with nested structs, nonempty fixed arrays and fixed C callbacks as fields | by value |\n| packed records and records with a flexible array member | by pointer only |\n| fixed arrays | as fields or pointees, never as a by-value argument or result |\n| C enums | as their integer values |\n| unions, bitfields, globals, thread-locals, nullable callbacks | through the generator's representations and adapters |\n\nAnything else a header can say, such as `long double`, 128-bit integers, complex or vector types, or forwarding a `va_list`, is refused by name rather than guessed.\n\nVariadic functions. A variadic C function writes `, ...` after at least one fixed parameter. This `...` is C's variadic tail, unrelated to [0960]'s `! ...`.\n\n    extern(c) printf: (format: ptr u8, ...) -> (written: i32)\n\n    say_count: (format: ptr u8, count: i32) -> none =\n        _ = printf(format, count, 1.5)\n    end say_count\n\n- Calls, direct or through a function value, are positional only, including the fixed parameters.\n- The variadic tail takes scalars, pointers and fixed C callbacks, not structs, arrays, slices, atoms or `any`.\n- C's promotions apply: `f32` becomes `f64`, and `bool` and narrow integers become C `int`. An untyped literal is `i32` or `f64`.\n- A variadic function value may be stored and called in Landin, but it cannot fill a C callback field or parameter.\n- A Landin definition cannot receive varargs; the generator writes a C adapter from an explicit extraction schema instead.\n- Cortex-M declares no variadic C function yet. Write a C function of fixed arity that makes the variadic call, and import that one.\n\nExact rules: spec [1975].
C	1590	Linking a library	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1590	`linker.library` asks the C driver for a library, as `-lNAME` asks it in C. Write it next to the declarations that need it, not in a separate build file. `linker.directory` says where to look, relative to the file it is in.\n\n    linker.library("raylib")\n    linker.library("m")\n    linker.directory("vendor/lib")\n\nThis links `libraylib` from `vendor/lib` beside the source, and `libm` from wherever the C driver keeps it.\n\n- The name is a fixed text literal of ASCII letters, digits, `_`, `-` and `.`. It is nonempty, does not begin with `-` and is not only dots. The driver takes a shared library or an archive of that name, as it would for a C program.\n- Order. Active directives reach the linker after the program, in source order, repeats included. So moving one among the module's declarations can change how archives resolve. This is the one place where declaration order matters. A directive in an inactive arm of a `fixed if` ([1500]) adds nothing.\n- A directory is a fixed, nonempty text literal: relative to the directory of the file that names it, or absolute. One that does not exist is refused before anything is linked.\n- **`-L DIR`** on `refine compile`, `run` or `check` names another directory, relative to where the build runs. It is searched first, so a build can put its own copy of a library ahead.\n- At startup. Each directory is also where the program looks for a shared library when it starts.\n- A missing library. A library the link cannot find is named with every directory searched.\n- On Linux a library links beside the C library, so a build that asks for one needs `--link=libc`. The default static link ([1650]) refuses a library, and refuses a directory too.\n- Cortex-M firmware links each library as a static archive built for its core, after the program and before the compiler's runtime. It refuses one that brings C constructors, thread-local storage or a dynamic linkage, none of which its startup can honour.
C	1600	Exporting to C	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1600	Give an `extern(c)` declaration a body and you have defined a C function in Landin. Make it `public` and C code can call it by its name.\n\n    public extern(c) my_add: (a: i32, b: i32) -> (r: i32) =\n        r = a + b\n    end my_add\n\n`extern(c)` chooses the calling convention and nothing else:\n\n- Without a body it imports.\n- With a body it defines.\n- `public` is what exports, making the declared name a global symbol.\n\nA private C definition is still useful: its address can be handed to C as a callback.\n\nLimits:\n\n- A C signature is not generic, takes only `in` parameters and returns at most one value.\n- Landin's declared failures do not cross. Recover inside the body and return the status or value the C interface promises.\n- Nothing is promised if a foreign exception or a `longjmp` crosses Landin frames.\n- On Cortex-M a C signature cannot be variadic: import a fixed-arity C function that makes the variadic call instead.
C	1610	Choosing a symbol's linker name	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1610	`link(symbol: "...")` gives a declaration a linker name its Landin name cannot spell, or does not want. It follows `extern(c)` for a C import or definition, or stands alone before a native Landin function or a module datum.\n\n    link(symbol: "native_identity") identity: (value: i32) -> (result: i32) =\n        result = value\n    end identity\n\n    extern(c) link(symbol: "foreign_add") add: (a: i32, b: i32) -> (r: i32)\n\nLandin code still calls these `identity` and `add`: `link` changes neither lookup nor signature nor Landin visibility. The standalone form keeps the native Landin convention and still needs `= body end`; `link` never means C and never means bodyless.\n\nIt does export. Which symbols the linker sees:\n\n- A link name is a global symbol whether or not the declaration is `public`. That is how you export a module datum deliberately.\n- Without `link`, C imports and public C definitions use their declared name.\n- The program's entry is global, and so are a public definition in a machine convention and a Cortex-M definition with [1640]'s section, alignment, vector or `keep` (spec [1975]).\n- Every other function and datum, public or private, is a local symbol under its own name, so no C library can collide with it. It is renamed, with its module path, only when the program holds that name twice.\n\nThe rules for a link name:\n\n- A link name matches `[A-Za-z_.$][A-Za-z0-9_.$]*`: no whitespace, no `@` suffix, no assembler expression.\n- It is the name before the platform's prefix. ELF uses it unchanged; Darwin adds one underscore, so `foreign_add` becomes `_foreign_add` and `_entry` becomes `__entry`. The backend quotes it where the assembler needs that. Native and C link names follow the same rule.\n- Bodyless C declarations may share a symbol with each other and with one definition if their signatures agree. Disagreeing signatures and a second definition are refused. `escaping` counts, although C has no such word: an import of a C function that keeps its pointer must say so, as the definition does.\n\nExact rules: spec [1975].
C	1615	Storage local to each thread	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1615	`link(thread)` before a module `mut` binding gives every thread its own instance of it. A thread reads and writes only its own, and each one starts at zero when its thread starts.\n\n    link(thread) mut last_failure: i32\n\n    note_failure: (number: i32) -> none =\n        last_failure = number\n    end note_failure\n\nTwo threads calling `note_failure` at once each keep their own number, so this needs no lock. `hosted/system` keeps each thread's last errno this way.\n\n- There is no initial value: write none, and use a type that has a zero, so not a pointer or a slice.\n- It takes no `symbol` or `section`, so a C thread-local is not named this way; use the binding generator ([1580]).\n- On a microcontroller, which runs one thread, it is ordinary module storage.\n- Its address is good while its thread runs. Do not hand it to a thread that may outlive the one it belongs to.\n\nExact rules: spec [1996].
C	1620	Atomics	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1620	Atomic operations are `compiler` builtins, not assembly, so the compiler knows which memory they touch and can still allocate registers around them. The ordering is a fixed atom.\n\n    bump: (p: ptr mut u32) -> none =\n        _ = compiler.atomic_add(p, 1, compiler.acq_rel)\n    end bump\n\n`core/atomic` wraps one `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64` in a cell whose operations carry their orderings in their names:\n\n| operations | ordering |\n| --- | --- |\n| `load` | acquires |\n| `store` | releases |\n| `exchange`, `add`, `compare_exchange` | acquire and release |\n| `load_relaxed`, `store_relaxed`, `add_relaxed` | order nothing else |\n\nCortex-M0 has no read-modify-write atomics, so there a cell has no `exchange`, `add` or `compare_exchange`, there is no `u64` cell, and the compiler reports a call to one. What it has is `sole_add`, the single writer's add: a load and a store, correct while only one context, say an interrupt handler, writes the cell. State that several contexts write needs `platform/cortex_m`'s critical section instead.\n\nA cell, and the single writer's add on it:\n\n    import core/atomic\n\n    mut ticks: atomic.cell(u32) = zeroed\n\n    count_tick: () -> none =\n        _ = atomic.sole_add(addr ticks, 1)\n    end count_tick\n\nEach tool for shared memory does one thing:\n\n| tool | what it gives |\n| --- | --- |\n| atomics | synchronization of coherent CPU memory between threads |\n| volatile accesses ([0850]) | every access happens, as written; no synchronization between threads |\n| compiler barrier | the compiler forgets what it knew about memory; no hardware ordering |\n| the target's device and completion barriers | hardware ordering and completion of the accesses before them |\n\nA direct memory access (DMA) buffer stays an ordinary slice. When the device has finished, by its own protocol and not merely because an interrupt arrived, make its writes visible with the target's barriers or cache maintenance and a compiler barrier. Then read the buffer. Masking interrupts does not stop DMA.\n\n`spec.md` defines the supported operations, the exact orderings, alignment traps, happens-before and what a race may do.\n\nExact rules: spec [1990].
C	1630	Inline assembly, for what has no builtin	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1630	`assembler.block` takes fixed quoted or raw text in a function body, and after it the operands that carry values in and out. An operand names its direction, its name, its type and the register it is placed `at`:\n\n    disable_interrupts: () -> (previous: u32) =\n        previous = assembler.block("mrs {mask}, primask\\ncpsid i",\n                                   out mask: u32 at general)\n    end disable_interrupts\n\n    restore_interrupts: (previous: u32) -> none =\n        assembler.block("msr primask, {mask}\\nisb sy",\n                        in mask: u32 at general = previous)\n    end restore_interrupts\n\n- The register is a name the target answers for, never text. `general` asks the compiler to choose one, and `{mask}` in the text is where the chosen register goes, spelled at the width the operand's type selects. A fixed register is the architecture's own full-width name, and the text may use it directly.\n- The direction: `in` carries a value in, `out` carries one out, and `inout` does both through one register.\n- The value. The outputs are the block's value, as a function's named returns are its: one is a scalar, several are an anonymous result you destructure.\n\n    (low, high) := assembler.block("rdtsc", out low: u32 at rax,\n                                   out high: u32 at rdx)\n\nWhat an operand can be.\n\n- An integer scalar that fits one register, placed `at general` or at an integer register.\n- An `f32` or `f64`, placed `at float` or at a float register: `xmm3`, `v3`, `f3`, or `d3` on a Cortex-M7 whose description has its float unit. A target without float registers, such as a Cortex-M with no float unit, refuses a float operand.\n- A pointer crosses as `usize(p)` and comes back through `ptr(u)`, whose zero check then happens there. The integer keeps no permission. So a function around a block that writes storage takes it as `ptr mut u8` or `[]mut u8`: its callers are checked against that parameter, and an immutable buffer is refused there rather than handed to the system.\n- A flag comes back as `x <> 0`.\n\nInputs are evaluated once, left to right, before the block runs.\n\nLandin has no square-root builtin, so a block is how you reach the instruction. `float` chooses a float register, as `general` chooses an integer one, and the text spells it at the operand's width: `%xmm1` for either on x86-64, `d1` or `s1` on arm64.\n\n    root: (x: f64) -> (r: f64) =\n        r = assembler.block("sqrtsd {x}, {r}", in x: f64 at float = x,\n                            out r: f64 at float)\n    end root\n\nWhat a block may touch.\n\n- Every block may overwrite the registers a call may, and the flags.\n- A register a call must preserve is declared, as an operand or as a discarded output `out _ at rbx`, or `out _ at v8` for a float one. That declaration is what makes the function save it.\n- The frame, stack and link registers are never named, so a block cannot break a backtrace.\n- The language reserves no register of its own.\n- A block that changes x86-64's direction flag, or a float unit's rounding mode or exception flags, puts them back before it ends.\n\nEvery block is opaque to the compiler. Memory knowledge is invalidated and memory accesses cannot be moved across it, which is exactly what a critical section wants. It is not itself a hardware barrier.\n\nAn ordinary block is straight-line code, with no labels or calls; a system call returns to the next instruction, so it is straight-line too.\n\nThe older Cortex-M0 form stays as a shorthand: `assembler.block(text, value)` passes one `u32` in and out of r0, and the text names r0 itself.\n\nThe common blocks, already written. `platform/cortex_m` wraps them:\n\n- `disable_interrupts()` returns the prior PRIMASK, and `restore_interrupts(previous)` puts it back, so nested critical sections do not enable interrupts too early. Both work in thread and handler mode. They do not stop DMA or mask NMI or HardFault.\n- `wait_for_interrupt()` issues DSB, then WFI. Waking up is a reason to check the device again, not proof that it finished.\n- `compiler_barrier`, `device_barrier` and `completion_barrier` are the three distinct boundaries of [1620]. There is no cache or scheduler API.\n\nA naked body. A naked body ([1570]) owns its control flow, so its block may use labels and branches. This entry runs after the compiler's reset has initialized data and stacks:\n\n    extern(naked) start: () -> none =\n        assembler.block("""\n            1:\n            wfi             @ sleep until an interrupt\n            b 1b            @ then sleep again\n            """)\n    end start\n\nThe compiler request names the source entry:\n\n    refine compile main.ldn --target=cortex-m0 --firmware-entry=start --emit=exe\n\nA naked entry may set up PSP or call explicitly linked ordinary code, but it must then meet that code's eight-byte stack alignment, r9 and frame obligations. `none` is not a promise never to return: the compiler traps if the entry returns or the naked block falls through. There is no hosted caller to return to.\n\nComments in the text. A line of the text may end in a comment, written as the target's own assembler writes one: `@` on Cortex-M, `//` on arm64, `#` on x86-64 and RV64. The compiler removes it before it reads the text, so a register or a `{name}` in a comment means nothing, and it never reaches the assembly the compiler writes. Any other form, `/* */` or another target's, is refused, and so is a number with a `_` in it: the text is the assembler's, and its numbers take no separator.\n\nExact rules, with each target's registers, the text rules and your obligations: spec [1990].
C	1640	Placing code and data on a microcontroller	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1640	On a firmware target, a `link(...)` annotation also places a declaration: in a section, at an alignment, in an interrupt vector slot, and kept against the linker's section garbage collection. Cortex-M, RV32 and Xtensa all place declarations this way. The example and the vector table below are Cortex-M's; RV32 and Xtensa have tables of their own, and the compiler checks a slot against the one selected.\n\n    link(vector: 16)\n    extern(interrupt) device_handler: () -> none =\n        assembler.block("nop")\n    end device_handler\n\n    link(section: ".rodata.firmware_mark", align: 16, keep)\n    firmware_mark: [4]u8 = [55, 48, 49, 0]\n\nSlot 16 is IRQ0 in the selected profile: a vector number is the absolute slot in the table, not an IRQ number or a peripheral's name.\n\nCalling convention, symbol name, placement and retention are four independent choices; none implies another.\n\nThe vector table. The compiler owns it. Its first word is the initial stack pointer, its second the compiler's reset, reserved slots are zero, and `vector` annotations fill in handlers with their types checked. So a stack address, a reserved word and a handler can never be mixed up. A vector annotation needs a firmware-entry request ([1650]).\n\nWhat survives the link.\n\n- The table is kept and refers to each handler in it, so those handlers survive.\n- An interrupt function nothing refers to and nothing keeps can disappear.\n- `keep` retains the section that holds the declaration. Several objects placed in one section share that retention.\n- A link name alone retains nothing.\n\nWhere things go.\n\n| what | sections |\n| --- | --- |\n| functions | `.text.*` in flash, or `.ramtext.*`, copied to RAM at reset |\n| immutable data | `.rodata.*` |\n| mutable data | `.data.*`, or `.bss.*` when zeroed |\n\n- `align` is a power of two up to 256. It places the object and does not change its type's layout.\n- `align` and `vector` take decimal literals; digit separators are fine, hex and expressions are refused.\n- `region: "NAME"` places a function or module datum in a region of the device description, by name rather than by section. Code needs a region that may execute and mutable data one that may be written, and reset copies or clears it there.\n- Without a device description, the image has the reference firmware profile's 32 KiB of flash and 16 KiB of RAM, whose top 4 KiB is reserved for stacks; a description gives its own. The linker checks bounds and overlap.\n- A generic function is a function for each instance, and every instance goes to the section, alignment or region it is placed in. A vector slot, the boot stage and `keep` each name one function, so a generic one takes none of them.\n- The compiler refuses reserved vectors, a section that does not match the declaration, duplicate attributes and symbol collisions.\n- There is no module initialization in user code ([1460]).\n\nA second boot stage. Some boot ROMs run a second stage before the image: RP2040's reads its flash through one. On such a chip that stage lives in the device description, as a naked function marked `link(boot_stage)`. The description's boot kind places it at the start of the image, and the compiler seals it with the checksum the ROM checks. Nothing else is marked that way, and nothing else in a description is code.
C	1650	Where a program starts	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1650	A hosted program starts at `public main: () -> (code: i32)` in the entry module, and `code` is the exit status, passed through the system's C ABI.\n\nArguments. The arguments are not parameters. You ask the host for them, as `io.argument_at(host, 0)` does in "Reading a file" at the top: the host keeps the argument table and lends each argument as a host string ([1660]). The first argument is the one after the program's own name. C's `argc` and `argv` shape could not be indexed in Landin without turning a pointer into a slice, which Landin does not do ([0500]).\n\nThe C library. A Linux executable needs no C library. It starts at `platform/linux`'s `_landin_start`, which calls `main` with the process's arguments; `--link=libc` links the C runtime instead. Darwin and FreeBSD always link their C library.\n\nThe argument root. A program that imports `hosted/system`, directly or through `hosted/blocking`, imports `platform/posix` with it. Its entry then first calls this C-callable function with the real values, before the body of `main` begins, so the environment is kept beside the arguments and lent the same way:\n\n    void _landin_host_initialize_arguments(int argc, char **argv, char **envp);\n\nWhen C owns `main` and calls exported Landin functions, it calls that function itself, with its own `envp` or C's `environ`:\n\n- Call it before `blocking.new()` acquires an argument capability, and before starting any thread that may acquire one. File, stream and heap work needs no argument root, so linking `core/io` alone does not require the call.\n- The first call with a nonnegative count and a non-null table sets the one root; a null environment is an empty one. Repeating exactly the same three values is harmless. Using the argument services before the call, or calling with different values, traps. No ordinary export or callback initializes or resets the root.\n- Nothing is copied. The C owner keeps the tables and the strings they name readable as long as any world, view or callback derived from them can use them.\n- The arguments start at `argv[1]`, so a C program run with only its own name gives Landin no arguments.\n\nFreestanding. There is no `main`. The compiler request names the entry: an infallible ordinary `() -> none` or `() -> noreturn` function, or a naked `() -> none` one, in the entry module ([1630] shows the request). The compiler's reset initializes RAM before calling it. Returning from it, or a failed check, traps, since there is no hosted exit to go to. General build and package orchestration are outside the firmware path.\n\nAn image loaded into RAM. For a debugger-loaded SRAM image, select `--firmware-layout=ram`. The compiler derives RAM placement from the same device description, retains BSS clearing and skips copies of data already in place. The board tool establishes the device state before entry. The default `boot` layout keeps the image its boot ROM needs; a RAM run does not test that boot path.\n\nExact rules: spec [1975] for hosted programs, spec [1990] for firmware.
C	1660	Where capabilities come from	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1660	The entry point is the usual place to make the program's roots — the host, an allocator, a diagnostics log — and pass them down as ordinary arguments. The language does not reserve that to the entry point: any function can call the constructors ([1680]).\n\nWhat a root imports:\n\n- A hosted root imports `hosted/blocking`, whose reads, writes, network calls and sleeps block the thread until they are done.\n- A program that serves several things at once imports `hosted/events` instead, whose waits let other fibres run ([1675]).\n- A program that never reads, writes or sleeps may use `system.new()` alone; it is not a world, since it cannot read or write.\n- A caller-backed root needs only `core/io`.\n\n`hosted/blocking` and `hosted/events` are both built over `hosted/system`, which keeps everything that does not wait: the arguments and environment, opening and closing files, directories, running programs, entropy and the wall clock.\n\nThis is the essential flow of `examples/derived_hosted`, a complete log filter. Its `main` is one line, `code = app.entry()`, and the work starts in `entry`, a public function of the program's own `app` module. That module imports `hosted/blocking`, `hosted/heap`, `core/region`, `core/diag` and `core/io`, and `run_logged` is the application's function that does the work:\n\n    public entry: () -> (code: i32) =\n        host := blocking.new()\n        world: any io.world = any(addr host)\n        heap := heap.new()\n        mut ledger: region.growing_space = zeroed\n        program := region.over(ledger, heap)\n        defer region.release(ledger, heap)\n        writer: any io.writer = any(addr host)\n        mut logger := diag.stream(writer, world.err())\n        log: any diag.log = any(addr logger)\n        kept: usize = run_logged(program, world, usize(4096), log) else (problem)\n            _ = problem\n            code = 1\n            return\n        end\n        _ = kept\n        code = if log.failed() then 1 else 0 end if\n    end entry\n\nRoots are handles. Each root is a small value, copied and passed by value, that refers to its state.\n\n- `blocking.new()` and `heap.new()` borrow nothing, because what they refer to belongs to the process: the argument root, the descriptors, the last errno and the heap. `blocking.new()` acquires the real argument table; it does not create or copy it ([1650]).\n- A caller-owned provider is made from state the caller declares, as the region is made from `ledger`. The handle cannot outlive that state, and the state cannot be released while the handle is still used.\n- An erased capability is built from the address of a handle binding, and its dispatch copies the handle from there. So `world`, `writer` and `host` itself can be used side by side, and nothing is locked.\n\nHanding it something else. Because the code below the root only sees what it is handed, you can hand it something else. A test gives the same `run_logged` an in-memory world from `core/io`'s `io.memory_over`, which takes caller-owned files, arguments and output storage and makes no host call, and the run cannot tell.\n\nThat works because I/O is a concept, not a type, so another provider can satisfy it. It travels as `any` rather than as a type parameter: an indirect call costs next to nothing beside the system call behind it. An allocator sits in hot loops, so it is passed as a type parameter instead. The machinery is the same, chosen case by case ([1690]).\n\nFour concepts. I/O is four concepts, because a provider should supply only what it has ([1260]):\n\n| concept | entries |\n| --- | --- |\n| `io.writer` | `write`, `write_some` |\n| `io.reader` | `read` |\n| `io.files` | open, close, `same_file` |\n| `io.process` | the three standard streams, the argument table |\n\n`core/io` has more concepts beside these four, each separate and not part of the world: `directories`, `environment`, `programs`, `file_system`, `terminals` and `entropy`.\n\n`io.world` composes the four for a root that has everything, and `world.write` on an erased world reaches the writer's entry. A UART implements `writer` and nothing else.\n\nA diagnostics log asks for `any io.writer`, which is why `entry` builds one from the same `host`: an `any io.world` is not an `any io.writer`, and neither converts to the other. A function holding only an erased world can go on in either of these ways:\n\n- pass it as it is to a function generic over a writer, or\n- make an `any io.writer` from the adapter `io.writer_of(world)` lends it.\n\nArguments and paths. Both providers lend each argument and path as a `text.host_string`: the bytes the system gave, unconverted and uncopied, so an argument passed on as a path reaches the system unchanged, whether or not it is UTF-8. Neither provider's arguments include `argv[0]`.\n\nThe library reference describes the system providers (`hosted/system`, `hosted/blocking` and `hosted/events`), the memory provider and host strings (`core/io`, `core/text`). The exact provider contracts — errno capture, whole and partial writes, retries, `same_file` — are in spec [1975].
C	1670	When a check fails	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1670	When a check fails — an index out of range, an overflow, a bad conversion, an `unreachable`, a fibre's stack run out ([1675]) — the program calls a fixed handler that never returns. With none of your own, a hosted program writes one line, `FILE:LINE:COLUMN: trap: KIND`, to standard error and stops; firmware just stops.\n\nTo replace the default, declare a public `panic_handler` of exactly this shape in the entry module:\n\n    import core/panic\n\n    public panic_handler: (kind: panic.panic_kind, site: u32) -> noreturn =\n        loop do\n        end loop\n    end panic_handler\n\nIt gets two scalars and no strings:\n\n- `kind` is one of `core/panic`'s `out_of_range`, `overflow`, `bad_conversion`, `unreachable` and `stack_exhausted`.\n- `site` is a plain `u32`, not [1040]'s `site` struct: a number the compiler gives the failing operation and its check family.\n\nFile and line live in an optional table outside the target, so a small firmware image carries no file names. `refine --panic-map` writes that table. `refine site PROGRAM SITE` resolves a site against the build that made it, and only that build.\n\nFine print:\n\n- The handler must have exactly this infallible form and atom domain. A linker symbol of the same spelling does not replace it.\n- A failed check does not unwind: the failed computation's `defer` and cleanup do not run.\n- Entering the handler a second time traps, including a check that fails inside it.\n- Caller coordinates are a separate value ([1040]).\n- Hardware faults and naked assembly keep their machine obligations.\n\nExact rules: spec [1960].
C	1675	Two things in flight: fibres	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1675	Concurrency is a capability, like an allocator or the host ([1660], [1680]). There is no `async`, no second calling convention and no coloured function type. A function that wants two things in flight asks for something that runs them, and whether they really overlap is that provider's answer, not the function's. Each one runs on a stack of its own, a fibre.\n\nA task is an ordinary function. It takes its state `inout` and fails with `core/failure`'s set, and nothing in it knows it runs on a fibre:\n\n    answers: type = struct\n        order: [2]u8\n        count: usize\n    end answers\n\n    asking: type = struct\n        clock: any time.clock\n        wait: u64\n        tag: u8\n        heard: ptr mut answers\n    end asking\n\n    ask: (inout self: asking) -> none ! failure.reason =\n        if self.wait > 0 then\n            self.clock.sleep(time.milliseconds(self.wait))\n        end if\n        self.heard.val.order[self.heard.val.count] = self.tag\n        self.heard.val.count += 1\n    end ask\n\nA group. A function starts tasks as a group, over storage it lends, and waits for them before it goes on, so whatever they borrow from it outlives them:\n\n    ask_both: (runs: any fibre.scheduler, clock: any time.clock,\n               inout heard: answers) -> none ! failure.reason =\n        mut stacks: [2 * 8192]u8 = zeroed\n        mut asks := try fibre.group_over(runs, stacks, 2)\n        defer fibre.join(asks) else none\n        a: asking = (clock: clock, wait: 20, tag: u8('a'), heard: addr heard)\n        try fibre.admit(asks, ask, a)\n        b: asking = (clock: clock, wait: 0, tag: u8('b'), heard: addr heard)\n        try fibre.admit(asks, ask, b)\n        try fibre.join(asks)\n    end ask_both\n\n- `group_over` cuts the backing into two equal stacks. Nothing is allocated: the stacks are the caller's bytes, and the group comes `from` the provider and the backing ([0790]).\n- `admit` waits for a free stack, copies the state onto it as a call passes an argument, and starts a fibre that calls `ask` with the copy. One group can hold tasks with different state types.\n- `join` waits until every task has ended, then fails with the first failure any of them had. Nothing cancels a fibre, so the others run to their own ends first.\n- A group must be joined before its backing goes. The `defer` does that on every way out, as it releases a region ([1660]); the compiler does not check that you wrote it.\n- The state is kept in the group until its task ends, so `admit` takes it `escaping into` the group ([0780]). `a` may point at `heard`, a parameter of the function that made the group; a local declared after the group is refused.\n\nProviders. Two concepts say what a provider is:\n\n- A `fibre.scheduler` may run each task to its end inside `admit`, before returning.\n- A `fibre.turns` is a scheduler with `yield`, and promises more: a fibre that yields lets every other unfinished fibre of its provider run before it goes on.\n\nThe blocking host and `fibre.whole` are schedulers. Over either of them, `a` sleeps its 20 milliseconds and is answered first. `stacks.round`, a round of fixed turns from `core/fibre/stacks`, provides `turns`. Give it a clock whose sleep takes a turn for each millisecond, and `b` is answered while `a` waits:\n\n    turning_sleep: (self: turning, span: time.duration) -> none =\n        deadline: u64 = self.reading.val + u64(span)\n        while self.reading.val < deadline do\n            self.runs.yield()\n            self.reading.val += u64(time.milliseconds(1))\n        end while\n    end turning_sleep\n\nOne `ask_both`, three providers, and the answers are `ab`, `ab` and `ba`. So a program written against `scheduler` must be right when every task runs to its end as it is admitted. A program that needs turns says so: `fibre.turns_over` takes an `any fibre.turns`, and handing it the host or `whole` is refused where the group is made, not when a task waits for ever.\n\nChoosing a provider on a hosted system. The choice is made where the roots are minted ([1660]), and the functions below never learn it:\n\n| provider | a call that waits | groups | signals |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `hosted/blocking`, `blocking.new()` | blocks the thread | `scheduler`: each task to its end | none: SIGTERM ends the process |\n| `hosted/events`, `events.over(state, entries)` | lets the other fibres run while epoll or kqueue waits | `turns` | `core/io/signal`'s `signals` |\n\n`events.over` takes a space the caller declares and a round's table, one entry more than the fibres unfinished at once. A signal is an event a fibre waits for with `next_signal`, so only a provider of turns gives one: over the blocking host a fibre waiting for SIGTERM would hold the program before it served anything.\n\nFibres are cooperative. A fibre gives the core away only inside a call to its provider, a `yield` or a call that waits, and nothing preempts it. The fibres of one provider are one execution context: between two such calls no other fibre of it runs, so a module counter or the last error a call left is not raced for. A switch is a full compiler memory boundary, and a fibre never moves to another thread.\n\nA fibre's stack does not grow. In a program that prepares a stack, a function compares its frame with the current stack's limit before it reserves the frame; the few that skip the check, small ones that call nothing, fit in a margin kept for them. Past the limit, the function traps `stack_exhausted` at its own declaration, before it has written below the stack ([1670]):\n\n    main.ldn:15:1: trap: stack_exhausted\n\n- The limit stands a margin above the stack's lowest byte, room for the handler to run in: 640 bytes on x86-64 and arm64, 768 on RV64, 384 on Cortex-M0.\n- A program that prepares no stack has no check, and its code is what it would be without fibres.\n- How deep a task goes depends on the target: `ask` takes up to 4.4 KiB of its stack on RV64 and less on the others, which is why its stacks are 8 KiB.\n- `refine compile --stack-report=PATH` writes each function's frame and the deepest stack its calls can reach, and names the `any` calls, recursion and foreign calls that leave that open. Size a stack from its task's row and the margin.\n- A backing too small for its stacks fails `mem.out_of_memory`, where the group is made or when a task is admitted.\n\nOn one core nothing runs at once, so there fibres are for structure: one takes the next request while another answers this one. A single-core device answers requests one at a time, in the order they arrived, and says `busy` when its queue is full; two answers are never in flight together.\n\nOn Cortex-M0 a fibre runs on the process stack and interrupt handlers on the main one, so a fibre's backing pays for one exception frame, 36 bytes, and the handlers' own frames are the main stack's. A handler never switches: it records what happened, and the provider looks before it waits.\n\nWriting a provider. An application makes a group, and at most a provider, as the round above. `core/fibre/stacks` also holds the switch, `prepare` and `switch` over records a provider keeps, for whoever writes a provider of their own, built on two `compiler` builtins.\n\n- A program over `whole` or the blocking host imports no switch and runs on every target.\n- The switch runs on every target with a native backend.\n- A debugger's backtrace through a switch shows `landin.stack_switch`, and a fibre's frames end at `landin.stack_start`.\n\nThe library reference describes `core/fibre` and `core/fibre/stacks`.\n\nExact rules: spec [1995].
C	1680	Pass the capability, don't track the effect	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1680	Landin has no effect system. A function that does I/O, allocates or reads the clock takes the thing that does it as a parameter: an allocator, an `io` writer, a peripheral handle, a random source. A caller can then hand it an in-memory world or a bounded allocator.\n\nThe parameter list says what a caller supplies, not everything the call can reach:\n\n- Any hosted function may call the public host and heap constructors itself.\n- A driver may make a pointer from an address [0460].\n\nCreating the roots in `main` [1660] is a convention the compiler does not check.\n\nIf you need to know that a call tree does no host I/O, read its calls and imports.\n\nExact rules: spec [1975].
C	1690	One mechanism, read two ways	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1690	Generic code and `any` share one foundation: evidence that a type satisfies a concept. Static generics and runtime dispatch are two readings of one feature, not two features ([1310], [1370]):\n\n- When the compiler knows the concrete evidence, it may specialize the call.\n- Otherwise the call goes through a table, and an `any C` value carries that table with it.
C	1700	Atoms are the same idea wherever they appear	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1700	An atom is identity without payload. Enumerations, error sets, variant tags, register encodings and panic kinds are all uses of atoms, not separate categories. There is no `enum` in the language because there is nothing left for it to be.
C	1710	How a new feature earns its place	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1710	When a program cannot be written cleanly, ask in this order:\n\n| ask, in order | then |\n| --- | --- |\n| can an existing mechanism express it? | a library |\n| can the compiler work it out itself? | no syntax |\n| must the programmer say it, and does saying it generalise or remove another mechanism? | a candidate |\n| does it only solve this one case? | not yet |\n\nA new mechanism should let two old ones leave the building.
C	1720	What Landin promises, plainly	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1720	Landin makes local checks: origins and escape, consumption [0910], reference permission [0430], bounds, conversions and arithmetic. It is not a memory-safe language and not a resource-safe one.\n\nWhat the checks do not cover:\n\n- Pointer-to-integer conversion and the C boundary leave the checked model altogether [0470].\n- A copy taken before a `sink` is not refused [0910].\n- Distinct pointer or computed-index paths may alias across `inout` [0900].\n- Two arenas look the same to the compiler [0860].\n\nThat is a smaller claim than "safe" and a larger one than C's: deliberately unsafe, with static help worth having. `spec.md`'s guarantee register classifies every observable failure boundary the compiler implements, and each new operation joins it.\n\nChecks are on by default. `unchecked` [1120] removes only the checks that entry lists, and only in the region where it is written. It tells the optimizer nothing: it emits fewer checks and gives no later pass a fact to assume. Optimization adds no undefined behavior, no-alias, overflow or floating-point assumption because of it, and keeps scalar results and the order of side effects and traps.
C	1730	Check once, then carry the proof	tour.md	https://www.701.dev/tour.html#1730	A successful check can produce a value that stands for what was checked. A buffer that passed the alignment test becomes a `dma_buffer`, and the DMA interface asks for nothing else. Distinct types, range subtypes and error sets are enough for this; it needs no feature of its own, only the habit.\n\nFor a range subtype, the proof starts with a checked subtype value, not with a guard on an ordinary integer.
C	1740	A source file is an import prelude and declarations in any order	spec.md	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#1740	A source file is a possibly empty import prelude followed by declarations in any order. All reached source files together are the program. Declaration order does not affect name lookup inside a module [0130]: names are collected as a set, and a name may be used above the line that introduces it. Active `linker.library` directives retain canonical source/declaration order for archive resolution (D202). 'public' rides on a declaration and not on a statement [0090]: what a module exports is decided where the module is written, never inside a body.\n\n    program     ::= import_declaration* declaration*\n    import_declaration ::= "import" import_path\n                           ("as" identifier | "(" identifiers ")")?\n    import_path ::= identifier ("/" identifier)*\n    declaration ::= "public"? (atom_declaration | binding | function\n                                | external_function | machine_function | linked_binding\n                                | type_declaration\n                                | concept_declaration)\n                    | conformance_declaration\n                    | fixed_conditional\n                    | option_declaration\n                    | tool_directive\n    option_declaration ::= "option" identifier ":" type "=" expression\n    tool_directive ::= tool_namespace "." identifier\n                       "(" (expression ("," expression)*)? ")"\n    tool_namespace ::= "compiler" | "assembler" | "linker"\n    fixed_conditional ::= "fixed" "if" expression "then" declaration*\n                          ("elsif" expression "then" declaration*)*\n                          ("else" declaration*)? "end" "if"\n    atom_declaration ::= identifiers ":" "atom"\n    identifiers ::= identifier ("," identifier)*
C	1750	A source file is bytes	spec.md	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#1750	A source file is bytes, a line ends three ways, and space separates tokens. A span in a diagnostic names a byte, and every later stage must be able to point at the same one, so the lexical rules are written over bytes. A line ends at LF, at CR followed by LF, or at a CR that is not followed by LF, and a file need not end with one at all. Text inside a literal or a comment may be any UTF-8 [0260]; nothing outside them may be. Space is a space byte, a tab, a line end or a comment [1780], and any run of them may sit between two tokens. Two tokens whose spellings would run together into one longer token need at least one, which is the whole of the rule: 'mut x' is two tokens and 'mutx' is one name. Otherwise space carries no meaning, and no rule below this layer mentions it. A line end therefore never terminates a statement: when the token after it can continue the expression or selection before it, it does. This is [1060]'s one-line rule read from the other direction. One `(` is read by where it stands: a `(` that begins a line, and whose matching `)` is followed by `:=`, begins [0990]'s destructuring binding rather than a call of the line above, because a call is no place and that reading could never derive.\n\n    space       ::= " " | "\\t" | line_end | comment\n    line_end    ::= "\\n" | "\\r\\n" | "\\r"
C	1760	Identifiers are lower case, and no identifier is a keyword	spec.md	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#1760	Identifiers are lower case, and no identifier is a keyword. Every name in the language has this one shape: types, functions, bindings and fields alike, which is why the tour never needs to say which case a thing is written in. Two rules narrow it. A word the keyword rule spells is that keyword and never a name, so 'if' is not available as a binding; that one is the tokeniser's. The other is in the rule itself: a name that starts with '_' needs something after it, so the lone '_' is the discard of [1020] and nothing may be called it. The kernel reserves fifty words; the reserved set of the whole language is larger, and each word joins it when its construct is enabled in the language. Once reserved, it is a keyword in every program, even one that does not use that construct. Type names are not among them: u32 and bool are names the kernel predeclares, and a program may declare the same spelling [0120]; [1790] says which of the two a type position names.\n\nControl words cannot name bindings, types, functions, parameters, results, fields, atoms, import bindings or loop and block labels. In particular, `begin = 10` and `begin: i32 = 10` are invalid; `(begin)` is not an identifier escape. A longer spelling such as `begin_value` remains an ordinary identifier. D225 records the reservation and its compatibility consequence.\n\n    identifier  ::= lower (lower | digit | "_")*\n                  | "_" (lower | digit | "_")+\n    lower       ::= "a" ... "z"\n    digit       ::= "0" ... "9"\n    keyword     ::= "addr" | "alignof" | "and" | "any" | "atom" | "begin"\n                  | "break" | "complete" | "continue" | "dec" | "defer" | "do"\n                  | "else" | "elsif" | "end" | "escaping" | "extern" | "fail"\n                  | "false" | "fixed" | "for" | "from" | "if" | "import" | "in"\n                  | "inc" | "inout" | "loop" | "match" | "mut" | "none" | "not"\n                  | "or" | "ptr" | "public" | "return" | "sink" | "sizeof"\n                  | "struct" | "then" | "true" | "try" | "type" | "unchecked"\n                  | "undo" | "uninit" | "when" | "while" | "with" | "zeroed"
C	1770	The kernel's literals include characters, floats and text	spec.md	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#1770	The kernel's literals are integers, floats, characters, quoted text, the two booleans, and contextual `zeroed` and `uninit`. Integer literals are untyped and take the type of their context [0190], defaulting to i32 with none [0200]; the bases and the separator are [0220]'s. Each integer digit run starts and ends in a digit of its base; any internal run of underscores separates digits. A number ends where its spelling ends: a letter, digit or underscore directly after one belongs to it, so `1u64` or `1.5f32` is one malformed literal rather than a number and a name (D245). `uninit` is D152's restricted private inline-array field initializer; it reserves storage without assigning an item image. It has no stand-alone value type. `zeroed` has no type of its own: [0540] gives it the all-bits-zero image of a directly supplied initializer, assignment or field-label context. D27--D30 establish fixed-array contexts, D39--D43 scalar contexts, D49 and D57--D59 whole array-field and ordinary-struct contexts, D62 the depth-one indexed field place, D64--D67 labelled struct fields and static images, D75/D76 variant-bearing struct storage and case payloads, and D87 depth-one nested ordinary storage. It remains refused where no enabled construct supplies that context. D161 admits [0260]'s quoted literal when its direct context is a read-only `[]u8`; the unescaped source content is UTF-8 [1750], and [0270]'s byte escapes are decoded into that view. Raw text [0280] takes the same direct byte-slice context by D164, but interprets no escape and removes a line-leading closing delimiter's indentation. The maximal opening quote run chooses the delimiter width; only a later run can close it. Adjacent quotes therefore cannot encode an empty raw literal. Intervening line endings remain content under D164; empty text uses `""`. D181 adds `utf8`, `utf16` and `cstring` contexts and makes `utf8` the contextless default. A scalar escape is encoded as UTF-8 or UTF-16 for those views; a byte escape remains exclusive to `[]u8`. D162 admits [0210]'s decimal float with [0220]'s optional exponent. D166 adds [0230]'s hexadecimal fraction and required binary exponent. D167 admits [0240]'s type-qualified `infinity` and `nan` values for f32 and f64. D163 admits [0250]'s single-quoted character as exactly one Unicode scalar value of fixed type `u32`. C	1810	Statements do one thing each, and only exits carry 'when'	spec.md	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#1810	Statements do one thing each, and only exits carry 'when'. Assignment is a statement and never an expression [0390]; there is no '++', and 'inc' and 'dec' are statements too [0400]; discarding a result is written out [1020]; the one-line form of every construct is [1060]. 'when' rides on an exit and on nothing else, which is what keeps a conditional statement from having two spellings. `return` carries no value. A named return is assigned like any other place and `return` leaves [0930], which is why the kernel needs no second way to say what a function hands back. `fail` is the other early exit [0970]: it carries one payload-free atom on the declared channel and does not read the successful named return. A direct or selected call, with positional or named arguments, is a statement as well as an expression, because a function returning none has nothing to bind. That is the only call the position takes: one that hands a result back is refused there, recovered or not, because [1020] wants a result discarded on purpose rather than by omission, and `_ = call` is how it is written (D244). A labelled application in this position must resolve to a function call; the shared construction syntax still requires its ordinary value context and does not make constructed values standalone statements. A standalone `try call` explicitly propagates its failure and discards any successful result, whatever its shape. `defer` and `undo` each register one call when their statement is reached and evaluate the callee and arguments only on applicable exits from the lexical block [1100] [1110]. They are statements rather than expressions and so cannot supply a block's final value. A match is D77's exhaustive tag selection or [0640]'s exhaustive atom-set selection. A variant subject is one directly selected variant part and each case arm carries one statement or one expression; a bare `begin` block makes a multi-statement arm. D78 extends the arm with positional payload bindings. An `if`, a `match`, and a bare `begin` block retain their statement forms and also occupy expression positions under [1820]. Used as a statement, one takes no value from its branches, so a branch, an `elsif` or `else` arm, a `match` arm or the block itself, that ends with a value is refused, as a call standing alone that hands one back is: nothing would take the value, and [1020] drops none by omission. The refusal names the two routes, a branch written as a statement and, where the value followed a call's `else` that divided an `if` [1820], the recovery parenthesised or bound. A place is [1820]'s indexed selection, so a binding, a field of a struct, or an enabled array element is written and stepped exactly as the binding holding it is. What may be written is [1900]'s and not this rule's: a field is writable when the binding it belongs to is.\n\nD165 enables [0390]'s compound forms. Each reads the selected place, applies the corresponding [1820] binary operator to that value and the right-hand expression, then writes the result back. The place is evaluated once before the right-hand expression [0410], must already be assigned [1910], and needs the same write permission as `=` [1900]. The operator keeps its ordinary type, known-operand, trapping and wrapping rules.\n\nThe kernel admits the statement forms of [1130], [1140], [1170], [1180], and [1190]. An unconditional loop tests nothing; a `while` condition is evaluated before every iteration and must be `bool`. `break` transfers to the point after its target loop and `continue` transfers to that loop's next condition test (or next unconditional iteration). Without a label they target the nearest loop; with one they target the nearest enclosing loop, or labelled bare block, carrying that ordinary name. A labelled loop or block closes with its label. A block is left only by a plain `break`: `continue` naming one and `break with` targeting one are refused (D234). Their optional `when` condition is evaluated once and must be `bool`; its false edge continues with the following statement. Both transfers leave every lexical block between the statement and the loop edge, so [1100]'s `defer` runs and [1110]'s `undo` does not. A conditional loop's optional `complete` block runs only when its condition becomes false; a `break` skips it. After a loop, a name is definitely assigned when it is assigned on every edge that leaves the loop: a `while`'s false test and a `for`'s exhaustion, through `complete` when there is one, and every `break` (D430). `break with` and value-producing loops are D158's extension. D159 enables the integer-range form of `for`: both bounds are evaluated once, from left to right, and have one integer type. `a..<b` visits the ascending values for which the element is less than `b`; `a..b` also visits `b`. Either form is empty when its first value is already beyond its last. The element binding is an immutable copy with the range's type; an optional index is an immutable `usize` beginning at zero. `continue` advances both before the next test, and the inclusive form completes at its maximum integer endpoint without first overflowing it. D160 enables collection traversal over a slice or a fixed array: the source is evaluated once, the element binding is a place in that storage rather than a copy, and the optional index is an immutable `usize` beginning at zero. The element is writable over `[]mut T` and over a fixed array held in a place the body could assign; over `[]T` and over any other array it is read-only [1160]. A body that writes the storage by index observes the write through the element, and the reverse. Elements that are themselves fixed arrays or slices retain their complete shape under D178, including when copied out through a loop value. An `any C` element retains its erased identity and evidence under D179. A source that would need [1320]'s iterable evidence is enabled by D180 when its type is a struct or `any C` and exactly one conformance to the unambiguous concept named `iterable` supplies `Cur`, `Item`, and [1320]'s four exact, infallible signatures. The source expression is evaluated once and copied into private traversal state. `first` is called once. Each test calls `at_end`; a false result calls `item` before entering the body. Fallthrough and `continue` run applicable cleanup and then call `next`; a `break` runs applicable cleanup and skips `next`. The optional immutable `usize` index begins at zero and advances with each `next` call. `try for` additionally admits the exact `fallible_iterable` concept with associated `Cur`, `Item`, and atom error set. Its four providers declare that same error set. A failed provider runs active failure cleanup and propagates its atom; it neither enters `complete` nor calls a later provider. When both conformances exist, `try for` selects `fallible_iterable`; ordinary `for` continues to select only `iterable`.\n\nThe cursor keeps its complete type identity between calls. The element is an immutable copy of the exact `Item` result, not an alias into the source, and therefore carries only the origin allowed by [1320]'s source-free result. An `any C` source and an `any C` item each retain their own erased concept and evidence identities; neither two-cell value is ever interpreted as a slice. Missing or ambiguous concept identity, or missing, ambiguous, or non-exact iterable evidence, is L0348. Integer ranges and fixed-array or slice storage traversal retain D159--D160 and D178--D179 unchanged.\n\nD184 admits the exact `utf8`, `utf16`, and `cstring` identities through three intrinsic conformances to [1320]'s four-operation traversal contract. These do not search, add, reorder, or expose a source-declared evidence table, and an ordinary slice or pointer does not acquire them from its representation. Each uses exact `usize` Cur and `u32` Item identities. Cur is a private physical code-unit offset: bytes for `utf8` and `cstring`, UTF-16 code units for `utf16`. Item is an immutable copied Unicode scalar with no reference origin. It is not an encoded subview and is never an alias into the retained read-only source.\n\nThe source expression is evaluated once and its complete carrier and origin are retained before conceptual `first` produces offset zero. Every test calls `at_end`; a false result calls `item`, which decodes exactly one validated scalar before the body. Fallthrough and `continue` run applicable cleanup and then `next`, which advances Cur by that scalar's physical width and advances the optional immutable `usize` loop index by one. `break` skips `next`. For `utf8` and `utf16`, `at_end` is Cur equal to the retained code-unit length. For `cstring`, it is the first zero byte; that terminator is not an Item, so an embedded U+0000 ends the C string in the same way as its trailing terminator.\n\nD187 enables [1120]'s statement form. `unchecked begin` opens a region and `end unchecked` closes it. D225 reserves both opener words under [1760]; neither can name a binding or label. The region is a lexical block with its own scope and it is not an expression: the block forms that also occupy expression positions are the `if`, the `match` and the bare `begin` named above, and this is not one of them. Nesting is idempotent and there is no counter-word. A [1100] `defer` or [1110] `undo` call is checked as its registration is written and not as the exit that runs it, so a `return`, `break` or `fail` inside a region keeps every edge of a cleanup registered outside one. Which check edges the region removes, which it never removes, and what a removed one leaves behind are D187's.\n\nThese intrinsic providers declare no atom error. D181 validates `utf8` and `utf16` views, and D183 preserves that validity across text slices, so a well-formed view of either identity does not trap during traversal. A literal `cstring` is also valid UTF-8.
