D	274	The library says what it does	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d274-the-library-says-what-it-does	Chosen: a module is named by a short noun or a conventional abbreviation. `core/small` is `core/spill`, whose type is `spill.list`, and `core/failing` is `core/fault`, whose type is `fault.injector`. `core/mem.failing`, a bump arena with a budget that counted only successes, is withdrawn: `fault.new` over `mem.arena_over`, `fault.over` since D288, is the one injector, and its budget spends a permit on every call that reaches the provider, including one the arena refuses.\n\nA name says what the declaration does. `mem.reserve`, a view over caller bytes, is `mem.storage_over`, so that `reserve` always allocates; `mem.initialized` is `mem.length`; `raw_full` and `raw_not_empty` are `mem.full` and `mem.not_empty`; `transfer_zero_prefix` is `transfer_prefix` for any item size, and `drain_zero_prefix` is `mem.clear`. The equality entry is `equal`, beside `less`, and `text.eq` is `text.equal`. `text.ordinal`, a byte offset that would index `utf8` as a scalar count, is `text.offset`; `text.at`, which lends nothing, is `text.cursor`; `text.written` is `text.prefix` and reports `past_end`. `diag.note_at`, a copy, is `diag.get`; `diag.to` is `diag.stream`; `diag.stored` is `diag.length`. The pool's counters are `allocations`, `frees` and `rejected_frees`, so `frees` no longer reads as the number of free slots.\n\nThe map's `capacity` is D269's room: the entries that fit before the next new key rebuilds the table, three quarters of its `slots`. A new key taking a free bucket meets the pressure check with tombstones counted. The table is rebuilt at its size while its live entries with the new key fit in half its capacity, and grows otherwise, so tombstones make up at least half of any pressure that rebuilds in place and two rebuilds are at least half a capacity of operations apart. Hashes are spread with MurmurHash3's finalizer before reduction, since the shipped integer hashes are the identity. `reserve(n)` allocates the smallest table whose capacity holds `n`, and counts the tombstones as D379 says. Release clears a storage's prefix in constant time rather than withdrawing each item.\n\n`spill.list` drops the `zeroable` constraint D152 had left with no effect, so it stores pointers and atom-bearing records. Public signatures spell the public alias of a private type. `mem.aligned_offset`, the bump arithmetic, and `text.valid`, the UTF-8 check `from_bytes` makes, are public; the hosted heap's state is opaque. A generic routine's signature that applies one of its own parameters as a type, as `storage: storage(item)` does, is L0304 at the declaration, called or not, as the same application in a plain signature is, and a name in it that names nothing is that signature's L0304 or L0201 rather than a failed match that let the program reach the lowering.
D	275	The compiler finds its library beside itself	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d275-the-compiler-finds-its-library-beside-itself	Chosen: the library ships with the compiler and the compiler finds it. An installation is a prefix holding `bin/refine` and `lib/landin` with the three namespaces in it; the flake's packages and the release archive are laid out so. `refine` asks the host for its own executable's directory, with links resolved, and takes the first of `../lib/landin` and, for a compiler built in a checkout, the checkout six directories up that holds `core`. `--library=DIR` names another: a build that stages only the library modules it reaches, as the firmware lanes do, names its staged tree, so the sources it hashes and debugs are the ones compiled. A directory holding none of the three is refused as a bad root is. The library root follows every `--root`; an import of `core`, `hosted` or `platform` resolves from it alone, and one of anything else from the roots in their order. With no `--root`, the named files are still one module and reach the library and whatever it imports. A `--root` naming the library's own directory is searched once, under the user's spelling, so a build that names the checkout records the paths it always did. `refine version` and its JSON name the library, and the language server finds it the same way. A user's home root and every other default stay with the Companion tool and ecosystem. Since D366 a named root holding a module the library supplies is warned about, with `--library` as the way to compile against it.
D	276	The hosted operating-system boundary is library source	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d276-the-hosted-operating-system-boundary-is-library-source	Chosen: the compiler names no host routine but one. The public module `platform/libc` declares the C library beneath the hosted providers as ordinary `extern(c)` imports: `open`, variadic as C declares it, `read` and `write` returning `isize`, `close`, `strlen`, `malloc` returning an `allocation` union whose empty arm is the atom `no_allocation`, `free`, `stat`, and `errno_cell`, linked to `__errno_location` on Linux and to `__error` on Darwin and FreeBSD by `fixed if compiler.os`, which `hosted/system` reads on Darwin and FreeBSD. The errno constants `eperm`, `enoent`, `eintr`, `eacces`, `erofs` and `enotdir` (D287), the flags `o_rdonly` and `o_wronly`, the per-system `o_creat` and `o_trunc`, `timespec`, the per-system `file_status` record and `file_status_size` are source declarations selected by `compiler.os` and the C ABI and checked against each system's C headers. Like every hosted module it is refused on firmware (D267). `hosted/system` and `hosted/heap` reach the host only through it; the 0666 creation mode stays in `hosted/system` as provider policy. On Linux `hosted/system` and `hosted/heap` use `platform/linux` instead (D279, D282), and since D297 both reach the host only through `platform/posix`; every `platform/libc` declaration is bodyless, so a program naming none of them needs no C library.\n\n`hosted/system` holds the argument root in two module cells, and since D288 the process's last-error cell in a third, and defines in source the public C routine `_landin_host_initialize_arguments`, whose signature is `(count: i32, escaping values: ptr ptr u8) -> none`, to which D311 adds the environment's table as a third parameter. D208's rules are unchanged: the first nonnegative-count, non-null-table call establishes the root without copying; an identical repeat is a no-op; an invalid call, use before initialization or replacement traps; the published count is `max(argc - 1, 0)` without `argv[0]`. Indexed lookup reads the `argv` entry by address and traps on a null entry. Each of these traps is the library's own `compiler.unreachable()` (D278), so a panic handler receives `unreachable` at a site in `hosted/system` where the bridge reported it at a synthetic site zero.\n\nThe compiler's one hosted contract is that call. When a hosted entry is selected and the program defines a C routine with the link symbol `_landin_host_initialize_arguments`, the hosted `main` calls it with its incoming `argc` and `argv`, and since D311 its `envp`, before its body. A program that defines none calls nothing, so a hosted program that never imports `hosted/system` links without it. Beside a hosted entry every declaration carrying that symbol must be exactly `extern(c) (i32, ptr ptr u8) -> none`, with `escaping` immaterial, or it is refused with L0347. The symbol is an ordinary default-visibility global rather than a hidden one, and a C-owned `main` still calls it explicitly. The names `strlen`, `malloc`, `free`, `open`, `read`, `write`, `close` and the errno accessor are no longer set aside for the backend: they are `platform/libc`'s imports, and ordinary symbol allocation keeps a private Landin definition of the same spelling from capturing them.
D	277	The hosted heap over-allocates in source	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d277-the-hosted-heap-over-allocates-in-source	Chosen: `hosted/heap` performs the same over-allocation in source over `platform/libc`'s `malloc` and `free` (D276). It asks `malloc` for the request plus `alignment - 1` bytes and one `usize` word, refusing with `mem.out_of_memory` before the call an addition that would overflow or a total above `(0 -% 1) >> 1`, the host's `PTRDIFF_MAX`. It aligns within the block and writes the address `malloc` returned into the word before the aligned block a byte at a time, because for an alignment that is not a multiple of the word the word is unaligned; release reads it back the same way and passes it to `free`. A `no_allocation` result is `mem.out_of_memory`. D195's contract is unchanged: every `usize` alignment is accepted, zero and one meaning byte alignment, and a zero-byte request returns a distinct non-null token. On Linux, D282 replaces this provider, and D300 replaces it on Darwin and FreeBSD too.
D	278	An explicit trap is a `compiler` builtin	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d278-an-explicit-trap-is-a-compiler-builtin	Chosen: `compiler.unreachable()` on the toolchain module [1560], with no import and no keyword. It types as a call of a `() -> noreturn` routine: a statement, the value of an `if` or `match` arm, or the end of any path, and definite assignment, named results and `noreturn` bodies treat it as not returning. It takes no arguments; misuse is refused as the same misuse of such a routine would be, L0327 for an argument, L0331 for a value and L0329 for `try` or `else`, and naming it without calling it is L0203. Reaching it raises `unreachable` through D232 at its own numbered site, with the panic map entry a compiler check has, or the terminal default trap when no handler is selected. It is a statement and not a check, so `unchecked` never removes it. It is available on every target, firmware included. `hosted/system` stops on every misuse of the argument root with it.
D	279	Linux's system interface is `platform/linux`, with no C library	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d279-linux-s-system-interface-is-platform-linux-with-no-c-library	Chosen: the public module `platform/linux` declares Linux's system calls in source, inside `fixed if compiler.os == linux`. It declares nothing on Darwin and FreeBSD, and because Landin has no conditional import, `hosted/system` and `hosted/heap` import it on every hosted system. Each call is one ordinary assembly block: x86-64 `syscall` with the number in rax, arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9, and rcx and r11 overwritten; arm64 `svc #0` with the number in x8 and arguments in x0–x5; RV64 `ecall` with the number in x17 (a7) and arguments in x10–x15 (a0–a5). rax, x0 or a0 carries the result. Its wrappers are `read`, `write`, `openat`, `close`, `statx`, `mmap`, `munmap` and the `noreturn` `exit_group`, to which D294 adds `getdents64`, `mkdirat` and `unlinkat`, a public raw `system_call` and every call's number. A failure is minus its errno in the result; there is no errno cell. The `*at` calls take `at_fdcwd`, and `statx`'s `file_status` is the kernel's one 256-byte record on every architecture. Every public routine has the link name `_landin_linux_` followed by its own name, so none of them replaces the C library's function of the same spelling when a program also links libc.\n\nThe module owns the process entry. `_landin_start` is a naked routine that clears the frame pointer (and the link register on arm64 and RV64), aligns the stack where the ABI requires it and calls `_landin_start_main` with the initial stack's address. That routine reads argc, argv, envp and the auxiliary vector after envp's terminator, keeps the environment and auxiliary roots for `environment()` and `auxiliary(tag)`, and calls C's view of the program's entry: a bodyless `extern(c) link(symbol: "main")` of `(i32, ptr ptr u8, ptr ptr u8) -> i32`, which the checker admits beside the native hosted `main` as the same symbol. It ends the process with `exit_group` and main's result. No C library initialisation runs and no thread-local storage exists. Under `--link=libc` (D280) the C runtime starts the program, and the argument initializer passes `platform/linux.adopt_start` the `argc`, `argv` and `envp` C's `main` was given (D311). It takes the environment and the auxiliary vector after `envp`'s null only when the tables have the initial stack's layout: `argv` above the calling frame, `envp` directly after `argv`'s null, at least one string and every string above the tables, AT_NULL within 64 entries below the lowest string with every tag below 4096, AT_PAGESZ a power of two of at least 4096, and AT_RANDOM's sixteen bytes between the vector and the lowest string. Nothing above the lowest string is read. Otherwise `environment()` is `no_environment`, `auxiliary` finds nothing and `page_size()` falls back to 4096. The alternatives were the C library's `getauxval`, which a static link would refuse with L0500 since nothing tells the library its link mode; `PR_GET_AUXV`, Linux 6.4's; `/proc/self/auxv`, which needs `/proc`; and trusting any `envp`, which `setenv` may have moved and a C `main` may have built, sending reads into unmapped memory. `abi/auxiliary-from-c` pins the adoption and each refusal.\n\nNaked routines are admitted on hosted x86-64, arm64 and RV64 for this entry. Their text is the routine's whole body followed by a trap, keeps [1990]'s uniform text rules except that it may transfer control, and takes no operands. Their CFI marks the return address undefined, so a debugger's stack ends at `_landin_start`.
D	280	A hosted Linux executable links statically by default	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d280-a-hosted-linux-executable-links-statically-by-default	Chosen: `--link=static|libc` chooses how a hosted executable is linked. Linux defaults to `static`: the driver loads `platform/linux` from the compiler's library (D275) and links with `-nostdlib -static -no-pie -Wl,-e,_landin_start` and `-Wl,--gc-sections`, with no C runtime object, no C library and no dynamic loader. `--link=libc` keeps the C runtime's link. Darwin and FreeBSD reach their systems only through their C libraries and link with `libc`, their only mode; `--link=static` there is a usage error, as is `--link` on a target with no hosted system or without `--emit=exe` or `--emit=asm`. A static request is refused with L0500 before any tool runs, naming `--link=libc`, when no library holding `platform/linux` was found, when the program asks for `linker.library`, or when it refers to a bodyless external symbol no program item defines. The refusal counts only what the entry reaches, since every backend collects per-item sections (D303), and names each missing symbol with the routine that refers to it, `dlopen, which platform/posix's open_library refers to`, so a program loading a library learns which of its calls asked for the C library (D336). `-v`, `--dry-run` and the build report name the mode. An emitted `.s` under static mode includes `platform/linux` and still links under a C driver. `refine check` gives the refusals of a C library asked for and of a C symbol nothing defines, as compiling does (D443).
D	281	RV64's system call has the standing of `syscall` and `svc`	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d281-rv64-s-system-call-has-the-standing-of-syscall-and-svc	Chosen: an ordinary RV64 assembly block admits `ecall`. Like x86-64's `syscall` and arm64's `svc`, it enters the kernel and returns to the next instruction, so the block stays straight-line. `ebreak`, `c.ebreak`, `mret` and the other control transfers stay refused.
D	282	The Linux heap keeps size classes over its own mappings	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d282-the-linux-heap-keeps-size-classes-over-its-own-mappings	Chosen: on Linux `hosted/heap` maps its own memory, now through `platform/posix`, which makes `platform/linux`'s calls (D279, D297). It keeps eight size classes from 32 to 4096 bytes. A class with no free slot maps a 64 KiB chunk and links its slots into a free list; a freed slot returns to its class's list and is handed out before any new chunk is mapped; chunks are never unmapped. A request whose extent exceeds 4096 bytes is a mapping of its own, rounded to the page size and unmapped when freed. Two words precede every block, the slot's or mapping's start and its extent, at the multiple of the word at or below a header before the block, so they are aligned whatever the block's alignment and every `usize` alignment works, a power of two or not; a zero-byte request is a distinct token. An addition that would overflow, or an extent above `PTRDIFF_MAX` less the page rounding, is `mem.out_of_memory` before any state changes, as is a failed mapping. The provider was single-threaded; D502 puts its classes behind a lock once a thread has started. D300 makes it the heap of every hosted system.
D	283	Zero-image data are laid out smallest first	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d283-zero-image-data-are-laid-out-smallest-first	Chosen: zero-image module data are laid out smallest first, ties in item order, on x86-64 and RV64, so one object as large as RIP-relative or `auipc` addressing reaches cannot push another datum out of reach. arm64's ±4 GiB reach is unchanged. The implicit `platform/linux` roots of a static link (D280) exposed it.
D	284	A static Linux executable holds the processor to its level in the entry	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d284-a-static-linux-executable-holds-the-processor-to-its-level-in-the-entry	Chosen: `platform/linux`'s `_landin_start_main` holds the processor to the executable's level before `main` runs. The level is the compile-time `compiler.feature` facts: `fixed if` selects, for each level, its name, its checks and its `check_level`, and the baseline's `check_level` is empty, so a baseline executable runs no check. On x86-64 the check reads `cpuid` leaves 1, 7 and 0x80000001 for D255's v2, v3 and v4 features in D255's order, and above v2 requires the system to save the state the level uses: OSXSAVE and XCR0's SSE and AVX bits for v3, and the opmask and ZMM bits for v4, read with `xgetbv`. On arm64 it reads AT_HWCAP for armv8.1-a's atomics, CRC32 and RDM. On RV64 it asks `riscv_hwprobe` for Zba, and a kernel that cannot answer does not confirm the level; no Linux interface reports XTheadBa, so it is not checked. A processor without a feature writes one line to standard error, `landin: this executable needs LEVEL, and the processor lacks FEATURE`, and ends the process with status 127, the status glibc's loader gives when it refuses an executable's ISA level, so a static and a libc build of one program end alike on one machine. Under `--link=libc` the C runtime starts the program, the loader's note applies on x86-64, and the entry check does not run. `level`, `read_cpu_words` and `missing_feature` are public, so the check can be tested on injected words.
D	285	Standard input is the process concept's third stream	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d285-standard-input-is-the-process-concept-s-third-stream	Chosen: `process` gains `input: (self: provider) -> (stream: file)`, taking the handle by value as every I/O entry does (D288), read through `reader` like any opened file: zero from a nonempty read is the end of input. `hosted/system` answers descriptor 0. `core/io.memory` answers handle 0 over the caller's `input` bytes, the argument `memory_over` takes after the argument table; the `read_limit` and `fail_read_at` of its `io.memory_space` apply to it as to a file, and closing it ends it. The five free functions `io.input`, `io.out`, `io.err`, `io.argument_count` and `io.argument_at` take the handle `in` as `host: provider`, as `io.read`, `io.write` and the `files` functions do, so a caller always passes the handle, `io.write(host, io.out(host), ...)`, and nothing is locked; `argument_at` lends its result `from host`, and two arguments lent from one handle are live at once. A runtime or ABI fixture names the file its program reads as standard input with `stdin:`, relative to the fixture and below it; without the key every lane gives the program an empty input, never the harness's own. A fixture that reads standard input is hosted: firmware refuses it by name (D267) and the memory provider runs the same routine there.
D	286	Decimals of every unsigned width, over bytes	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d286-decimals-of-every-unsigned-width-over-bytes	Chosen: `text.write_u64` and `text.write_usize` have `write_u32`'s shape: they count the digits by division and report `no_space` before writing. `text.parse_u32`, `parse_u64` and `parse_usize` read decimal digits from `[]u8` and report `invalid_number` or `number_overflow`, whichever the scan from the left meets first; `usize` is the target's width, so firmware parses 32 bits. `to_u32` over `utf8` parses the text's bytes. `core/diag`'s position writer, the derived hosted program and the fizzbuzz and fannkuch writers use them; the configuration parser keeps its recursive digit parser, which the debugger sessions stop in. D355 retires the slice writers: the builder's appends are the one decimal writer, and the parses live with the signed and hexadecimal ones.
D	287	A path through a file is not found	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d287-a-path-through-a-file-is-not-found	Chosen: ENOTDIR, 20 on Linux, Darwin and FreeBSD, is `not_found` from `open_read` and `open_write`, and an output path that meets it is absent, so `same_file` answers false. `last_errno` still holds 20 for a caller that needs the difference.
D	288	A service is a handle, made from state its caller declares	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d288-a-service-is-a-handle-made-from-state-its-caller-declares	Chosen: a value that is edited, a container or a bounded log, stays `inout`. A service is a handle: a small copyable record, passed `in`, that refers to its state through a pointer and whose lifetime is checked once, where it is made from that state. `mem.allocator`'s `alloc`, `grow` and `free` and every entry of `core/io`'s `reader`, `writer`, `files` and `process` take `self: provider` by value, and a conformance changes state through the handle. Free functions take `memory: provider` for an allocator and `host: provider` for I/O, passed `in`, and `core/vec`, `core/map`, `core/tree` and `core/spill` take `memory: provider`; a call is spelled as before.\n\nCaller-owned state is a type the caller declares `zeroed`; `over` takes it `inout`, fills it and returns the handle `from` it. `mem.arena_space` and `mem.arena` have `arena_over(inout state, escaping base, size) -> (handle: arena from state, base)` and `arena_over_unchecked` with a plain `base`; `pool.space` and `pool.provider` have `pool.over(inout state, base, extent, slot_size, slot_count, slot_alignment, bookkeeping)`, which reports `mem.out_of_memory` before changing the state; `fault.space` and `fault.injector(P)` have `fault.over(inout state, inner, allowed_attempts)`; `region.space(fixed capacity)` and `region.region(P)` have `region.over(inout state, parent)` and `region.release(inout state, parent)`, a capacity of zero growing the ledger through the parent and a positive one holding that many records in the state; and `io.memory_space` and `io.memory` have `memory_over(inout state, files, arguments, input, output, errors)`. `io.memory_space` is public, so its limits, failure points and counters may be read and set while the handle lives; the handles are opaque. A state type holds only scalars, because `zeroed` has no image for a pointer, a slice or a pointer union (L0328), so a reference the caller supplies lives in the handle. Since the handle is `from` its state, returning it past that state is L0314, and `release`, which takes the state `inout`, is L0315 while the handle is still used; using the handle is an `in` use and locks nothing.\n\nA provider stacked on another holds a copy of the other's handle: the region, the injector, `io.writer_of`'s lent writer, `writer_of(host: any world) -> (adapter: lent_writer from host)`, and `diag.stream(host: any io.writer, where_to: io.file) -> (result: streaming from host)`, which takes both by value. `region.release` takes the parent again because a zeroable state cannot hold the parent's handle (L0328), and keeping the parent in caller state through an `escaping` parameter would refuse every frame-local parent with L0314. The `diag.log` concept keeps `self: ptr mut logger`, because a bounded log is an edited value. Process-wide state belongs to the process, so its handles borrow nothing and are bound without `mut`: `system.new()` returns a handle holding the argument table, its count and the process's last-error cell, `heap.new()` is unchanged, and the Linux heap's size classes are module state (D282). An erased capability is built from the address of a handle binding, `any(addr host)`, which D289 dispatches; an immutable binding suffices.\n\nThe last error is the one value the system provider writes on behalf of its caller, so the handle names the cell it records into, `failure: ptr mut i32`, and `system.last_errno(host)` reads that cell. Every handle from `system.new()` shares the process's cell, a private module `mut` of `hosted/system`. `system.over(inout state: system.space) -> (handle: system from state)` fills a caller-declared, zeroable `system.space` holding one `failure: i32` and returns a handle that records its last error there instead, for a C thread calling into Landin or a library that keeps its own detail. Either handle shares the process's arguments and descriptors, and either traps before the argument root exists. D207's thread-local meaning is therefore kept by ownership until thread-local storage exists: a thread over its own cell reads only its own failures.\n\nAn allocation still borrows nothing from its allocator: [0810]'s integer conversion is kept. A block returned `from self` and kept in a container's `inout` storage would be L0314, and making the handle `escaping` to allow it would refuse every handle over frame-local state.
D	289	An erased entry may take a record `self` by value	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d289-an-erased-entry-may-take-a-record-self-by-value	Chosen: an entry whose first parameter is `self: t`, taken by value, is object-safe when the conformance's `t` is a record. Dispatch passes the pair's data pointer as the record's address carrier, the one D94 gives a by-value aggregate argument, and the callee copies the handle from it, so the provider changes state only through the pointers the handle holds. A scalar `t` taken by value has no such carrier and is L0342. A by-value entry writes nothing through the pair, so it asks no mutable permission: a read-only pointer builds the `any`, and `any(addr host)` over an immutable binding is accepted, while D146's construction rule still holds for a `ptr mut t` entry. The pair still erases a pointer, never a value (D145), so `any(host)` of the handle itself is L0342. Hidden `t` still appears nowhere else in the entry, the pair carries the origin of its pointer operand as D146 says, and a result lent `from self` keeps the erased value's origin. With this, `any mem.allocator` and the four I/O concepts are object-safe over a record provider.
D	290	A generic `from` asks nothing of a source whose instance type holds no reference	Decisions: Lifetime, escape and allocation	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d290-a-generic-from-asks-nothing-of-a-source-whose-instance-type-holds-no-reference	Chosen: in a generic instance (D138), a `from` name whose parameter's declared type is a type formal asks nothing of that parameter when the instance's type for it holds no reference: such an argument has no origin to supply, and the clause is compared over its other names. Where the instance's type holds a reference, the name binds as written and the exact comparison applies. A parameter of any other type keeps the exact rule, so naming a reference-free one is still L0316. `region.over(state, parent) -> (handle: region(P) from state, parent)` (D288) is the case: a pool's handle carries references into its backing that the region must keep, and `heap.new()`'s handle carries none.
D	291	A view taken again through an `inout` call ends the old one at its assignment	Decisions: Lifetime, escape and allocation	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d291-a-view-taken-again-through-an-inout-call-ends-the-old-one-at-its-assignment	Chosen: the old view ends at that assignment, so it is not in use while the call runs, unless the call's recovery can `break` or `continue` past the assignment. On such an edge the binding keeps the old view, a later read of it is a use, and the `inout` call is L0315.
D	292	A cleanup on a return or failure edge has no later statement to conflict with	Decisions: Lifetime, escape and allocation	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d292-a-cleanup-on-a-return-or-failure-edge-has-no-later-statement-to-conflict-with	Chosen: on a return or failure edge the deferred call is checked against what is live on that edge, and no statement after the return or failure runs there, so a handle used later on the fall-through path is not in use. On the fall-through exit the cleanup runs after the handle's last use, as it always did.
D	293	A directory is a value read through a fifth concept	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d293-a-directory-is-a-value-read-through-a-fifth-concept	Chosen: `io.directories` is a fifth concept, outside `world`, with `open_directory`, `read_entry`, `entry_size`, `close_directory`, `make_directory`, `remove_file` and `remove_directory`; the listing consumer has to build and clear its own tree. Its provider is a handle (D288); an open `io.directory` is a value the caller edits. `open_directory(host, path, buffer)` returns a directory `from` a buffer the caller supplies, `read_entry` takes it `inout` and returns an entry whose name is lent `from` it until the next read, and `close_directory` takes it `sink`. An entry is its name as `[]u8` and its kind, `regular | subdirectory | symbolic_link | special`, never following a link; where the file system records no kind the provider asks the entry itself, and skips one removed in between. An empty name is the end of the directory, as zero bytes is the end of a read; `.` and `..` are never entries. `entry_size` gives a `u64` relative to the open directory without following a link, and a name that is empty, holds `/` or NUL, or is 1,024 bytes or longer is `not_found` without asking the host. `io.directory_buffer` is 1,024 bytes, the hosted providers' smallest buffer, which every hosted system's entries fit. A missing path or a file used as a directory is `not_found` (D287), EPERM, EACCES and EROFS are `no_access`, a name `make_directory` finds taken is the new atom `io.already_exists`, and anything else is `io_failed` with its errno kept. A directory dropped without `close_directory` keeps its descriptor until the process ends; `defer io.close_directory(...)` is the idiom. On Linux, `getdents64` fills the caller's buffer, and every record is held to lie inside what was filled, to be long enough for its header and to end its name inside itself, so a bad record is `io_failed` rather than a trap. Darwin and FreeBSD open with `O_DIRECTORY` and read through `fdopendir`, `readdir` and `closedir`, copying each name into the caller's buffer, and make and remove with `mkdirat` and `unlinkat`. The memory provider's directories are the slot names' parts before a `/`, and a slot ending in `/` is an empty directory; it refuses changes other than an existing directory's `already_exists` with `no_access`, so `memory_over` keeps its signature.
D	294	Every Linux system call is reachable by number	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d294-every-linux-system-call-is-reachable-by-number	Chosen: the raw call is public as `system_call`, six integer arguments and an integer result, minus the errno on failure. `platform/linux/numbers` names every call's number for x86-64, arm64 and RV64 by one rule, the kernel's table name followed by `_number`, which no reserved word or wrapper can meet. The numbers are generated by `scripts/linux_syscalls.py` from a pinned kernel release's own tables, x86-64's `syscall_64.tbl` with the common and 64 ABIs and the generic table for arm64 and RV64 with each architecture's own entries, and the generated file names the release and its checksum; the generator can check the committed file instead of writing it. With no release named it holds `numbers.ldn` to being its own rendering under the pin and writes or checks the wrappers from it, so adding a typed wrapper needs no kernel source; the release is needed only to change the pin. The wrappers take their numbers from the same tables, through a private generated file, so there is one source of numbers. The numbers are a module of their own, imported by a program that calls by number, so `platform/linux` stays the wrappers every static Linux program imports; a program pays only for the numbers it uses (D296). Typed wrappers stay for the calls the library itself makes, `getdents64`, `mkdirat` and `unlinkat` among them.
D	295	`try` of a callee whose error set is inferred waits for the set	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d295-try-of-a-callee-whose-error-set-is-inferred-waits-for-the-set	Chosen: a `try` whose callee's set is still being inferred is asked again once every set is final, and refused then only if the solved set is empty.
D	296	A routine or module binding the program cannot reach is not emitted	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d296-a-routine-or-module-binding-the-program-cannot-reach-is-not-emitted	Chosen: when the entry module declares a public `main`, a module routine, generic instance, evidence table or binding is lowered and emitted only if the program can reach it. The roots are every routine the entry module defines, so `main`, D232's `panic_handler` and a firmware entry among them; a binding with a link symbol; a C definition that is public or has a link symbol; a definition in a machine convention, as the process entry `_landin_start` is; a definition whose link name a bodyless import names; a routine or binding with a placement, a section, an alignment, a vector or `keep`; one whose name or link name, or `_` and either on Mach-O, is a word in an `assembler.block`'s text; and every module declaration that is neither a routine nor a binding, a type whose length names a constant among them. A reached routine or binding reaches what any resolved reference in it names, in any position, the generic instance any of its calls selects, and the conformance whose table a selection, an `any` construction or a `for` reads; a reached instance reaches its template and the conformances it receives; a reached conformance reaches its providers and, for an erased table, D145's parent conformances. `public` alone is not a use, and neither is a native routine's link symbol, which [1975] makes its linker identity rather than an export. Every declaration is still checked, so an unreached declaration's errors are still errors, except a target-limited builtin's refusal, which D564 makes where the call is reached. Reachability can keep too much but never too little, and kept items are numbered in declaration order, so the output stays a function of the sources. Any compilation without a public `main` keeps everything.
D	297	The hosted library stands on a POSIX layer	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d297-the-hosted-library-stands-on-a-posix-layer	Chosen: four layers. Each system's own interface stays raw under `platform/`: `platform/linux` with its numbers (D279, D294) and `platform/libc` (D276). `platform/posix` gives POSIX's facilities in Landin types, written once over each (D298). The portable concepts in `core` name no POSIX type, so `io.file` is a `distinct usize`, an open directory holds a `handle: usize`, and no integer descriptor, mode bit, owner, signal number or errno is in a `core` signature. `hosted/system` and `hosted/heap` are written once over `platform/posix`, with no code of their own for any system. All three `platform` modules are scoped to the hosted POSIX systems, Linux, Darwin and FreeBSD, by namespace and by a `compiler.assert`, and firmware refuses them by name with L0015; `platform/libc` serves Linux too, under `--link=libc`. Every public routine of `platform/posix` has a `_landin_posix_` link name, so none replaces a C library function of the same spelling. A BSD and Darwin module for kqueue comes with the event-driven Io that needs it.
D	298	POSIX's descriptor, errors and status in Landin types	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d298-posix-s-descriptor-errors-and-status-in-landin-types	Chosen: `posix.descriptor` is a `distinct i32`, with `standard_input`, `standard_output`, `standard_error` and `working_directory`, the `*at` calls' AT_FDCWD. Every errno any of the three systems defines is an atom named after its C macro in lower case, 154 of them and `unlisted`, in the atom set `posix.errno`; an alias has no atom of its own, so EWOULDBLOCK is `eagain`, and ENOTSUP is its own atom only on Darwin. `number` gives an atom's number on this system and `errno_of` a number's atom, through tables generated from Linux's, FreeBSD's and Darwin's headers. The calls are POSIX's own: `open_at`, `read`, `write`, `close`, `status_at` with a `status` of device, inode, kind and size, the directory calls over a caller's buffer, which list `.` and `..` as POSIX does, `make_directory_at`, `unlink_at`, `remove_directory_at`, `map`, `unmap`, `page_size`, `exit` and `poll`, whose events are a `distinct u16` flag set (D302). None retries EINTR or completes a short transfer; that is provider policy in `hosted/system`. Each path is copied with its NUL into a per-system `PATH_MAX` buffer, so the terminator never reaches a caller; a path holding a NUL is `einval` and one too long `enametoolong`. The argument root lives here, with the environment's table since D311, read from the initial stack on a static Linux program and through the C runtime otherwise, as a real `ptr ptr u8` (D301).
D	299	A host string is passed through unconverted	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d299-a-host-string-is-passed-through-unconverted	Chosen: `text.host_string` is one opaque type whose representation is chosen in one place by target, bytes on every system today, so a 16-bit representation for Windows goes there. `text.host_over` makes one lending its bytes, `text.host_bytes` gives the bytes back, `text.from_host` converts to `utf8` and fails `invalid_text` when it is not, and `text.host_equal` compares with a literal. Every path the `files` and `directories` concepts take, every argument and every directory entry's name is a host string, so a value passed from an argument to `open` is never converted. `io.terminate_path`, the `_bytes` and `_text` open variants, `io.copy_argument`, `io.argument` and the atoms `empty_path`, `path_contains_nul`, `path_too_long` and `argument_too_long` are withdrawn; those cases are now the system's own answer, `not_found` for ENOENT and `io_failed` for EINVAL and ENAMETOOLONG, their errno kept. The memory provider's argument table is `[][]u8`, which firmware can declare as static data.
D	300	One heap on every hosted system	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d300-one-heap-on-every-hosted-system	Chosen: D282's size-class heap is the heap of every hosted system, over `platform/posix`'s `map` and `unmap`, so `hosted/heap` has no code of its own for any system. It is single-threaded everywhere; a heap that threads share is the threads item's, on every system alike, which D502 and D514 give it.
D	301	Static storage satisfies a read-only `from` clause	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d301-static-storage-satisfies-a-read-only-from-clause	Chosen: a reference is static when it reaches storage no frame owns, a module binding or what one points to. A result with no writable reference whose edge carries a static reference satisfies a named source it does not derive from, because static storage outlives every source. A parameter the clause leaves out is still refused, and a writable result keeps D222's refusal.
D	302	Two values of one distinct scalar type compare equal, and flags combine	Decisions: Declared types, ranges and layout	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d302-two-values-of-one-distinct-scalar-type-compare-equal-and-flags-combine	Chosen: `==` and `<>` take two values of the same distinct type whose base is a scalar. `&`, `^`, `|` and `~` take values of the same distinct type whose base is an unsigned integer, and their result keeps that type. `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` take two values of one distinct type over a scalar, in the base's own order, an amendment D315's durations and instants prompted: integers by value and sign, `bool` with false first, and floats by IEEE comparison with NaN unordered. Arithmetic, shifts and updating assignment stay refused, `|=` with a note to write it out. A distinct value never meets its base or another distinct type without a conversion, and the refusal says so. D427 later extended equality to distinct atoms, pointers and function values and admitted `&=`, `^=` and `|=` over an unsigned base.
D	303	Every routine and datum has its own section, and a static link counts what it reaches	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d303-every-routine-and-datum-has-its-own-section-and-a-static-link-counts-what-it-reaches	Chosen: the ELF backends for x86-64, arm64 and RV64, on Linux and FreeBSD, give every routine, datum and evidence table its own section, named by item index so the output stays a function of the sources, with zero-image data in their own `.bss` sections; Mach-O keeps `.subsections_via_symbols` and Darwin links with `-dead_strip`; Cortex-M keeps its per-item sections under its own script. Every ELF link passes `--gc-sections`. A static link's L0500 counts only the references the entry reaches, from `_landin_start`, `main`, the argument initializer, `panic_handler`, every `keep` item, every datum and the entries D374 keeps of every evidence table, through calls and taken addresses, an external C name leading to the routine that defines it.
D	304	Byte blocks over slices	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d304-byte-blocks-over-slices	Chosen: `mem.copy(into, source)` copies with `memmove`'s rule, from the last byte down when the destination starts inside the source after its first byte and from the first up when it starts at or before the source, so overlap is always safe; one wholly after the source may go either way. It fails `out_of_bounds` before writing when `into` is shorter; a longer destination keeps its tail. `mem.fill` sets every byte. `cmp.compare` answers the atom set `less | equal | greater`, bytes unsigned and a proper prefix first. `mem.find` gives the first match's index or the source's length, so `source[0..<find(…)]` is always valid.
D	305	A text builder writes whole pieces into the caller's buffer	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d305-a-text-builder-writes-whole-pieces-into-the-caller-s-buffer	Chosen: `text.builder` is a value the caller edits `inout`. `text.over(buffer)` makes one bounded by the caller's buffer, and `text.growing(allocator)` one that starts empty and doubles through an erased `mem.allocator`, resizing its storage through the allocator, which grows it in place or moves it (D337), and given back with `text.release`. Bytes, a byte, `utf8`, host strings, signed and unsigned decimals of every width and lower-case hexadecimal are appended; each piece is written whole or not at all, failing `no_space` with the builder unchanged, which is also a growing builder's answer when its allocator refuses. `text.align_right` and `text.align_left` pad what was written since an earlier `text.length`. The allocator is erased because the `formattable` entry must name one builder type.
D	306	`text.format` takes `{}` and checks its count when it runs	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d306-text-format-takes-and-checks-its-count-when-it-runs	Chosen: `text.format(into, template, values)` writes `template` into a builder with each `{}` replaced by the next value, an `any text.formattable` whose one entry appends the value; `{{` and `}}` are a brace. The whole template is checked before anything is written: a count that disagrees with the values, or a stray brace, is `invalid_format` and writes nothing, and `no_space` part-way restores the builder's earlier length. Width, fill and radix are the builder's typed calls, not the template's. The integer types, `bool`, `utf8`, `[]u8` and host strings conform. Formatting is the same in every locale and keeps no global state.
D	307	Parsing mirrors what the builder writes	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d307-parsing-mirrors-what-the-builder-writes	Chosen: `core/text` parses signed and unsigned decimals of every width and hexadecimal over bytes. A signed value takes an optional `-` and never a `+`, because no append writes one, and `-0` is zero; hexadecimal takes either case and no prefix. Overflow is found during the scan against the type's own limit, so the first problem from the left is the one reported, as `number_overflow` or `invalid_number`.
D	308	A buffered writer is flushed explicitly, and a line reader lends its lines	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d308-a-buffered-writer-is-flushed-explicitly-and-a-line-reader-lends-its-lines	Chosen: `io.buffered_writer(provider)` is a value edited `inout` over a writer's handle and a caller's buffer. `io.put` buffers what fits, flushing first when it does not, and writes a piece at least the buffer's size straight through. `io.flush` writes with `write_some` until the buffer is empty, so after a failure exactly the unwritten bytes stay at its front and a later flush writes each byte once; a writer that makes no progress is `io_failed`. Bytes still buffered when a program ends are never written: `defer io.flush(…)` and a final flush whose failure is reported are the idiom, documented as a hazard wherever the writer is. `io.line_reader` lends each line until the next read, as a directory lends its names (D293): a line ends at `\\n`, a `\\r` before it belongs to the ending, a lone `\\r` is a byte, and the last line need not end. A line and its ending must fit the buffer; a longer one is `io.line_too_long` and is skipped, so the next read gives the following line. End of input is a line marked `finished`, asked again as often as the reader likes.
D	309	An array is lent whole to a slice parameter	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d309-an-array-is-lent-whole-to-a-slice-parameter	Chosen: an array literal, or a fixed-array place, is the argument of a slice parameter `[]T` passed `in`. A literal is formed in written order in the caller's frame each time the call runs and lent read-only, with frame origin, so a result `from` that parameter cannot leave the caller. A place, a binding, a module array, a parameter, a named return or an admitted array field, lends its own storage for its type's whole length and keeps the place's origin. A `[]mut T` parameter takes a writable place, as a range slice of it would, and never a literal. A `utf8` parameter takes neither. A generic routine's slice parameter takes a place as any other routine's does (D372), and a literal when its element type names no formal (D419); one whose element type is a formal still refuses a literal, which D138 types before the parameter is known.
D	310	A call that returns nothing takes no value in its `else`	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d310-a-call-that-returns-nothing-takes-no-value-in-its-else	Chosen: the recovery of a call with no results is checked like any statement block: a last line that is a value is L0331, "this call returns nothing, so its `else` has no result to stand in for", whose note names the block form, `else (problem) ... end`.
D	311	The hosted entry hands the argument initializer the environment too	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d311-the-hosted-entry-hands-the-argument-initializer-the-environment-too	Chosen: `_landin_host_initialize_arguments` takes C's three `main` arguments, `(count: i32, escaping values: ptr ptr u8, escaping environment: ptr ptr u8) -> none`, and the hosted `main` passes its `envp` with the rest; it is already in the third argument register on every architecture, so no backend moves anything. A null table is an empty environment, and a repeat must repeat all three. A static Linux program's entry passes the initial stack's table and the C runtime passes its own, so both reach the environment through one routine. The table is counted again on every read, because C code may change it in place.
D	312	The environment is a read-only concept of its own	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d312-the-environment-is-a-read-only-concept-of-its-own	Chosen: `io.environment` is a concept outside `world`, with `variable_count`, `variable_at` and `variable_named`, the first match by bytes, failing `no_variable`. An `io.variable` is a name and a value, both host strings (D299), lent `from self`, which D301's static origin satisfies on a hosted system; an entry without `=` is a name with an empty value. There is no setter: a program's own environment is not changed beside threads, and a child gets the environment its parent builds. `io.variables_over` gives a provider over `NAME=value` byte strings that firmware can declare as static data.
D	313	A program is run by its path and reported as ending one of two ways	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d313-a-program-is-run-by-its-path-and-reported-as-ending-one-of-two-ways	Chosen: `io.programs` is a concept outside `world`, shaped like D293. `io.spawn(host, path, arguments, environment, streams)` runs the program at the path as given, with no search and no shell; its first argument is the path, and its environment exactly what the caller built. Each of its three streams is `inherited`, `discarded` or `piped`, with presets `inheriting`, `capturing` and `discarding`. A running child is a value the caller edits: `io.write_child` and `io.close_input` feed it, and `io.read_child` waits on both piped outputs and reads whichever is ready, so a child is never stalled on a full pipe. `io.wait` takes the child `sink`, closes its pipes and answers `io.ending`, `exited(code)` or `signalled`; the signal's number is hosted detail, `system.last_signal(host)`, kept in a cell of the handle's `system.space` beside its last error. `io.scripted_over(world, programs)` gives scripted children whose output, errors, code and ending are given, recording how often each started, its argument and variable counts and the input written to it.
D	314	Every descriptor the POSIX layer makes is closed on exec, and a child starts clean	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d314-every-descriptor-the-posix-layer-makes-is-closed-on-exec-and-a-child-starts-clean	Chosen: `platform/posix` opens every descriptor close-on-exec, files, directories and pipes. `posix.pipe` is `pipe2(O_CLOEXEC)` on Linux and FreeBSD and `pipe` followed by `fcntl` on Darwin, which has no `pipe2`, so it is not atomic there. `posix.spawn` builds the argument and environment tables in a temporary mapping and first moves any stream descriptor below 3 that is not its own number above 2. On Linux it is a `clone` with SIGCHLD and nothing shared, whose child sets its streams with `dup3`, closes the rest with `close_range(3, ~0, CLOSE_RANGE_CLOEXEC)` and calls `execve`; an exec failure reaches the parent through a close-on-exec pipe and the child is reaped. On Darwin and FreeBSD it is `posix_spawn`, with `POSIX_SPAWN_CLOEXEC_DEFAULT` and `posix_spawn_file_actions_addinherit_np` on Darwin and `posix_spawn_file_actions_addclosefrom_np(3)` on FreeBSD. `posix.wait` is `wait4` or `waitpid` and answers `exited(code)` or `signalled(signal)`; the hosted provider retries EINTR. A stream that is already its own number is D378's, which amends this decision.
D	315	Time is a count of nanoseconds, and the wall clock seconds and nanoseconds	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d315-time-is-a-count-of-nanoseconds-and-the-wall-clock-seconds-and-nanoseconds	Chosen: `time.duration` and `time.instant` are each a `distinct u64` of nanoseconds, about 584 years, and ordered and compared as their base is (D302). `time.wall_time` is a record of `seconds: i64` and `nanoseconds: u32`, UTC since 1970 without leap seconds. Spans are made with `time.nanoseconds`, `time.microseconds`, `time.milliseconds` and `time.seconds`, which trap past the range; `time.elapsed` traps when its second reading is the earlier one; `time.later` makes a deadline, and `time.in_milliseconds` rounds down. There is no other arithmetic on time. Calendars, time zones and their formatting are the locale record's in the roadmap's register.
D	316	A clock, a wall clock and entropy are concepts of their own, and a sleep never returns early	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d316-a-clock-a-wall-clock-and-entropy-are-concepts-of-their-own-and-a-sleep-never-returns-early	Chosen: `time.clock` holds `now` and `sleep` together, because a sleep is measured on that clock and its fake must advance it; `time.wall_clock` holds `wall_now`, apart, because firmware may count time without knowing the date and the wall clock jumps; `io.entropy` holds `fill_random`. All three are outside `world`, with fakes in `core/io`: `fake.clock_over` gives a `manual_clock` a test advances, whose sleep advances it by exactly the span, and `fake.entropy_over` gives scripted bytes. Reading a clock cannot fail; a failure of the system's own is `compiler.unreachable()`. A sleep cannot fail and never returns before `now` has reached its start plus the span: the hosted provider takes a deadline from the monotonic clock and sleeps for what is left, at most a million seconds a call, treating any failure, EINTR among them, as a reason to read the clock again; a deadline that would overflow is the clock's last instant. Entropy is fallible, and on Linux is `getrandom` with no flags, which waits only before the kernel's pool is first ready, looping over short reads and EINTR; on Darwin and FreeBSD it is `arc4random_buf`, which cannot fail.
D	317	Linux reads its clock through the vDSO	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d317-linux-reads-its-clock-through-the-vdso	Chosen: `platform/linux/vdso`'s `vdso.symbol` (D346) finds the clock function the auxiliary vector's AT_SYSINFO_EHDR names: `__vdso_clock_gettime` at `LINUX_2.6` on x86-64, `__kernel_clock_gettime` at `LINUX_2.6.39` on arm64 and `__vdso_clock_gettime` at `LINUX_4.15` on RV64. It reads the first load segment and the dynamic table, counts symbols from `DT_HASH` or else `DT_GNU_HASH`, since only x86 forces both, and requires the version, or the name alone where there are no version tables. Every offset is held inside the image before it is read, by arithmetic that cannot overflow, and the image is bounded by its first page for the headers and its first load segment, at most a mebibyte. The function's address is cached in a plain module word on first use, a relaxed `u64` cell of `core/atomic` since D502, and called through D335's conversion of that address to a C function value. A missing symbol, a malformed image or a nonzero answer falls back to the system call. Since D279's adoption it serves `--link=libc` too, and `time.now` costs about 116 ns either way.
D	318	`core/random` is xoshiro256**, the same everywhere and not cryptographic	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d318-core-random-is-xoshiro256-the-same-everywhere-and-not-cryptographic	Chosen: `random.generator` is xoshiro256** 1.0 (Blackman and Vigna, 2021), whose multiplications by 5 and 9 are shifts and additions, so drawing needs no helper on Cortex-M0. `random.new(seed)` seeds it through splitmix64, as its authors advise; `random.from_entropy` reads 32 bytes from an `io.entropy` provider and replaces the impossible all-zero state with `new(0)`'s. `random.below` masks to the bound's width and draws again when the value is too large, so it has neither division nor bias, and traps on a bound of zero, with `overflow` since D342; `random.shuffle` is Fisher and Yates'. A fixed seed's sequence is the same on every target. It is not cryptographic, as its documentation says.
D	319	A network is a concept of its own whose connections are readers and writers	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d319-a-network-is-a-concept-of-its-own-whose-connections-are-readers-and-writers	Chosen: `net.network` is a concept outside `world` that also conforms to `reader` and `writer`, so a connection is a `file` that `io.read`, `io.write`, the line reader and the buffered writer take. Its entries are `connect`, `listen`, `accept`, `open_datagram`, `send`, `receive`, `send_to`, `receive_from`, `shutdown`, `local_address`, `peer_address`, `set_timeouts`, `set_no_delay` and `close_socket`. A system's errors become atoms: ECONNREFUSED is `refused`; ENETUNREACH and EHOSTUNREACH `unreachable`; EADDRINUSE `address_in_use`; EADDRNOTAVAIL, EAFNOSUPPORT and EPFNOSUPPORT `address_unavailable`; EACCES and EPERM `no_access`; a limit passing, or ETIMEDOUT at connect, `timed_out`; EPIPE, ECONNRESET, and ETIMEDOUT or ENOTCONN on a connection, `disconnected`; anything else `io_failed` with its errno kept. The calls block. `set_timeouts(receive, send)` sets limits, zero meaning none; a limit passing leaves the socket usable, and `accept` keeps the receive limit on every system, by `poll` on Darwin and FreeBSD. `connect` has no limit of its own; D580 adds `connect_within`, which has. Every listener reuses its address and every IPv6 socket is IPv6 only, so an address names one family everywhere; the backlog is 128. The hosted provider retries EINTR, waits out an interrupted connect and reads its error, takes the next connection after ECONNABORTED and sends until every byte is sent.
D	320	An address is a family, sixteen bytes and a port, written as the RFCs say	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d320-an-address-is-a-family-sixteen-bytes-and-a-port-written-as-the-rfcs-say	Chosen: `net.address` is a public record, as D293's directory is, so a provider in another module builds one, of an `ipv4` or `ipv6` family, sixteen bytes and a port; it has no zone, so `%zone` is `invalid_address` and a link-local address waits. D581 amends this: an IPv6 address has a zone. IPv4 is four decimal parts with no leading zero, as `inet_pton` reads them. IPv6 is RFC 4291's form in either case, with one `::` and an IPv4 tail; it is written as RFC 5952 says, in lower case with the longest run of two or more zero groups compressed, the first on a tie, and only an IPv4-mapped address dotted. With a port it is `a.b.c.d:p` or `[v6]:p`. `net.parse_ip`, `net.parse_address`, `net.append_ip` and `net.append_address` read and write them, and an address is `formattable`.
D	321	A loopback network in memory never waits	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d321-a-loopback-network-in-memory-never-waits	Chosen: `fake.network`, from `fake.network_over`, is one machine with only loopback addresses, over socket records the caller declares, each record's buffer its receive buffer. Delivery is at once, whole and in order; a datagram no socket takes, or one its buffer has no room for, is lost. It never waits: wherever a real call would, it answers `timed_out` at once, after a send has delivered what fits. A send to a closed peer is `disconnected` the first time. Ports are given from 49152, and a port overlaps as on Linux, the unspecified address taking every one. A test can turn IPv6 off, fail a chosen call and read the counters. Resets, partial reads and TIME_WAIT are not modelled. Its conformance links every entry, about 40 KB, so it does not fit a Cortex-M0 image.

D	325	The rest of the file system is a concept of its own	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d325-the-rest-of-the-file-system-is-a-concept-of-its-own	Chosen: `io.file_system` is a concept outside `world` beside `files` and `directories`, with `open_file`, `rename`, `status_of`, `status_of_file`, `set_read_only`, `synchronize`, `truncate`, `read_at`, `write_at`, `make_temporary` and `current_directory`. The fakes are `fake.volume`, a node-based volume for all five file concepts, which does not fit Cortex-M0 because its conformances link every entry, and `fake.terminals`.

A refusal leaves the block, its bytes and the provider as they were. D	338	A branch whose arms only compute is a choice	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d338-a-branch-whose-arms-only-compute-is-a-choice	Chosen: the IR has `Choose`, whose bool operand picks one of two scalar values of its result's type, neither carrying a function, atom set or pointee, in routines only. Lowering never makes one. Under size and speed, `Landin.IR.If_Conversion` rewrites a block that ends in a branch whose two sides meet again, each side at most one block that ends in a jump, when neither arm can do anything a program could observe if the other arm were taken: it loads and stores only private slots, scalars that nothing names but their own loads and stores, and otherwise computes with operations that cannot trap — constants, comparisons, bitwise and wrapping arithmetic, float arithmetic, total conversions, and integer operations whose checks were proved or lie in an `unchecked` region. Integer division never qualifies, because x86-64 refuses a zero divisor in the hardware itself. The block then computes both arms, chooses each stored slot's value and jumps to where the arms met. One trapping operation qualifies: a checked integer addition or subtraction that updates a slot from the value it had before the arm, `x = x + k` or `x = x - k`, when the other arm leaves the slot alone. It becomes `x + (if c then k else 0)`, which traps exactly when the arm would have and at the same point in the program's order, since nothing observable lies between the branch and the arm or the arm and its end; an update that cannot trap takes the same form. Each arm is held to six operations besides its constants, loads and stores, and a conversion to four chosen slots. A branch whose condition is computed from a slot an arm stores stays a branch: the choice would wait for a comparison that waits for the choice before it, a chain a predicted branch does not wait on. x86-64 selects `cmov` or `setcc`, arm64 `csel`, `fcsel` or `cset`, both testing the flags of a comparison right before the choice when it has no other use; RV64 and Cortex-M0, which have no conditional move, use the condition's own zero or one for a choice of one or zero and otherwise branch around one load inside the choice.
D	339	At speed a small direct call is a copy of its routine	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d339-at-speed-a-small-direct-call-is-a-copy-of-its-routine	Chosen: at `--optimize speed`, before simplification, a direct call is replaced by a copy of the routine it names when that routine has a body in the program and nothing takes its address (no function value, image or evidence entry names it, and it is not an entry, an import or an export), it is not the routine making the call, it uses the ordinary convention and Landin's own transport, it returns, it is not variadic, it has no placement and no assembly block, every aggregate it is passed or returns has a nominal shape, and it weighs at most 64 of D211's weighted operations as lowering made it. The copy's own calls stay calls: one level. A routine grows by at most the larger of 512 and its own weight; calls inside loops are copied first, then the lightest. `none` and `size` copy nothing, and neither does Cortex-M0, whose backend does not read the objective. One pass measures every routine and one copies, so the work is linear but for ordering each caller's calls.\n\nA copy does what the call did. Its arguments were evaluated where the call stands, left to right; each is stored into the copy of its parameter, and a by-value aggregate is copied, or cleared for D97's zero carrier, as the routine's entry would have done it. When the routine only reads the aggregate and nothing could write the caller's storage while the copy runs (no `addr` of it is kept, no slice is over it, and no address of it reaches a parameter that may escape), the copy reads it where the caller keeps it, as `Landin.IR.In_Place` would have the routine read it. A parameter given a constant is read as that constant. Each `return` copies a stored result to the storage the call named, as the routine's way out does, and goes on with the rest of the caller's block; the caller's values that crossed the call wait in slots, or are made again when they are constants. A routine that can fail is copied only where its call is followed by lowering's failure test, nothing else reads the call's status, and the value the call stored is read only on the succeeding way: each `fail` stores its atom and goes the test's failing way, and each return the other way, which is the choice the test would have made, so propagation and call-site recovery are unchanged; a routine that declares errors and never fails stays a call. Every operation of a copy is the routine's own, with its source site and its check, in the order the routine ran them, so each trap is where and when the call's would have been and D232's site is the routine's; a check is removed only when, as anywhere, it is proved unable to fail. Cleanup is the routine's own code and runs where it ran, before the caller's recovery.\n\nEach copied block, slot and source alias names the copy it belongs to, which names the routine, the call it replaced and that call's scope. A native debugger reads it as DWARF4's `DW_TAG_inlined_subroutine`: the routine is described once more, abstractly, with `DW_AT_inline`, its parameters, locals and lexical blocks; each copy, inside the caller's lexical block that held the call, has that abstract origin, its address ranges and the call's file, line and column, and its own parameters, locals and blocks with locations in the caller's frame. A stop in a copy is a frame of the routine inlined into its caller's frame, which shows its own variables as it would across a call; a backtrace has both frames; a breakpoint on one of the routine's lines can stop in a copy, and a step enters and leaves one as it would a call. The routine's own out-of-line description is unchanged, and at `none` and `size`, where nothing is copied, so is every debugger session.

D	358	`refine fmt` writes a source into its own file	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d358-refine-fmt-writes-a-source-into-its-own-file	Chosen: the formatted bytes are written through the descriptor that read the original source, retained throughout formatting (D907), into the same inode, so it keeps its owner, group, extended attributes and ACLs, those the caller cannot list among them, and every name a hard link gives it, which sees the formatted bytes too. Writing in place is not atomic, so before the first byte changes the original bytes, read back through the descriptor that will be written, are copied into a new file beside it, `.fmt-original-` and an exclusive per-invocation suffix, and the copy and its directory are synced. Then the new bytes are written from the start, the file is cut to their length and synced, and the copy is removed. A failed write puts the original bytes back from memory and removes the copy; a write that cannot do even that keeps the copy and names it, which is also what a crash during the write leaves. A path names a symlink's target; a file that is not ordinary or that no one may write is refused. A renamed-in save is never written: a changed pathname observed before writing refuses the operation; one changed after that check still names a different inode from the retained descriptor, and the command reports that its layout was not installed at that name, retaining its recovery copy. Concurrent writes through another descriptor to the same inode are unsupported; neither an identity check nor an advisory lock excludes that writer. What a write itself takes away is checked first: the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits a write clears are set again and read back, so a file whose bit the caller could not set again, as its owner and for set-group-ID in its group, is refused before it is written, and so is a Linux file with capabilities, which a write removes and only a privileged process can give back. Nothing needs privilege. Each refusal names its cause, and says whether the original bytes are back or where their copy is.

D	371	A one-line function-typed module binding is a binding	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d371-a-one-line-function-typed-module-binding-is-a-binding	Chosen: a top-level `name: (...) -> returns = value` is a binding when the value is a name, or a name selected from a module, that ends its line on the declaration's line, and the next line does not begin with `end`. A function always closes with `end`, so such a line declares no function, and every function the corpus writes is read as before. A function-typed value written over several lines, such as an anonymous function, is still read as a function and still needs the alias.
D	372	A generic call types a literal from its parameter and lends an array	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d372-a-generic-call-types-a-literal-from-its-parameter-and-lends-an-array	Chosen: an untyped integer or float literal argument waits until every other argument of the call has been matched. Its parameter pattern is then normalized with what they bound: a pattern that names an integer type gives an integer literal that type, a float type a float literal, and the literal is checked there as [1880] checks any literal in context. A pattern still unbound, or of another class, leaves [0200]'s default, which then decides the pattern as before. Because every literal waits for every other argument, `second(4, u16(30))` and `second(u16(30), 4)` both make `t` `u16`. A fixed-array place, a binding, a parameter, a named return or an admitted field, matches an outer slice pattern `[]t` through its element, and the instance's ordinary call check then lends it as D309 does, refusing a read-only place where `[]mut t` is written. D	373	A note explains in words, and a cited label stands beside them	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d373-a-note-explains-in-words-and-a-cited-label-stands-beside-them	Chosen: every note the compiler emits says what the rule is in plain words. A paragraph or decision label may stand beside those words, first as the code's catalogue row does, but never instead of them, and no note quotes a grammar production, its `::=`, `?` or `*`. Where a note needs the shape of a construct, it shows a short example of the source, as `for item in source do`. `check.py` reads every note literal out of the compiler and refuses one that is a bare label or quotes a production.
D	374	A table names only the entries something can project	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d374-a-table-names-only-the-entries-something-can-project	Chosen: every backend, on every target, keeps entry N of a table only when code that can run projects entry N from a table of the same concept, direct tables and erased tables apart. The concept, not the table a projection names, is the unit, because a projection's table at runtime may be any table of its concept: an `any C` value carries whichever conformance built it, and an instance's hidden table is any of its concept's. Code that can run starts from the roots: a routine with a reference no call makes (a function value, an image, an export, an import, a link name, a placement, a non-ordinary convention or the C ABI), one without parameters, as a firmware entry is, and the panic handler the backend calls. A routine a routine that can run calls, takes the address of, or names in an `assembler.block`'s text can run, and an entry's target can run once that entry is kept; a routine that only routines that cannot run call cannot run either, so what it projects keeps nothing. An entry left out is a zero word in its place, so a table's size, its order and every offset D144 and D147 give stay as they were, and the two identities of one physical table keep the same entries. The routine a zero word replaced is linked only if something else reaches it, and D303's L0500 count follows the kept entries. Calling through a left-out entry cannot happen, since nothing reads it.
D	375	A writable result may carry static storage it reaches only through read-only views	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d375-a-writable-result-may-carry-static-storage-it-reaches-only-through-read-only-views	Chosen: D222 asks about an independent alternative only when a writable reference in the result may reach it. An erased value is judged by what it erased: `any` admits no entry whose `self` asks more permission than its operand gives, so `any` of a read-only pointer reaches what the pointer reaches. A call's writable result counts every independent storage its named arguments carry, since the callee's permission, not the argument's type, decides what the result can write. The binding's own mutability does not matter; the view's does, as it does for D301. The writable parts of the result still derive exactly from the clause; an erased view of mutable storage through a `ptr mut`, or of a binding that holds a writable view, is still refused; and frame storage still escapes.
D	376	`else none` ignores the failure of a call that returns nothing	Decisions: Functions, calls and returns	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d376-else-none-ignores-the-failure-of-a-call-that-returns-nothing	Chosen: `recovery ::= "else" "none"` is a recovery of its own. It is admitted only on a call that returns none, where it means exactly the empty bound block: the call's effects up to its failure stay, and the statement after the call runs next, whatever failed. `none` begins no expression or statement, so an `if`'s own `else` can never begin with it, and `else none` is the call's recovery in an `if` arm as anywhere else [1820]. D	378	A child receives every stream it is handed, closed on exec or not	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d378-a-child-receives-every-stream-it-is-handed-closed-on-exec-or-not	Chosen: `spawn` duplicates every stream below 3 above 2 for the call, its own number included, with `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`, and closes the duplicate after, so each stream reaches its number in the child by a duplication from another descriptor, which clears the close-on-exec flag in the child alone: `dup3(source, target, 0)` on Linux and `posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2` on Darwin and FreeBSD. The parent's descriptors and their flags are never changed. The same descriptor may be given for several streams. D	379	A reservation counts the tombstones	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d379-a-reservation-counts-the-tombstones	Chosen: the promise is kept. After `reserve(n)`, inserting new keys until `length` reaches `n` neither grows nor rebuilds the table, as long as nothing is removed in between. A table too small for `n` is replaced by the smallest whose capacity holds `n`, as before. A table already that large keeps its size, and is rebuilt at it when its tombstones and `n` together exceed its capacity, which drops the tombstones; otherwise it is left alone and nothing is allocated. Since a new key rebuilds once the live entries and the tombstones reach the capacity, `n` entries fit beside the tombstones exactly when the two together do. A rebuild in `reserve` is an allocation like any other: a refused one keeps every entry and tombstone. This amends D274.

D	386	A pool grows a block within its own slot	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d386-a-pool-grows-a-block-within-its-own-slot	Chosen: the pool's `grow` keeps the block in its slot to any extent the slot holds and records that extent for the block's free, as `resize` does, and refuses a larger extent, a block that is not a live slot of `old_size` and an address inside a slot rather than at it, with the pool unchanged. The block does not move, so it keeps the alignment it was allocated with. `free`, `grow` and `resize` find their slot through one private routine, so they refuse alike, and `resize` is a growth or shrink in place.
