D	444	A program starts fibres as a group it joins	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d444-a-program-starts-fibres-as-a-group-it-joins	Chosen: `core/fibre` has three layers. The switch, `prepare` and `switch` over a caller's record and stack, is for whoever writes a provider. Two concepts say what a provider is: `scheduler`, whose `start` may run a task to its end before returning and whose `wait` returns once one of its fibres has finished, or at once when none is running; and `turns`, a `scheduler` that adds `yield`, whose contract is that a fibre that yields lets every other unfinished fibre of the provider run before it resumes. A provider that runs everything to its end has no `yield`, so a program that needs turns says so in the concept it asks for and is refused where it asks. The blocking host and `fibre.whole` provide `scheduler`; a device's round of turns, the event-driven Io and an RTOS's scheduler provide `turns`. The library carries the switch, `whole` and one round of fixed turns over caller records, with the wait when nobody can run supplied by the provider built on it; priorities, timers and preemption stay out of it.\n\nAn application uses the third layer only. `group_over` takes a `scheduler` and `turns_over` a `turns`, with a backing the caller lends and a count, and cuts the backing into equal stacks; the group comes `from` the provider and the backing. `admit` waits, through the provider, for a free stack, copies the task's state onto it as a call passes an argument, and starts a fibre that calls an ordinary routine with that copy; one group holds tasks of different state types. A task's error set is `failure.reason`: the group keeps the first failure and `join` fails with it, after every admitted task has ended, since nothing cancels a fibre. A task with atoms of its own maps them before returning, as `core/failure` asks of a set that holds both. A group must be joined before its backing goes, and the program's `defer` does it, as it releases a region.
D	445	A parameter may be kept in another parameter's storage	Decisions: Lifetime, escape and allocation	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d445-a-parameter-may-be-kept-in-another-parameter-s-storage	Chosen: a parameter may be marked `escaping into p`, where `p` names another parameter of the same routine. The routine may keep the reference in `p`'s storage, and nowhere else. At a call, the argument for it must outlive the origin of the argument for `p`, which is decided locally, as [0780]'s same-origin update already is: a parameter of the caller, static storage and an allocation outlive anything the caller's frame holds; a local outlives another local of the same frame when it is declared before it; and a frame reference never outlives a parameter's storage. A writable reference kept this way must name every place it is kept, as D222 requires of a result. `escaping` alone keeps its meaning. The form is enabled, the tour's [0780] teaches it, and D455 decides what the rule left to the checker.
D	446	A fibre switches only inside its provider, and is no context of its own	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d446-a-fibre-switches-only-inside-its-provider-and-is-no-context-of-its-own	Chosen: fibres are cooperative. A fibre gives the core away only inside a call to an entry of the provider that runs it, and a provider states which of its entries may switch, as `hosted/system` states which retry; a query that does not wait, `last_errno` among them, never switches. The fibres of one provider are one CPU execution context in D227's sense: a switch is sequenced-before within it, and it is a full compiler memory boundary, as D227's explicit primitives are, so no ordinary access is carried across one in a register. A fibre does not move between threads. Threads are not a provider of the fibre concepts: a provider of them runs at most one of its fibres at a time, and state shared with a thread is the atomic wrapper's or a lock's.
D	447	What a switch owes the machine and the debugger	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d447-what-a-switch-owes-the-machine-and-the-debugger	Chosen: a stack's limit is checked by every routine that runs on it: in a program that prepares a stack, each routine compares its frame with the current stack's limit in its prologue and enters the program's [1670] handler past it (D471), and the limit travels in the frames a switch saves (D472); which panic kind that is, D451 says. The compiler reports, for each routine a program admits to a group, the deepest stack of the call graph it can close, and names where an `any` call, recursion or a foreign call opened it. On Cortex-M, fibres run on the process stack pointer and handlers on the main stack, so handlers' own frames and every nested exception are paid once, by the main-stack reservation, and a fibre's stack holds its own calls and the one hardware exception frame the core pushes when it interrupts the fibre (D461); the reset stack stays on the main stack. A fibre's first frame ends the frame-pointer chain and says so in its unwind information; `switch` is written so that, stopped anywhere in it, the frames above are the leaving fibre's; and the records are ordinary data a debugger script walks to show a suspended fibre's frames. No debugger is taught about fibres.
D	448	On one core, requests are answered one at a time, in order	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d448-on-one-core-requests-are-answered-one-at-a-time-in-order	Chosen: on one core, an operation in flight is a request whose answering has started and not finished. A device answers in arrival order, one at a time, and answers `busy` when the requests waiting for it fill its queue; receiving goes on in a fibre of its own. Fibres on a device are for structure, taking input while answering, and not for overlapping answers. A trace of the derived firmware shows answers in request order, none starting before the previous one has finished.
D	449	What the second Io and the atomic wrapper owe fibres	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d449-what-the-second-io-and-the-atomic-wrapper-owe-fibres	Chosen: nothing cancels a fibre. A program stops one by failing the I/O it waits on: an Io that runs fibres wakes every fibre waiting on a descriptor when it is shut or closed through the provider, and the woken call fails `io_failed`; a signal reaches the provider as an event read by an entry that waits like a receive, never as a handler running Landin code on a fibre's stack. A fibre that never ends holds its group's `join` for ever, and one never resumed never runs its `defer`s; both are stated, not prevented. An interrupt handler never switches: it records what happened for the provider to see before it waits. The atomic wrapper names the single-writer update, a load and a store, as an operation of its own on every target, and refuses a shared read-modify-write where the target has none, naming the critical section. The fake network, given a scheduler that takes turns, yields where a call would wait and answers `timed_out` only after a whole round in which nothing it waits for arrived; without one it behaves as now, and the library reference's reason is reworded.
D	450	The stack switch is two compiler builtins	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d450-the-stack-switch-is-two-compiler-builtins	Chosen: two `compiler` members, ordinary calls in source like the atomics, each evaluating its arguments once from left to right.\n\n- `compiler.stack_prepare(stack, entry, argument)` takes a `[]mut u8`, a function value of type `(argument: usize) -> noreturn` and a `usize`, and returns the `usize` stack pointer a later switch resumes. It aligns the top of `stack` down to the target's call alignment and lays out a first frame that, when resumed, calls `entry(argument)` with the frame-pointer chain and unwind information ending there, and the stack's limit, its base and D472's margin. A slice too small for that frame and the margin traps `stack_exhausted` (D451).\n- `compiler.stack_switch(save, resume)` takes a `ptr mut usize` and a `usize`. It saves the callee-saved registers, the frame pointer and the current stack's limit on the current stack, stores the stack pointer through `save`, and resumes the context `resume` names, its limit included, returning there. It is a full compiler memory boundary. It took a third argument, the leaving stack's limit, which it checked the stack pointer against, until D472 retired it.\n\nOn Cortex-M a prepared stack runs on the process stack pointer, and a switch between the reset stack and a prepared one changes CONTROL's stack selection; handlers keep the main stack (D447), and D460 says how a saved context records which stack pointer it resumes. The builtins name no library type: `core/fibre` builds its records, scheduler and group over them, and keeps the integer-made pointers that carry its state inside itself [0810]. Both are admitted on every target with a native backend; synthetic-32 admits neither.
D	451	A stack past its limit is a fifth panic kind	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d451-a-stack-past-its-limit-is-a-fifth-panic-kind	Chosen: `core/panic` gains `stack_exhausted`, and `panic_kind` is the union of five. D232's handler contract takes the five-atom domain; a handler written with `panic.panic_kind` accepts it unchanged, and one that matches the kind completely gains an arm. The hosted default handler reports it as it reports the others, and firmware keeps its bare instruction. A prepare too small for its first frame (D450) and a routine whose frame would go below its stack's limit (D471) raise it.
D	452	A panic site reserves five numbers per source byte	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d452-a-panic-site-reserves-five-numbers-per-source-byte	Chosen: each source byte, including its one-past-end position, reserves five numbers, `base + 5 * first_byte_offset + family_offset` with family offsets zero through four in `core/panic`'s order, `stack_exhausted` fourth. Every other rule of D232's site space is unchanged, and a site number is still not persistent across changed source inputs.
D	453	The stack builtins' refusals, and a backend that does not emit them yet	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d453-the-stack-builtins-refusals-and-a-backend-that-does-not-emit-them-yet	Chosen: the stack builtins are refused with L0344, as the memory intrinsics are: an argument outside D450's contract, a missing argument, a recovery, and a target that does not admit them. A target whose backend does not emit them yet refuses both by name, "not yet emitted on" the target, rather than admitting a call its backend cannot carry; each backend lifts the refusal for its targets as it lands, which leaves D450's admission the rule once all have. D564 amends where a target's refusal is made: only where the program reaches the call. An argument that is not a `usize` is the ordinary type disagreement, L0301, as an atomic's value operand is.
D	455	What `escaping into` compares, and where its target stands	Decisions: Lifetime, escape and allocation	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d455-what-escaping-into-compares-and-where-its-target-stands	Chosen: the named parameter may stand earlier or later in the list, so two parameters may each name the other, as `push_front`'s do. `into` is a contextual word, a target only when a second name follows it. The name must be another runtime parameter of the same signature, whose type holds a reference; an unknown name, a parameter naming itself and a target that can hold nothing are L0339. The parameter is not `escaping`: it may be kept in the named parameter's storage, in storage of its own origin and in the frame, and anywhere else is L0314. The contract is part of the function's type, so a function value, a concept entry and a generic instance carry it and a call through any of them is checked as a direct call is; two types that differ in it do not agree.\n\nAt a call, the kept argument's origin is its value's, as `escaping` reads it. The origin of the argument for the named parameter is read as a call's `from` result reads it: an `inout` argument is its place, and any other is what its value refers to. A local is declared before another when it comes first in the same block or an enclosing one, and a frame reference with no declaration to order it, a literal or a copied subject, is refused. An untracked argument is the program's claim [0470], as for `escaping`, and a holder whose origin is not known is taken to outlive the call. After the call, the frame storage the holder's argument reaches, and an `inout` place, hold what was kept, so returning or keeping it later is checked against the kept origin. The code generator treats the parameter as escaping, since it outlives the call.
D	460	On Cortex-M0 a saved context records which stack pointer it uses	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d460-on-cortex-m0-a-saved-context-records-which-stack-pointer-it-uses	Chosen: the saved word is the stack pointer itself, and the frame it points at records the selection. A switch pushes r4 to r7 and the return address, then a scratch word and the current stack's limit (D472), then CONTROL's value with r8 to r11 above it: forty-eight bytes, CONTROL lowest. Resuming reads the CONTROL word at the resumed address, writes the address into PSP when that word's SPSEL bit is set and into MSP when it is clear, writes CONTROL, executes an ISB, which makes the written pointer the current one, and pops the frame. `compiler.stack_prepare` aligns the slice's top down to eight and lays a frame whose CONTROL word is two, SPSEL set and privileged, with the argument in r4, the entry in r5, zero in r11 and the other registers, the stack's limit, and the start routine as the return address; a slice whose aligned top leaves less than those forty-eight bytes and D472's margin traps `stack_exhausted`. So a prepared stack always runs on PSP, and the reset context, saved by its first switch with CONTROL as reset left it, resumes on MSP. CONTROL's other bits travel with each context, as the limit does. A switch in handler mode, where the stack pointer is always MSP and SPSEL cannot be written, or in unprivileged thread mode, where neither CONTROL nor MSP can, is outside the contract and is not checked: D446 makes a provider's entries the only places a fibre switches, and they run in thread mode.
D	461	A fibre's backing on Cortex-M0 holds one exception frame	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d461-a-fibre-s-backing-on-cortex-m0-holds-one-exception-frame	Chosen: a fibre's backing holds, beyond its own deepest calls and the forty-eight-byte frame a switch saves (D460), one exception frame: thirty-two bytes, and four more when the core aligns the frame to eight bytes, which ARMv6-M always does, so thirty-six at most. It is paid once per fibre, not once per level of nesting: a nested exception is taken in handler mode and stacks on MSP, as every handler's own frames and calls do. The main-stack reservation pays for those. D447's sentence now says so, and a measurement of a fibre's stack charges it the thirty-six bytes.
D	462	The stack builtins' fixtures run on firmware as they are	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d462-the-stack-builtins-fixtures-run-on-firmware-as-they-are	Chosen: both are freestanding, so every target runs one source. The round trip's status says what its line said: the order the two stacks ran in, the module value folded on both and the local kept across both switches; its backing is two KiB, which the corpus's twelve KiB of static RAM holds. The handler fixture's fibre recurses past its stack's limit, and its handler records the kind and resumes the context `main` saved when it switched to the fibre, so `main` returns the stack_exhausted arm's code. A handler that switches away does not return, so D232's rule for a returning handler is not engaged; the panic latch stays claimed, and a later check in that image reaches the terminal default instruction. That is a property of the fixture and not a recovery idiom: [1670]'s handler still ends the program's checked computation.
D	463	The switch is a module beneath `core/fibre`	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d463-the-switch-is-a-module-beneath-core-fibre	Chosen: `core/fibre` holds the concepts `task`, `scheduler` and `turns`, the record `space`, `whole` and the group, and calls no builtin. The switch, `prepare` and `switch`, and the round of fixed turns built on it, `round`, are the submodule `core/fibre/stacks`, as `core/io/fake` is `core/io`'s. A program that never switches a stack, a group over `whole` or over the blocking host, is then admitted on every target, firmware and synthetic-32 included; one that imports `core/fibre/stacks` is admitted where its backend emits the builtins. `hosted/system` provides `fibre.scheduler` in a file of its own and imports `core/fibre` and not its switch, so no hosted target is refused for it. There is no import cycle: `core/fibre` imports `core/failure` for its error set and `core/mem`, and neither imports anything hosted. The price is the closure: every hosted program now reaches `core/fibre`, `core/failure` and the `core/map` and `core/tree` that `core/failure` names atoms from, which made a hosted program's debug compile about a tenth slower when it was measured and its executable no larger.
D	464	The spellings `core/fibre` changed from prototype 5's sketch	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d464-the-spellings-core-fibre-changed-from-prototype-5-s-sketch	Chosen: four spellings and one representation, each because the sketch's would not compile or would not hold. `task`'s entry is `run: (self: ptr mut task_type) -> none`: an `inout self` has no erased table (D146), and a provider is handed `any task`. The switch's, the providers' and the group's failure is `mem.out_of_memory`, where the sketch had `stack_too_small | stack_misaligned`: `failure.reason` must hold whatever `admit` fails with, which would make `core/failure` import `core/fibre`; a stack is aligned by `stack_prepare` and never misaligned; and caller-lent backing too small for its use is out of memory, as `core/arena`'s and `core/pool`'s is. `prepare` takes a fourth record, `after`, the one a fibre resumes when its task has ended: the sketch's "switches back to whoever started it" is not the round's next turn, and a provider is the one that knows. A round's wait when nobody can run is the concept `stacks.idler`, given to `round_over`, with `stacks.spin` returning at once; it is called after a whole round in which every unfinished entry yielded and nothing started or ended. And a group made over `turns` keeps its provider as `any turns` beside an unused `any scheduler`, because the one does not convert to the other.
D	465	Where a record's limit stands	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d465-where-a-record-s-limit-stands	Chosen: `prepare` sets the limit 1 KiB above the stack's lowest byte, and refuses a stack smaller than 2 KiB. The check is made at a switch, inside the provider, after the provider's own calls on the way to it, and those took several hundred bytes below the task's frame at the higher optimization profiles; with the limit at the lowest byte, a task's overflow reached its own record, below the stack, before any switch read the limit from it, and the program ran on into a fault. With the room, a task whose calls go a little past the limit between two switches traps `stack_exhausted` at the next before it has written below its stack. One that goes further has written there already: the check is late, as D447 said, and the depth report it names is what bounds a stack.
D	467	The depth report covers every emitted routine, from its caller's stack pointer	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d467-the-depth-report-covers-every-emitted-routine-from-its-caller-s-stack-pointer	Chosen: `--stack-report=PATH` writes, beside emitted assembly or an executable, one JSON row for every routine the backend emitted, with whether its address is taken, so whoever starts a fibre reads its entry's row. A routine's frame is the backend's own figure: how far its code takes the stack pointer below where its caller's stood before the call, so x86-64's return address, every frame record, the frame, and the largest area it reserves around one call or pushes for a moment. Its depth is its frame plus the deepest of its callees' depths, of what `compiler.stack_switch` saves on the leaving stack where it switches, and of a failed check's call where one calls out. A switch is not a call into the context it resumes. A selected handler runs on the stack that failed, and a check failing in its own calls enters it once more as far as its frame before trapping, so the handler is measured with its own frame as that cost and every other routine with what that measured; D361's report costs what its routine takes. The hosted entry's call to the argument initializer is counted from its whole frame. What `compiler.stack_prepare` lays at a stack's top and how far below the top the entry starts are the target's, reported once; on Cortex-M0 the exception frame is D461's. A report holds frames and depths and no backing arithmetic: alignment of the top, the `starting` record, D461's thirty-six bytes and the margin above a stack's base (D472) are the consumer's sums. Calls are read from the unit the backend was given, so a call it closed by inlining is not one.
D	468	What opens a call graph	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d468-what-opens-a-call-graph	Chosen: a report lists each opening once, with its kind, the routine it is in and where, and each routine the openings its calls reach; such a routine is not closed, and its depth is what the rest closes. The kinds are: `any`, a call through an erased table; `evidence`, a generic's call through a table a caller handed it; `function value`, a call through any other function value; `foreign`, a call to a declaration no emitted routine defines under its link name, or through a C function value; `recursion`, each call inside a cycle, whose depth is not followed; `helper`, a routine that calls the target toolchain's runtime, as Cortex-M0's `__aeabi_*` division does; and `assembly`, a naked routine, whose text owns the stack, or a [1630] block whose text pushes, pops, enters, leaves, calls or names a stack pointer. A call through a routine's address or a constant table computed in the same routine is a call to that routine; a value traced through slots names only the opening's kind, because a slot may be written through its address. A failed check's own openings are the report's `trap`: the handler's, or D361's report calling the C library's `write` off Linux on the stack it was called on, which D491 leaves only in a program that prepares no stack.
D	469	The switch and start routines have names a debugger shows	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d469-the-switch-and-start-routines-have-names-a-debugger-shows	Chosen: both are local function symbols with their sizes, `landin.stack_switch` and `landin.stack_start`, which Mach-O spells with its underscore and LLDB shows without it. No Landin routine can be spelled with the dot, so no routine of a program takes either name; an explicit link name beginning `landin.` moves the prefix, as one beginning with a local label's prefix moves that. On Mach-O each still begins an atom of its own. The start routine's symbol begins at its opening nop, and a prepared first frame returns past the nop, so the return address less one that a debugger looks up lies in the start routine's symbol as well as in its unwind description. Neither routine has a DWARF subprogram, as no routine the compiler writes for itself has: a debugger names the frame from the symbol and shows no line or variables for it. Their unwind information is D447's, unchanged.
D	470	What a fibre consumer's capacity on Cortex-M0 counts	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d470-what-a-fibre-consumer-s-capacity-on-cortex-m0-counts	Chosen: flash is the highest end of the image's flash load, and static RAM the highest end of its RAM load, alignment and zero fill included; a fibre's backing that the program declares as module storage is static RAM, identified by its symbol's extent, and is counted there once. The reserved RAM is static RAM and the main-stack reservation. A fibre's backing is the stack a group cuts for it, its record at its base included; the peak simultaneous backing is the sum of the backings live at once, which for a group is every stack it cut from admission to join. A fibre's peak is the deepest byte written below its stack's top in a run of the consumer, read from paint laid before the group cuts the backing, and it fits when that peak and D461's thirty-six bytes lie within the stack above the record. The consumer fits the profile when its flash is at most 32 KiB, its reserved RAM at most 16 KiB, its main stack's painted peak within the reservation and every fibre fits. Paint is an observation of this consumer's run, not a bound on any stack (D447), and a stack's limit, its base and D472's margin, is a trap, not a measure of depth.
D	471	Every routine checks its frame against its stack's limit	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d471-every-routine-checks-its-frame-against-its-stack-s-limit	Chosen: a program whose whole program holds a `compiler.stack_prepare` checks every ordinary routine's frame in its prologue. After the frame record and before the frame is reserved, the routine compares the stack pointer less its frame with one cell, the current stack's limit, and when it is below traps `stack_exhausted` at its own site, its declaration's: through the selected handler or the hosted default report, from its frame record, with nothing of its frame reserved or written. A call's argument area larger than the target's unchecked figure (D472) is checked the same way before it is reserved, at the routine's site. The cell holds zero on the stack the program started on, so routines running there never trap, and a switch installs the resumed context's limit (D472). These are not checked: a routine that makes no call and whose frame is no larger than the unchecked figure, which the margin pays for; a naked routine, whose text owns the stack; the selected handler, which instead stores zero in the cell, so that it and what it calls run on what a failed check left without a check that would enter it again, D232's latch still refusing a second entry; and on Cortex-M0 an interrupt handler, which runs on the main stack that no prepared stack's limit describes: it keeps the interrupted context's limit below its frame record, zero in the cell while it runs, and puts the limit back as it returns. On Cortex-M0 a call-free routine whose frame is larger than the unchecked figure keeps the frame record its check needs. A program with no `compiler.stack_prepare` has no check and no cell, and its code is byte for byte what it was. The cell is the running thread's (D497). A check is one load, one compare and one branch, with the instructions that form the frame's address and the cell's and the test of that address's borrow (D1111): five instructions on x86-64, whose load is `%fs`-relative; six on Linux and FreeBSD arm64 and eight on Darwin, which read the thread pointer first (D506); and nine on RV64 and on Cortex-M0, whose branch to the trap is a far one.
D	472	A saved context carries its limit, a margin above its stack's base	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d472-a-saved-context-carries-its-limit-a-margin-above-its-stack-s-base	Chosen: `compiler.stack_switch(save, resume)` has two arguments. The switch saves the cell's value in the frame it pushes on the leaving stack and, once the resumed stack is current, loads the value saved in that frame into the cell: x86-64 pushes it as an eighth word, a 64-byte frame; arm64 stores it at 144 in a 176-byte frame, below its frame record (D475); RV64 in the frame's lowest word, which was unused, keeping 208; and Cortex-M0 pushes it with a scratch word between r4 to r7 and the rest of D460's frame, 48 bytes. The switch checks nothing: the routine that calls it checked its frame, and its save is inside the margin. `compiler.stack_prepare` lays the stack's limit in the same place of the first frame, the slice's base plus the target's margin, and traps `stack_exhausted` when the slice cannot hold the first frame and the margin.\n\nThe margin pays for what runs below a checked frame with no check of its own: a call area or a call-free routine's frame, each up to the unchecked figure; the frame record a callee pushes before its check; the switch's save; and a failed check's call of the handler or the default report, and the handler's own depth; on Cortex-M0 also D461's thirty-six bytes, which an interrupt may stack at any instruction. The worst before a handler's own frames is two unchecked figures, a frame record and the call, except on Xtensa: it checks every ordinary frame, including call-free routines, and a frame holds its routine's outgoing area (D1110), so no area is unchecked. The failed callee's 32-byte ENTRY and a 16-byte ABI spill cushion are 48 bytes, well below its conservative 416-byte allowance, which still counts a 256-byte area. Window exceptions use the existing ABI spill areas and recorded backchains without reserving another frame, and the stack pointer they are found from stays where the prologue left it.\n\n| Target | Margin | Unchecked | Switch frame | Before the handler | Left for the handler |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| x86-64 | 640 | 64 | 64 | 152 | 488 |\n| arm64 | 640 | 64 | 176 | 144 | 496 |\n| RV64 | 768 | 64 | 208 | 144 | 624 |\n| Cortex-M0 | 384 | 64 | 48 | 188 | 196 |\n| Xtensa | 1024 | 256 | 336 | 416 | 608 |\n\nRV32 keeps RV64's 768 (D675), and a Cortex-M profile with a float unit adds 72 bytes each for the extended exception frame and the larger switch frame (D620), 528 in all.\n\nThe default report needs 8 to 24 bytes of that. What is left is sized from the depth report's `trap` figure, which counts a handler's frame twice (D467), for the corpus's selected handlers that run on an overflowed stack, at every profile: those of `runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler` and `runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`, which match the kind and switch away, took at most 384 bytes on x86-64 and arm64 and 544 on RV64, at `none`, and 160 on Cortex-M0. On both Xtensa configurations these handlers take at most 544 bytes across the six profiles, leaving 64 bytes within their 608-byte handler allowance. The complete window context is 336 bytes. A 1536-byte margin left existing 2 KiB prepared stacks too little room for ordinary frames. Compact ordinary word homes and a 1024-byte margin retain the measured handler bound while admitting those unchanged consumers. A margin of 1 KiB, which covered handlers three times their size, made `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave`'s 4 KiB stacks too small at `none`, and so was declined. The report's `margin_bytes` and `unchecked_bytes` give the two figures beside the `trap` depth, so a reader sees whether a program's handler fits; one that does not is refused (D474). The default report always fits. A switch between two contexts that were never prepared, both on the stack the program started on, carries zero, as that stack's limit is.
D	473	What `core/fibre/stacks` keeps of a stack's limit	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d473-what-core-fibre-stacks-keeps-of-a-stack-s-limit	Chosen: `fibre.space` keeps where its stack pointer was saved and its status, and no limit; `stacks.switch` names neither record's limit; and `stacks.prepare` keeps no room of its own. It fails `mem.out_of_memory` for a stack smaller than 128 words beside its `starting`, which holds the first frame and the margin of every target of that word size, 976 bytes at most of 1,024 on the 64-bit targets and 432 of 512 on Cortex-M0, so a stack too small is out of memory, as D464 has it, rather than the builtin's trap. How deep a task goes is the stack's business: a deeper one traps at the routine that overflows. `runtime/fibre-same-source-any-provider` keeps the 8 KiB stacks its task needs on RV64, where it takes 4.1 to 4.4 KiB at every profile: 4 KiB stacks would now trap `stack_exhausted` there instead of writing below the stack. For the same reason the 4 KiB stacks of `runtime/fibre-turns-interleave` and `runtime/fibre-join-first-failure` became 8 and 5 KiB: their tasks went deeper than 4 KiB less the margin on RV64, into D465's room, which the late check let them use. On the retained Cortex-M0 profile the measured consumer (D470) no longer needs D465's 2 KiB: its two fibres fit on backings of 1,472 bytes where they had 2,176, painted to at most 904 at every profile, and its reserved RAM fell from 8,576 to 7,168 bytes; the checks cost it 744 bytes of flash at `none` and 864 at `size`.
D	474	A selected handler must fit a prepared stack's margin	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d474-a-selected-handler-must-fit-a-prepared-stack-s-margin	Chosen: a program whose whole program holds a `compiler.stack_prepare` and whose entry module selects a `panic_handler` (D232) is refused with `L0508` when the handler does not fit the target's margin. What it needs is D472's worst before the handler, 152 bytes on x86-64, 144 on arm64 and RV64, 188 on Cortex-M0 and 416 on Xtensa, which the report gives as `handler_entry_bytes`, and the depth report's `trap` figure, which counts the handler's frame twice for a check failing in its own calls (D467); the margin is 640, 640, 768, 384 and 1024 bytes. The refusal gives both, the margin and the target, and the handler's deepest path, at the handler. A handler whose calls reach an opening of D468, `any`, `evidence`, `function value`, `foreign`, `recursion`, `helper` or `assembly`, has no depth to compare and is refused too, though since D570 a call through `any`, a table or a function value opens it only when the program holds no routine it can reach, naming the first opening's kind and routine and pointing at it, with how many more there are. The depth is the emitted code's, on the target and profile being compiled, so the rule is decided after emission and before anything is written, for `--emit=asm` and `--emit=exe` alike, a dry run included; `--emit=ir` has no frames and does not raise it, `refine check` and the server decide it from the frames the backend would emit (D572), and a handler that fits at one profile may not at another. A program that prepares no stack is not refused, however large its handler: no fibre can exist there, and its handler runs on the stack the program started on. A program that selects no handler is never refused: D361's report takes 8 to 24 bytes and Cortex-M0's trap instruction none beyond D461's exception frame, which the figure before the handler holds, so the default fits every margin with at least 464 bytes to spare on the hosted targets and 196 on Cortex-M0. Off Linux the default report calls the C library's `write`, whose stack the compiler does not know, on a stack of its own (D491), so the margin pays only its frame. The handlers of `runtime/stack-exhausted-reaches-the-handler` and `runtime/stack-frame-past-limit-traps`, which match the kind and switch away, need at most 536 bytes on x86-64, 528 on arm64, 688 on RV64 and 348 on Cortex-M0, at `none`.
D	475	The switch routines' names stand alone, and the switch keeps a frame record	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d475-the-switch-routines-names-stand-alone-and-the-switch-keeps-a-frame-record	Chosen: every FreeBSD link passes `-Wl,--discard-locals`, which drops the local symbols whose names begin `.L` from the image and keeps the global ones, so an explicit `.L` link name still resolves and a debugger finds only the routines' own names at their addresses. The objects keep their labels, as `-L` asks; the image is what a debugger reads. Linux assembles with GNU as without `-L` and its output is unchanged; on Mach-O no `L` label reaches an object and the link drops every linker-private `l` name.\n\nThe arm64 switch routine opens with the frame record, then lowers sp by 160 and stores x19-x28 and d8-d15 from the frame's bottom, the stack's limit at 144 and a pad word; the frame stays 176 bytes, and a prepared first frame lays the same bytes, its record x29 zero and x30 past the start routine's nop. Its unwind rule is x29 plus 16 from the record's opening, and the switch points x29 at the resumed stack's record before loading that stack's sp, so the debugger's frames become the resumed context's at that instruction, whether it reads the unwind information or the frame record; the rule returns to sp once the saved registers are released. The start routine alone is exempt from the contract, by its name: its return address is undefined so that a walk ends there (D447), which a record would contradict.
D	476	The hosted services split into the system and two waiting providers	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d476-the-hosted-services-split-into-the-system-and-two-waiting-providers	Chosen: three modules. `hosted/system` keeps the services that do not wait and are the same whoever waits: the arguments, the environment, opening and closing files, directories, running programs, entropy and the wall clock, and the last-error and last-signal cells. It is no longer a world, because reading and writing can wait. `hosted/blocking` is the provider whose waiting operations block the thread: reading and writing, the network, the monotonic clock's `sleep`, and `fibre.scheduler`, running each task to its end. `hosted/events` is the provider whose waiting operations switch fibres over the system's event mechanism. Each of the two is built over a `hosted/system` handle and supplies `io.world` and the concepts the system supplies, by handing it what does not wait. A program mints its root from the one it chooses, `blocking.new()` or `events.over(...)` (`events.new` until D1032); a program that never waits on anything may still use `system.new()` alone. Every hosted source and document moves from `system.new()` to `blocking.new()`. D479 amends this list: starting a program stays with the system, and reading its pipes and waiting for it are the waiting providers'.
D	477	Only a provider that takes turns waits for signals	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d477-only-a-provider-that-takes-turns-waits-for-signals	Chosen: `core/io`'s `signals` concept is provided only by providers of `fibre.turns`. A program that waits for a signal asks for both, so over `hosted/blocking` it cannot be written and the process keeps the system's default disposition: SIGTERM ends it. Prototype 5's derived server takes its signal waiter only when it was given a provider of turns, and the choice is made where the providers are minted.
D	478	Which side of the split each hosted concept is on	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d478-which-side-of-the-split-each-hosted-concept-is-on	Chosen: `hosted/system` supplies `files`, `process`, `environment`, `directories`, `programs`, `file_system`, `terminals`, `entropy` and `time.wall_clock`. `process` is the standard streams' descriptors and the arguments, which do not wait; reading a stream does. `file_system`'s `read_at` and `write_at` stay with it, because a regular file is always ready and no event mechanism waits on one. `programs` stays with it as D476 says, its pipes read and written and its children waited for by blocking the thread whatever provider is built over it. Entropy stays with it: `getrandom` waits only once, at boot, for a pool no event announces. D479 amends the placement of `programs`: the waiting providers supply it, and the system keeps only `start`, which they build on. `hosted/blocking` supplies `reader`, `writer` and so `world`, `net.network`, the monotonic `time.clock`, since `now` cannot be supplied without `sleep`, and `fibre.scheduler`, and supplies every concept of the system's by calling the system's own entry on its handle. Its handle is a struct holding the system's; there is one last-error cell, the system handle's, which `hosted/system` lets a provider built over it clear and fill with `clear_errno` and `record_errno`, and `is_socket` tells such a provider which of the system's files it writes by sending. The file encoding, `descriptor_of`, `file_of` and `socket_of`, stays the system's alone, so a program that converts a descriptor imports both modules.
D	479	Starting a child is the system's, and waiting on it is a waiting provider's	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d479-starting-a-child-is-the-system-s-and-waiting-on-it-is-a-waiting-provider-s	Chosen: `io.programs` keeps its one shape, and the providers that wait supply it, as they supply reading and writing: `hosted/blocking` and `hosted/events`, each in its `programs.ldn`. `write_child`, `read_child` and `wait` are the entries that wait; `spawn` and `close_input` do not. Starting a child stays in `hosted/system`, as the public routine `system.start(handle, path, arguments, environment, streams)`, which makes the pipes and `/dev/null`, calls `posix.spawn`, maps its errno onto the concept's atoms in the handle's last-error cell, and answers an `io.child` whose pipes are files of the system's, which the provider reads, writes and closes as its own. `system.process_of` gives the child's `posix.process_id` for the provider to wait for, and `system.ended` turns the status it waited for into `io.ending`, keeping the signal in the handle's last-signal cell. `hosted/system` is no provider of `io.programs`. The blocking provider polls both output pipes and reads with its `read`, as before; the event provider sets the parent's ends non-blocking and waits on them as on any file, and waits for the end of a child through `pidfd_open` on Linux (D487), and kqueue's `EVFILT_PROC` with `NOTE_EXIT`, which `platform/kqueue` names as `note_exit`, on Darwin and FreeBSD, before reaping it with a `wait` that does not block. This amends D476's list of the system's services and D478's placement of `programs`.\n\n`posix.spawn` starts every child with an empty signal mask, on Linux by `rt_sigprocmask` in the child between the copy and the exec, and on Darwin and FreeBSD by `posix_spawnattr_setsigmask` with `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGMASK`. Beside SIGPIPE, which D322 already gives back, it gives the child the default disposition of each signal named to `posix.default_in_children(signal)`, which a provider calls for every signal it takes from its disposition; `POSIX_SPAWN_SETSIGDEF` carries them on Darwin and FreeBSD, and `rt_sigaction` in the Linux child. A signal nobody named keeps whatever disposition the parent gives it, so a shell's background job, started with SIGINT ignored, and a program under `nohup` pass their ignores on as POSIX programs do. `default_in_children` refuses with `einval` a number that is no signal, one past 64 or Darwin's 31, and SIGKILL and SIGSTOP, which a child could not be given.
D	480	The event loop sleeps in its wait, and needs no descriptor to wake it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d480-the-event-loop-sleeps-in-its-wait-and-needs-no-descriptor-to-wake-it	Chosen: the loop's sleep is the wait's own time limit: `epoll_pwait`'s milliseconds, a part of one counting as a whole one, and `kevent`'s `timespec`. A fibre's deadline is kept by the provider and checked against the monotonic clock when the wait returns, so a limit rounded up wakes the loop late by less than a millisecond and never early. Nothing outside the loop's own thread can make it ready while there is one thread and no handler runs Landin code (D449), so there is no waking descriptor. `platform/linux` therefore wraps `epoll_create1`, `epoll_ctl`, `epoll_pwait`, `signalfd4` and `rt_sigprocmask` and neither `eventfd2` nor the timerfd calls, and `platform/kqueue` names the timer filter, which a program may use, and not the user filter. Their numbers stay in `platform/linux/numbers` for a program that wants them.
D	481	kqueue is a module named for the facility, declared on the two systems that have it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d481-kqueue-is-a-module-named-for-the-facility-declared-on-the-two-systems-that-have-it	Chosen: `platform/kqueue`, one file, `kqueue.ldn`, declaring `kqueue`, `kevent`, each system's `struct kevent` as `event_record`, the filters and flags the two share and each system's timer units under `compiler.os`, and nothing on Linux. Its scope is the hosted POSIX systems, Linux included, as `platform/linux`'s is, so a provider written once imports both and selects its own routines by `compiler.os`; firmware refuses it by name. It imports `platform/libc` for `timespec` and leaves the errno to `libc.errno_cell`. The calls a signal waiter needs beside it, `sigprocmask`, `kill` and `getpid`, are every system's C library's and are declared in `platform/libc`.
D	482	Signals are a module beneath `core/io`, and an arrival names its signal portably	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d482-signals-are-a-module-beneath-core-io-and-an-arrival-names-its-signal-portably	Chosen: the concept is `signals` in `core/io/signal`, a module beneath `core/io` as `core/io/fake` is, which imports `core/fibre` and `core/io`: `signals: type = concept (provider: type) is fibre.turns`. Its entries are `watch`, which takes one signal from the system's default disposition and delivers it as an event from then on; `next_signal`, which waits, taking turns, for the next arrival; and `stop_watching`, which gives every watched signal back to its default disposition and wakes every waiter, whose call fails `io_failed`, as D449 stops a fibre by failing what it waits on. Only `next_signal` switches. A signal is named by the atom set `kind`: `interrupt`, `terminate`, `hangup`, `child`, `user1` and `user2`, the six a server cares about, and an arrival is an `event` of its `kind` and the system's own number. One signal at a time is watched, so both mechanisms implement it directly: signalfd adds it to the blocked mask and the descriptor's set, kqueue ignores it and adds an `EVFILT_SIGNAL` filter. Two arrivals before a read may be one event, as both systems keep them. The fake, `fake.signals`, is given the turns it waits on and passes `fibre.turns`' entries to them, so it is a provider of both; `raise` delivers a signal into it, one nobody watches is counted and dropped, and it numbers signals as Linux does on x86-64 and arm64.\n\nWriting this found that the checker counted only a parent concept written as a bare name: a parent named through its module, `fibre.turns` here, `io.reader` beneath `net.network`, was skipped, so a conformance to the child was accepted without one to the parent. The concept body's parents now include a qualified reference, as its accessor's postcondition already said.
D	483	The fake network is given its turns by a second constructor	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d483-the-fake-network-is-given-its-turns-by-a-second-constructor	Chosen: `network_over_turns(state, sockets, runs)` makes the network over a `fibre.turns` it borrows for as long as it is used, beside `network_over`, which keeps a scheduler that is never called and waits for nothing. A call that would wait, `accept`, `send`, `receive`, `receive_from` and the reader and writer entries over them, yields and looks again. The network counts in `moves` each change something could wait for: a connection made or taken, bytes or a datagram delivered or taken, a shutdown and a close. A call that yielded and finds `moves` unchanged has seen a whole round of every other fibre in which nothing moved, and so nothing it waits for arrived, and fails `timed_out`; one that finds it changed looks again. A call whose socket was closed, or shut for receiving, while it waited fails `io_failed` when it wakes, as D449 asks of an Io that runs fibres. `turns` counts the turns its calls took.
D	484	A direct table's entry no selection names is not lowered	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d484-a-direct-table-s-entry-no-selection-names-is-not-lowered	Chosen: a direct table's entry is reached only by a reached selection that names it: a constrained generic body's `t.entry`, in the instance's own view, which is the only way code reads a direct table, so the selection names the exact conformance the instance receives. A reached instance makes the tables of its evidence exist without reaching any of their entries. An erased table, built where an `any` is constructed or an erased entry selected, still reaches every entry and D145's parents, because an `any` value may have any entry read, and so does a `for`'s iterable conformance, which names no entry. A direct table's entry that nothing reaches is absent: its provider is not lowered, the IR entry names no routine and no signature, it keeps its place so D144's and D147's offsets stand, and every backend emits it as D374's zero word, which a projection elsewhere in its family can therefore not keep. The verifier refuses a projection of an absent entry.
D	485	The event provider is made over its caller's round and loop, and a wait is kept on its fibre's stack	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d485-the-event-provider-is-made-over-its-caller-s-round-and-loop-and-a-wait-is-kept-on-its-fibre-s-stack	Chosen: `events.over(state, entries)`, `events.new` until D1032, fills an `events.space` the caller declares `zeroed`, the round's state and the event loop's, and returns a handle `from state, entries`, where `entries` is the round's table, one more than the fibres that may be unfinished at once. It fails `mem.out_of_memory` for a table of fewer than two and `io_failed` when the system makes no queue. The handle runs its fibres on core/fibre/stacks' `round`, whose idler is the loop, and passes the round's entries on through their evidence, so it is a `fibre.turns`. An operation that waits fills a record on its own fibre's stack, links it into the loop's list and takes turns until the loop answers it: the fibre does not return from the call before then, so the list never holds a record whose frame has gone, and the provider needs no table of waits for the caller to size. The hosted/system handle beneath is the process's, `system.new()`, as `blocking.new()`'s is, so `last_errno` reads the process's cell. The queue is closed on exec and stays open until the process ends; there is no call that closes it.
D	486	A wait is submitted and answered, and the loop sleeps only when every fibre waits	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d486-a-wait-is-submitted-and-answered-and-the-loop-sleeps-only-when-every-fibre-waits	Chosen: a waiting record names a descriptor and a direction, a child (kqueue's), a signal or a deadline on the monotonic clock, and the loop answers it `ready`, `expired` or `failed`; the operation then makes its call again. Submitting arms the descriptor once, `EPOLLONESHOT` for the union of the directions every record on it waits for and kqueue's `EV_ONESHOT` per filter, and after a report the loop arms it again for the records still waiting. The round calls the loop when every fibre has taken a turn since anything last started or ended. The loop then waits without a limit, until the earliest deadline, or not at all when a fibre took a turn of its own through `yield`, which is runnable work; with no record waiting and no such turn it returns at once. Closing a file, a socket or a child's pipe through the provider answers every record on its descriptor `failed` and removes it from epoll before the descriptor closes; shutting a socket's side answers that side's records. The provider's sockets and a child's pipes are non-blocking; a file it did not make, a standard stream or a file opened by path, is polled with no limit first and read or written once ready, so a regular file, always ready, is read at once, and the program's terminal is never made non-blocking behind its shell. While such a file is blocking, a write to it is handed no more than a pipe reported ready takes without waiting, unless it is a regular file (D1045). A socket's limits are kept as the system's own time limits, which a non-blocking socket never waits on, and each wait reads them back, `platform/posix`'s `send_timeout` beside `receive_timeout`; a limit the system does not give back, as QEMU's user emulation does not, is none. A connect has no limit.
D	487	A child's end is a pidfd on Linux and kqueue's process filter elsewhere	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d487-a-child-s-end-is-a-pidfd-on-linux-and-kqueue-s-process-filter-elsewhere	Chosen: on Linux the provider opens a pidfd for the child, waits for it to be readable as for any descriptor, closes it and reaps the child with `posix.wait`; a kernel without `pidfd_open`, before 5.3, has the reap wait the thread instead. On Darwin and FreeBSD it adds a one-shot `EVFILT_PROC` filter for `note_exit`, and a child the queue refuses with ESRCH has ended already and is reaped at once. `spawn` starts the child through the system handle and sets the parent's pipe ends non-blocking; `read_child` reads the output when it has anything, its end included, then the errors, and when neither is ready waits for both and goes on with whichever the loop answers first.
D	488	The event provider reads every watched signal through one descriptor, and stopping reads what came	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d488-the-event-provider-reads-every-watched-signal-through-one-descriptor-and-stopping-reads-what-came	Chosen: on Linux one signalfd reads every watched signal, its mask growing with each `watch`, and the loop watches it from the first. On Darwin and FreeBSD each watched signal is ignored and reported by an `EVFILT_SIGNAL` filter, except SIGCHLD, whose default already ignores it: an ignored SIGCHLD reaps every child before `wait` could. Each signal is named to `posix.default_in_children` before it is taken, so no child keeps the block or the ignore. The loop keeps each arrival in order of arrival, two of one signal before a read being one, until a fibre reads it with `next_signal`, which waits as a receive does. `stop_watching` first reads what arrived, so that unblocking a signal that came while it was watched does not deliver it with its default, then closes the signalfd, unblocks or restores every watched signal, forgets the arrivals and fails every waiter `io_failed`; a later `next_signal` fails at once until `watch` is called again.
D	489	Prototype 5's derived server, and where it departs from the sketch	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d489-prototype-5-s-derived-server-and-where-it-departs-from-the-sketch	Chosen: `examples/derived_server` has the sketch's four modules. Its `app` reads `--io=blocking` or `--io=events` and `--port=N` through a `hosted/system` handle, and its two minting routines are the only code that knows which provider it got. Over the blocking provider it calls `server.serve`, which announces the address and serves with no signal waiter, so SIGTERM ends the process by its default disposition. Over a provider of turns and signals it calls `server.serve_until_terminated`, which watches SIGTERM, announces, and runs a fibre that waits for the signal, then shuts both directions of every connection being served and closes the listener; the accept and every receive fail `io_failed` (D449), and the server ends cleanly, with the count of requests it answered, only when the waiter stopped it. Such a provider is lent three ways, as `fibre.turns`, `signal.signals` and `fibre.scheduler`, since the three do not convert (D464). An `any C` is a provider of C and of the concepts C refines (D492), so the erased network goes to `net`'s routines, `io.lines_over` and `io.buffered_over`, and the erased clock to `protocol.answer`, generic over its clock, as the sketch wrote them, with no adapter. The protocol separates words by one space, takes a tag of at least one byte and no space, and refuses a wait over a minute; every other line, one too long for the session's buffer among them, is answered `malformed`.
D	490	Prototype 5's two-process evidence observes the order without turns	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d490-prototype-5-s-two-process-evidence-observes-the-order-without-turns	Chosen: the fixture's program is both parts. Run without arguments it is the harness: it starts itself again through `io.programs`, by `posix.program_name()`, with `serve`, the provider's `--io=` and `--port=0`, and the child calls the same `app.entry` as the example's `main`. The harness reads the child's first output line for the address, sends `WAIT 1000 a` on one connection and `NOW b` on another, and reads the second with a receive limit of 500 milliseconds: an answer within it came before `a`, which the server sends no sooner than 1000 milliseconds after it was asked, and none means `a` came first. It needs no turns, so it runs over the blocking provider on every hosted target. It sends SIGTERM, `kill` on Darwin and FreeBSD and the system call on Linux, reads the rest of the child's output and waits for it: over the blocking provider the child must have been ended by the signal and written nothing more. The same exchange then runs with `--io=events`, over `hosted/events`, and requires `b` first, `stopped after 2 requests` as the child's last line and status 0: the server's signal waiter, not the signal's default, ended it. The server's source is the same in both children; only `app`'s minting routine differs. The QEMU cross lanes, which cannot start the program's own child without a binfmt_misc handler, list the fixture in `compiler/tests/cross-lanes.json`, and the gate's RV64 lane registers one (D1037).
D	491	Off Linux the default report writes on a stack of its own	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d491-off-linux-the-default-report-writes-on-a-stack-of-its-own	Chosen: off Linux, in a program that prepares a stack, the report routine pushes its frame record on the stack it was called on, as before, and then moves the stack pointer to the top of a 16 KiB stack of its own in zeroed storage, aligned for C, before it calls `write`. The report never returns, so nothing moves the pointer back. The frame address still names the record on the failed stack, so a debugger that stops on the terminal instruction unwinds to the failed check as before. The stack that failed pays only the report's frame, which D472's figures already count, so the margin and D474's verdicts are unchanged, and the stack report's `trap` in such a program is closed while `foreign_write` still says that the C library is called. A program that prepares no stack keeps the report on the stack it is called on, which is the one the program started on, and its `trap` stays open, as D468 has it. Linux's report is a system call, which needs no stack, and is unchanged, as are Cortex-M0's bare instruction and every program that prepares no stack. The storage is one per program, which a thread claims before it uses it (D498). 16 KiB is ten times what either FreeBSD guest measured and holds the largest vector state x86-64 saves.
D	492	An `any C` is a provider of C and of the concepts C refines	Decisions: Concepts, generics and runtime dispatch	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d492-an-any-c-is-a-provider-of-c-and-of-the-concepts-c-refines	Chosen: an `any C` is a provider of C and of every concept C's erased table flattens (D147): its represented formal's constraint and its parents, transitively, compiler concepts excepted. The conformance is the compiler's, interned in the whole-program register with the key (concept, `any C`) when a constraint first asks for it, and a program that declares one is refused as L0319, as one declaring a `zeroable` conformance is. It provides no other concept, not even one every provider of C happens to conform to: that is L0318, whose note says to erase the provider as an `any` of the wanted concept where it is made. A conformance a program declares for `any C` to a concept outside that closure stays the program's.\n\nThe conformance has no provider routines and no table. In an instance whose type formal stands for `any C`, a selection `t.entry(first, ...)` is an erased call through its first argument: D146 makes `self` an entry's first parameter, so with `t` the pair it is `self: any C`, the pair itself, or `self: ptr any C` or `ptr mut any C`, a pointer to it, read when the call is made, as a provider called through a table would read it. The call dispatches through C's flattened erased table at the entry's flattened position, described by the first conformance of C as an erased call's own dispatch is, and is answered late (D377) when C has none yet; a concept no conformance answers traps there as D377 says. No hidden table is passed for the formal, so its selections reach no direct table (D484). The lowering, the IR, the verifier and every backend see the erased call they already had.\n\nPermission and origin are the pair's own, as a value's. A `ptr mut` provider parameter wants a writable pointer to the pair, so the address of an immutable `any` binding is refused as L0340, whatever write authority its data pointer carries (D146): writing through that pointer may replace the pair. A result `from host` carries the pair's origin (D146), so a line reader over an erased network made from a local does not outlive its frame. An entry that is not object-safe is refused where it is selected, as an erased call's is.\n\nOptimization is honest by construction (D211): the call is erased, never an evidence call, so dispatch specialization never makes it direct, and a build report lists it in `left_indirect` as a call through `any`. An instance at `any C` is one instance whichever provider the value holds.\n\nAn `any C` is already its own provider, so it is not erased again: `any(pointer)` whose pointee is an `any` is refused as L0318. A pair over a pair would dispatch twice through two tables, and an `any P` made from a pointer to an `any C`, P a parent of C, would be the conversion D145 declines.
D	493	A sleep on a clock beside the fake network is a move to come	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d493-a-sleep-on-a-clock-beside-the-fake-network-is-a-move-to-come	Chosen: `clock_over_beside(state, start, wall, network)`, named `clock_beside` until D1032, makes `core/io/fake`'s manual clock beside a network, and over a network that takes turns its `sleep` takes the network's turns. While it sleeps the network counts it in `sleepers`, and a call that waited a round finding `moves` unchanged fails `timed_out` only while `sleepers` is zero. The clock moves only after a whole round in which nothing in the network moved, when every other fibre waited: the sleeper that saw the round advances it by a millisecond, or by what is left of its sleep when that is less, and counts the advance in `moves`, so a second sleeper in the same round does not advance it again and sleepers wake in the order of their deadlines, to the millisecond. Beside a network that takes no turns, and from `clock_over`, the clock is as before: `sleep` advances it at once. The only new surface is the constructor and the `sleepers` count.
D	494	A program starts threads as a group it joins	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d494-a-program-starts-threads-as-a-group-it-joins	Chosen: `hosted/thread` starts threads as `core/fibre`'s application layer starts fibres. A group is made over a `hosted/system` handle, a backing the caller lends and a count; `admit` copies a task's state onto a free stack and starts a thread that calls an ordinary routine with that copy, waiting for a stack to come free when none is; the group keeps the first failure in a ledger the threads share through the atomic wrapper, and `join` fails with it once every admitted thread has ended. A task's error set is `failure.reason`, as D444's is, and a task with atoms of its own maps them into it before returning. With the fibre group and the thread group both carrying their caller's failures so, that mapping is the way a generic facility carries a caller's error set, rather than a stopgap until error sets become generic parameters. D445's `escaping into` and the `defer` that joins are as for fibres. A successful `admit` synchronizes with the new thread's first action and a thread's end with the return of the `join` that waits for it, as D227 has it; a failed start establishes neither edge and starts nothing. A static Linux program starts a thread with `clone` and waits for its end on the word the kernel clears; under `--link=libc`, on Darwin and on FreeBSD the C library starts it with `pthread_create` and waits with `pthread_join`. A thread begins with every signal blocked, so the signals a provider reads through a signalfd or kqueue reach that provider and no worker's default disposition. `join` blocks the calling thread whatever provider it runs under, so a fibre that joins holds its round. A worker may run a round of fibres of its own; a fibre never moves between threads.
D	495	A thread runs on a stack its caller lends, and checks it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d495-a-thread-runs-on-a-stack-its-caller-lends-and-checks-it	Chosen: as a fibre group does, a thread group cuts its caller's backing into equal stacks and prepares each with `compiler.stack_prepare`, so a program that starts a thread checks every routine against the running thread's own limit (D497) and a worker past its stack traps `stack_exhausted`. Where the C library starts the thread, its own start frames and, under glibc, the thread's block are placed in the same backing. A stack smaller than the system's minimum is refused when the group is made; the item that implements the group records the figures. Starting a thread allocates nothing and maps no guard page.
D	496	Per-thread module storage is placed by `link(thread)`	Decisions: Modules and compile time	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d496-per-thread-module-storage-is-placed-by-link-thread	Chosen: `link_attribute` gains `thread`. A module `mut` binding written `link(thread) mut cell: T` has one instance in every thread, each zeroed when its thread begins, so it takes no initializer and its type must be zeroable. A thread's reads and writes reach its own instance. On a hosted target the storage is the system's own: ELF thread-local storage in the local-exec model on Linux and FreeBSD, which a static Linux program sets up itself and the C library sets up otherwise, and Darwin's thread-local variables. On a target with no threads it is ordinary module storage, shared with interrupt handlers as any module storage is. It does not combine with `symbol` or `section`, so no C thread-local is named through it. What an instance's address may outlive, since the instance ends with its thread, is settled by the item that implements the form, in a record of its own.
D	497	A thread's limit cell is its own, in its system's thread storage	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d497-a-thread-s-limit-cell-is-its-own-in-its-system-s-thread-storage	Chosen: the cell is per thread. On Linux and FreeBSD it is ELF thread-local storage the image addresses in the local-exec model, so on x86-64 the check compares the stack pointer with an `%fs`-relative word. A static Linux program sets up its own thread pointer and block: its entry for the first thread, and the thread facility for each thread it starts, through `clone`'s `CLONE_SETTLS`. Under `--link=libc` and on FreeBSD the C library sets up the storage of every thread. Darwin has no ELF thread-local storage: there the cell is the slot of a pthread key the program creates before it runs Landin code, which the check reads inline through `tpidrro_el0`, and the program's start compares that read with `pthread_getspecific` and ends with a report if they disagree. A thread whose cell holds zero never traps, as D471's first stack never does: the thread a program starts on, and a C thread calling into Landin. D472's frames are unchanged; a switch saves and loads the running thread's cell. A program that prepares no stack and starts no thread still has no cell and no check.
D	498	One report stack serves every thread, claimed before it is used	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d498-one-report-stack-serves-every-thread-claimed-before-it-is-used	Chosen: the stack stays one per program. Before the report moves to it, it claims a latch of its own with an atomic exchange; a thread that finds the latch claimed writes nothing and waits, without returning, for the report that claimed it to end the process. The report's frame on the failed stack, and therefore D472's margins and D474's verdicts, are unchanged. Linux's report, a system call that needs no stack, takes no latch: each trapping thread's line is one `write`. D232's panic latch is the selected handler's and is unchanged.
D	499	An atomic is fenced as its ordering asks	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d499-an-atomic-is-fenced-as-its-ordering-asks	Chosen: each backend lowers an atomic by its ordering, by the mapping of its architecture's memory model: on x86-64 a load and a relaxed or release store are a plain move, a seq_cst store an exchange, a read-modify-write a locked instruction with no fence, and only a seq_cst fence an `mfence`; on arm64 acquire and release accesses are `ldar` and `stlr` or their exclusive and LSE forms, and fences `dmb ishld` or `dmb ish`; on RV64 the mapping the RISC-V memory model gives, with `.aq` and `.rl` on its atomic instructions; and on Cortex-M0 a `dmb` only where an acquire or a release needs one, or at `armv8-m.main` the `lda` and `stl` that acquire and release (D606). Every atomic stays a full compiler memory boundary, and the alignment check is unchanged.
D	500	`core/atomic` wraps one scalar, and its operations carry their orderings	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d500-core-atomic-wraps-one-scalar-and-its-operations-carry-their-orderings	Chosen: `core/atomic` gives a cell over one `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64`. A load acquires and a store releases; exchange, add and compare-exchange are acq_rel, a failed comparison acquiring; a relaxed family loads, stores and adds for counters and caches; seq_cst stays with the builtins. The single-writer update, a relaxed load and a release store, is an operation of its own, correct while one context writes the cell, on every target. On Cortex-M0 exchange, add and compare-exchange are refused at the caller's use, the refusal naming the single-writer update and `platform/cortex_m`'s critical section, as are the eight-byte cell's operations there.
D	501	A lock waits on its word through the system	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d501-a-lock-waits-on-its-word-through-the-system	Chosen: `hosted/thread` gives a lock over one word of the atomic wrapper, which an uncontended lock takes and gives with one read-modify-write each, and which waits and wakes through the system's own wait on an address: the futex on Linux, `_umtx_op` on FreeBSD and `os_sync_wait_on_address` on Darwin, which `platform/posix` names on each. Waiting blocks the thread, so a fibre that holds a lock across a switch can hold another fibre of its round. On Cortex-M0 the critical section is the lock.
D	502	The heap is shared, and the vDSO cache is relaxed	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d502-the-heap-is-shared-and-the-vdso-cache-is-relaxed	Chosen: `hosted/heap`'s size classes are behind one lock (D501). A mapping of its own needs no lock. The vDSO cache is a relaxed atomic word, whose value every thread computes alike, and which D499 makes a plain move. D	503	The process's own state beside threads	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d503-the-process-s-own-state-beside-threads	Chosen: `hosted/system`'s last-error and last-signal cells are `link(thread)` storage (D496), and a handle from `system.new()` records into the cell of the thread making the call, not the one that made the handle, so handles shared across threads keep D207's thread-local meaning; `system.over` still records into a cell of its caller's own. D	504	A static Linux program lays its first thread's storage before anything is checked	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d504-a-static-linux-program-lays-its-first-thread-s-storage-before-anything-is-checked	Chosen: platform/linux's naked `_landin_start` calls `_landin_start_thread` with the initial stack before anything else. That routine walks the auxiliary vector to the program headers, keeps what the TLS segment says (its image, the bytes of it that are initialized, its size rounded up to its alignment, and where in a block the image and the thread pointer go on this architecture), maps a block for the first thread with `_landin_start_map`, and returns its thread pointer; an executable with no TLS segment gets its control words in 48 bytes of module storage and maps nothing. The entry makes the pointer the thread's: `arch_prctl(ARCH_SET_FS)` on x86-64, `msr tpidr_el0` on arm64 and `mv tp` on RV64, the last of which only a naked routine may write. `_landin_start_main` then lays the block, zeroing it, copying the initialized image and, on x86-64, storing the pointer in the word it names, before it holds the processor to its level and calls `main`. A routine whose symbol begins `_landin_start` runs before the pointer exists and is not checked against a stack's limit, which on Linux are exactly these; `_landin_start_thread` therefore calls nothing but the map routine, whose system call it makes itself. For the threads the program starts, the module gives `thread_block_bytes`, the bytes a block and room to align it take, and `thread_block_lay(block)`, which lays a block in the caller's memory and returns the value `clone` takes with `CLONE_SETTLS`. Under `--link=libc` none of this runs: the C library lays every thread's storage and `thread_block_bytes` is zero.
D	505	A thread's instance lives as long as its thread, and is tracked as module storage	Decisions: Modules and compile time	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d505-a-thread-s-instance-lives-as-long-as-its-thread-and-is-tracked-as-module-storage	Chosen: an instance's address is valid while its thread runs, and every frame of that thread is inside that time, so the origin rules treat it as a module binding's: `addr`, an `inout` argument, a pointer kept in a local, and a result that returns it are all admitted as they are for module storage, and no new refusal applies. The thread's instances can keep the address only as an integer, since thread storage holds no pointer and no pointer union (L0328). What outlives the thread is another thread's storage or memory a thread hands another, and a pointer there is the program's to keep valid, as D446 leaves every reference shared with a thread to the program. A module binding can hold such a pointer only through a pointer union or an integer, since a module image holds no address and a module pointer has no zero image (L0328). The refusals of the declaration are L0347's, which already says what a link annotation may place, and L0328's, whose zero-image rule a binding with no value already meets; neither takes a code of its own.
D	506	Darwin's cell is a key the image's initializer makes and checks	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d506-darwin-s-cell-is-a-key-the-image-s-initializer-makes-and-checks	Chosen: a program that uses the stack builtins on Darwin carries a compiler-owned routine, `landin.thread_start`, in its image's initializers (`__mod_init_func`), which the loader runs before `main`. It makes the key with `pthread_key_create`, keeps eight times the key, the slot's offset from the slots' base, in a word of module storage, stores a probe, its own frame address, with `pthread_setspecific`, requires the inline read and `pthread_getspecific` both to give the probe, and stores zero again. A read is `mrs` of `tpidrro_el0`, its low three bits cleared, as the system's own accessor clears them, plus the offset word: a check is eight instructions, against six on Linux and FreeBSD arm64. A key that cannot be made, or a read that disagrees, ends the process with status 127 and one line on standard error, as a processor below the executable's level does on Linux. A thread a C library starts begins with its slot zero, and so with no limit.
D	507	The report's latch is one exchanged word, and the loser spins	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d507-the-report-s-latch-is-one-exchanged-word-and-the-loser-spins	Chosen: the latch is one zeroed 32-bit word beside the report stack, in exactly the programs that have that stack: those that prepare a stack, on Darwin and FreeBSD. The report exchanges one into it, with `xchg` on x86-64 and an acquire-release exclusive pair on arm64, whose baseline has no LSE, and moves to the report stack when it read zero. A thread that read one spins on `pause` or `wfe`, writing nothing, until the claimant's trap ends the process. The frame record is pushed on the failed stack first, as D491 has it, so a debugger stopped in either thread unwinds to its failed check.
D	508	A thread's instance is described where the target's assembler can spell it	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d508-a-thread-s-instance-is-described-where-the-target-s-assembler-can-spell-it	Chosen: a `link(thread)` datum's location is its offset in its module's thread block and `DW_OP_form_tls_address`, which a debugger resolves for the thread it has selected: `x@dtpoff` on x86-64, `.dtpreldword` on RV64 and the variable's descriptor on Darwin. arm64 ELF has no directive for the offset in GNU as, and its datum is described with no location, as GCC describes one.
