D	509	A handle from `system.new()` names the calling thread, not a cell	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d509-a-handle-from-system-new-names-the-calling-thread-not-a-cell	Chosen: `hosted/system`'s handle holds, for each of its two cells, D189's one-atom pointer union of `calling_thread` and the caller's cell. `new` stores the atom, and every record and read through the handle matches it, reaching the `link(thread)` cells `thread_errno` and `thread_signal` of whichever thread runs; `over` stores the caller's own cells, as before. The checker says such a missing conformance of one of `core/atomic`'s concepts for one of the four scalars as the target's refusal, L0344, at that use: when the target has no atomic access of the scalar's width, that it has no cell of it, naming a cell of four bytes or fewer and the critical section; when it has the accesses but no read-modify-write, that a cell has no exchange, add or compare-exchange there, naming `atomic.sole_add` and the critical section. Which refusal it is comes from the target's own admission of the builtins (D227), at the build's level since D690, not from a list of targets. D	511	The cell's operations, and the single writer's add	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d511-the-cell-s-operations-and-the-single-writer-s-add	Chosen: `atomic.cell(T)` is a struct of one field, opaque outside the module, which module storage starts `zeroed` and `atomic.new(value)` makes for a local or a field. Its operations take the cell's address: `load` and `store`, acquiring and releasing; `load_relaxed`, `store_relaxed` and `add_relaxed`; `exchange`, `add` and `compare_exchange`, which return what the cell held, an add wrapping at the scalar's width. The single-writer update is `atomic.sole_add(cell, value)`: a relaxed load, a release store of the wrapping sum, and what the cell held, correct while one context alone writes the cell, and on every target. Each operation calls its concept's entry, which `--specialize` makes a direct call, so a cell operation costs a call more than the builtin until the inliner takes it. The name is provisional: `sole_add` was chosen to say in the operation's own name that it has one writer, which `advance` would not, and its shape, an add rather than an update taking a routine, because the consumer it serves is a count and a handler should not call through a function value.
D	512	A wait on an address takes a `u32` cell, and may return early	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d512-a-wait-on-an-address-takes-a-u32-cell-and-may-return-early	Chosen: `posix.wait_on(word, expected)` sleeps while the `atomic.cell(u32)` at `word` holds `expected`, and `posix.wait_on_within(word, expected, span)` does for at most a span on the monotonic clock, failing `etimedout` after it and `einval` for a span no `time_value` may be; `posix.wake_one(word)` and `posix.wake_all(word)` wake one or every waiter. The word is four bytes, the one width all three systems wait on, and private to the process. Either wait returns at once when the cell does not hold `expected`, and may return with nobody having woken it, so a waiter reads the cell again; neither has any other failure, since the systems' others are an address the cell's type rules out. On Linux they are `platform/linux`'s `futex_wait` and `futex_wake` over `FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE` and `FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE`, the operations private to the module; on FreeBSD `_umtx_op` with `UMTX_OP_WAIT_UINT_PRIVATE` and `UMTX_OP_WAKE_PRIVATE`, a span given as a `struct _umtx_time` on `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`; on Darwin `os_sync_wait_on_address`, its `_with_timeout` form on `OS_CLOCK_MACH_ABSOLUTE_TIME`, and `os_sync_wake_by_address_any` and `_all`, which macOS 14.4 added.
D	513	The lock is three states over one cell, and the start is a flag beside it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d513-the-lock-is-three-states-over-one-cell-and-the-start-is-a-flag-beside-it	Chosen: `hosted/thread/lock` is a module beneath `hosted/thread`, so that the heap can import it without importing the facility, which never imports the heap. A `lock.lock` is one `u32` cell, free, taken, or taken with a thread waiting, as Drepper's "Futexes Are Tricky" gives it: `lock.take` takes a free lock with one compare-exchange, and otherwise marks it waited for with an exchange and waits on the cell until an exchange finds it free; `lock.give` frees it with one exchange and wakes one waiter when it was waited for; `lock.take_if_free` never waits. A zeroed lock is free. It is neither reentrant nor owned. The flag is a relaxed `u32` cell of the module's, set by `lock.note_start()`, which the thread facility calls before its first start, and read by `lock.threads_started()`. On Cortex-M0 there is no lock: the critical section is one.
D	514	What the heap's lock costs a program with one thread	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d514-what-the-heap-s-lock-costs-a-program-with-one-thread	Chosen: `hosted/heap` reads the flag once for each slot it takes or gives, and takes the lock around the class's list, mapping a chunk under it; a block larger than the largest class takes none. Measured on Linux x86-64 with the debug compiler, twenty million allocations and frees of 24 bytes, each pair: at `--optimize size` 78 ns before, 197 ns with the flag clear and 460 ns with it set; at `--optimize speed` 28 ns, 145 ns and 367 ns. Those figures predate D499, under which every atomic was fenced before and after. With D499's lowering, measured again on the merged item the same way, three runs each: at `size` 76 ns before, 100 ns with the flag clear and 135 ns with it set; at `speed` 27.5 ns, 37.7 ns and 53.6 ns. The flag is a plain load now, and what a pair still pays with it clear is the register's to find. The vDSO cache is a relaxed `u64` cell, a plain move (D317), and `child_defaults` is a `u64` cell a compare-exchange adds a signal to and a spawn reads once with an acquiring load.
D	516	A naked routine is called through a C import of its symbol	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d516-a-naked-routine-is-called-through-a-c-import-of-its-symbol	Chosen: a bodyless `extern(c)` declaration with an explicit `link(symbol: ...)` may name the symbol a naked routine with a body defines under the same written link name, as a C header declares a routine written in assembly: ordinary code calls the naked text through the import's C signature, and the text owns honouring it. The checker admits the pair beside each other, as it admits C's view of `main` (D279), and the verified IR's agreement of a symbol's declarations takes the pair as one; any other pairing of a naked definition and a declaration of its symbol is still L0347, a public naked routine's own spelling among them since D770. The naked routine is reached through the import, rather than kept as every machine-convention definition is, so a program that never calls the import carries neither. `platform/linux`'s `clone_thread` is such an import, and its text has no label: the creator and the new thread run the same instructions after the call and each picks its next step with a conditional move, or on RV64 a mask, since a hosted body then admitted no label.
D	517	A thread starts on an area at its stack's top, and switches to the prepared stack	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d517-a-thread-starts-on-an-area-at-its-stack-s-top-and-switches-to-the-prepared-stack	Chosen: each of a group's stacks holds its record at its base, the task's own stack above it with the task's state at that part's top, and, at the stack's top, the area the thread starts on. A static Linux program calls `clone` with `CLONE_VM`, `CLONE_FS`, `CLONE_FILES`, `CLONE_SIGHAND`, `CLONE_THREAD`, `CLONE_SYSVSEM`, `CLONE_PARENT_SETTID` and `CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID`, and `CLONE_SETTLS` with the thread's own block, on that area; the thread's first routine runs there, calls `hosted/thread`'s, and ends with the thread's own `exit`, never `exit_group`, so the kernel clears the record's word and wakes a futex waiter only once nothing of the thread runs. `join` waits with `FUTEX_WAIT` on that word, not the private form, because the kernel's wake is not private, until an acquire load reads zero. `platform/linux`'s `futex_wait`, which waits private as a lock's word may, is therefore not the join's: a join that slept through it was never woken. Elsewhere the C library is given the area with `pthread_attr_setstack` and the routine with `pthread_create`, and `pthread_join` waits. On the area, `hosted/thread`'s routine first writes a `link(thread)` byte of its own, so that Darwin's dyld makes the thread's storage there, in a slow path no check or depth report counts, rather than at a first access on the prepared stack, and then switches with `compiler.stack_switch` to the prepared stack, whose first frame runs the task and switches back; the routine then marks the record ended and returns. Every asynchronous signal is blocked around the start and the caller's mask put back after it, so the thread begins with them blocked (D521).
D	518	FreeBSD links libthr for a program that starts a thread	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d518-freebsd-links-libthr-for-a-program-that-starts-a-thread	Chosen: a FreeBSD program whose reached code imports `pthread_create` is linked with `-lthr`, after the archives the program asks for; one that imports none links libc alone, as before. glibc has held its threads in libc since 2.34 and Darwin's are libSystem's, so neither needs a library named. libthr keeps its own record of each thread and its thread's storage beside the area it is given, as Darwin's `pthread_create` does; glibc keeps both in the area (D495).
D	519	The least stack of a thread group, on each system	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d519-the-least-stack-of-a-thread-group-on-each-system	Chosen: a stack is its record, at least 4 KiB for the task's own stack, which holds `compiler.stack_prepare`'s first frame and D472's margin and a few calls, and the area the thread starts on, which is the system's: 2 KiB and the thread's own storage on a static Linux program, for the start's frames and the switch's; glibc's PTHREAD_STACK_MIN under `--link=libc`, 16 KiB on x86-64 and RV64 and 128 KiB on arm64, which `pthread_attr_setstack` refuses below; and 16 KiB on Darwin and FreeBSD. Darwin's minimum is 16 KiB too, and it takes a stack only page-aligned in whole 16 KiB pages, so every stack of a Darwin group is cut in whole pages and is at least 32 KiB. FreeBSD's PTHREAD_STACK_MIN, 2 KiB on x86-64 and 4 KiB on arm64, is too little for libthr's own start and end, whose calls the run-time linker binds lazily on that stack, which took 1,664 bytes on FreeBSD arm64 (D491). `thread.least_stack()` gives the figure, and `group_over` fails `mem.out_of_memory` below it.
D	520	A thread group waits for a free stack by joining, and a refused start fails as out of memory	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d520-a-thread-group-waits-for-a-free-stack-by-joining-and-a-refused-start-fails-as-out-of-memory	Chosen: `admit` takes a stack no thread runs on; failing one, it joins a thread whose task has said it ended, and failing that, the thread started first. A start the system refuses fails `admit` with `mem.out_of_memory`, as POSIX's EAGAIN says the system lacked what another thread needs, and keeps the errno in the group's `hosted/system` handle for `system.last_errno`; the stack stays free and nothing was started. The first failure is claimed with a compare-exchange on the ledger, so only one task writes it, and `join` reads it after every thread's end.
D	521	A thread starts with the asynchronous signals blocked, and a fault's own not	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d521-a-thread-starts-with-the-asynchronous-signals-blocked-and-a-fault-s-own-not	Chosen: this amends D494's "every signal". A new thread begins with every signal blocked but the six a fault raises in the thread that made it: SIGILL, SIGTRAP, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV and SIGSYS, which keep the disposition the process gives them, so a trap's terminal instruction ends the process on every system alike. Every other signal is blocked while the thread starts and in the thread, as D494 has it; the caller's mask is put back after the start.
D	522	Each backend's ordering mapping is its architecture's published one	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d522-each-backend-s-ordering-mapping-is-its-architecture-s-published-one	Chosen: the mappings of the C/C++11 orderings the architectures' authors publish: x86-TSO's and ARMv8's from Sewell's collection (<https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~pes20/cpp/cpp0xmappings.html>), ARMv7's from the same collection for Cortex-M0 at the levels with no acquire or release instruction and ARMv8's at `armv8-m.main` (D606), and Table A.6 of the RISC-V unprivileged ISA's memory model appendix for RV64.\n\n- x86-64. Every load is a `mov`; a relaxed or release store is a `mov` and a seq_cst store `xchg`; exchange, add and compare-exchange are `xchg`, `lock xadd` and `lock cmpxchg` at every ordering; an acquire, release or acq_rel fence emits nothing and a seq_cst fence `mfence`.\n- arm64. A relaxed load or store is `ldr` or `str`, an acquire or seq_cst load `ldar`, a release or seq_cst store `stlr`. A read-modify-write's exclusive loop reads with `ldaxr` when its ordering acquires and `ldxr` otherwise, and writes with `stlxr` when it releases and `stxr` otherwise; at `armv8.1-a` it is `swp`, `ldadd` or `cas` with no suffix, `a`, `l` or `al`. An acquire fence is `dmb ishld`, every other `dmb ish`. Darwin and FreeBSD share it.\n- RV64. A relaxed load or store is plain; an acquire load is followed by `fence r, rw` and a seq_cst one also preceded by `fence rw, rw`; a release or seq_cst store is preceded by `fence rw, w`. An AMO carries `.aq`, `.rl` or `.aqrl`, seq_cst taking `.aqrl`; an LR/SC loop, compare-exchange and the one- and two-byte masked loops, puts `.aq` on the LR for an acquire, `.aqrl` for seq_cst, and `.rl` on the SC for a release. The four fences are `fence r, rw`, `fence rw, w`, `fence.tso` and `fence rw, rw`.\n- Cortex-M0. A relaxed access is plain; an acquire or seq_cst load is followed by `dmb sy`, a release store preceded by one and a seq_cst store has one on each side; every thread fence is `dmb sy`, the only option ARMv6-M's DMB has. At `armv8-m.main` an acquire or seq_cst load is `lda` and a release or seq_cst store `stl`, each in the access's width, with no `dmb`; the fences are unchanged (D606).\n\nA compare-exchange is lowered by its success ordering, never weaker than its failure ordering (D227), so the acquiring read a failed comparison may ask for is already there. The device, completion and compiler barriers, the alignment checks and the panic latch's sequences are unchanged; every atomic remains a full compiler memory boundary, which the IR and the allocators already kept without the instructions.
D	523	Under `--link=libc` a library is the C driver's `-lNAME`	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d523-under-link-libc-a-library-is-the-c-driver-s-lname	Chosen: under `--link=libc`, which Darwin and FreeBSD always use, each active `linker.library("NAME")` reaches the C driver as `-lNAME`, in D202's source order with its repeats, after the program's assembly. The driver resolves it as it would for C, a shared library before an archive of the same name in one directory where its linker prefers one. The C runtime's own libraries, `m` among them, therefore link as the driver links them for C: a dynamically linked Linux executable no longer takes glibc's static `libm`, whose ifunc members ask the dynamic loader for CPU features no static member provides. The default static Linux link still refuses the directive (D280); firmware refused it too (D229) until D923 made it a static archive there. `--dry-run` and `-v` show the `-l` operands. This amends D202's archive-only resolution on every hosted target, and Darwin's `-print-file-name` query goes with it.
D	524	`linker.directory` and `-L` say where libraries are, at link and at run time	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d524-linker-directory-and-l-say-where-libraries-are-at-link-and-at-run-time	Chosen: `linker.directory("DIR")` is a tool directive taking one fixed text literal, decoded by the ordinary text decoder and nonempty. A relative directory is resolved against the directory of the file that declares it, so a project's `lib` beside its source is found wherever the build runs; an absolute one is used as written. `-L DIR`, repeatable on `compile`, `run` and `check`, names one relative to the working directory, as a C compiler's does. Both reach the driver as `-L` with the absolute path, before the program's assembly: the command line's first in their order, so whoever builds can put another copy of a library ahead without editing the source, then the directives in source order, then the driver's own directories. Each named directory is also the executable's runtime search path, `-Wl,-rpath,DIR`, in the same order on every hosted target, so a program linked against a shared library in a named directory starts where it was built, as `refine run` runs it; the executable then records that path on the machine that built it. A directive in an inactive arm adds nothing, and repeats of one directory are kept. A directive naming a directory that does not exist is L0391 at the directive, and such an `-L` is a usage error, both before any tool runs. Wherever `linker.library` is refused, `linker.directory` and `-L` are too: the static Linux link, with D280's L0500 naming `--link=libc`, and, until D923 admitted all three there with no runtime path, firmware. `refine check` gives these refusals as compiling does (D443).
D	525	A library the link cannot find is named with the directories searched	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d525-a-library-the-link-cannot-find-is-named-with-the-directories-searched	Chosen: only when the link fails, refine looks for each requested library: in each named directory, in D524's order, for `libNAME.so` and `libNAME.a`, or `libNAME.tbd`, `libNAME.dylib` and `libNAME.a` on Darwin, and then through the driver's `-print-file-name`, which knows the driver's own directories and not the named ones. Apple's driver answers that query from its own directories and not from the SDK it links against, so on Darwin the SDK's `usr/lib`, which `xcrun --sdk macosx --show-sdk-path` names and `SDKROOT` overrides, is searched last; a host whose `xcrun` cannot answer settles nothing, and the library counts as found. A library found nowhere is L0509, given instead of the linker's text. It names the library at its directive, every named directory with where it was named, and says that the C driver's own directories were searched as well; its note names `linker.directory` and `-L`. A failed link whose libraries are all found stays L0501 with the tool's output. A successful link searches nothing, so it runs no more tools than before.
D	526	`refine run` compiles to a temporary executable and runs it	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d526-refine-run-compiles-to-a-temporary-executable-and-runs-it	Chosen: `refine run [options] SOURCE... [-- ARGUMENT...]` takes `compile`'s options except `--emit`, `-o`, `--keep-asm`, `--depfile` and `--dry-run`. Its `--` ends refine's operands and begins the program's arguments, which the program receives exactly; a source spelt with a leading hyphen is written `./-name.ldn`. It runs only the compiler's own host: another `--target` is a usage error naming `refine compile --target`. The executable is written into a new directory only its user may enter, under `TMPDIR` or `/tmp`, and is named after the entry source without `.ldn`, so its `argv[0]` and a trap report name the program. The program runs in the caller's working directory with refine's environment, standard input, output and error, and no time limit; while it runs refine ignores the terminal's interrupt and quit signals, which reach the program, and passes on a termination or hangup sent to refine itself (D730). The directory is removed when the program ends, and on every way out before it: a refusal, a failed link, a program killed. refine exits with the program's status. A program ended by a signal makes refine write one line naming the signal and exit with 128 and its number, as a shell reports it. A program refused before it runs exits with refine's own statuses, which a script cannot tell from the program's.\n\nBare `refine FILE`, after a check that found no error, writes one line to standard error: that it checked and wrote nothing, with `refine run FILE` to run it and `refine compile FILE -o NAME` to build it, each repeating the options that chose the program (D731). `-q` silences it, and `refine check` stays silent, since it is the form tools call.
D	527	`io.write_format` writes a template and its values in one call	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d527-io-write-format-writes-a-template-and-its-values-in-one-call	Chosen: `core/io` gains `write_format`, generic over a `writer` like `write`: a host, the file to write, a template and its values as `[]any text.formattable`, failing `io_failed` or `text.invalid_format`. It checks the template against its values before writing anything, as D355's `format` does, so a mismatch writes nothing. It formats into a small store of its own on the stack and writes the store to the file whenever it fills and at the end, so a line that fits is one write and a value of any length is written in pieces: it never reports `no_space`. Every target has it. The tour prints a value with it before its first loop, and keeps the buffered writer for a program that writes many pieces. An unknown `core/io` member spelt as another language's print, `print`, `println`, `printf` or `puts`, is L0201 whose fix shows the call. Floating-point values stay unformatted.
D	528	An identifier with capitals is one L0012, and a C name's says `link(symbol: ...)`	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d528-an-identifier-with-capitals-is-one-l0012-and-a-c-name-s-says-link-symbol	Chosen: a word of ASCII letters, digits and underscores that begins with a letter or underscore and holds a capital is one L0012 spanning the word, and the parse continues as if it were an identifier of that spelling, so the word is not reported again. When the word is the name of a function declared `extern(c)` without `link(symbol: ...)`, the note shows that declaration with `link(symbol: "InitWindow")` and the name in lower case with underscores, `init_window`. Elsewhere the note offers the lower-case spelling. A run holding a byte no rule spells keeps its own report. Each place the word is written is its own report, the declaration's and every use's, and a word whose lower-case spelling is a keyword, `End`, is told that spelling is reserved. The scan reads the word as an identifier and leaves its report to the parse, which alone knows whether the word names such a function, so the command line and `refine lsp` say the same.
D	529	L0346 names the record that is not `layout(c)`	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d529-l0346-names-the-record-that-is-not-layout-c	Chosen: a C signature whose parameter or result is a record without `layout(c)` is L0346 naming the part and the record, "C cannot take `tint`: `color` is not `layout(c)`", with a note saying to declare the record `layout(c) struct` and why its layout is otherwise Landin's own, which C does not share ([0750]). The other faults of a C signature keep their notes. The row keeps one note and one secondary label. A result is "C cannot return `result`", and a `layout(c)` record holding such a struct by value is the same refusal at its field, "a C record cannot hold `offset`: `vector2` is not `layout(c)`"; a parameter's and a field's note also offer `ptr` to the struct. A struct behind a pointer crosses as it did, and a pointer union, a variant or a `layout(packed)` register image keeps [1580]'s whole rule.
D	530	`refine explain` answers a construct and a decision	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d530-refine-explain-answers-a-construct-and-a-decision	Chosen: `refine explain` takes `[1590]`, `1590`, `D275` or `d275` beside a diagnostic code. For a construct or a decision it prints the title, the document and, for a decision, its register section, and its page on <https://www.701.dev>. `--full` adds the text: a construct's section up to its next heading, and a decision's `Chosen` paragraph. The table is generated by `python3 check.py --catalogue` from `tour.md` and `spec.md`, and the check holds it to them; D1240 says where the compiler reads it. A number that names nothing is refused as an unknown code is. The page is the address the site gives the heading: a construct's number, `tour.html#1590`, and a decision's heading as the renderer slugs it, `spec.html#d275-the-compiler-finds-its-library-beside-itself`, and the register section is named as the site heads it. The text is shown for a terminal: a code span keeps its backticks, as an explanation's does, a link is its text and bold its words, a paragraph is one line and a fenced block is indented four spaces. `--full` may stand anywhere among what is asked, and a decision's `Chosen` text runs to the next paragraph that opens with a bold label.
D	531	A released compiler carries no debug information, which ships beside it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d531-a-released-compiler-carries-no-debug-information-which-ships-beside-it	Chosen: the release workflow takes the debug information out of the released `refine` before packaging: `objcopy --only-keep-debug`, a `.gnu_debuglink` and `strip --strip-debug` on Linux, `dsymutil` and `strip -S` on Darwin. It publishes the debug information as an asset of its own beside the archive, with its checksum, and the archive's layout is unchanged. The README's install route states each archive's size. A released compiler's internal error prints addresses, which a debugger or `addr2line` given the debug asset resolves. Checkout, Nix and debug builds keep their information.
D	532	Cortex-M links through the pinned arm-elf GCC or a distribution's	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d532-cortex-m-links-through-the-pinned-arm-elf-gcc-or-a-distribution-s	Chosen: the Cortex-M toolchain identity is `arm-eabi`. With no `--toolchain`, a Cortex-M link tries `arm-eabi-gcc` and then `arm-none-eabi-gcc`, and runs the first the host can start, as D364's Linux candidates are tried; a dry run, `-v` and the build report name the one run. `--toolchain=NAME` is still the only one tried. With neither, L0500 names both and what installs each: a distribution's package, or the arm-elf archive. The archive's GDB is built without Python, which the debugger sessions run, so the lane keeps its pinned `gdb-multiarch` and QEMU.
D	536	A static image's runs are written without expansion	Decisions: Arrays, slices and text	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d536-a-static-image-s-runs-are-written-without-expansion	Chosen: every native backend writes a run of one element through the one set of helpers in `Landin.Backend`, so the four, arm64 for Linux, FreeBSD and Darwin alike, agree on its form:\n\n- A run that writes only zero bytes is one `.zero`: a repeated zero scalar, a hybrid's zero suffix, and a repeated aggregate or array element whose whole image is zero, with its padding.\n- A run of a scalar of one, two or four bytes is one `.fill count, size, value`, which both assemblers hold as one fragment.\n- What is left, a run of a nonzero composite element, of an address, of an atom, or of an eight-byte scalar whose high half `.fill`'s four-byte value field would drop, is repeated. A count above 256 is written in base 256: for each nonzero digit, a `.rept` of that digit around as many nested `.rept 256` as its place, around the body. A count up to 256 is one `.rept` as before.\n- Inside a body that is itself repeated, a zero gap or a scalar run of at most 16 bytes is written as plain values, `.byte 0, 0, 0` for a record's padding, and only a longer one as `.zero` or `.fill`.\n\nA body is therefore written once per nonzero digit, at most eight times, and the text an assembler expands at once is the body's own times at most 256. Nested runs multiply their digits, which D537's budget bounds: within 4 GiB at most three dimensions of an image exceed 256. The object bytes are those the earlier `.rept` sequences assembled to.
D	537	One image budget on every target, before emission	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d537-one-image-budget-on-every-target-before-emission	Chosen: one check, before anything is emitted, holds every target's static images to a budget in target bytes. It counts every datum the compilation lowers, before optimization and before section GC: a program with a public `main` lowers what that reaches, and one without, a firmware image or an object, lowers everything. Written images, those with bytes in the object, count against the initialized budget; mutable written images also against the writable one; zero images the loader or startup clears count only against the address space.\n\n| Target | Written images | Mutable written images | Zero images |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| linux-x86-64, freebsd-x86-64 | 2 GiB, the small code model's reach | 2 GiB | 2^64 - 1 bytes |\n| darwin-arm64 | 2 GiB, a Darwin static image | 2 GiB | 2^64 - 1 bytes |\n| linux-arm64, freebsd-arm64 | 4 GiB, ADRP's reach | 4 GiB | 2^64 - 1 bytes |\n| linux-rv64 | 2 GiB, AUIPC's reach | 2 GiB | 2^64 - 1 bytes |\n| cortex-m0 without a firmware request | 2^32 - 1 bytes, the address space | 2^32 - 1 bytes | 2^32 - 1 bytes |\n| cortex-m0 firmware, reference profile | 32 KiB, its flash | 16 KiB, its RAM | 2^32 - 1 bytes |\n\nA firmware image takes its profile's capacities as the check's argument, so a profile with more flash raises its budget without another rule. A scalar datum counts as written whatever it folds to. The refusal is L0505, which names the bytes the images take, the budget they exceed and what sets it, the code model, the address space or the profile's flash or RAM.\n\nThis states the per-target limits that the roadmap's emission policy left open. The check is not a placement verdict: code is not counted, and the linker remains the authority for the map, the stack reservation and a zero image past a code model's reach.
D	542	A device description is a module of directives, and its generated half has one text	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d542-a-device-description-is-a-module-of-directives-and-its-generated-half-has-one-text	Chosen: a device is described in Landin source, as one module made only of tool directives in [1740]'s `tool_directive` form. Each argument is positional: a text is a text literal, decoded by the ordinary text decoder as `linker.library`'s is, and an integer is a fixed integer expression in D202's closed fold, so `0x2000_0000` and `256 * 1024` are both written as they read. The directives are:\n\n| directive | arguments | says |\n|---|---|---|\n| `compiler.device(name)` | lowercase ASCII letters, digits and hyphens, beginning with a letter, at most 32 bytes | the device's identity; the module holding it is a description |\n| `compiler.core(name)` | `cortex-m0`, `cortex-m0plus`, `cortex-m3`, `cortex-m4`, `cortex-m7` or `cortex-m33` | the core, and through it the architecture level: `armv6-m`, `armv6-m`, `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m`, `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main` |\n| `compiler.vectors(count)` | an integer | the vector table's whole length in words, the initial SP and reset included |\n| `compiler.interrupt(name, irq)` | an ASCII letter, then letters, digits and underscores, at most 64 bytes; an integer | that external interrupt `irq` is implemented, at absolute slot 16 + `irq` |\n| `compiler.boot(kind)` | a boot image kind | how the image begins |\n| `compiler.float_unit(name)` | `fpv5-d16` | the core's float unit, which changes the C ABI (D615) |\n| `linker.region(name, origin, length, access)` | an ASCII letter, then letters, digits and underscores, at most 32 bytes; two integers; `"rx"`, `"rw"` or `"rwx"` | one memory region |\n| `linker.place(kind, region[, size])` | `"vectors"`, `"text"`, `"rodata"`, `"data"`, `"bss"` or `"stack"`; a region's name; for `"stack"` alone, its size in bytes | where the compiler places that part of the image |\n\nA slot no `compiler.interrupt` names is reserved and holds zero. The directives' order carries no meaning.\n\nA description is usually two files, which the compiler does not tell apart. `interrupts.ldn` holds `compiler.device`, `compiler.core`, `compiler.vectors` and the interrupts, and is generated from the device's CMSIS-SVD file; `memory.ldn` holds the regions, the placements, `compiler.boot` and any `compiler.float_unit`, and is written by the developer, since an SVD says nothing of the first three and too little of the last (D615). A generated `interrupts.ldn` has exactly this text, so that whatever generates it, and a reviewer, can compare bytes:\n\n1. Line 1 is `-- Interrupts of the NAME, from its SVD: vendor VENDOR, version VERSION.`, with the SVD's `device/name`, `vendor` and `version` as written, surrounding whitespace removed; a clause whose element the SVD lacks is left out with its comma.\n2. Line 2 is `-- SVD SHA-256 HEX.`, the lowercase SHA-256 of the SVD file's bytes.\n3. Each nonempty line of the SVD's `licenseText`, its surrounding whitespace removed, follows as `-- LINE`.\n4. Then `-- Generated from the SVD; memory.ldn beside it is written by hand.`; then, for each interrupt correction of the generator's reviewed policy (D556), in the policy's order, one line: `-- The policy adds NAME at VALUE: SOURCE.` for an interrupt the SVD does not name, `-- The policy moves NAME from OLD to VALUE: SOURCE.` for one it numbers otherwise, or `-- The policy removes NAME at OLD: SOURCE.`, OLD being each value the SVD gives it, joined by ` and `; and one empty line.\n5. `compiler.device("ID")`, ID being `device/name` in lowercase; `compiler.core("CORE")`, from `cpu/name`, where `CM0`, `CM0PLUS`, `CM3`, `CM4`, `CM7` and `CM33` are the six cores above; and `compiler.vectors(N)`, N being 16 plus the larger of `cpu/deviceNumInterrupts` and one more than the highest interrupt value, or plus the latter alone when the SVD has no `deviceNumInterrupts`.\n6. One `compiler.interrupt("NAME", VALUE)` for each distinct pair of an `interrupt` element's name and value in any peripheral, derived ones included, as the corrections leave them, ordered by value and then by the name's bytes; VALUE is decimal with no separators. The count of step 5 is of the corrected pairs.\n\nThe file is ASCII with LF line ends, one directive or comment per line, no trailing spaces, no other empty line, and it ends with one LF. It is the form `refine fmt` leaves unchanged. RP2040's SVD gives 48 slots: it says 26 interrupts and names 32, the last six its spare software interrupts, and pico-sdk's vector table has 48 words.\n\nThe repository keeps a description in `devices/descriptions/DEVICE/`, beside and apart from the register modules under `devices/generated`, which are regenerated byte for byte; a program imports it as `descriptions/DEVICE` with `--root=devices`, a name no root of register modules can hold. The constrained reference profile is a description in refine's own library, `platform/cortex_m/reference`, so an installed compiler finds it as it finds `platform/cortex_m`.
D	543	A program selects its device by importing its description	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d543-a-program-selects-its-device-by-importing-its-description	Chosen: the firmware entry module imports its description, directly or through any module it imports; a description is the module holding `compiler.device`, and at most one is in the reached graph. On a Cortex-M target, a program that reaches none is given the library's `platform/cortex_m/reference`, the constrained profile [1990] fixed written as a description, and on `rv32` `platform/riscv/reference` (D661), which the loader adds once everything the imports reach is read; its sources join the program as any library module's do, and its directives emit nothing, so the assembly of a program that imports no description is what it was. A host whose library lacks it can still check and emit a program with no vector or region placement, and refuses one that has either, or a firmware request, as L0518, saying to import a description or name a library with `--library=DIR`.\n\nThe directives join D202's closed configuration fold. Each is a module-level directive of the description's own module, outside every fixed arm, active or not, as an option is; one in another module, or in an arm, is L0513, and so is an import or any other declaration in a description but its boot stage (D587), and a second description. A description names its device, core, vector table and boot image kind once each, and places each of `vectors`, `text`, `rodata`, `data`, `bss` and `stack` once; an argument outside its row's form is L0399. Once all are read: regions do not overlap; a placement names one of the description's regions, code and the vector table one that may execute, and data, BSS and the stack one that may be written; the vector table, aligned to its length rounded up to a power of two and no less than 128 bytes, fits its region past the boot kind's prefix; the table is no longer than the core's architecture allows, 48 words on ARMv6-M and 512 on ARMv7-M, and on a RISC-V core what D662 gives it; each interrupt's slot is inside it; and the stack fits its region; and in an image that boots from its own memory, `text` is with the vectors or in a region that may not be written, and `rodata` there or with `text` (D1116). Those are L0514. `.ramtext` is placed with `data`, and every load image in the region `text` is placed in.\n\nA description's core must execute what the request builds: the target is its core's family's, `cortex-m0` for an Arm core and `rv32` for a RISC-V one (D662), and `--level` is the core's own level or a lower one of its family. On `rv32`, `rv32imc` is below `rv32imac`, so an `esp-rv32imc` builds at `rv32imc` alone and a `hazard3`, a `sifive-e31` or an `esp-rv32imac-clic` at either. On the M profile, `armv6-m` is below `armv7-m`, and `armv7-m` below both `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main`, neither of which holds the other: Armv8-M's DSP instructions are an optional extension of its core. So an RP2040, a `cortex-m0plus`, builds at the default `armv6-m` and no higher, a `cortex-m4` builds at `armv7e-m`, `armv7-m` or `armv6-m`, and a `cortex-m33` at `armv8-m.main`, `armv7-m` or `armv6-m`, its vector slots its core's at any of them; a level above the core's, or a target of another family, is L0515, naming the levels the core executes. A description with a float unit builds only at the level that holds the unit, and a lower one is L0546 (D615). The constrained reference alone is used at every level, with its ARMv6-M slots, because it is the profile the levels were always tested on and remains so. The maintainer chose the lower levels over requiring the core's own: code built for less runs on the core, and a baseline build of a later chip is a choice a developer makes. `refine lsp` checks a module that imports a description against that profile, with the target and level it is given, and reports the same refusals at the directives.
D	544	The selected profile decides which vector slots a handler takes	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d544-the-selected-profile-decides-which-vector-slots-a-handler-takes	Chosen: a handler's `link(vector: N)` takes slot N when the selected profile admits it: a core slot of the description's core, NMI 2, HardFault 3, SVCall 11, PendSV 14 and SysTick 15, with MemManage 4, BusFault 5, UsageFault 6 and DebugMonitor 12 on ARMv7-M, or 16 + IRQ for an interrupt its description names, and below its `compiler.vectors` count. The table has that many words; an admitted slot holds its handler or the unhandled loop, and every other slot holds zero. The checker, the verifier and the backend read one profile, which the IR carries. A slot the profile reserves is L0347, naming the device and the slots its core takes. The constrained reference keeps [1990]'s table byte for byte: 48 words, IRQ5 and IRQ26–31 reserved. RP2040's description names all 32 of its interrupts, so a handler at slot 21, `USBCTRL_IRQ`, occupies that word.
D	545	The linker script is derived from the description, and boot kinds are the compiler's	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d545-the-linker-script-is-derived-from-the-description-and-boot-kinds-are-the-compiler-s	Chosen: the driver writes the derived script as `OUT.ld`: a MEMORY line for each region in the description's order, the stack at the top of its region, the vector table at the start of its region, past the boot kind's prefix, then text, read-only data and the unwind tables in their regions, initialized data and RAM code in the data region loaded from the text region, BSS, and each region a `link(region: ...)` uses (D547). It asserts the vector address and length, the stack's alignment, that nothing placed in the stack's region reaches the stack, whichever sections those are (D1114), and that the last load image ends inside the text region. A section that would begin at address zero leaves its first eight bytes unused (D1115). Reset copies and clears what the script places, by the `_landin_firmware_*` symbols. For the constrained reference the script is, byte for byte, the one D229 fixed.\n\nA boot image kind is a fact of the target, not of a device. The closed set is `vector-table`, the plain table at the boot address; `rp2040-boot2`, a 256-byte second stage at the start of the vectors' region, in a `.boot2` section, with the table after it at 256-byte alignment, as pico-sdk lays it out; `rp2350-image-block`, the plain table at the start of the vectors' region followed directly by one IMAGE_DEF block in an `.embedded_block` section (D637); and the reserved `esp-app-image`, which a description may name and refine refuses as L0516 until it builds it. The second stage's code is the description's, a `link(boot_stage)` naked routine (D587), and the slot, its 252-byte limit and its checksum are the boot kind's, which refine emits and seals (D588); until the first board it held 256 zero bytes, which the boot ROM's check refused. The firmware build report records the selected device, core, boot kind, vector address and length, the bytes the boot kind puts before and after the table as `boot_prefix` and `boot_suffix`, regions and placements beside the capacities, which are the text region's length and the data region's less a stack it holds, for `rp2040-boot2` the stage (D588), and for `rp2350-image-block` the block (D638).
D	546	A developer's linker script is held to a written contract	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d546-a-developer-s-linker-script-is-held-to-a-written-contract	Chosen: `--linker-script=FILE` links firmware with FILE in place of `OUT.ld`, which refine still writes beside the image. It is refused unless the request is `--target=cortex-m0 --firmware-entry=NAME --emit=exe`. refine does not parse the script: after the link it reads the ELF and holds it to four clauses, in order, and a broken one is L0519 naming it, the executable is removed and the derived script is offered:\n\n1. the vector table: `_landin_firmware_vectors` at the profile's boot address, its whole length loaded there, its first words the initial stack pointer and reset, for `rp2040-boot2` the second stage at the start of its region, its last word the CRC-32 of its first 252 bytes (D588), and for `rp2350-image-block` the image block refine checked, its words as D637 gives them, ending in the first 4 KiB of the vectors' region (D638);\n2. the startup symbols: every `_landin_firmware_*` symbol reset reads, the stack's two, and each used region's;\n3. the stack: in a writable region of the description, its top aligned to eight bytes, its size the description's, and no data, RAM code or BSS reaching into it;\n4. the initialized images: each load image of data, RAM code and a used writable region in the region text is placed in, held in the file.
D	547	A declaration can be placed in a named region	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d547-a-declaration-can-be-placed-in-a-named-region	Chosen: `link_attribute` gains `region: text`, which places a routine or module datum in a region of the selected description by name, without a section: a routine needs a region that may execute, a mutable datum one that may be written. A routine and initialized data in a writable region are copied from their load image in the text region by reset, and zero data is cleared, after `.data`, RAM code and `.bss`; in a read-only region they run and are read in place. A region the description does not have, a region beside a section, or a region whose access does not hold the declaration is L0517, and a region placement with no profile is L0518. On a hosted target placement is L0347, as every placement is.
D	555	refine reads a device's SVD with its own strict XML reader	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d555-refine-reads-a-device-s-svd-with-its-own-strict-xml-reader	Chosen: `refine` reads the SVD itself, through `Landin.Xml`, a reader of XML 1.0's well-formed documents in the subset an SVD is written in: an optional byte order mark and XML declaration whose encoding is UTF-8, elements, attributes, character data with the five predefined entities and character references decoded and line ends read as XML says, CDATA sections, comments and processing instructions. It refuses, never raises, and places each refusal by line and byte column: a document type declaration and every entity but the five, bytes that are not UTF-8 and characters XML does not admit, an end tag that closes something else, an attribute given twice, `<` in an attribute value, `]]>` in character data, `--` in a comment, text outside the root element, and nesting deeper than 64 elements. A refused SVD is L0525.
D	556	`refine svd` reads an SVD and a selection policy	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d556-refine-svd-reads-an-svd-and-a-selection-policy	Chosen: `refine svd --policy=POLICY.json --out-dir=DIR DEVICE.svd`. The command is named for the format it reads, as `fmt` and `lsp` are for what they serve. The policy is JSON, read by the reader refine already has for its language server, and it has schema 2. It names the SVD it was reviewed against by `device`, `svd_version` and `svd_sha256`, and an SVD that is not that file is L0527: a review covers one file, not its successors. It gives the `notice` lines each module begins with, which is where a derivative carries the licensor's notice; the layout under the output directory, as `modules`, `prefix`, `correspondence`, `manifest` and `description`, each with a default; the `selection`, each peripheral's registers in the order they are generated; one access policy per selected register, its `read` `normal`, `modify` or `refused`, its `write` `normal`, `one_clears` or `refused`, its `reserved` bits `zero` or `preserve` and an optional `write_mask`; `numeric_enums`, the fields whose vendor enumeration is read as a number; `reset_mask_overrides`, the reset knowledge a reviewer promises instead of the SVD's; and `reset_corrections`, a reviewed reset value with the source it was read from; and `field_corrections`, a field's reviewed `bits` or that it is to be omitted, or a field the SVD lacks, added with its `bits` and `access` (D652), with its `source`, which the correspondence records beside the SVD's; and `interrupt_corrections`, an interrupt to add or move to a `value`, or to `omit`, with its `source`, which `interrupts.ldn` says in a line of its own (D542). Any other member is refused, except `provenance`, the reviewer's notes, which is not read. A policy refine cannot read is L0526, and one that selects what the SVD lacks L0530.
D	557	What the projection reads, and what it writes	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d557-what-the-projection-reads-and-what-it-writes	Chosen: each selected register's properties are inherited from the register, its peripheral, the peripheral that one is derived from, and the device, in that order; size, reset value, reset mask and access are read so. A peripheral `derivedFrom` another takes its registers and keeps its own name and base address, once: a derived peripheral that gives registers of its own, or is derived from a derived one, is refused. An `alternateRegister` is a register of its own at the address it shares, which must be its alternate's, and the correspondence records it. A field lies where its `bitRange`, its `bitOffset` and `bitWidth`, or its `lsb` and `msb` say. A register may leave its access to its fields, which must then each say theirs. A field with enumerated values becomes an encoded type unless the policy reads it as a number; one without becomes `uN`. Numbers are decimal, `0x` hexadecimal or `#` binary. Names are lowercased; fields take `f_`, atoms the register's and field's names, and two vendor names that become one Landin name are refused. Only 32-bit registers are generated.\n\nL0528 refuses, for a selected register, what is not read: `dim` arrays of peripherals, registers or fields, a register in a `cluster`, a register or field derived from another, derived enumerated values, an `alternateGroup`, a default enumerated value, a number with a multiplier or don't-care bits, another width, and a core other than the six D542 names. An enumerated value named otherwise than an identifier cannot be an atom: every selected field with one is named in one refusal, each with its first such name, and with the policy's `numeric_enums` as the way out, rather than one field a run. L0529 refuses what cannot be generated as it is said: overlapping fields, a field outside its register, an enumerated value that does not fit or is given twice, a property given nowhere it is inherited from, an address that is not a word-aligned 32-bit address, and an alternate at another address, which for an alternate that names an element of a register array is the element's own, the array's `addressOffset` and its position's `dimIncrement`s. D1062 adds what an SVD omits, overstates or says twice, and D1063 a name Landin reserves.\n\nWhat is written is the text the RP2040 fixture was first generated in, byte for byte: one module per selected peripheral, `PREFIX/NAME/device.ldn`; the correspondence, every selected register and field as the SVD gave it beside what was generated, as JSON indented by two spaces with sorted keys; the manifest, each of those files' SHA-256; and `interrupts.ldn` in D542's text. An SVD without `deviceNumInterrupts` has as many slots as its highest interrupt needs.
D	558	`refine svd` replaces its outputs whole or not at all	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d558-refine-svd-replaces-its-outputs-whole-or-not-at-all	Chosen: D907's shared publication group replaces these outputs. Nothing is published until every destination is checked: the output directory must be one, no destination may be a directory or have a file where a directory is needed, no staged or kept copy of an earlier run may be beside one, and the manifest found there may name only paths below it. Each new file is written in exclusive private staging beside its destination and read back, and only then is each destination replaced, its old bytes kept until every replacement is done. A failure restores what this invocation replaced without clobbering a concurrent change, or names the kept copy it could not put back. A file whose bytes are already the new ones is left alone. The manifest is how refine knows which files are its own: a file the old manifest names that this run does not make is removed with the rest, while it is still the bytes the manifest records (D1064). A refusal before writing is L0531; a write that fails is L0005. This recovers from a failure; it is not a snapshot for a concurrent reader.
D	559	Vendor inputs are pinned by URL and SHA-256 and fetched	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d559-vendor-inputs-are-pinned-by-url-and-sha-256-and-fetched	Chosen: no vendor input is in the tree. `devices/inputs.json` pins each SVD and each vendor header the generated modules are checked against by the URL it is fetched from and its SHA-256, and `scripts/fetch_inputs.py`, standard-library Python, fetches each into `$LANDIN_INPUTS` or `~/.cache/landin/inputs`, verifies it every time it is used, and never caches bytes of another hash. An input a job must not fetch is pinned the same way and marked `"fetch": "by hand"`: one its publisher will not serve to a script, ST's RM0433, or one whose URL serves whatever release is current, the RP2350 datasheet and the ESP32-C3 and -C5 manuals, so a job depending on its hash would fail the day a new release appeared. A person downloads it and puts it in the cache, and the fetcher verifies that copy, never downloads one, and without one says where to put it. No test reads a manual; the literals reviewed from one stay in the tests, each citing its section and page, and its pinned hash names the document they were reviewed against. A licence's notice stays in the tree, as a notice: the generated modules are derivatives of the SVD, BSD-3-Clause asks that a redistribution of source in any form keep the licence's whole text, and Apache-2.0 that a recipient be given a copy, so `devices/notices/LICENSE.pico-sdk` and `devices/notices/LICENSE-Apache-2.0.stm32h7` are kept and each module's notice names its own. `check.py` runs `devices/test.py` offline: the lock and the policies agree, every generated file is the one its manifest hashes and carries its notice. The regeneration and the vendor-header checks need the inputs, so the gate's `cortex-m` job fetches them and runs them.
D	560	The STM32H753 is learnt for prototype 1's UART and DMA, with reviewed corrections	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d560-the-stm32h753-is-learnt-for-prototype-1-s-uart-and-dma-with-reviewed-corrections	Chosen: the STM32H753 is learnt from ST's own SVD, the copy in Arm's `STM32H7xx_DFP` at tag `v4.1.3`, under Apache-2.0, pinned by hash and not vendored. Its policy selects the RCC clock enables for GPIO port D, USART3 and DMA1 (`AHB4ENR`, `APB1LENR`, `AHB1ENR`); port D's `MODER` and `AFRH`, for PD8 and PD9's alternate function 7; USART3's `CR1`, `CR3`, `BRR`, `ISR`, `ICR`, `RDR` and `TDR`; DMA1's `LISR`, `LIFCR` and stream 0's `S0CR`, `S0NDTR`, `S0PAR` and `S0M0AR`; DMAMUX1's channel 0, `DMAMUX_C0CR`; and TIM2's `CCMR1_Input`, prototype 1's timer and the selection's alternate register. These use every form D557 reads: GPIOD and USART3 are derived from GPIOA and USART1, every reset mask is the device's, and no selected field but DMAMUX1's enumerates values, which are read as numbers. Status is read and not written, a clear register written as one-clears and not read, and USART3's receive register read with one load.\n\nWhere the SVD and ST's CMSIS header disagree, the reference manual decides: RM0433 Rev 9, pinned by its SHA-256 and supplied by hand (D559). Where it says the SVD is wrong, the policy carries a reviewed correction with the section and page it was read at: `RCC_AHB1ENR`'s bit 18 is reserved, not a field (8.7.41, p. 454); port D's mode register resets to 0xFFFF FFFF, all analog, where the SVD gives port A's 0xABFF FFFF by deriving port D from it (11.4.1, p. 541); and the RAMECC diagnostic interrupt is at 145, which the SVD omits (Table 147, p. 759). It is named `ECC`, the header's `ECC_IRQn`, because the manual gives that one line three acronyms, `RAMECC1` to `RAMECC3`. Where it says the SVD is right, nothing is corrected and the check names the header's disagreement: DMAMUX1's `DMAREQ_ID` is bits 6:0 and `SYNC_ID` bits 26:24 (17.6.1, p. 708), where the header's masks are DMAMUX2's, and `WWDG1_RST` is at 143, which the header omits.\n\nA policy may so add, move or remove an interrupt, each with a cited source, as it corrects a field. `interrupts.ldn` then carries the corrected table, and D542's form says each correction in a line of its own after the line that says the file is generated from the SVD, so a reader of the description sees which interrupt is not the SVD's and why.
D	561	A consumer's device accesses are read from its linked image	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d561-a-consumer-s-device-accesses-are-read-from-its-linked-image	Chosen: `devices/consumers/stm32h753` configures the UART transmit with whole images computed in the program, and `devices/thumb.py` reads the linked image: from its reset vector it evaluates the ARMv6-M instructions the backend emits over memory that is the image's own bytes, and records each store to a device window, with its address, width and value, until the first WFI. The check compares that list, in order, with one reviewed from RM0433's memory map and register descriptions, and requires that nothing enables or maintains the M7's caches. The evaluation models no peripheral, exception or clock: it reads the image, it does not run a chip.
D	562	The STM32H753's description is cacheless and keeps DMA out of the TCMs	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d562-the-stm32h753-s-description-is-cacheless-and-keeps-dma-out-of-the-tcms	Chosen: `devices/descriptions/stm32h753/memory.ldn` describes 2 MiB of flash from 0x0800_0000, the 64 KiB ITCM at 0, the 128 KiB DTCM at 0x2000_0000, 512 KiB of AXI SRAM at 0x2400_0000, SRAM1, SRAM2 and SRAM3 at 0x3000_0000, 0x3002_0000 and 0x3004_0000, and SRAM4's 64 KiB at 0x3800_0000, each checked against the base addresses of ST's header. The boot kind is `vector-table`, the plain table at 0x0800_0000. The profile is cacheless: compiler-owned startup leaves the M7's caches disabled, as reset leaves them. DMA1 and DMA2 reach neither TCM, so initialized data, BSS and the stack, where prototype 1's buffers are, are placed in the AXI SRAM, which both streams reach; the DTCM is described and holds only what a program places there by name. This profile stays the board's cacheless one, its bytes and checks unchanged, beside the cached profile admitted with its provider, `devices/descriptions/stm32h753_cached`, which a program selects by importing it instead (D974).
D	563	An empty first directory does not hide a later root's module	Decisions: Modules and compile time	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d563-an-empty-first-directory-does-not-hide-a-later-root-s-module	Chosen: first-root precedence stands, and the directory the first root supplies is still the import's. When that directory holds no direct regular `.ldn` source and a root after it holds a directory of the same path that does, the import is refused as L0532, at the import, naming the empty directory, the later root and its directory, and saying to name that root first or give the empty directory a source. A later directory that is empty too is passed over for the next; an empty module that no later root rivals stays legal, and so does one rivalled only by empty directories. A first directory holding a source wins as before, whatever later roots hold. An import of the library searches the library alone (D275), so it has no rival. This amends D150's discovery paragraph.
D	564	A target-limited builtin is refused where the program reaches it	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d564-a-target-limited-builtin-is-refused-where-the-program-reaches-it	Chosen: this amends D453. A refusal that names the target, L0344's "needs a native backend", "is not yet emitted on" and "memory operation or width unavailable on target", is made by the checker as before, with the same message, site, second place and note, and held against its call rather than reported; the call is otherwise checked and typed as an admitted one. Once the lowering knows which code the program keeps, which D296's walk from the entry module's routines decides, it reports each held refusal whose call is in kept code, and lowers nothing when any is. A compilation with no `main` to root the walk keeps everything, so a module checked on its own still reports every one, as a firmware image does. A refusal of the call's own form, an argument outside the contract, a missing argument or a recovery, is reported where it is written, as every other checker refusal is. A held refusal joins the report only when the checker accepted the rest of the program.
D	565	What an option needs of its request is the command catalogue's	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d565-what-an-option-needs-of-its-request-is-the-command-catalogue-s	Chosen: the catalogue says, for each option, what it needs of the rest of its request: nothing, a source to compile (`--optimize`, `--specialize`, `--build-report`, `--firmware-entry`, `--link`), emitted machine code (`--debug`, `--panic-map`, `--stack-report`), an executable (`--keep-asm`), or something emitted at all (`-o`); and it writes the one sentence for a request that does not meet it, for an option given twice, for a value an option does not take, naming the values it does, and for a compilation option beside `--help` or `--identify`. `refine compile` and `refine run` hold their requests to those requirements as they parse, and the driver holds the request it is handed to them, so both refuse one combination with one sentence. The options the driver reads are the catalogue's compile options less the commands' own, and its usage is the catalogue's overview. A command-line change is a change to the catalogue.
D	570	The depth report closes a call through a table or a function value	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d570-the-depth-report-closes-a-call-through-a-table-or-a-function-value	Chosen: the report closes such a call over the routines the whole program holds that it can be. A call through a table read from a value reaches entry N of every table of the same concept, direct and erased apart, which is the set D374 already relies on: a left-out entry is a zero word, so a table outside it could not be called through at all. A call through any other function value, however the value was kept, reaches every routine whose address the program exposes, by a function address, an image, an export or an import, and every table entry it may project, whose signature agrees with the call's, which is what the checker and the IR's verifier require of every function value that reaches a call. A routine that is neither emitted nor supplied by the link is left out, since nothing that names it was kept. A call stays open when it has no such routine, when its signature is a C function type, whose value may be one C made, and through a code address; recursion, foreign calls, runtime helpers and assembly stay open as D468 has them, and a closed call may meet recursion through what it reaches. A value made from integers or written by foreign code is outside the bound, as it is outside D374. The depth is then a bound over every task the program can start on a stack, not a measure of one run: the deepest provider of the concept counts wherever the call is, and on a hosted Linux target the vDSO's clock, a foreign call, still opens a task that may reach it.
D	571	A round's yield calls nothing beneath it but its sweep, its idler and its switch	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d571-a-round-s-yield-calls-nothing-beneath-it-but-its-sweep-its-idler-and-its-switch	Chosen: `sweep` empties the ended entries and counts the unfinished in one pass that calls nothing; `round_yield` takes its count, searches for the next entry in its own body with no division, which Cortex-M0 would call its runtime for, and switches through `compiler.stack_switch` directly. Beneath a yield there are then only the sweep, the round's idler and the switch, and in the depth report a yield with a spinning idler goes no more than D465's 1 KiB deeper than its switch on every target at every profile, 688 bytes at most, on x86-64 at `none`; the round's wait goes no deeper than through its yield. With RV64 reusing its scalar homes, a yield takes, with what the switch saves, 456 bytes on x86-64 at `size` and 392 at `speed` where it took 552 and 600, 800 and 400 on arm64 where it took 960 and 560, 960 on RV64 where it took 2,160 and 2,416, and 352 on Cortex-M0, its device idler included, where it took 504. At `none`, where every value keeps a home of its own, a yield takes about 2.1 KiB on the 64-bit targets, as the chain did. The round's code is smaller than it was, which a 32 KiB Cortex-M0 image near its limit needs. The idler is the provider's to choose and runs where the yield does: the event provider waits for its events there.
D	572	A check decides whether a handler fits from the frames it would emit	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d572-a-check-decides-whether-a-handler-fits-from-the-frames-it-would-emit	Chosen: in a program that prepares a stack and selects a handler, on a target with a backend, a check runs the optimization pipeline and the backend in memory, keeping nothing, and judges the handler as compiling does, with the same L0508 at the same place. `refine check` measures at its own profile, `none` unless `--optimize` names another, and the server at `none`, which no setting changes yet; a handler that fits there may still be refused at another profile, as D474 says. A program that compiling refuses before it emits, for an image past its budget, a frame the target cannot address or a vector with no firmware entry, is left to that refusal, which a check does not raise. Every other program, the great majority, prepares no stack or selects no handler, and costs a check nothing more.
D	575	`platform/cortex_m` declares nothing off an M-profile target	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d575-platform-cortex-m-declares-nothing-off-an-m-profile-target	Chosen: the module `platform/cortex_m` is available on every target and declares its operations only on an M-profile one, inside one `fixed if compiler.arch == cortex_m0`, as `platform/linux` declares nothing off Linux (D350). D	580	A connection's limit is a second entry, `connect_within`	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d580-a-connection-s-limit-is-a-second-entry-connect-within	Chosen: `net.network` gains an entry, `connect_within(to, limit)`, and `core/net` its free function: a connection made as `connect` makes it, or `timed_out` once `limit` has passed with no answer, the socket it began closed. The limit is a `time.duration`, and zero is none, as `set_timeouts` reads one; the connection made has no limit of its own on what it sends and receives. `connect` stays as it was. The blocking provider makes the socket non-blocking for the connection alone, waits with `poll` for what is left of the limit on the monotonic clock, rounded up to the millisecond and asked again after EINTR, takes the outcome from `SO_ERROR`, and makes the socket block again; the limit passing is ETIMEDOUT, which D319 maps to `timed_out`. The fake network connects or refuses at once, so its limit is never reached.
D	581	An IPv6 address keeps its zone as text, and the provider looks it up	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d581-an-ipv6-address-keeps-its-zone-as-text-and-the-provider-looks-it-up	Chosen: `net.address` gains `zone: [16]u8`, the zone's bytes and zeros after them, at most `net.zone_room`, 15, of them: an interface's name on every hosted system, whose IFNAMSIZ counts a NUL after them. A zone is text in the address rather than the system's interface number, because `core/net` reads and writes addresses on every target, firmware included, with no system to ask: `parse_ip` reads `fe80::1%eth0`, `parse_address` reads `[fe80::1%eth0]:80`, the zone inside the brackets as it is written rather than as a URL escapes it, `%25eth0`, and `append_ip` and `append_address` write them back. A zone is one to 15 bytes, none of them NUL, kept as written, Go's rule; an empty zone, a longer one and a zone after an IPv4 address are `invalid_address`. `with_zone` gives an IPv6 address a zone, or takes it away given an empty one, and `zone_length` measures it. A zone of decimal digits is the interface's number, RFC 4007's numeric form.\n\nWhere an address meets a socket, `posix.internet_address` writes the zone's interface into `sin6_scope_id`: digits as the number they spell, and a name as `posix.interface_index` finds it, which is `SIOCGIFINDEX` on a Unix-domain socket on Linux and the C library's `if_nametoindex` on Darwin and FreeBSD. It now fails, `enodev` for a zone that names no interface, and each provider makes that `address_unavailable`, as it does ENODEV and ENXIO from the system, and `unreachable` for `send_to`, whose atoms have no other. A record read back, a peer's, a socket's own or a datagram's sender's, gives its scope as a zone through `posix.interface_name`, `SIOCGIFNAME` or `if_indextoname`: the interface's name, or its number in decimal for an interface that has gone.

D	588	refine emits the stage at the start of its slot and writes its checksum into the object	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d588-refine-emits-the-stage-at-the-start-of-its-slot-and-writes-its-checksum-into-the-object	Chosen: the backend emits the stage at offset 0 of `.boot2`, labelled `_landin_firmware_boot2`, with nothing before its first instruction: the boot ROM copies the slot to SRAM and enters the copy at its first byte in Thumb state, with lr zero. Its literal pool follows it, so its literals stay in the slot, then zeros to the stage's limit, written so that a stage longer than the limit still assembles and is refused for its size rather than for an assembler message, then a zero word for the checksum. The stage runs from the copy, at an address it is not linked at, so it must be position-independent: no relocation may be in it, and none in an image section may refer to it.\n\nrefine has no assembler of its own, so only the assembled bytes can be summed. Once the firmware assembly succeeds, the driver reads the object's `.boot2`: a section that is not 256 bytes is a stage and literals past 252 bytes, and a relocation in it, or one in an allocated section against a symbol defined in it, is a stage the ROM's copy would not run as linked; each is L0538, naming the size or the relocation, its offset and its symbol, before anything is linked. Otherwise refine computes the boot ROM's CRC-32 over the first 252 bytes, polynomial `0x04c11db7`, initial value all ones, neither input nor output reflected and no final exclusive or, and writes it into the last four, little-endian, in the object file, in place. Every object and executable refine writes for an `rp2040-boot2` profile therefore carries the right checksum, a link with `--linker-script` among them, and D546's first clause checks the linked slot's checksum again; `--emit=asm` keeps the zero word, which no assembler can fill. The firmware build report gives the stage as `boot_stage`: its source routine, its address, its length as the assembler wrote it, the slot's length, and the checksum and the address it is written at.

D	594	On the RP2040 a receive snapshot reads the live count, and stop aborts	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d594-on-the-rp2040-a-receive-snapshot-reads-the-live-count-and-stop-aborts	Chosen: a snapshot does not pause the channel. It reads CTRL_TRIG and TRANS_COUNT live; the count drops when a transfer is issued, before its write lands (2.5.3.2), and the driver's stated premise is that the write lands before the byte is copied out, a bus latency of a few cycles against the hundreds a snapshot and its copy take. The board's oracle checks every echoed byte against what was sent, which a stale read would fail. `stop` records what the count says, disables the channel's interrupt, writes CHAN_ABORT, waits at most 1000 polls for BUSY to fall, which 2.5.5.3 says takes a few cycles once the transfers in flight complete, and clears the completion interrupt RP2040-E13 says an abort may raise; bytes received after that last count are discarded with the epoch. A stopped descriptor answers from the count it kept. `restart` re-arms the channel only after BUSY has fallen. While the channel is exhausted or stopped, UART0's 32-byte FIFO holds what arrives and a byte past it is lost; the UART flags that in UARTRIS's OERIS, and a snapshot reports it as `overrun`, so no byte is lost unreported. A board run found the loss silent before: a 4096-byte epoch exhausted while the application still echoed its ring lost 116 bytes in the 13 ms before its restart.
