D	616	A float unit selects AAPCS32's VFP variant, for C and for Landin	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d616-a-float-unit-selects-aapcs32-s-vfp-variant-for-c-and-for-landin	Chosen: a program whose description has `fpv5-d16` uses the VFP variant of AAPCS32, hard float and not `softfp`. In the C convention a VFP candidate is an `f32` or `f64`, or a composite of one to four members all of one of those types, nested aggregates and arrays included. Each candidate takes the lowest-numbered run of free registers of s0-s15 that holds it, a double or an aggregate of doubles an even-aligned run, so a single back-fills the slot a double's alignment left. Once a candidate finds no such run every VFP register is unavailable, the candidate goes to the stack at its own alignment, and no later argument takes one, even a single that would fit a slot left free. Candidates consume no core register; everything else is placed in r0-r3 and on the stack exactly as before, sharing the stack with the candidates in argument order. A candidate result is returned in s0 or d0, an aggregate in s0-s3 or d0-d3 whatever its size; any other composite result keeps its r0 or hidden-address placement. A variadic call uses the base PCS throughout, its fixed arguments included. s16-s31, d8 to d15, are call-preserved, and s0-s15 and FPSCR's flags are call-clobbered.\n\nThe internal Landin convention uses the same bank for its own floats: an `f32` or `f64` parameter is placed as the C convention places it, and an `f32` or `f64` result is s0 or d0; aggregates, arrays and multiple results stay by address in core registers, and r12's outcome is unchanged. `Backend.Arm32_ABI` plans both, its locations naming the first single slot and how many a candidate takes. D920 enables C interoperation on Cortex-M, so the C half is the convention every C signature of a program with the unit uses, still measured against GCC as below; D922 leaves the variadic call the planner places unused.
D	617	With a float unit, floats are computed in VFP instructions	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d617-with-a-float-unit-floats-are-computed-in-vfp-instructions	Chosen: with `fpv5-d16`, f32 and f64 addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are VADD, VSUB, VMUL and VDIV, negation VNEG, and a comparison VCMP for equality and inequality or VCMPE for an ordered relation, VMRS of the flags and a branch on the condition that is false when unordered. A conversion between the widths is VCVT, and a narrowing keeps Landin's finite-overflow guard; one from an integer of at most 32 bits is VCVT from s32 or u32; and one to such an integer widens an f32 to f64 exactly, traps unless the source lies strictly between the type's lowest less one and highest plus one, which a NaN does not, and then truncates with VCVT, so D171's checks are unchanged. A conversion from or to a 64-bit integer keeps the runtime's base-PCS conversion or the integer decoding, since no VFP instruction converts 64 bits, and a float's test as a bool keeps its comparison of the carrier. Operands and results move between their homes and s0-s2 or d0-d2 by VLDR and VSTR, and a banked argument or result between its home and its register the same way; a value's home and every other move are unchanged. No arithmetic, comparison or 32-bit conversion helper is called. FPSCR keeps its reset default: round to nearest even, no flush to zero and no default NaN.\n\nSelection names no call-preserved VFP register. An assembly block's text can, and the compiler does not read that text for registers, so a framed routine that holds a block on a profile with a unit stores d8-d15 in its frame with VSTM after it reserves its homes, between them and the incoming staging, and loads them with VLDM before its epilogue, each with its CFI offset. That is not D471's unchecked area above the frame record, as a VPUSH before the record would be, so the limit check covers it. A call-free leaf holds no block.\n\nThe assembly says `.fpu fpv5-d16`, and declares `Tag_ABI_FP_number_model` IEEE 754 and `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` VFP registers, which the assembler does not infer from its flags; the assembler and the linker are given `-mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv5-d16`, from which GCC selects the `thumb/v7e-m+dp/hard` libgcc multilib, so refine names no multilib path. The linker compares objects' `Tag_ABI_VFP_args` only when both declare a number model: a soft-float C object is then refused, and a libgcc helper object, which declares none, leaves the image's attribute standing. Without a unit the flags and the code are as they were, and the assembly declares what D780 says.
D	618	Reset enables the float unit, and handlers take extended frames	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d618-reset-enables-the-float-unit-and-handlers-take-extended-frames	Chosen: with a float unit, compiler-owned reset gives CP10 and CP11 full access in CPACR, 0xE000ED88, then DSB and ISB, right after it initializes r9 and r11 and before anything that can execute a float instruction, the copies and the entry included. FPCCR keeps its reset default, automatic state preservation with lazy stacking, so an exception that interrupts a context with an active float state, CONTROL.FPCA set, reserves ARMv7-M's extended frame, s0-s15, FPSCR and a reserved word beyond the basic eight, and fills it only if the handler executes a float instruction. A handler's EXC_RETURN is then `0xffffffe1`, `0xffffffe9` or `0xffffffed`, a handler, a thread on MSP or a thread on PSP from an extended frame, and its epilogue's BX LR returns through either kind. A handler is an ordinary framed routine and needs nothing more: s0-s15 are the hardware's to restore, and d8-d15 are preserved as every routine preserves them (D617).

D	630	Float assembly operands are a second class, `float`	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d630-float-assembly-operands-are-a-second-class-float	Chosen: an operand's type may be `f32` or `f64`, placed at a fixed float register or at the class `float`, spelled the same on every target as `general` is. A fixed float register is the architecture's full-width name, and the operand's type selects its spelling in the text, as `w9` and `x9` do for an integer:\n\n| target | float operand registers | text spelling | `float` chooses from, and every block overwrites | saved by the routine when named |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| hosted x86-64 (Linux, FreeBSD) | `xmm0`–`xmm15` | `%xmmN` at both widths | all | none |\n| hosted arm64 (Linux, Darwin, FreeBSD) | `v0`–`v31` | `sN` for `f32`, `dN` for `f64` | `v0`–`v7`, `v16`–`v31` | `v8`–`v15` |\n| RV64 Linux | `f0`–`f31`; the text's `ft`, `fa` and `fs` aliases are those registers | `fN` at both widths | `f0`–`f7`, `f10`–`f17`, `f28`–`f31` | `f8`, `f9`, `f18`–`f27` |\n| Cortex-M with FPv5-D16 (D615) | `d0`–`d15`; the text's `s(2n)` and `s(2n+1)` are `d(n)`'s halves | `s(2n)` for `f32`, `dn` for `f64` | `d0`–`d7`, and FPSCR's flags | `d8`–`d15` |\n\nAn integer is placed at an integer register or `general` and a float at a float register or `float`; each misplacement is L0330, naming the register and the type. The two classes count apart, each only the registers of its own row the block does not otherwise name, and every output keeps a register distinct from every input unless it is `inout`. A text register at any width or view counts as its full-width register, `d8` and `q8` as `v8` and `ymm3` as `xmm3`, so the callee-saved float registers that D248 left never named are declared as the saved integer registers are, by an operand or by `out _ at v8`, and the routine then saves and restores them. A profile with no float registers, Cortex-M at `armv6-m` and any description that selects no float unit, refuses a float operand as L0304, whose standing is now that profile's recorded boundary rather than a transfer, and the refusal names the profile. It is reported in place of a refusal of the block's text there, since a float instruction is no instruction on that profile either and the operand says why. The float unit's rounding mode and exception flags, MXCSR, FPCR and FPSR, `fcsr` and FPSCR, are the programmer's to restore, beside x86-64's direction flag. On Cortex-M a routine that holds a block keeps d8-d15 in its frame whatever the block declares (D617); a block that names one now declares it, as on the hosted targets. Each backend lowers a float operand by moving it between its frame home and its register at its own width, and the verified IR keeps one instruction with declared register effects, whose empty register is the class its operand's type selects.

D	648	On the STM32H753 an epoch is taken in laps, each armed by the stream's completion	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d648-on-the-stm32h753-an-epoch-is-taken-in-laps-each-armed-by-the-stream-s-completion	Chosen: USART3 receives through DMA1 stream 0, paced by DMAMUX1's channel 0 with usart3_rx_dma, request 45 (Table 124, p. 697), into a 256-byte ring, keeping D593's public receive contract with its atoms and its order of checks. The stream has no ring address, and a circular stream reloads its count where no reader can see how often, so the stream runs in normal mode, which stops at zero with EN clear (15.3.15, p. 654), and an epoch's budget is taken in laps of the ring's size, the last one shorter when the budget is not a multiple of it. The stream's transfer-complete interrupt arms each next lap from the ring's start until the budget is reached; an error leaves the stream disabled and its flag in DMA_LISR. A snapshot reads DMA_LISR and DMA_S0NDTR with interrupts masked and counts the laps completed and, of the lap armed, what the count says, or all of it when its completion is still pending. Stop clears EN and the completion interrupt in one write, so that no lap is armed after it, waits at most 1000 polls for EN to read 0, which 15.3.16 (p. 654) says it does once the transfer in progress completes, and keeps what the count then says was transferred; bytes received after the last snapshot before a stop are discarded with the epoch. USART3 runs in FIFO mode (48.5.4, p. 2023), for its transmitter: the shared loop echoes each byte as it is read, and with FIFO mode off the transmit data register is the only byte of slack, so the work between two reads idled the line and the echo fell behind the line it echoes. The first board run found that: a 4,094-byte stream at line rate fell more than the ring behind after some 2,600 bytes and was discarded as an overrun. With its 16-entry TXFIFO the line stays busy across that work. While a stream is exhausted or stopped, or between a lap and the next, the receiver then holds 17 bytes, the RXFIFO's 16 (Table 402, p. 2018) and one in the receive data register, the 17th setting no ORE (48.5.4, p. 2023; note 2 of p. 2067), and the next is lost; the USART sets ORE (48.5.6, p. 2030), and a snapshot reports it as `overrun`, so no byte is lost unreported. The board run held 17. A lap is re-armed within an interrupt's latency, far inside the 87 microseconds of a byte at 115,200 baud.\n\nTRBUFF, DMA_SxCR's bit 20, is set, since RM0433 says it must be for a stream that serves a USART (15.5.5, p. 662); the SVD omits the field, and the policy adds it (D652). The board's oracle reads the stream's configuration over SWD and refuses a run without it.

IDLE alone is no wakeup for a stream that never falls quiet: the first board run's application slept from one lap's end to the next, found the ring full each time it woke, and discarded it as an overrun, 262 bytes in every 327. So SysTick interrupts every millisecond, slot 15, the role RP2040's timer played, and the stall counts its interrupts; the oracle requires them to advance.

D	656	The RV32 unhandled entry records the trap in memory before it waits	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d656-the-rv32-unhandled-entry-records-the-trap-in-memory-before-it-waits	Chosen: on `rv32` the unhandled entry records the trap before it masks interrupts and waits, in five words of `.bss.landin_firmware_trap`, which any probe reads as memory: `_landin_firmware_trap_cause` (mcause), `_landin_firmware_trap_pc` (mepc), `_landin_firmware_trap_value` (mtval), `_landin_firmware_trap_sp`, the sp the trap interrupted, and `_landin_firmware_trap_count`, how many traps have reached it since reset, in that order. The derived script places the cells first in `.bss`, so they are at `_landin_firmware_bss_start` in every image of a profile; a developer's script places them wherever it collects `.bss.*`. Reset clears them, so a record is read before the next reset.\n\nCortex-M keeps its loop as it is. What an RV32 core keeps in CSRs, an Arm core keeps where every probe reaches it: the fault status and address registers of an M3 and later, CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR and BFAR, are memory-mapped in the System Control Block, the stacked frame holds the faulting pc and xPSR, whose exception number is IPSR's, and sp and the core registers are read through the debug port's core register transfer, not the CSR reads that failed. An M0 has no fault status register to copy.

D	662	A RISC-V core's interrupt model decides what a slot is	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d662-a-risc-v-core-s-interrupt-model-decides-what-a-slot-is	Chosen: a description may name four RISC-V cores, each of family RV32: `hazard3` (RP2350), `sifive-e31`, `esp-rv32imc` (ESP32-C3) and `esp-rv32imac-clic` (ESP32-C5), at `rv32imac`, `rv32imac`, `rv32imc` and `rv32imac`. D	671	RV32 is RV64's emitter at XLEN 32, with eight-byte values in pairs	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d671-rv32-is-rv64-s-emitter-at-xlen-32-with-eight-byte-values-in-pairs	Chosen: one emitter, `Landin.Backend.RiscV`, asks the target its XLEN and selects at it: an immediate, a memory access, an extraction, the overflow test's sign bit and every word of a frame, a switch frame, an evidence table and a slice image are XLEN wide, and RV32 has no float register, no `.option pic`, no thread pointer and no default report, which are Linux's. Every value keeps its home in the frame, as on RV64, so an eight-byte value is a register pair only while one operation reads or writes it: the low word in the register named and the high word in a fixed partner, x27 beside the x5 every value passes through and the next argument register beside an argument's, so the moves, loads, stores, unaligned byte accesses, choices and fills that never look inside a value move both words by the same code. x27 is therefore saved by every RV32 routine, as RV64 saves its fixed scratch registers. The operations that look inside an eight-byte integer are selected for the pair x10:x11 and x12:x13: addition and subtraction with the carry or borrow recovered by `sltu`, the checked forms testing the high word's carry or sign as RV64 tests its one word; bitwise operations word by word; comparison of the high words, signed or not, then of the low words unsigned; shifts split at 32 with the crossing bits moved by a shift of one and then of 31 less the amount, so a shift by zero moves none, and an amount past the width giving zero as RV64's does; and negation, extension, narrowing and range checks in words. A product is the low 64 bits of M's `mul` and `mulhu` partial products, one sequence for both signednesses; a checked product first proves that the magnitudes' whole product has no word above 64 bits and fits the result's sign, inline. A packed member of an eight-byte carrier is shifted and masked as a pair. A quotient and a remainder are libgcc's `__divdi3`, `__udivdi3`, `__moddi3` and `__umoddi3`, after the language's zero-divisor and minimum-over-minus-one guards, which are the language's and not the helper's.

An item that asks for nothing keeps RV64's section.
D	677	RV32's C transport is the planner's ilp32 at XLEN 32	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d677-rv32-s-c-transport-is-the-planner-s-ilp32-at-xlen-32	Chosen: `Landin.Backend.RiscV_ABI` plans `ilp32` as the integer calling convention LP64D already holds, at the target's XLEN: four-byte carriers in a0-a7, then four-byte words of the outgoing area, an argument aligned there to its own alignment up to sixteen; a scalar or record of up to eight bytes in one or two registers, low word first, split between a7 and the area when one register is left; a larger record by address, and a larger result through a hidden pointer in a0; a variadic eight-byte value in an even pair; and no float bank, so an f32 is a word and an f64 two. The planner is held to GCC by direct checks, as D616 held the M7's: each row is where `riscv64-elf-gcc` 16.1 at `-march=rv32imc -mabi=ilp32` reads or writes the same C signature's arguments and results. Executable C interoperation stays disabled on RV32, though D920 enabled Cortex-M's.
D	678	RV32 keeps its firmware text near the size of Thumb's	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d678-rv32-keeps-its-firmware-text-near-the-size-of-thumb-s	Chosen: at XLEN 32 a routine saves and restores its callee-saved registers at the frame's stack pointer, where each is one compressible instruction, and only those its text names, by number or, in an assembly block, by ABI alias; their homes stay in the frame. Where every region of the profile is at most 1 MiB, a jump is `j` and a branch is written as itself, which GNU as lengthens with a JAL past 4 KiB, since a routine is one input section within one region. A word loaded from the home the line before stored it from is not loaded again. A dead value's home is reused at every objective, as Cortex-M0 reuses it, where RV64 gives each value its own home at `--optimize=none`, since firmware's stack is a few KiB.\n\nOver a representative 24 fixtures, the runtime corpus's largest among them, RV32's `.text` went from 1.66 times Cortex-M0's at `armv6-m` to 1.04 at `--optimize=none` and from 1.69 to 1.02 at the default, and its average frame from about twice Cortex-M0's to 1.1 to 1.35 times it.
D	679	No RISC-V epilogue reads below the stack pointer	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d679-no-risc-v-epilogue-reads-below-the-stack-pointer	Chosen: at both XLENs the epilogue loads the return address, raises sp only to the frame record, loads x8 from it at sp and then releases the record, with the CFA moved to sp before x8 changes. Nothing is read below sp at any instruction. The other backends' epilogues and every other sequence that raises sp already read only at or above it: arm64's `mov sp, x29` and post-indexed `ldp`, x86-64's `movq %rbp, %rsp` and `popq`, Cortex-M0's `mov sp, r6` with its loads at sp and sp + 4, the RISC-V switch's loads after `mv sp, x11`, and an assembly block's set-aside word read before its sixteen bytes are released.
D	680	An RV32 image's traps follow its core's interrupt model	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d680-an-rv32-image-s-traps-follow-its-core-s-interrupt-model	Chosen: compiler-owned code enters every handler, and no handler takes an exception: an exception, mcause's interrupt bit clear, reaches the unhandled loop, which records it in memory first (D656). Each model sets mtvec its own way:\n\n- `vectored`, the E31's and the ESP32-C3's: mtvec holds the table in vectored mode, 1, and the core jumps to slot N for interrupt code N and to slot 0 for every exception. Each slot is one `j`: to the unhandled loop, to a naked routine itself, or to a stub of the handler's, `_landin_firmware_slot_N`.\n- `clic`, the ESP32-C5's: mtvec holds `_landin_firmware_trap`, aligned to 64 bytes, in CLIC mode, 3, and no interrupt is selectively hardware vectored. The CLIC specification sends every trap of a non-vectored interrupt to mtvec's base, and its interrupt id is mcause's low twelve bits, in its non-vectored mode; the entry saves the registers, reads mcause, and calls slot `id` of the table, whose `j` reaches the handler. ESP-IDF's own vectors set `mtvt` and each interrupt's `shv` instead (`components/riscv/vectors_clic.S`); that needs a write per interrupt the program enables, which the program owns, and a table of addresses beside the table of jumps. D830 supersedes this in part: mtvt names such a table, and an interrupt whose `shv` the program sets enters its slot's stub through it.\n- `xh3irq`, Hazard3's: mtvec holds the table in vectored mode, and slot 11, the machine external interrupt, jumps to `_landin_firmware_external`, which saves the registers and, while meinext names an IRQ, calls slot 16 + IRQ through the table, as pico-sdk's `isr_riscv_machine_external_irq` loops over meinext, which gives the IRQ times four in bits 2 to 10. Bit 31, no IRQ, ends the loop.\n\nA slot the profile does not admit, or one no handler takes, jumps to the unhandled loop rather than holding zero, which D544 gives the NVIC: a RISC-V slot is an instruction, and zero is an illegal one, whose trap would overwrite the mcause a debugger reads. An `extern(interrupt)` routine is an ordinary routine. Its stub lowers sp by 64 bytes, saves ra, t0-t6 and a0-a7, the registers a call may change, calls it and restores them, then `mret`; its unwind rules give mepc as the return address, which nothing changes until `mret`, so a debugger unwinds from the handler into the interrupted code. A naked routine in a hardware-entered slot is jumped to, and owns its saves and its `mret`. A slot the core's dispatch enters, every slot under the CLIC and slot 16 + IRQ on Hazard3, is called, so a naked routine there is L0347, saying to write it `extern(interrupt)`. There is no nesting: mstatus.MIE stays clear from the trap to `mret`. When the program prepares stacks ([1995]), the stub saves the stack limit's cell, stores zero in it while the handler runs and restores it, 80 bytes in all: a handler runs on the interrupted stack, which a switch may be moving between, and is not checked, as on Cortex-M0.
D	681	A boot kind is read by one family's boot ROM, or by both	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d681-a-boot-kind-is-read-by-one-family-s-boot-rom-or-by-both	Chosen: `rp2040-boot2` begins with a stage of Thumb code, so only an Arm core's description may select it, and `esp-app-image` is what an ESP32-C3's or ESP32-C5's ROM loads, so only a RISC-V core's may. `vector-table` and `rp2350-image-block` serve both: RP2350 boots either family from one block format. A description that selects another family's kind is L0576, at its `compiler.boot`, naming the core.
D	682	An RV32 `rp2350-image-block` image begins with its entry word	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d682-an-rv32-rp2350-image-block-image-begins-with-its-entry-word	Chosen: on `rv32` the image is its entry word, then the table at the first address its alignment allows, then the IMAGE_DEF block directly after it, still ending in the first 4 KiB. Hazard3's boot ROM, given a block with no ENTRY_POINT, enters a RISC-V image at its first byte, which is the entry word. The block's IMAGE_TYPE is 0x1101, an executable for RISC-V, for RP2350, of no stated security, in the item format D637 cites, so its second word is 0x11010142, the word the Pico 2 booted on the rig; D638's read-back and D546's first clause check that word on `rv32`, reading an EM_RISCV object.
D	683	`esp-app-image` is a RAM-only image the ROM loads, its chip the description's	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d683-esp-app-image-is-a-ram-only-image-the-rom-loads-its-chip-the-description-s	Chosen: the kind stops being reserved, and L0516 is retired. An ESP32-C3's and an ESP32-C5's ROM load an application image from flash into RAM and enter it with no second stage, as the rig's spikes showed from power-on on both chips, in the format ESP-IDF's `esp_app_format.h` and `esp_image_format.h` declare: a header, 0xE9, the segment count, the flash mode and the size and frequency byte, and the entry; an extended header naming the chip, its minimum and maximum full revisions and that a hash follows; each segment as its load address, its length and its bytes; zeros to the last byte of a sixteen-byte boundary, which holds the exclusive or of every segment byte seeded 0xEF; then the SHA-256 of everything before it. Chip id, revisions and offset are the chip's, not the compiler's: a description that selects the kind writes `compiler.esp_image(chip, min_revision, max_revision, flash_offset)` once, the chip id as `esp_chip_id_t` gives it, 5 for the C3 and 23 for the C5, the revisions as major * 100 + minor, and the offset where its ROM reads, a multiple of 4096, 0 on the C3 and 0x2000 on the C5. A description of this kind without it, or one of another kind with it, is L0575; an argument outside its range is L0399. The image is RAM-only: its code runs from SRAM, flash execute-in-place is a register row, the flash mode byte is DIO and the size and frequency byte 0x20, which neither ROM reads to load a RAM image, and the legacy one-byte minimum revision is zero, as the images both ROMs booted on the rig were. The C3's ROM refuses an image whose checksum is wrong, and with secure boot off only warns of a wrong SHA-256 and boots it, so the hash is evidence the image is whole rather than a gate the ROM keeps; refine's read-back (D685) holds both.
D	684	An RV32 description's stage runs from the entry word, before reset	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d684-an-rv32-description-s-stage-runs-from-the-entry-word-before-reset	Chosen: on `rv32` an `esp-app-image` or `vector-table` description may hold one `link(boot_stage)` naked routine, labelled `_landin_firmware_reset_stage` in `.text.landin_firmware_reset_stage`, and the entry word jumps to it instead of to reset. It runs before reset has set the stack pointer, so it may use neither the stack nor RAM, and it ends in compiler-owned reset, which it names: a stage that names no `_landin_firmware_reset` is L0560, and one that reaches the stack through `sp`, `x2` or a compressed instruction that addresses through it, `lwsp`, `swsp`, `addi16sp` or `addi4spn`, is L0561, each saying the RISC-V form. D	688	RAM code runs in a region code runs in, or is refused	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d688-ram-code-runs-in-a-region-code-runs-in-or-is-refused	Chosen: RAM code is placed where code runs. D	690	RV32's read-modify-writes are its level's, the one checking rule a level decides	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d690-rv32-s-read-modify-writes-are-its-level-s-the-one-checking-rule-a-level-decides	Chosen: the admission of D227's exchange, add and compare-exchange is the one checking rule a level decides. On every other target the level changes no admission: Cortex-M0 refuses the read-modify-writes at each of its levels, since no Thumb-2 level's exclusives are lowered yet, and the hosted targets admit them at each. The checker reads the build's level, which `refine check`, `refine compile` and every other command take as `--level` and `refine lsp` as its `level` option, so an editor shows the refusal the build makes. The verified IR is held to what some level of its target admits, not to the build's level, so the target-neutral IR still depends on no level; a read-modify-write that reaches RV32's backend at `rv32imc` has passed a checker that refused it, and is the compiler's defect. A builtin refused at the build's level but admitted at another says so: "memory operation unavailable at rv32imc; a build at rv32imac admits it". The A extension's AMOs and LR/SC are four bytes wide; how the one- and two-byte read-modify-writes are lowered over the aligned word is the backend's.

D	702	The ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C5 are learnt from their SVDs, ESP-IDF and their manuals	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d702-the-esp32-c3-and-esp32-c5-are-learnt-from-their-svds-esp-idf-and-their-manuals	Chosen: the C3 is learnt from `espressif/svd` at `be20aa12560889d6125d144cdb48cf615ac17628`, Espressif's repository of SVDs and its newest commit, and the C5 from `esp-rs/esp-pacs` at `a96d437ebad40b00854aa3e78011ad7732713a4d`, `esp32c5/svd/esp32c5.base.svd`, since Espressif's repository has no C5. esp-pacs is Espressif's own Rust team's, whose commits correct the base file in place, so it is the vendor's copy and not D560's declined third-party collection; its policy says `modified from it`. ESP-IDF v6.1, commit `fff9895c82d744c7237be8847347bdd1b07c6643`, is each chip's oracle: its `reg_base.h`, `soc.h`, the selected peripherals' `*_reg.h`, `interrupts.h` and the C5's `clic_reg.h`. The C5's: the interrupt matrix's mapping registers from MSPI's on are eight bytes higher than the SVD puts them, UART0's at 0x0BC and SYSTIMER_TARGET0's at 0x0F4 (11.6, p. 480; D704); each mapping register's PASS_IN_SEC, bit 8, is added (11.7, p. 485); the timer groups' WDT_USE_XTAL is omitted (Register 15.10); thirteen sources the SVD omits and the manual and the header number alike are added, and BUS_MONITOR at 27, which the header calls ASSIST_DEBUG (Table 11.5-1); and the CLIC is added (D705). Where the manual agrees with the SVD the check names the header's disagreement: the C3's RTC and super watchdog keys reset to zero, and the C5's pin hysteresis bits exist. The selections are what the boards' port touches: UART0, its pins and an indicator, the clock and reset gates of UART0 and the system timer, UART0's and the system timer's routing, the C3's line enables, types, priorities 1 and 2 and threshold, the C5's CLIC configuration and identities 17 and 18, the system timer for a millisecond wakeup, every watchdog a flash boot leaves running, and the last reset's cause. Generated modules carry Apache-2.0's notice, in the tree as `devices/notices/LICENSE-Apache-2.0.espressif`.
D	703	An element of a register array is a register	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d703-an-element-of-a-register-array-is-a-register	Chosen: a policy selects an element of a register array by its name, the array's `%s` replaced by one of its indices: those `dimIndex` gives, as a range `LOW-HIGH` or a list `A,B,C`, or 0 to dim - 1 without one. A `dimIndex` whose count is not `dim` is L0529; an index the array lacks, L0530, saying how an element is named; an array whose name has no `%s` or is written `[%s]`, an element that is an alternate, and arrays of fields, clusters or peripherals stay L0528. Amends D557.

D	721	The ESP ports receive by interrupt and hold their lines off by threshold	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d721-the-esp-ports-receive-by-interrupt-and-hold-their-lines-off-by-threshold	Chosen: `compiler/tests/board/esp32c3` and `esp32c5` keep the receive contract's interface and atoms, and receive UART0 by interrupt: the interrupt matrix routes source UART0 to a CPU line, the C3's line 1 at priority 1 in its vectored table (TRM v1.4, 1.5), the map register holding the line, and the C5's external interrupt 1, CLIC identity 17, at level 63 with MNLBITS 3 (TRM v1.1, 2.8.2), the map register holding the identity itself, 16 to 47 (11.5.3), each `link(vector: N)` its slot (D680). D	730	`refine run` passes a termination or hangup on to its program	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d730-refine-run-passes-a-termination-or-hangup-on-to-its-program	Chosen: while the program runs, refine catches `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP` and sends each to the program. D	731	The bare form's line repeats what chose the program	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d731-the-bare-form-s-line-repeats-what-chose-the-program	Chosen: the commands the line names repeat the options that chose the program and how it is compiled, in the order given: `--target`, `--level`, `--root`, `--library`, `-L`, `--option`, `--build-mode`, `--optimize`, `--specialize`, `--link` and `--firmware-entry`. D	760	A float literal's f32 rounding may not change an integer conversion	Decisions: Operators, conversions and traps	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d760-a-float-literal-s-f32-rounding-may-not-change-an-integer-conversion	Chosen: an integer conversion whose operand is an untyped float literal, negated any number of times, converts it as an f32 still, and is refused, L0350, when the literal's f64 value would convert to a different integer, or one of the two converts and the other does not. The report names both outcomes, and its note names `f64(...)` around the literal for the written value and `f32(...)` for the rounded one; either is typed, and a typed operand keeps its width and is never compared. A literal whose rounding leaves the integer alone, `i64(45.7)` or `u8(-0.75)`, converts as before, and an operand that is an expression of literals rather than a literal is not compared. The comparison is the checker's exact decimal evaluation at each width and D171's truncation, so it does not depend on the host.

D	790	Frame preflight answers from a bound, and a routine's one plan serves emission and its debugger	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d790-frame-preflight-answers-from-a-bound-and-a-routine-s-one-plan-serves-emission-and-its-debugger	Chosen: preflight answers from the reference frame, which gives every slot and scalar value a home of its own, with room for one more home per value, one per register the target may save and the frame's rounding, each eight bytes padded to the stack's alignment. D	791	Every backend fills every build-report counter with one meaning, and a routine's stack beside its frame	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d791-every-backend-fills-every-build-report-counter-with-one-meaning-and-a-routine-s-stack-beside-its-frame	Chosen: every backend fills every field of a row for every routine it emits. `frame_bytes` is what the prologue reserves below the frame record and the registers it pushes, for slot cells, spill and save homes and incoming register homes; `stack_bytes`, which the row now carries, is D467's frame, the routine's own stack from its caller's stack pointer. `save_bytes` are the callee-saved registers the routine saves, in its frame or pushed beside its frame record, never the record itself. `register_count` is the distinct registers the allocation holds a value or slot in, saved or not, so zero on RISC-V and Cortex-M0, which give every one a home. A refusal is a diagnostic: a request written wrong is L0002, a header or policy that cannot be read L0003, a policy that is not one L0579, a Clang that cannot be used as asked L0580, a selection that cannot be bound L0581, outputs in the way L0582, and a replacement that fails L0005.

D	880	A refusal spells a type and a concept as the program reading it writes them	Decisions: Modules and compile time	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d880-a-refusal-spells-a-type-and-a-concept-as-the-program-reading-it-writes-them	Chosen: a refusal names a type or a concept as the source it is reported in would write it. D	900	A RAM firmware layout is derived from the same device description	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d900-a-ram-firmware-layout-is-derived-from-the-same-device-description	Chosen: `--firmware-layout=boot|ram` selects the artifact layout for Cortex-M and RV32 firmware, with `boot` the compiler default. An ESP RAM-only description retains its instruction/data mappings. Vectors, text and read-only data move to that region; data, BSS and the stack retain their described placements. A valid description-owned reset stage is the vector's entry when present, in both layouts. The build report distinguishes `layout`, `described_boot` and the effective `boot`, reports code and RAM capacities, and gives each linked load segment's physical and runtime addresses and file and memory sizes. D	901	Board development enters SRAM under an explicit warm contract	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d901-board-development-enters-sram-under-an-explicit-warm-contract	Chosen: board tools default to `--mode=ram`, distinct from explicit `--mode=boot`. A pinned probe-rs session helper halts and reinitializes the supported board-port state without flash programming or a system reset. It retires active Arm and C5 handlers, resets Hazard3's interrupt context, enable/force windows and priorities, and stops application DMA and interrupt sources before replacing SRAM. It parks the other RP core, checks the supported clock and cache baseline and configures the STM32 supply before writing RAM. Before hardware access the tool checks the helper's offline description against its compiled source identity and pinned probe-rs revision. It validates load ranges and vector bytes independently, verifies SRAM readback, establishes instruction visibility, and sets vector/trap base, stack and entry before compiler startup. The C5's active CLIC level is retired by returning from its handler, not by clearing its threshold. Unsupported prior state is refused with the boot check named. This is a defined warm entry, not a claim that arbitrary device state was reset.\n\nEach board retains a fixed application-silent flash image. A boot check loads and cold-starts the ordinary image, exercises its boot oracle, then restores and checks the fixed image. Boot image-format and startup changes, item closure and the physical board gate require this separate evidence. Pico 2 architecture changes are explicit setup/boot operations off the cascade: install and verify the intended architecture's fixed image before repeated RAM runs on that architecture. One resident image does not promise a ROM-free switch between Arm and Hazard3. Boot and corrupted-image work also stays off the cascade; probe attachment in BOOTSEL is always refused. D906 lets a Pico 2 on a power-only cable do its boot checks and its architecture change on the cascade. Hardware USB-JTAG remains available on the ESP chips. Every hardware phase still holds the host rig lock and stops on kernel USB trouble. Runs record their mode, input identities, elapsed time, warm preparation or boot evidence and physical oracle results.\n\nThe RP UART protocol uses ACK, boot frame, GO and readiness before its scenario. Loading precedes the UART connection because independent UDP clients cannot share a probe slot's sequence. The handshake tolerates early bytes lost before UART setup and keeps its bytes outside DMA epochs.
D	902	Offline board builds compare artifact records and carry checked inputs	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d902-offline-board-builds-compare-artifact-records-and-carry-checked-inputs	Chosen: the offline builder prepares every supported port without USB, probes, the rig lock or network access. D	903	Xtensa levels share the windowed ABI and retain distinct instruction configurations	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d903-xtensa-levels-share-the-windowed-abi-and-retain-distinct-instruction-configurations	Chosen: one firmware target, `xtensa`, with `compiler.arch == xtensa` and the two D255 levels. Both use little-endian ELF32 and windowed ILP32: four-byte pointers, `usize`, C `int` and C `long`, eight-byte alignment for 64-bit scalars, sixteen-byte alignment for 128-bit scalar storage and the stack. C `char` is unsigned, and C `double` and `long double` are eight bytes. `compiler.c_xtensa_windowed_ilp32` identifies that ABI. As on RV32, though not since D920 on Cortex-M, public C signatures, C records and variadic calls remain disabled; the identity describes the runtime boundary and does not admit those source forms.\n\nThe pinned vendor C compilers do not admit `unsigned __int128`. The sixteen-byte scalar-storage alignment is Landin's layout fact, not a claim of a vendor C 128-bit integer mode; independent vector-storage alignment and the supported C scalar carriers are checked separately.\n\nCalls use `call8` or `callx8`, `entry` and `retw`. Arguments use six words, `a2` through `a7` in the callee and `a10` through `a15` in the caller, with aligned multiword arguments. An argument that cannot fit the remaining registers goes wholly to the stack, and subsequent arguments follow it. Results through sixteen bytes use `a2` through `a5`; larger results use a hidden first pointer. Float carriers use integer registers even though both chip configurations include single-precision floating-point hardware. `a0` and `a1` are the link and stack registers; the backend keeps `a7` as its frame pointer and reserves optional FP, boolean, MAC and vector banks from ordinary allocation. Every windowed frame includes the ABI's spill space. Compiler-owned startup initializes window state and provides all six CALL4/CALL8/CALL12 overflow and underflow vectors. Ordinary interrupt handlers admit CPU lines at levels one through three, which both exact configurations mask while PS.EXCM is set. The compiler saves all physical address registers and the floating state before calling a handler, with ordinary interrupts masked for its duration. Higher-priority, debug and NMI entries stop; they cannot borrow that shared context or the interrupted stack. Read-only byte-addressed data remains in data SRAM even when the selected layout is RAM. CALL0 objects are not compatible peers merely because their scalar layouts match.\n\nBefore an Xtensa pre-reset device stage, architectural entry establishes WINDOWBASE/WINDOWSTART, VECBASE and the declared internal DRAM stack with its ABI spill backchain, with ordinary interrupts masked and window exceptions enabled. The stage may use that stack for windowed ROM calls; static data and BSS remain uninitialized, and the naked stage form does not admit ordinary Landin calls. Compiler reset repeats architectural initialization after the stage. Other families retain their stack-free pre-reset stage contracts.\n\nA naked Xtensa assembly block admits at most 32768 decoded ASCII bytes, enough for a self-contained stage that compares its pinned ROM routines' instructions and literals before calling them. Ordinary blocks and all other target families retain the 4096-byte bound. The larger text allowance admits no directives, data emission or additional description declarations.\n\nThe default and explicit baseline levels select the ESP32 configuration; S3 selects its own. `salt` is the exposed distinguishing fixed feature. The configurations both include density, loops, integer multiplication and division, NSA, min/max, sign extension, MAC16, release synchronization and S32C1I; optional instructions remain subject to their selected assembler configuration, not a generic Xtensa instruction list. A source can query `compiler.feature.salt` without changing layout or the ABI. Unknown or foreign-family levels are L0009, including the server's initialization refusal. A common-baseline artifact is compatible only after its linked instructions and runtime helpers have been checked against both exact configurations. An S3 execution of that artifact proves no ESP32-only instruction or arbitrary ESP32 helper compatible.\n\nThe toolchain selects Espressif's chip-specific wrappers from `esp-16.1.0_20260609`, GCC 16.1.0 and Binutils 2.46.0. The selected wrapper supplies the configuration plugin to both compiler and assembler and selects the matching runtime multilib; generated instructions and source assembly therefore reach the same assembler configuration. The assembler ABI tag is `--abi-windowed` and the compiler ABI is `-mabi=windowed`. Both default and explicit levels must reject valid Xtensa instructions absent from the selected configuration. Assembly operands use integer registers; `a0`, `a1` and `a7` are reserved. Atomic loads and stores through four bytes and fences are admitted; atomic read-modify-writes and eight-byte atomics are refused.\n\nSources are Espressif's pinned GCC layout and ABI definitions, argument and frame implementation, configuration overlays and tool wrappers.
D	904	Physical boards run in the gate on trusted events only, and their evidence is never reused	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d904-physical-boards-run-in-the-gate-on-trusted-events-only-and-their-evidence-is-never-reused	Chosen: `gate.yml` runs every supported board port on the maintainer's rig through one non-ephemeral GitHub Actions runner on rigpi, labelled `landin-rig` alone and run as a system user with the device groups and no privilege, keys or secrets, registered once with a one-hour registration token and configured in the maintainer's NixOS configuration for rigpi. Its board-scope events are a push to `main`, a weekly schedule on `main` and a manual dispatch, in this repository only; a dispatch's `scope` is `full`, every software lane and the boards, or `boards`, the boards with the inputs, document and script jobs. A branch push or pull request never reaches the rig, and its green gate is software evidence only. A fork's pull request runs its own workflow files, so a workflow's `if:` is no control: the runner's job-started hook, `environments/rig-runner/hook.py`, refuses before any step every job but a push or schedule on `main` or a dispatch from a branch by an allowed actor, each of `gate.yml` at the run's ref with no pull request in its environment or payload. GitHub fails a job whose pre-job script exits nonzero before its first step. The repository's approval setting for fork pull requests is a second layer, not the control.\n\n`board-bundles` builds the release compiler and every bundle from the commit, strict against the hardware records; each port's leg checks out exactly that commit, takes the artifact by id against its digest, checks its file list and provenance, and runs `environments/boards/gate.py`: the port's RAM run from the verified fixed image the last run left, then its boot check, which restores and verifies that image again, so a board rests on its fixed image rather than on a RAM application left running; the Pico 2's four steps in order; one leg at a time under one lock. After an run that did not leave its board on that image, a port first takes the boot check that restores it. On a board-scope event the aggregate fails unless every leg succeeded with the outcome `passed`; physical jobs are never reused, so a `main` push that reuses a software pass runs the boards fresh, and a `main` run whose boards fail has a failed gate and serves as no reuse base. A candidate is promoted after its complete software gate and a passed boards dispatch on the identical tree, which a declared explanatory edit skips; `main`'s own push gate is then followed to its end, its failure investigated rather than rerun, and an unavailable rig blocks promotion.
D	905	A board run reports one outcome, stops cleanly when cancelled, and shares one rig state	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d905-a-board-run-reports-one-outcome-stops-cleanly-when-cancelled-and-shares-one-rig-state	Chosen: every board tool's `result.json` keeps its `status` and adds an `outcome`, one of `passed`, `failed`, `usb-stopped`, `unavailable`, `rig-busy`, `rig-tool-mismatch`, `needs-setup`, `needs-operator` and `cancelled`, each refusal naming its own; `gate.py` adds `incomplete` for a step that left no readable result. D	907	A command publishes its outputs without destroying conflicting inputs or saves	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d907-a-command-publishes-its-outputs-without-destroying-conflicting-inputs-or-saves	Chosen: one publication contract in `Landin.Platform`. Commands register protected input paths and original read identities, and prepare every output's expected version, including its absence, before producing its replacement. Compiler reads supply bytes and identity from the same open descriptor. Consumed response files, selected tools, supplied tool inputs and known resolved libraries join the source closure; bindings also records Clang's consumed-header paths. Dependency filenames establish an external tool's known input closure, not identities from its read descriptors. This does not sandbox arbitrary wrappers, interpreters or implicit toolchain internals. Unsupported indirect file directives refuse with an absolute-path or standalone-input route rather than changing their meaning silently. Executable launch still resolves a pathname: observing its identity does not pin execution against a noncooperating replacement of that namespace. Tool capture bytes stay in retained descriptors. Private scratch directories retain directory authority for reads, writes, tool output and cleanup, so replacing an ancestor does not redirect those effects or authorize deleting the replacement directory. Uncertain cleanup retains and names its recovery.\n\nGenerated files are verified in exclusive private staging beside the destination. The output directory is pinned; lookups below its chosen root, staging writes and tool output use that directory authority without following links. A dangling link is an occupied entry. The actual old destination is captured into recovery storage and checked against its expected version and protected inputs. The new version is installed only into an absent public name, using no-replace rename or, for regular files, no-clobber hard-link publication. A changed captured entry is restored without overwriting a newly occupied name, or retained under the recovery path the refusal names. Rollback applies the same rule to this invocation's installed entries; it never unlinks a public name on the strength of an earlier identity check. Prior versions remain recoverable through verification of the artifact group, an ESP image included. Manifest-listed stale outputs receive the same checks. Unchanged bytes keep their original file. Directory artifacts, including a Darwin debug bundle, have checked trees. Earlier retained transactions are diagnosed rather than removed to make progress. Separate transactions in one process cannot reserve the same destination name or an alias of that directory entry while its arena remains active. The refusal asks the caller to retry after the owning transaction completes; distinct hard-link names remain separate destination entries.\n\nA cooperative producer retains a write lease on its first sealed destination record. An inspector can prepare an unrelated target while that producer's tools have extra temporary entries in staging: every destination record must still validate, its names must be separate from the requested target, and the recovery inventory must contain only registered names. The inspector leaves the peer's staging untouched. Unexplained staging without a live producer lease refuses. The lease is an observation of a cooperative producer, not a lock on public destinations or a promise of future liveness; publication still checks the actual expected version and never uses a process identifier as authority to signal another process.\n\nAn initially absent bindings output tree is reserved as an absent directory artifact before generation. Its missing ancestors are staged privately too, starting at the first absent component below an existing parent. Invalid input or a failed tool creates none of those public names. The reservation refuses an entry already present at preparation, and publication refuses a tree that appeared afterwards; it never adopts and replaces that tree. An existing bindings output directory retains per-file publication so unrelated files beside the generated ones remain its owner's. Creating staged directories uses the same retained directory authority as staged file writes.\n\nAfter the last publication in an arena finishes successfully, its remaining descriptors and bookkeeping are released. Native staging helpers refuse unrecognized or retired spellings containing a `.refine-publication-*` component instead of using ordinary-path fallback. Scratch helpers similarly reserve the `.refine-private-` marker. These are spelling guards, not filesystem canonicalization through aliases. Repeated removal of an absent scratch root performs no write; no unbounded retired-path history supplies later write authority.\n\nCompilation artifacts and reports require an existing, available parent. A missing parent is named with the route of creating it or choosing an output pathname under an existing directory. The command does not create missing parent directories. These destination-parent and direct source/output-pair preflights describe unknown identity as uncertain separation rather than proof of collision, retaining conservative refusal. This does not alter the separately specified bindings output-tree creation or formatter write behavior.\n\nFormatting is the inode-preserving mode, D358: its original read descriptor protects renamed-in saves without losing invisible metadata or changing hard-link behavior. `--check` and `--stdout` acquire no writable lease. Noncooperating writes through another descriptor to the same inode remain unsupported. Identity is not a content-version lock. Private storage is not isolation from hostile processes with the same credentials or privileged processes.\n\nInterrupt, termination and hangup cancellation is recorded by signal-safe notification while the command holds something to recover (D1046). The supervisor forwards it to the active tool's process group, permits bounded shutdown, stops remaining ordinary group members and reaps its direct child before cleanup. That unreaped child reserves the identifier while signaling is possible. Tools that escape their group or change credentials are outside this supervision contract. Filesystem and Ada cleanup run in ordinary control flow. Cancellation returns 128 plus the host signal number after recovery, and at once when nothing is held (D1046); inherited ignored signals remain ignored. Spawning refuses before creating a child when `SIGCHLD` is ignored or `SA_NOCLDWAIT` would discard its exit status. The refusal asks for a default, waitable child-exit policy rather than changing the inherited disposition. Native callers must leave that policy unchanged and must not reap these children through another waiter or signal handler. An observed loss of wait-status ownership clears the saved identifier before exception cleanup.\n\nThis is loss-preserving publication, not kernel conditional-inode rename. A destination can briefly be absent; a group is not an atomic snapshot for concurrent readers. Ordinary failure/cancellation recovery is distinct from power-loss durability. Files and directory entries are synced where supported; uncertain or conflicting recovery is retained and reported, never described as an untouched preflight refusal.
D	920	Cortex-M's C ABI is AAPCS32, named by `compiler.c_aapcs32` and enabled at both variants	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d920-cortex-m-s-c-abi-is-aapcs32-named-by-compiler-c-aapcs32-and-enabled-at-both-variants	Chosen: `cortex-m0`, at every level, `armv6-m`, `armv7-m`, `armv7e-m` and `armv8-m.main`, has the C ABI AAPCS32, and `compiler.c_aapcs32` is its fixed bool fact: true there and false on every other target, as each C fact names one ABI. C signatures and `layout(c)` records are enabled for it, through `Backend.Arm32_ABI`, and `platform/c` is available (D921). The fact does not say which of AAPCS32's variants a build uses. That is the description's float unit's to say, as D616 has it: with `fpv5-d16` every C signature, imported, exported or called through a C function value, uses the VFP variant, and without a unit the base PCS. A program reads the unit through `compiler.feature.fp` and `compiler.feature.fp_dp` (D615), so a second C fact would only repeat them. D780's attributes keep an object of one variant from linking with one of the other, in either order, whichever of them is C. D	945	Positions over `utf8` step a whole scalar	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d945-positions-over-utf8-step-a-whole-scalar	Chosen: `text.start(source)`, `text.done(source, at)`, `text.width(source, at)` and `text.step(source, at)` take a `utf8` and the existing `text.position`. `start` is offset zero, the end itself for empty text; `done` holds at or past the byte length; `width` is the one to four bytes encoding the scalar at `at`; and `step` is `at` advanced by that width. `width` and `step` read the scalar as `source[at]` does, so they trap exactly where D182 and D249's position index traps, at the end and on a continuation byte, through the same checked-address failure, and declare no atom. Every position they return is therefore a scalar's start or the end, which are the offsets D183's ranges accept, and `text.offset` gives either kind of position's byte offset. The byte cursors keep their names and contracts. A scope gives one name to one thing [1850], so the scalar forms are four new names, each taking its text first as D269's accessors take their subject: `start` beside `first`, `done` beside `at_end`, and `step` beside `next`, because it moves by a scalar and needs the text to know how far. A firmware entry named `start` keeps its own symbol beside this one, since an export is never the item D417 qualifies.
D	946	A search over text returns where the match begins	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d946-a-search-over-text-returns-where-the-match-begins	Chosen: `text.find(source, sought)` and `text.find_from(source, sought, at)` return the position at which `sought` first begins, in all of `source` or at or after `at`, and `text.find_scalar(source, scalar)` and `text.find_scalar_from` the position of the first scalar equal to `scalar`; each reports the new atom `text.not_found` when there is none. Empty text is found where the search begins, `start` or `at`, as `contains` finds it. The text searches and `contains` share one private Two-Way routine, so `contains` keeps its result, its empty-text rule and its linear time, and a search from `at` costs the same over what follows it. A search from `at` takes that rest as D183's range `source[offset(at)..<lenof source]`, which traps on a position inside a scalar or past the end. A scalar search encodes the scalar as D947 does and searches for those bytes as for text; a surrogate or a value above U+10FFFF is `not_found`, since no text holds one.\n\nShortest-form UTF-8 synchronizes itself: a leading byte never equals a continuation byte, so a match of valid sought text in valid text begins at a scalar's start and ends at one. The parts of the source before, at and after a match are therefore D183 ranges of it, `utf8` views with its origin and read-only permission and nothing copied, and returning one needs the exact `from source` as any range does. `not_found`'s words are `not in the text`; `failure.reason` holds it (D388).
D	947	The encoder writes a whole scalar or nothing	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d947-the-encoder-writes-a-whole-scalar-or-nothing	Chosen: `text.encode(scalar, into)` writes the shortest-form UTF-8 encoding of `scalar`, one to four bytes, at the front of `into` and returns how many; a caller encodes at an offset by passing what follows it, `buffer[at..<lenof buffer]`. A surrogate, U+D800 to U+DFFF, or a value above U+10FFFF reports `invalid_scalar`, and a scalar wider than `into` reports `no_space`. The width is known before the first store, and `invalid_scalar` is reported first, so a value that is no scalar is refused the same way whatever the room. Either refusal writes no byte: `into` is as it was, which is the encoder's whole partial-update rule. `text.append_scalar(into, scalar)` appends the same bytes to a byte builder through its room check, whole or not at all as every append is (D305), with the same two refusals in the same order and the builder unchanged by either; a growing or draining builder makes room as it does for any piece. `invalid_scalar`'s words are `not a Unicode scalar value`.
D	948	A `utf8_builder` holds only whole scalars	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d948-a-utf8-builder-holds-only-whole-scalars	Chosen: `text.utf8_builder`, made by `text.utf8_over(buffer)` over the caller's buffer, is a byte builder whose only appends keep its bytes UTF-8: `utf8_append_text`, `utf8_append_scalar`, and the decimal and hexadecimal appends of every width, whose digits and sign are ASCII. Each is the byte builder's call with `utf8_` before it and writes the same bytes: whole, or `no_space`, or for a scalar `invalid_scalar` first, with its length and buffer unchanged. It has no append of bytes, of a byte or of a host string, no alignment, whose fill is a byte, and is not a `format` destination, since a `formattable` may append any bytes. `utf8_truncate` keeps the whole scalars of the first `count` bytes: a count inside a scalar cuts back to that scalar's start, so the bytes stay UTF-8, and a count at or past the length changes nothing. `utf8_clear`, `utf8_length` and `utf8_capacity` are the byte builder's. `utf8_used` lends what it holds as one `utf8` view and `utf8_bytes` as bytes, each `from` the builder, which is `from` its buffer, so a view of a frame's storage cannot be returned past that frame. The text view is made with D949's `compiler.utf8_unvalidated` and nothing is scanned: the appends and cuts are what make the bytes UTF-8. The prefix is D269's, for a module that holds several types.

D	955	A serial line's settings and its divisor are `core/line`'s, and a driver writes nothing it refuses	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d955-a-serial-line-s-settings-and-its-divisor-are-core-line-s-and-a-driver-writes-nothing-it-refuses	Chosen: `core/line` is a shared freestanding module with no register in it. `line.settings` is a record of a `u32` rate in bits per second, `u8` data bits, a `line.parity` atom set, `no_parity`, `even_parity` or `odd_parity`, and a `line.stop_bits` one, `one_stop_bit` or `two_stop_bits` (D350), so one and a half stop bits cannot be asked for; `line.default_settings` is 115,200 8N1. `line.check` refuses a rate of zero with `line.unsupported_rate` and data bits outside 5 to 9 with `line.unsupported_format`; `line.divisor(clock, rate, oversampling, fraction_bits, least, most)` gives the integer nearest `clock * 2^fraction_bits / (oversampling * rate)`, halves up, as the register holds it, and refuses with `unsupported_rate` a value outside the register's range or a rate it misses by more than `line.tolerance` (D956). One routine serves the families the ports program: a PL011, 16 times a bit with 6 fraction bits; an STM32 USART, whose BRR is the divisor of its kernel clock, oversampling 16 or 8 with 4 bits; and an Espressif UART, once a bit with 4. The arithmetic is integer only, in `u64`, which a Cortex-M0 links as libgcc's helpers, and exact for every `u32` clock and rate. Both atoms are in `failure.reason` with words. A driver computes every register image through the module and its own encoding first, refuses what its peripheral cannot carry, and writes only then, so a refusal leaves every register and the line as they were; each port's own refusals are D957 to D961's.
D	956	A divisor may miss its rate by two percent	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d956-a-divisor-may-miss-its-rate-by-two-percent	Chosen: `line.tolerance` is 20 parts per thousand: `divisor` refuses a value whose rate is more than two percent from the one asked for, measured exactly, `|clock * 2^fraction_bits - value * oversampling * rate|` against `value * oversampling * rate`. A receiver finds a frame by the falling edge of its start bit and samples each bit at its middle; it reads the first stop bit, the last bit it samples, correctly while the drift between the two ends stays under half a bit. Over the longest frame a port here admits, a start bit, eight data bits and parity, the middle of that stop bit is 10.5 bit times in, and a receiver sampling 16 times a bit may find the edge a sixteenth of a bit late, so the two clocks together may differ by `(1/2 - 1/16) / 10.5`, 4.2 percent. Two percent is half of that, the other half the far end's. It holds no margin for a slow edge or for a receiver that votes on three samples, which is why the ports' own divisors are well inside it: every PL011 rate at 48 MHz within 0.79 percent, BRR 556 at 0.08.
D	957	The derived driver opens any line its PL011 can carry	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d957-the-derived-driver-opens-any-line-its-pl011-can-carry	Chosen: `uart.open(settings: line.settings, budget, escaping buf)` computes IBRD, FBRD and LCR_H through `uart.line_registers` for the synthetic UART's declared 48 MHz clock and writes them in that order, LCR_H last so that its write latches both divisors: 46 to 3,000,000 baud, 5 to 8 data bits, any parity and one or two stop bits; LCR_H keeps the FIFOs on and sets neither break nor stick parity. Nine data bits are refused with `line.unsupported_format`, since WLEN reaches eight. `bad_baud` is gone: the driver fails with the shared `line.unsupported_rate` and `line.unsupported_format` in its place, checked after the buffer and before `busy`, and both precede any device write. 115,200 8N1 is still 26, 3 and 0x70, and the application opens `line.default_settings`. Retires the 115,200 bound.

D	970	Cache maintenance is `core/cache`'s concept, over whole lines, with a cacheless provider everywhere	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d970-cache-maintenance-is-core-cache-s-concept-over-whole-lines-with-a-cacheless-provider-everywhere	Chosen: `core/cache` is a shared freestanding module holding one concept, `maintenance`, with four entries: `line`, the bytes in one line; `clean`, which writes a range's dirty lines to memory and keeps them; `invalidate`, which discards a range's lines; and `clean_invalidate`, both. Each operation takes a `[]u8` range and returns once its maintenance is complete at the point a device observes, its provider's completion barrier issued last, so D227's order is the caller's to write and the barrier's to keep: clean before a transmit is enabled, clean and invalidate before a receive is armed, invalidate once a completion or count observation says the device's bytes are written, the device barrier before an enable staying the driver's. A range that does not begin on a line, or whose length is not a whole number of lines, is refused with the recoverable atom `cache.misaligned` and nothing is maintained; it is never rounded out, because a rounded line can hold bytes the caller does not own, whose dirty copy an invalidate loses or whose stale copy a clean writes over a device's data. An empty range is no lines, and its operation is the barriers alone. `cache.lines(line, range)` is that check, which every provider calls. The generic entries `cache.clean` and its siblings take the provider's handle as `core/time`'s do; a handle is a small value passed `in` (D269's service convention), and the parameter is `caches`.\n\nThe cacheless provider is `cache.cacheless(line)`, named for what it is since `maintenance`, the principal type, is a concept (D1032), a `cache.barriers` handle on every target: its operations check the range against LINE and issue the completion barrier, which is all memory no cache stands in front of needs, and a line that is not a nonzero power of two is `cache.bad_line`. It refuses exactly what a cached provider of that line refuses, so a driver checked against it on Cortex-M0 or a hosted target takes the cached profile's refusals. Both atoms have phrases in `core/failure`.

A program reads it as `compiler.feature.cache`, true when the selected description declares a cache, and `compiler.cache_line`, the declared line in bytes and 0 without one, each read as D615's features are, before any option or fixed condition. D	973	Reset enables a described cache once memory is written, and the entry's return disables it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d973-reset-enables-a-described-cache-once-memory-is-written-and-the-entry-s-return-disables-it	Chosen: a cached profile's compiler-owned reset, once `.data`, `.ramtext`, BSS and every placed region are written with the caches still off and their DSB and ISB issued, selects the level 1 data cache in CSSELR, reads its sets and ways from CCSIDR and invalidates every set and way through DCISW, completes that with DSB, invalidates the instruction cache through ICIALLU with DSB and ISB, and sets CCR's DC and IC, bits 16 and 17, with DSB and ISB, as the Cortex-M7's manual and CMSIS's `SCB_EnableDCache` and `SCB_EnableICache` enable them; then it enables interrupts and calls the entry. D	979	The cached board's transmit raises its request only once its stream has its first byte	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d979-the-cached-board-s-transmit-raises-its-request-only-once-its-stream-has-its-first-byte	Chosen: a transmit writes the stream's addresses and count, clears its flags, configures it and enables it with CR3's DMAT clear; clears TC through ICR's TCCF; and only then sets DMAT, so USART3's request rises after the stream has preloaded its first byte. It waits for the stream's EN to clear with its count at zero, clears DMAT, and waits for TC before the CPU writes another frame, as RM0433's transmission using DMA orders the end (48.5.19, p. 2057). In direct mode a memory-to-peripheral stream preloads its first byte once enabled and sends it at the peripheral's first request (15.3.8, p. 644; 15.3.14, p. 653), and a request raised before that preload is an underrun that sets FEIF (15.3.20, p. 657). Success is the count at zero with no transfer error; FEIF and DMEIF are reported and decide nothing, since neither stops the stream.\n\nThe two chip runs before it showed both halves. The first ended its wait on FEIF with the stream still feeding the FIFO, and the CPU's next frame raced it for the FIFO's last slot, losing five bytes at each edge. The second, with that wait corrected but DMAT held set across both transmits from before either stream was enabled, reported TCIF, HTIF and FEIF and a count of zero at each, and each lost its first byte.
D	985	The Cortex-M corpus runs an ABI fixture's C freestanding, by one contract	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d985-the-cortex-m-corpus-runs-an-abi-fixture-s-c-freestanding-by-one-contract	Chosen: an `abi/` fixture whose inventory row says `execute` is built and run as a runtime fixture is, at every profile and level, with its C. Each `c-sources` entry is compiled by the pinned `arm-eabi-gcc` with the flags of the level's lane, the processor and float ABI the harness start is assembled with, soft on the micro:bit, AN385 and AN505 and `-mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=fpv5-d16` on the AN500, `-ffreestanding -nostdlib -O1 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`, then `-std=c11 -nostdinc -fno-short-enums`, GCC's own include directory, the fixture's directory, each pinned input directory the new `c-inputs` key names, fetched by hash, and the fixture's `c-args`. Int-sized enums are what Cortex-M's C boundaries use, Clang's default and the generated bindings' assertion, so the lane passes them rather than each fixture. No C library is reachable: the headers are GCC's freestanding ones, and the link is the harness's start, refine's object, the C objects, the four routines GCC requires of a freestanding program, `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset` and `memcmp`, each in its own section, and libgcc. Every object's float-argument attribute is held to the lane's before the link, apart from GNU ld's check, and a C peer compiled for the other variant must be refused by both, the linker in either order; no object may declare short enums, which the linker only warns of, and a peer built with them must be refused by that assertion. `abi/cortex-c-peer` also takes the route a program does, refine's own firmware link of its C as archives named by `linker.library` with `-L` (D923), under compiler-owned startup.
D	986	A corpus restriction names the stage that stops it, and the lane reaches it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d986-a-corpus-restriction-names-the-stage-that-stops-it-and-the-lane-reaches-it	Chosen: a restriction is built at none/off on each lane it runs on as an `execute` row is, and names in `stops` the first stage that must stop it: `defect`, refine fails internally; `c-options`, the pinned GCC refuses one of its `c-args`; `c-headers`, a C source includes a header no freestanding C has; `c-source`, a C source does not compile for the target; `link`, the image names a symbol nothing linked defines; or `oracle`, it builds and links, and its oracle needs standard input, arguments, files or output. The lane requires the stage it reached to be the row's, and records what stopped it, read from the build, as an L0015 refusal's modules are read. A fixture refine refuses is no restriction but a `refuse` row with its codes; one that gets past every stage is stale and must be made `execute`. Each of the 65 was decided again by that rule: 8 execute, 36 refuse with their codes, and 21 are restrictions with their stops. Two of the eight first stopped at `defect`: Cortex-M emission had no trap class for a `code_address`, which the integer-to-pointer check gives a C function value made from an address, as it gives a pointer's. The Xtensa corpus, which reads the same inventory, holds its restrictions to the same stages, an ABI fixture's C compiled by the chip's GCC, and a row whose verdict differs there carries its `targets.xtensa` disposition.
D	987	The generated Cortex-M bindings' layouts are held to both compilers at both variants	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d987-the-generated-cortex-m-bindings-layouts-are-held-to-both-compilers-at-both-variants	Chosen: `environments/cortex-m/abi.py` compiles each Cortex-M binding fixture's generated adapters with `-fsyntax-only`, by the pinned GCC at `-mcpu=cortex-m0 -mfloat-abi=soft` and `-mcpu=cortex-m7 -mfpu=fpv5-d16 -mfloat-abi=hard` and by Clang at `thumbv6m-none-eabi` and `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`, each with its freestanding headers. The VFP fixture's records must hold at both rows under both, AAPCS32's layout being one for both variants; the CMSIS fixture must hold at the base row and be refused by its header's `#error` at the VFP one; and its adapters built with short enums must be refused by their own assertion. Where no Clang is on PATH its half is recorded as skipped, never as held.

D	1022	A platform module with no scope is available nowhere	Decisions: The toolchain, C and the machine	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d1022-a-platform-module-with-no-scope-is-available-nowhere	Chosen: a `platform/*` module is available only where the compiler gives it a scope. Any other `platform/*` import is L0015 on every target, and its note says that the module declares no targets, which is a fault of the library, not of the program. Since D275 these modules come only from the compiler's own library, so a program cannot meet this unless its library is a maintainer's work in progress.
D	1031	Spans, instants and addresses ship their comparison evidence	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d1031-spans-instants-and-addresses-ship-their-comparison-evidence	Chosen: `core/time` imports `core/cmp` and declares `duration` and `instant` `equatable`, `hashable` and `ordered` as their counts compare, each hash the count as `u64`'s is. `core/net` declares `address` `equatable` by `same_address`, family, octets, port and zone, and `hashable` with 64-bit FNV-1a over the bytes that equality reads: a family byte, 4 or 6, the sixteen octets, the port high byte first and the sixteen zone bytes. An address has no order a program could rely on, so it is not `ordered`. Each type's evidence is in its own module, as `utf8`'s is in `core/text` (D273), so a program that names the type has its evidence, and re-declaring any of it is D270's collision.
D	1032	A handle that borrows nothing is `new`, and a second way to make one keeps `over`	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d1032-a-handle-that-borrows-nothing-is-new-and-a-second-way-to-make-one-keeps-over	Chosen: `l1.handle` is `platform/cortex_m/l1`'s only type, so its constructor is `l1.new()`, as `heap.new()` and `system.new()` are. D	1033	A library name is public when a program has a use for it	Decisions: The core library and the derived programs	https://www.701.dev/spec.html#d1033-a-library-name-is-public-when-a-program-has-a-use-for-it	Chosen: a library declaration is public when a program uses it: a routine or value a program calls or reads, and a type a program has to write to use the facility.
